paragraphs.text: FROM ORIGEN ON THE PSALMS

Because of the psalms that bear the title "To the end," we have selected the definitions of the term "end." From Aristotle we have these: The end is that for the sake of which other things exist, while it exists for the sake of nothing. Or: that for the sake of which other things exist, while it does not exist for their sake. Or: that on account of which a person does other things, while it is done on account of nothing else. From Herophilus's work On the Stoic Use of Terms we have this: They say that the end is a predicate for the sake of which we do everything else, while it is done for the sake of nothing. What is paired with it, as happiness is paired with being happy, they call the goal. This is the last of the things worth choosing.

You yourself must judge whether the definitions of God, and the various meanings of the word "God," will also be of use to us, once we have picked out those that bear on Scripture. The same Herophilus says: In the most general sense they call God an immortal, rational living being, so that every rational soul is God. In another sense, God is an immortal, rational living being that exists on its own. On this view the souls contained in us are not gods, but they will become gods once they are released from their bodies. In yet another sense, God is said to be an immortal, rational, virtuous living being, so that every refined soul is God, even if it is contained in a human being. In another sense, God is said to be an immortal, virtuous living being that exists on its own. On this view the souls contained in wise men are not gods. They also define God in yet another way: an immortal, virtuous living being that has some charge over the world in governing it, as the sun and the moon do. In another sense he says that God is the first governor of the world. Above all, they call God an incorruptible and unbegotten living being and the first king, the role held by the universe as a whole.

The Hebrews divide the book of Psalms into five books. The first runs from "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly" to the end of the fortieth psalm. The second runs from "As the deer longs" to the seventy-first. The third runs from "How good God is to Israel, to the upright in heart" to the eighty-eighth. The fourth runs from "Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation" to the hundred and fifth. The fifth runs from "Give thanks to the Lord" to the very end.

I used to think that the book of Psalms contained only one psalm with the title "A prayer of Moses, the man of God." Later, though, I was discussing certain oracles of God with Iullus the patriarch and with a man who was counted among the wise by the Jews. From them I heard a rule that holds throughout the whole book of Psalms, starting from the first and second psalms. Some psalms have no title among the Hebrews, and others have a title but do not name the writer. These belong to the person named in the most recent psalm before them that has a title. Speaking about these psalms, he first said that thirteen belong to Moses. But when I myself put to him what I had heard, [he said] that there are eleven. Then I asked the man they regard as wise, and I learned that there were eleven. The 89th begins "Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation." The next one, which we number as the ninetieth, began "He who dwells in the help of the Most High," and he said that this one was also by Moses. He also attributed to Moses the psalm that has a title but does not name its writer. I mean the ninety-first, which is titled "A psalm of a song for the sabbath day" and begins "It is good to give thanks to the Lord, and to sing praise to your name, O Most High." The psalm numbered ninety-second also had no title. It begins "The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself in majesty," and he said that this one too was by Moses. The same went for the ninety-third, which begins "The Lord is a God of vengeance"; the ninety-fourth, which begins "Come, let us rejoice in the Lord"; the 95th, which begins "Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth"; and the ninety-sixth, which begins "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice." So too the 97th, whose title was simply "A psalm." The words "of David," found in some copies, appeared neither in the Hebrew nor in the other versions. Its beginning was "Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things." The 98th was also said to be his. It begins "The Lord has become king; let the peoples rage." So was the ninety-ninth, titled "A psalm for thanksgiving," which begins "Shout for joy to the Lord, all the earth." After these eleven psalms, both the Hebrew and all the versions had the title "A psalm of David," and the hundredth was no longer by Moses.

In discussing the psalms that the Hebrews attribute to Moses, the Jew foresaw an objection and offered the solution that seemed right to him. He saw that someone might argue that one of the eleven psalms, the 98th, is not by Moses, on the basis of these words: "Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at the footstool of his feet. Holy are Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call on his name. They called upon the Lord, and he heard them; in a pillar of cloud he spoke to them." The objector would ask how Moses could have put the name of Samuel in his own psalm, when Samuel lived many generations later. His answer was that there is nothing surprising in Moses foretelling the name of Samuel. Samuel was a holy man, and Jeremiah ranks him with Moses in the words "Even if Moses and Samuel were to stand." Besides, in the book of Kings Josiah was foretold: "Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son is born to David; Josiah is his name."

I often looked into why "diapsalma" is written between passages of the psalms. Later I examined the Hebrew and compared the Greek with it, and I found a pattern. Where the Hebrew has "sel," and the Greek has "always" or something equivalent, the Seventy, Theodotion, and Symmachus put "diapsalma." It does no harm to confirm this with examples. Take the 74th psalm, which begins "We will give thanks to you, O God, we will give thanks to you, and call upon your name." After "I have made its pillars firm," the Seventy, Theodotion, and Symmachus have "diapsalma." In its place Aquila has "I have weighed its pillars always"; the Fifth version has "I am the one who prepared its pillars always"; and the Sixth has "I have made its pillars firm forever." In the Hebrew, "sel" stood after "amuda," which means "its pillars." Again, in the 75th psalm, which begins "God is known in Judea," we found "diapsalma" in the Seventy and Theodotion after "weapons, and sword, and war." Symmachus likewise has "diapsalma" after "shield and sword and war." In its place Aquila has "always" after "buckler and war and sword," and the Sixth has "to the end" after "weapon and sword and war." Again, in the Hebrew, "sel" came after "umalama" [?], which means "and war." Further on in the same psalm, after "to save all the meek of the earth," Symmachus likewise has "diapsalma." Aquila has "always" after "all the meek of the earth." The Fifth version also has "always" after "all the meek of the earth," and the Sixth has "to the end" after "to save the meek of the earth." In the Hebrew, "sel" comes after "anie ars," which means "meek of the earth." We found that this observation held without exception, and so we have recorded these things. You yourself may consider whether the translators wrote "diapsalma" because the musical melody or rhythm changes at that point, or whether they had some other reason.
FROM ORIGEN ON THE PSALMS

There are three psalms entitled "For the winepresses": the eighth, the eightieth and the eighty-third. They seem to me to point to the gathering of the Church and to the crowds who come together in one place. In the churches, a single prayer and a single hymn rise to God from many people, just as in the winepresses a single blend of wine is made from many different vines. Long ago there was one winepress in one place, Jerusalem, where people came together and sent up their prayers. Isaiah mentions it when he says: "And I built a tower, and dug a wine vat in it." The tower stands for the temple, and the wine vat for the altar. But since he threatened to tear these down, and did tear them down, he set up many winepresses in place of the one: the churches throughout the whole world. That is why the eighth psalm says: "O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!" It clearly points to God's winepresses throughout the whole world. The eightieth is also a psalm "for the winepresses", and it urges all the nations to offer their hymn to the God of the prophets. It says: "Rejoice in God our helper; shout aloud to the God of Jacob." Then, further on, it points to the rejection of the former people: "But my people did not listen to my voice, and Israel paid no heed to me. So I sent them away according to the ways of their hearts." The eighty-third has the same title, and it shows that there is not one tabernacle or one altar in Jerusalem but many tabernacles and many altars. So, since these tabernacles and altars are themselves many winepresses, it bears the title "For the winepresses". It says: "How beloved are your dwellings, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord." It adds: "Your altars, Lord of hosts." And again it speaks in the plural: "Behold, O God our protector, and look upon the face of your Christ; for one day in your courts is better than thousands." Notice that here it even names Christ. I take the two psalms entitled "For the eighth" to hint at the saving day of the Lord's resurrection. In the sixth, David, who has committed a sin unto death, pleads not to feel God's wrath or anger but asks that his soul may find mercy and healing. He foretells that this will happen when he says: "Turn, O Lord, rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy. For in death there is no one who remembers you, and in Hades who will give you thanks?" He is all but begging the Lord himself to rescue his soul from death. Further on, he shows that his prayers have been granted: "The Lord has heard the sound of my weeping; the Lord has heard my plea; the Lord has accepted my prayer." With these words he hinted at his own return from death to life, which came about together with the resurrection of Christ. The eleventh is likewise entitled "For the eighth" and contains a similar plea from David: "Save me, O Lord, for the godly man has failed." Then he goes on to say, not in veiled terms but quite plainly: "Now I will arise, says the Lord; I will set him in safety." I think the psalm was given this title because of the Lord's resurrection, which took place on the day after the Sabbath, the eighth day, as a type of new life. There are four psalms in all entitled "For those who will be changed". Of these, the fifty-ninth seems to me to signify the change in the nations, which they went through when they turned from superstitious error to the worship of the God of all. It says: "God has spoken in his sanctuary: I will exult and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of tents. Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head; Judah is my king. Moab is the cauldron of my hope. Over Idumea I will stretch out my sandal; foreigners have been made subject to me." So along with the tribes of Israel he has taken in Moab, Idumea and the foreigners. The sixty-eighth has the same title. It speaks of the change and transformation of the one who for our sake went down into the depths of the spiritual sea. It also speaks of his passion, which it shows in the words "They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." And it speaks of how those who plotted against him turned for the worse, as it also shows when it says: "Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs continually," and what follows. The forty-fourth belongs to the sons of Korah and is entitled "For those who will be changed" and also "For the beloved". It too speaks of the change concerning God's beloved. In it the psalmist sets out his divinity and also shows the Church of the Gentiles turning to him, with the words "Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear," and what follows. The seventy-ninth is Asaph's and has the same title. It again describes how the former people turned for the worse, saying: "You brought a vine out of Egypt," and what follows. The beauty and fragrance of the flowers and lilies of the earth change very quickly and pass into decay, and this seems to be why the Hebrew reads "Concerning the lilies" or "Concerning the flowers". So in place of "for those who will be changed" Aquila translated "upon the lilies" and Symmachus "concerning the flowers". The psalms entitled "For the secret things" tell of a hidden, unseen war and of our Savior's victory over invisible, spiritual enemies. The ninth, for instance, says: "When my enemy is turned back," and what it adds after this points to the calling of the nations: "Sing psalms to the Lord who dwells in Zion; proclaim his deeds among the nations." The title of the psalm shows that these things were brought about in secret at the time of the passion, for it is entitled "For the secret things of the Son". In its place Symmachus has "For the death of the Son", and Aquila "For youth". This fits with the psalm's references to his return from death to life, as in "You who lift me up from the gates of death." The forty-fifth is likewise said to be "for the secret things", and it depicts the invisible, spiritual war: "The nations were troubled, kingdoms gave way," and what follows. Then, having pulled down the rulers who had long trampled the nations and having brought the nations under himself, he goes on to say: "I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth." The psalms entitled "For an inscription on a pillar" contain words of modesty and humility. That is why, in place of "inscription on a pillar", Aquila translated "of the humble, perfect one", and Symmachus "of the humble-minded and blameless one". Perhaps David, though he was king and ruler of all Israel, spoke such words in a modest and humble spirit. Or perhaps the Christ of God prophesied such things in humility, as he teaches with the words "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart." Either way, the words would deserve a pillar and a memorial for all ages, and that is what "inscription on a pillar" conveys. You will understand what I mean from the fifty-fifth, which is entitled "For an inscription on a pillar", or "Of the humble, perfect one", or "Of the humble-minded and blameless one". In it we read: "Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me all day long," and what follows. The fifty-sixth has the same title and again mentions those who trample him: "He has given over to disgrace those who trample me." If you go through the rest of the psalms with this title, you will find that they keep to the same sense. The psalms entitled "For remembrance, of David" seem to remind him of his sin concerning Uriah. The thirty-seventh has this title and says: "There is no peace in my bones because of my sins," and what follows. Throughout the whole psalm it describes his state after the sin he had committed. Likewise the sixty-fifth, entitled "For remembrance", pleads for God's help. Perhaps the psalms entitled "A prayer" are not psalms, songs or hymns at all but simply prayers. They suit the frame of mind and circumstances of those who prayed them, and of everyone who finds themselves in a frame of mind like theirs. The psalms entitled "Do not destroy, of David" are three in a row. The fifty-sixth of them was spoken when he fled from Saul into the cave. David was hiding in the cave when Saul came in without knowing he was there. David's companions wanted to kill Saul, but David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy" him, clearly meaning Saul. Perhaps this is why the words became part of the remembrance kept in the psalms with this title: God accepted a saying that showed the height of forbearance. The fifty-eighth reads: "Do not destroy, when Saul sent and watched his house in order to kill him." It seems to contain a command of God, who would not allow the men Saul sent to destroy David. Perhaps the seventy-fourth, entitled in the same way "Of Asaph", also has the same sense. The ninety-first, entitled "For the Sabbath", urges us to come eagerly to the assemblies for the study of divine teaching and then to give praise. It says: "To proclaim your mercy in the morning, and your truth by night." And again: "Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God." The ninety-ninth, entitled "For confession", teaches: "He made us, and not we ourselves." It shows the meaning of confession: we have nothing of our own, and whatever good there is in us, he made it. The thirty-third psalm is entitled "Of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech". It seems to call Abimelech the man named Ahimelech in 1 Samuel. In Hebrew the letters, I mean kaph and beth, look very much alike and differ only by a small stroke. The story goes like this: "And David comes to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech was astonished to meet him and said to him, 'Why are you alone, with no one with you?' David said to him, 'The king gave me an order today. He said to me, "Let no one know about the matter on which I am sending you and which I have commanded you." And I have given orders to the young men at the place called God's Faithfulness, Phelmoni Almoni. Now then, if you have five loaves at hand, give me whatever can be found.' The high priest answered him, 'I have no ordinary bread at hand, only holy bread. If the young men have kept themselves from women, they may eat it.' David answered the high priest, 'Indeed, we have kept away from women yesterday and the day before. When I set out on the journey, all the young men were purified. The journey itself is an ordinary one, and that is why it will be sanctified today because of the vessels.' So Ahimelech the priest gave him the bread of the presentation, because there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence, which had been taken away from before the Lord so that hot bread could be set out on the day he took it." So much for the story. In place of "at the place called God's Faithfulness, Phelmoni Almoni", Aquila says "to such-and-such a place of so-and-so", or "to such-and-such a place without an owner", and Symmachus "to a certain place". The title of the psalm, then, seems to point to the change in what David said to the priest, when it says "When he changed his countenance before Abimelech". Or it may point to a change of face, which is why in Symmachus it reads "When he transformed his countenance before Abimelech", while Aquila has "When he changed his taste". That is why further on in the psalm he says, seemingly hinting at the sacred food: "Taste and see that the Lord is good." Perhaps, then, in urging us to taste Christ himself, he was hinting at his body, of which the law also had a symbol, since the body of Christ in the Eucharist has taken the place of the bread of the presentation. There is also another change by David, when he changed his countenance before Achish, the foreign king of Gath, and pretended to be mad. But the psalm does not seem to refer to that change here. Some psalms have no title of either kind. I mean no "song", "hymn", "psalm", "melody", "praise", "prayer" or anything like that. They seem to contain useful teaching and words that exhort and urge people to take up a life of piety. One of these is the tenth, which says: "In the Lord I have put my trust; how can you say to my soul," and what follows. Another is the thirteenth, which speaks in the same way: "The fool has said in his heart." The rest likewise offer teaching full of benefit. Yet they were not counted among the psalms, hymns or songs, because they are not composed in the same manner as those just mentioned. Or perhaps they too were written to be sung with the psaltery, or as a song, or in one of the other ways mentioned, but it so happened that they were never performed that way. In that case they would have the same force as the psalms, songs and prayers but bear no title because they were not performed in that way. Or perhaps some were given no title for the first reason and some for the second. The fifty-first, for example, is neither of these kinds. It tells the story of Doeg: "Why do you boast of wickedness, you mighty man?" and what follows. Because it is so grim, it could not be performed in the manner of the psalms or songs. The same goes for the fifty-second, which also deals with grievous things. The fifty-fourth, which begins "Give ear, O God, to my prayer", has the form of a prayer. The twenty-sixth, "The Lord is my light and my savior", is no different from a prayer. Yet neither was given a title. The second reason probably applies to the seventy-first psalm, which says at the end of its prophecy: "The hymns of David son of Jesse are ended." Some have taken this saying to mean that David's hymns come to an end here. You should note that the sense of the Hebrew does not mean this. In place of "The hymns of David are ended", Aquila gave "The prayers of David have been completed", Symmachus "The prayers of David have been fulfilled", and the Fifth Edition "The prayers of David have been summed up." These renderings show that the words belong with what the psalm prophesies about Christ. The psalm is entitled "For Solomon", but what it contains refers both to Solomon himself and to the son who would be born of his seed. That is why it says: "O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son." Next come prophetic words about the king's son, that is, the one to be born of Solomon's seed, and these cannot fit anyone but the Christ of God alone. For "He will rule from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the inhabited world", and sayings like it, could not apply to Solomon himself, or to Rehoboam who succeeded to his rule, or to any other of his successors. They apply only to our Savior. David had prayed that the birth of Christ from his seed would come about, together with what was prophesied about it. That prophecy includes the contents of this psalm, which says at the end: "And all the nations will be blessed in him, and all the earth will be filled with his glory." So it is fitting that these words should be followed, in Aquila, by "The prayers of David have been completed", in Symmachus by "The prayers of David have been fulfilled", and in the Fifth Edition by "The prayers of David have been summed up." They were summed up in this: that all the nations would be blessed when the Savior of all nations appeared from his seed. Where the word diapsalma appears, Aquila has "song" in its place, and the Fifth Edition "always". In our copies and in Symmachus, the diapsalma seems to be marked where the musical melody or rhythm changes. Often there is also a change of thought at the diapsalmata, and sometimes even a change of speaker. One might suppose that every psalm with a title was performed on the musical instrument called the psaltery. But throughout the whole book, wherever the Seventy have the title "psalm", Aquila gives "melody" and Symmachus "song" or "ode". So I had to point this out, so that no one would think that all the psalms we have with this title were performed with the musical instrument. It would make no sense, for example, for the fiftieth, entitled "To the end, a psalm of David", to have been performed with the psaltery, for "music in mourning is an ill-timed tale." David spoke these words over a terrible offense, when God's anger against him was no ordinary anger and he had been threatened through the prophet. How could he have taken up the psaltery as if in a time of good cheer and performed the signs of luxury and merriment? What is there in these words that suits the psaltery? Are they not words of lament and weeping, which were most likely spoken to a mournful melody and not with the instrument? You could say the same of the third, which is entitled "A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son." Ask yourself whether, in such a disaster, having fallen from his throne and being driven out by his son, he had leisure for music. It would make sense that when he sent this plea up to God as well, he uttered it to a melody suited to the occasion. That is why the other translators have given "melody" and "song" in the titles of these psalms too. Examine the other psalms with similar titles in the same way. Wherever psalms are entitled "among hymns", Aquila has rendered this "among psalms" and Symmachus "with the psaltery". So according to their translation these alone were sung to the musical instrument. And it certainly makes sense that the fourth psalm, entitled "among hymns", was played on an instrument. The third had been spoken by David when he fled from Absalom his son. The fourth celebrates the victory in the war against his son, so it is fitting that it is entitled both "To the end" and "among hymns". That is why, in place of "to the end", Symmachus gave "a victory song" and Aquila "for the victor". What follows bears out this interpretation, where he says: "When I called upon him, the God of my righteousness heard me," and what follows. These words, then, were fit to be struck up with musical instruments, as at a victory celebration. The third, however, is not entitled "to the end". It was not yet a victory song, and it was spoken before the war had come to an end. Consider also whether the sixth is fittingly entitled "a victory song" and "with the psaltery", and in the Seventy "to the end" and "among hymns", since after the opening of the psalm he adds at the end: "The Lord has heard the sound of my weeping, the Lord has heard my plea; the Lord has accepted my prayer." The fifty-third, too, was spoken by David before his sin concerning Uriah, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, "Is not David hiding among us?" Since those who had slandered him to Saul achieved nothing, it is entitled "among hymns" in our version, and in the other translators "with the psaltery", "among psalms", "for the victor" and "a victory song". Consider in the same way the other psalms that have been given a similar title. It is generally agreed that most of the psalms after the fiftieth were spoken long before the fiftieth. And the fiftieth itself was spoken before the time of the third, which David uttered when he fled from the face of Absalom his son. That time came after the confession of the fiftieth. What, then, is the reason for such an order? One might say that it has some of the [?]

…of God who gave them, the power signified by the seal. About being locked and being sealed, John teaches us in the Revelation, saying: "And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one will open: I know your works. See, I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut." And a little later: "And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a scroll written inside and on the back, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice, 'Who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals?' And no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open the scroll or to look into it. And I wept, because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it. And one of the elders said to me, 'Do not weep. See, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he can open the scroll and its seven seals.'" About being sealed alone, Isaiah speaks as follows: "And all these words shall be to you like the words of this sealed book. If they give it to someone who knows how to read, saying, 'Read this,' he will say, 'I cannot read it, for it is sealed.' And this book will be given into the hands of someone who does not know how to read, and he will say, 'I do not know how to read.'" For we must not suppose that these things are said only of the Revelation of John and of Isaiah's book; they apply to the whole of divine Scripture. Even those with only a modest ability to understand the divine words agree that it is full of riddles and parables, of dark sayings, and of many other kinds of obscurity that human nature finds hard to grasp. The Saviour too wished to teach this. Since the key was in the hands of the scribes and Pharisees, who made no effort to find the way to open the door, he says: "Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge; you did not enter yourselves, and you did not let those who were entering go in."

I have said these things by way of preface, because I am now forced to descend into a very great contest, one that is admittedly beyond me and my capacity. Your great love of learning compels me, holy Ambrose, and I cannot refuse your kindness and your modesty. For a long time I held back, knowing the danger not only of speaking about holy things but, far more, of writing about them and leaving them to those who come after us. Yet you charmed me in every way, as a friend, and by advancing me in divine things you brought me to this task. Be my witness before God, when I am examined on my whole life and on what I have dictated, as to the purpose with which this has been done: that in some places we hit the mark, while in others we either force the text rather violently or only seem to say something; yet we have traced out what is written, not disregarding the saying, "When you speak about God, you are judged by God," nor that other well-spoken saying, "Even to speak the truth about God is no small danger." Since nothing can be good without God, and least of all the understanding of the divinely inspired Scriptures, we therefore ask you to approach God, the Father of all, through our Saviour and High Priest, the begotten God, with petitions that it may first be granted us to seek rightly. For the promise of finding is laid up for those who seek; but perhaps God does not count among seekers at all those who do not set about this task in the right way.
And after other things:

3. As we are about to begin the interpretation of the Psalms, we will first set out a most elegant tradition that the Hebrew handed down to us about all divine Scripture in general. He used to say that the whole divinely inspired Scripture, because of its obscurity, is like many rooms in one house, all locked. Beside each room lies a key, but not the key that fits it. So the keys are scattered among the rooms, and none of them fits the room it lies beside. The greatest task is to find the keys and match them to the rooms they can open. In the same way, the Scriptures, obscure as they are, are understood by taking the starting points for understanding from nowhere else than from one another, since the means of interpreting them lies scattered among them. I think, then, that the Apostle too was suggesting this way of understanding the divine words when he said: "These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual."
And after many other things, comparing the beatitudes stated in the singular with those spoken in the plural, he says:

4. "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in the fire, proved for the earth, purified seven times." The Holy Spirit has dictated them through the ministers of the word with all exactness and careful scrutiny. If this is so, do not let the analogy escape you: the wisdom of God has extended to all divinely inspired Scripture, down to the least letter. Perhaps this is why the Savior said: "Not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things come to pass." Consider the making of the world. There the divine craftsmanship appears not only in the heaven and the sun and moon and stars, pervading all those bodies. It has done the same on earth in humbler matter, so that the craftsman did not disdain even the bodies of the smallest animals. Much less did he disdain the souls that dwell in them, each of which has received some distinctive property, something that preserves it even in an irrational creature. Nor did he disdain the plants of the earth, for his craftsmanship is present in each of them, in their roots and leaves and in the fruits they can bear, and in the differences of their qualities. Just so, we hold that in everything written by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, the holy Providence that bestows on the human race, through these writings, a wisdom beyond human wisdom has sown saving oracles. It has sown traces of wisdom, so to speak, in every letter, as far as each letter can hold them. Indeed, whoever has once accepted that these Scriptures come from the Creator of the world must be persuaded that whatever confronts those who seek to understand creation also holds for the Scriptures. Now in creation, too, there are some things hard or even impossible for human nature to discover, and that is no reason to accuse the Maker of the universe. For instance, we do not find the reason why basilisks and other venomous beasts were created. Here it is pious to recognize the weakness of our race and that we cannot grasp the principles of God's craftsmanship, which have been contemplated with all exactness. The pious course is to leave the knowledge of these things to God, who will later reveal to us, if we are judged worthy, the matters over which we now pause in reverence. In the same way, then, we must recognize that many things are stored up in the divine Scriptures that are hard for us to explain. There are those who have abandoned the Creator of the world and run to the one they have fashioned for themselves as God, and who claim to have the answers. Let them solve the difficulties we put to them. Or, after so great an act of impious daring, let them at least persuade their own conscience to rest content with their hypotheses about the questions under inquiry and about the difficulties raised against them. For if there too the difficulties remain no less after they have abandoned the Godhead, how much more pious it would have been to keep to the conception of God, who is contemplated as the author of creation from the things he created, and to declare nothing godless or impious about so great a God!

The other translators speak of "scoffer" against the very people to whom the name "pestilent" applies, and not without purpose. For those who are wise in their own eyes and learned in their own sight scoff at everyone else, and especially at those who have believed according to sound doctrine.

But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night, etc. The one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night is not the one who takes up the words of the law to memorize them without the works that correspond to them. He is the one who practises them and goes on to do the appropriate works, until through continual practice of the works of the law he becomes ready, rendering all that is due from one who lives perfectly according to the law. In this way it will be possible to meditate on God's law all day and all night. For whether he eats or drinks or does anything at all, as the divine Apostle says, such a person does all things to the glory of God. So even in the time of sleep, when sleep comes as it should, his attentiveness reaches even to that and to the images that arise in it. This also solves the difficulty in the Apostle's saying: "Pray without ceasing." For how can someone pray while sleeping, or while doing some duty toward other people, or taking care of his own body? But on this point too we say that the perfect person, doing all things according to reason, cries out to God and asks him for the best things, calling on him to grant them, so that his every action is a prayer. Yet just as, in meditating on the law, one must not neglect meditation in the specific sense, so one must not neglect prayer in the specific sense, since to meditate and to pray also mean doing anything at all according to the law of the Lord. One might also consider whether, by the rules of anagogical interpretation, "day" can mean our state when we are free from trouble, and "night" our state when we are in trouble, because it is gloomier. But we must try to remain in the law not only when outward circumstances do not oppose us, but also when we fall into what are called temptations.

And he will be like the tree planted by the channels of the waters, which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall off; and all that he does will prosper, etc. Next let us take up Aquila's rendering, "transplanted." From where, then, has the tree spoken of here been transplanted to the divisions of the waters? The one who was rooted in the Father has been transplanted for the benefit of many, so that others too might share in his image, which is received through his being transplanted. This does not mean that he is no longer in the Father (for he is), but that he has also come to be among others. Or, on another approach, it is the soul of the Savior, the soul he took up, which was transplanted from here into paradise. The Gospel says that he was there after the passion, relating that he said to the repentant thief: "Today you will be with me in the paradise of God." He has been transplanted there so that those who are worthy to be with Christ may be enlightened by him with the illumination of knowledge, advancing in the contemplation of the things that are, according to the wisdom of God. We have understood the passage in this way because "bearing fruit" is properly said of trees, whereas "giving" better suits beings with a soul, and rational ones at that. We must also ask whether there is a season for the fruit of the tree of life, for it is not pious to say that wisdom is ever without fruit. That is why the text does not say, "which will bear its fruit in its season," but "which will give its fruit in its season." Its season for giving is the readiness of the one who receives. As far as it is concerned, it is always ready to give its fruit. For if the Word wants stewards to be faithful and wise, not simply handing out the ration of grain to their fellow servants but handing it out in due season, how much more will wisdom dispense its own fruits faithfully and wisely! The season for giving is the same as the season for the receiver to receive. It is also worth considering what is meant by the leaf of life, that is, of wisdom, that does not fall. This can be grasped only by those who have spent at least some time on the study of nature. Clearly the Creator commanded fruit-bearing trees to sprout for the sake of their fruits, and for the fruits' sake he made, as a consequence, the things they need. The fruits need covering from the leaves to protect them. The same can be seen in the wisdom that governs the universe, in which the Creator of the universe made all things. Some things come into being primarily, and others follow as a consequence, for the sake of the primary ones. The rational living being comes first, and for its needs come cattle and the things that grow from the earth. Perhaps, then, the principles of the things made primarily are the fruits of the tree of life, and the principles of the things created for their sake are the leaves. None of these is vain, and none deserves to be wholly despised as worthless, as though it might fall and drop off unguarded. This is even more true of what follows: "And all that he does will prosper." For even all the things that came into being as a consequence can be put to some necessary use. Christ's fruit would primarily be his teaching, the food of the more honourable, while the leaf would be the food of those less endowed with reason, just as human beings eat fruits and grazing animals eat leaves. One can also speak of certain fruits of Scripture, which the more rational take in, and of leaves, by which the simpler are nourished. As for the one who is called blessed and likened to the tree of life, his fruit could be said to be his principal works, such as doing good and devoting himself to wisdom. His leaves would be the activities of his everyday life. These too are not to be despised, nor do they drop off for one who does all things attentively and to the glory of God. In this way everything he does prospers.
Not so the ungodly; but they are like the chaff that the wind drives away from the face of the earth, etc. Neither the Hebrew nor any of the translators repeated the word.

Therefore the ungodly will not rise in the judgment, etc. Taking this verse as their starting point, the simpler among the believers think that the ungodly will not attain the resurrection. Yet they do not make it at all clear what they understand by the resurrection or what kind of judgment they imagine. Even if they seem to make pronouncements on these matters, examination will show that they cannot consistently hold to what follows from them. If we ask them whose resurrection takes place, they answer: that of the bodies we now wear. Then we ask further whether the whole substance of these bodies rises or not, and before examining the question they say: the whole. But suppose we go along with their simplicity and raise a further difficulty. Will the blood that has flowed out in bloodlettings rise with them? Will all the flesh and hair they have ever had rise too, or only what was pressed together [?] at the time of their departure? At this they run for refuge to the idea that God does whatever he wills. The more high-minded among them do not want their argument to force them to gather again the very blood that has often been separated from our bodies. So they say that the body we have at our end will rise. But we raised a further difficulty. Bodily nature is changeable. Just as foods are assimilated into our body and lose their former likeness, so our bodies too are changed and, in carnivorous birds and beasts, become parts of those creatures' bodies. Those creatures are in turn eaten by humans or other animals, and they change back and become the bodies of humans or other animals. As this goes on over a long time, the same body must often have become part of many human beings. Whose body, then, will it be in the resurrection? In this way we would end up falling into an abyss of absurd nonsense. After these difficulties they take refuge in the claim that all things are possible to God. They bring forward passages of Scripture that, taken in their obvious sense, can suggest what they think. One example is the passage in Ezekiel: "The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me out in the spirit and set me down in the middle of the plain, and it was full of human bones. He led me around them on every side, and behold, there were very many on the face of the plain, and behold, they were very dry. And he said to me, 'Son of man, will these bones live?' And I said, 'Lord God, you know this.' And he said to me, 'Prophesy, son of man.' And I said to them, 'You dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says Adonai the Lord to these bones: Behold, I am bringing into you the breath of life, and I will put sinews on you, and bring flesh upon you, and stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit upon you, and you will live; and I will set you upon your land, and you will know that I am the Lord.'" They use this passage as the more persuasive one. They also cite other texts from the Gospels, such as "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth" and "Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna," and the passage in Paul: "He will give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit that dwells in you." But every lover of truth should apply his own mind to these matters and contend for the doctrine of the resurrection. He must preserve the tradition of the ancients and also guard against falling into the nonsense of impoverished ideas that are both impossible and unworthy of God. On this subject, then, we must understand the following. Every body held together by a nature that takes in things from outside as food and excretes other things in place of what is taken in, like the bodies of plants and animals, never keeps the same material substrate. That is why the body has rightly been called a river. Strictly speaking, perhaps not even for two days is the primary substrate in our body the same. And yet Paul, say, or Peter is always the same, and not only in the soul, whose substance on our view neither flows nor ever has anything added to it. He remains the same even though the nature of the body is in flux, because the form that characterizes the body is the same. So the features that present the bodily character of Peter and Paul also remain the same. Because of this character, scars from childhood remain on bodies, along with other distinguishing marks such as moles. And if there is anything else of this kind, it is this bodily form, by which Peter and Paul are given their shape, that in the resurrection is again put around the soul. It is changed for the better, and it is by no means still the particular substrate that originally made it up. A person's form persists to the end of life, even though the features seem to change a great deal. In the same way we must understand that the present form is the same as the future one, though it will undergo a very great change for the better. For the soul, existing in bodily places, must use bodies suited to those places. If we had to become aquatic and live in the sea, we would certainly need a condition otherwise like that of fish. So too, since we are going to inherit the kingdom of heaven and to be in different places, we must use spiritual bodies. The former form is not obliterated, even if it is changed into something more glorious. Just so, the form of Jesus, of Moses and of Elijah was no different at the transfiguration from what it had been before. So do not take offence if someone says that the primary substrate will not be the same then. Reason shows those who are able to consider it that even now the primary substrate cannot stay the same for two days. It is also worth noting that what is sown is of one kind and what rises is of another: "For it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body." And to all this the Apostle adds a saying that practically teaches us that we will lay aside the earthly quality while the form is preserved in the resurrection: "This I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption." Perhaps there will be around the saint [?] something held fast by what once made the flesh its own. But it will no longer be flesh. Rather, what once gave the flesh its character will give its character to the spiritual body. To the passages of Scripture that our brothers cite, the following can be said, and first about Ezekiel. If we go by what the simpler believers want these words to mean, there will not even be a resurrection of flesh, but only of bones, skins and sinews. At the same time we must show them that they have been carried away because they have not understood what is written. When bones are named, these bones are not necessarily meant. They are not meant in the verse "All my bones are scattered," or in "Heal me, for my bones are troubled," where it is evident that bones are not spoken of in the ordinary sense. And indeed the passage goes on: "they themselves say, 'Our bones have become dry.'" Do they say "Our bones have become dry" because they want them to be gathered together and to rise? That is impossible. Rather, they would say "our bones have become dry" because they had gone into captivity and lost all their vital moisture. And indeed they add: "Our hope has perished; we are lost." So the promise is of the people's resurrection from their fall and from the deadness, as it were, into which they had been put to death when they were handed over to their enemies because of their sins. The Savior too says that sinners are tombs full of bones and all uncleanness. It befits God to open each person's tomb and bring us out of our tombs made alive, just as the Savior drew Lazarus out. As for "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth," we must put this difficulty to them. In this life the Creator fashioned every member for some use, and he made the teeth for chewing solid food. What need of teeth, then, do those who are being punished have? For by their own account people in Gehenna will not eat. We must also show that not everything is to be taken according to the letter. Scripture says, "You have broken the teeth of sinners," and "The Lord has shattered the molars of the lions." Who is so foolish as to suppose that God preserves the bodies of sinners intact and breaks only their teeth? Anyone who wanted these words to be taken literally would be hard pressed and dragged into allegory. In the same way we must look for the meaning of the gnashing of teeth among those being punished. The soul has a power of chewing, and at the time when it is convicted of its sins it will gnash its teeth over what it had in mind, as teeth clash together. The saying "Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna" perhaps teaches that the soul is incorporeal. It perhaps also shows that the soul will not be punished without a body, a point we have discussed in our natural inquiry into the form and the primary substrate. Then there is the Apostle's saying, "He will give life also to our mortal bodies." The body is mortal and does not share in true life. So the verse can show that the bodily form we have spoken of, which is mortal by nature, "when Christ our life appears," will itself be changed from being a body of death and made alive, because through the life-giving Spirit it has come to be of the spirit. And the verse "But someone will say, 'How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?'" plainly shows that the primary substrate will not rise. If we have rightly understood the illustration, we must say the following. The seminal principle in the grain of wheat lays hold of the matter around it and pervades the whole of it, grasping it with its own form. It imposes the powers it has on what was once earth, water, air and fire. Overcoming their qualities, it changes them into the substance of which it is itself the maker. In this way the ear of wheat is brought to completion, vastly different from the original grain in size, shape and variety.

By the same author. For the righteous, judgment is the passage from the body of the active life to angelic bodies. For the ungodly, it is the transfer from the body of the active life to dark and gloomy bodies. For the ungodly will be raised not in the first judgment but in the second.

For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly will perish. Nothing evil is known by God; only the way of the righteous is. For "the Lord knew those who are his." The way of the righteous is the one who said, "I am the way," of whom it was said, "See what the good way is." The way of the ungodly is the one walked by those who speak evil of the Creator. God is ignorant of evil things and does not know them. This is not because he cannot grasp all things and take them in with his mind (for it is unlawful even to think that about God). It is because they are unworthy of his knowledge. Perhaps this is why (and the argument will say this rather boldly) he asks about things he does not know. When Adam sinned, God did not know him, nor the place into which he had fallen in fleeing from God. That is why he says, "Adam, where are you?" In the same way, in the Gospel too, he asks about things that are not worthy of his knowledge. Since he does not know the demon or its name, he asks what its name is, and it answers, "My name is Legion." And before the woman with the flow of blood received the release that brought her salvation, he asks, "Who touched me?" So God does not know the way of the unrighteous, but he knows the way of the righteous. And what is the way of the righteous but the one who said, "I am the way," whom the Father knows? For "no one has known the Son except the Father." The terms that occur so often in the prophecies, God's remembering and God's forgetting, fit what has been said about God's knowing and not knowing. For it is often said in prayers, "Remember me," and, "Why do you forget our poverty?" God casts those who sin out of his memory, just as he admits those who repent again and takes them back into his memory.
Psalm 2.

Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ, etc. We came across two Hebrew copies. In one of them we found these words at the beginning of the second psalm, while in the other they were joined to the first. In the Acts of the Apostles, too, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you" was said to belong to the first psalm: "For as it is written," it says, "in the first psalm: You are my Son; today I have begotten you." The Greek copies, however, show that this is the second psalm. But we should be aware that in the Hebrew no number such as first, second or third is attached to any of the psalms. And who would be the speaker who utters the prophecy concerning Christ? It is either the Holy Spirit or the prophet himself. From the Diapsalma onward there is a change of speaker, for it is Christ, as we shall show when we examine the words. It is not surprising if in a single psalm the speaker is not one person, for this can be seen in many places, as we shall show as we go on. So much by way of introduction to the psalm. Now let us consider the words.

By the same. The text says that four kinds of men laid hands on Christ: nations raging against him, peoples devising vain things, and kings of the earth standing by with rulers gathered together. We take "nations" to mean people who are strangers to the faith, such as the soldiers who raged against him. The "peoples" are those from the tribes of the concision. (They should not properly be called "of the circumcision," since they did not accept the Savior.) These devised vain things, because they did not understand the Christ proclaimed in the prophetic words they meditated on. The kings of the earth and the rulers are Herod and Pontius Pilate and the leaders of the Jewish people. For the divine apostle Peter mentioned these specifically in the Acts of the Apostles, when he cited the present passage. But if you say that the invisible powers are meant as well, you would not be wrong. Indeed, the most wise Apostle attributed the crucifixion of Christ not so much to men as to ruling powers, when he said: "Yet among the mature we speak wisdom, though not a wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are passing away. But we speak God's wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God foreordained before the ages for our glory, and which none of the rulers of this age has known; for if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." For what rulers crucified Christ, the Lord of glory, not knowing the wisdom of God and supposing that they themselves had some kinds of wisdom? Who could they be, if not those whom the prophecies call the prince of the kingdom of the Persians and the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks, and, following on from these, the princes of the other nations? "The nations," then, "raged": that is, as Aquila translated more clearly, they "were in tumult." The word "raged" (ephryaxan) is onomatopoeic and expresses the inarticulate noise of people in uproar. For that is how people are when they are agitated at the time they plot against those they are fighting. And if the other translators had not said "were in tumult," and "stirs up," as Symmachus did, one could have taken "raged" to mean "boasted." We think the word has this meaning in one of the prophets: "According to the pride of the Jordan." Now "whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either," and "whoever receives" Christ "receives the one who sent him." Therefore whoever makes war on Christ commits impiety against the Father. So those who raged, devised vain things, stood by together and were gathered at once seemed to act against Christ alone. But what they did has been counted against them as done first against the Father. That is why they are said to have done these things "against the Lord and against his Christ." We should also know something about the name that the Greeks pronounce with the title "Lord" and the Hebrews with "Adonai." Among the Hebrews God is called by ten names, one of which is "Adonai," which is translated "Lord." In some places the Hebrews say "Adonai" and the Greeks say "Lord" because this is the word actually written in Scripture. At other times "Yah" stands in the text, and the Greeks pronounce it with the title "Lord," but the Hebrews do not, as in: "Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good." For here it said "Lord" instead of "Yah," and among the Hebrews the psalm begins with "Hallelujah." There is also among them a certain four-letter name that is not pronounced, which was inscribed on the high priest's golden plate. They read it with the title "Adonai," although that is not what is written in the four letters, while the Greeks pronounce it "Lord." In the more accurate copies the name is written in Hebrew characters, not the present ones but the most ancient. For they say that during the captivity Ezra handed down to them new characters in place of the earlier ones. We have mentioned these things because the four-letter name stands as "Lord" in "But rather in the law of the Lord," and in "For the Lord knows the way of the righteous," and now in "against the Lord and against his Christ." We should also note that the Seventy and Theodotion put everything in the past tense. Aquila put some things in the past and some in the future, and Symmachus put everything in the present. For the Seventy often report prophecies about Christ as though they had already happened, as in: "They gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots." And: "A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." We think they speak this way because God knows all things before they happen, including his Christ and what would happen to him in the incarnation. These things are counted as having already happened to the one who suffered this and that. The same applies if it is the Holy Spirit who is telling the things about him, as in the present passage. But we do not say this as though the prophecies about him never shift into the future tense. For it says, "Behold, my servant shall understand, and shall be glorified, and shall be exalted exceedingly," and so on.

Let us burst their bonds, etc. It seems to me that the first four lines were spoken by the angels who came down with the Savior. They were indignant at the plot against him by the invisible kings and rulers, and at the same time they wondered why these things were happening at all. Those powers were the ones who had bound human beings and laid their own yoke on them. So the Son of God answers the angels, urging them to imitate him as he bursts the bonds of sinners and throws off their yoke. Let us too burst the bonds that bound us when we sinned, for each person is held tight by the cords of his own sins. And perhaps it is better to burst the bonds, like Samson, than to have them loosed, as Jerusalem's sin was loosed when she received from the Lord's hand double for her sins. Whoever has thrown off the yoke just mentioned can take up the kindly yoke of Jesus, carry his light burden and become his beast of burden. And the disciples will untie his bond.

Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and in his anger he will trouble them, etc. Words of threat are words spoken in wrath. But God promises to relent from the evils he says he will do, if those who hear repent. God spoke in his wrath to the Ninevites through Jonah. And since they repented in sackcloth and ashes, they suffered none of what they had heard. When God sent Jonah, he foreknew the repentance that would follow; clearly he sent Jonah for their salvation. Perhaps here too he will speak in his wrath to the sinners themselves for their salvation. For he did not say: He will punish them in his wrath even if they repent.

By the same. Anger differs from wrath, as experts in the meaning of words also say. Anger is wrath that is smoldering up and still being kindled, while wrath is a desire for retaliation. So anger is, as it were, less complete than wrath, and wrath is already directed toward some result. But here, as applied to our usage, we must understand "retaliation" as the punishment for sins, and "desire" as will. Even in divine Scripture anger is something less than wrath. This is clear from the fact that rebuke is said to come with anger and discipline with wrath. For it says, "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath." A person who still has hope of being cured without torment is rebuked by a reproving word. But a person who has gained nothing from rebuke needs the discipline of whips and rods. For no discipline seems a cause for joy at the time, but rather for grief. Later, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. God, then, will speak in his wrath to the sinners whom he laughs at and mocks. These are still in their transgressions, and in their insensibility they pride themselves on their own evils as if these were good things. And when he has shown his anger, he will trouble them. For he does not bring on torments and punishments all at once, before they have rejected the gentler kinds of cure, since an angry word spoken beforehand to turn them back can produce repentance in them through fear. Thus the blessed Paul, writing to the Thessalonians about the Jews who crucified the Lord, says: "Wrath has come upon them to the uttermost." Or did the wrath foretold by the prophets not come upon them, when they suffered every terrible and irreparable thing at the hands of the Romans?

Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession, etc. For he has been appointed heir of all things as a man, as part of the divine plan of salvation. In this way he could then recover, as his own rightful portion, those on earth whom the devil and the evil powers with him had wickedly scattered. When this was accomplished, he says to his own Father about us: "Those whom you gave me out of the world were yours, and you gave them to me." See, then, how even in the flesh he returns to the riches that belong to him by nature. For if those in the world belonged to the Father, they could in some way be understood to belong also to the Word who is his counselor. This is why he also said: "All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine; and I have been glorified in them." How, then, is he told to ask? How does he receive nations as an inheritance and make the ends of the earth his possession? Humanity had broken away from service to God, to its own ruin. The Creator and Father wished to save it, and so he sent his only-begotten Word into this present world. The Word became flesh and was contained in a body, yet remained unchanged [?] in nature, so that he might proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind. So even if he is said to receive, and to be appointed heir, because of his humanity, let us not lose sight of the divine plan of salvation.

By the same. By "inheritance" he means rational nature. Rational nature itself also inherits wisdom, as well as knowledge, truth and righteousness. The inheritance of rational nature is the contemplation of bodily and bodiless things, and of God, the cause of them all.

You will shepherd them with a rod of iron; you will shatter them like a potter's vessels, etc. In the Apostle too the more severe kind of treatment is called a rod. This is the treatment that sinners need, and also the weaker among those thought to have believed. He says: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?" And earlier still, in the Prophet, the divine word threatens sinners with the rod and with whips because they need such treatment. Its purpose is that mercy should not be withdrawn from their Father, that is, Christ. For it says: "I will punish their transgressions with the rod and their sins with whips; but I will not take my mercy away from him." That is why Isaiah calls Christ himself a rod. But some people do not need harsh treatment, because they show themselves worthy of the kindness of the Word's contemplations. So the same prophet also calls him a flower: "For a rod shall come out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from the root. The Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the spirit of the fear of God shall fill him." So the more brutish among those who come to God through Christ need a shepherd's rod. Next, we must explain how the Father, who gave the Son the nations as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession, can say to him: "You will shatter them like a potter's vessel." For who gives an inheritance so that the heir will shatter it? We must therefore show from the Scriptures that for some people being shattered is for their benefit. In the fiftieth psalm we find: "A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise." And in another prophet it is said as a command: "Wail because of the breaking of your spirit." So there is a spirit in us that must be broken, so that once broken it may become a sacrifice to God. What else could this be but the worse part of us? It seems sound while it is active, but it has been broken when we have shattered its powers by the word of God. There is also a heart in us, at times when we pride ourselves on wicked doctrines that have been given body as a harmful, connected system. That heart is thought to be whole and lofty, but it must be broken and humbled. Then it will stop deserving God's contempt and can be brought near to him. He rewards those who become aware of themselves, who condemn their own wicked disposition and take refuge in the kindness of God, who alone can do them good. From what has been said, the meaning of "Wail because of the breaking of your spirit" is also clear. A broken spirit is to be offered to God as a sacrifice [?]. God does not despise a heart that is broken and humbled, since it has rightly come to be in this state, and he accepts a wailing sent up from a broken spirit. In the same way we shall understand the shattering that Christ brings about in obedience to the one who gave him the nations as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession. He shatters the earthy and material element that the passions and the marks of vice have added to the soul, the element that made them idolaters and fornicators. For it is said in the seventy-seventh psalm: "When he slew them, then they sought him; they turned back and came early to God, and they remembered that God is their helper, and God the Most High is their redeemer." So it is not absurd to be slain in this way, or to be shattered like a potter's vessel. For sinners, insofar as they are sinners, were reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of a potter's hands, as the prophet Jeremiah says.
By the same. If he shepherds according to God's promise, then Christ is a shepherd. He is a shepherd who shepherds with a rod of iron, and he is the good shepherd.
By the same. The rod of God is his authority, his punishment of the disobedient: that is, it is found in the cross. For its material is wood, but its strength is iron.

And now, kings, understand; be disciplined, all you who judge the earth, etc. It is in keeping with the Savior's kindness to speak to the kings of the earth who stood by with the rulers gathered against him and say: "And now, kings, understand." In other words: even if you plotted earlier in ignorance, now understand and repent. But since "of the earth" is not added here, perhaps by "kings" he means the saints. For in the proper sense a king is one who knows how to rule without having to answer to anyone. And how is someone not a king who inherits the kingdom of heaven and will be in the kingdom of God? A saint who strives to reign must begin with himself and his own impulses. He must first reign over these, and no longer be ruled by sin, which has made it its business to reign in our mortal body. Aquila's rendering, "acquire knowledge," seems more emphatic than "understand." It commands them to take up a knowledge that belongs to kings and to no one else. "Be disciplined, all you who judge the earth." Just as we took "kings" in two ways, we can also understand "those who judge the earth" in two ways. Either the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ could be called judges of the earth, since judging is the proper work of rulers. Or the saints are the ones who judge the earth, as we shall show. "Be disciplined" means either "hand yourselves over to discipline and teaching," or "hand yourselves over to the punishments that discipline those who need such remedies." Someone will probably ask whether anyone is commanded to be disciplined through punishment and to hand himself over to it willingly. Many points in this passage are puzzling, but in answer to this question we must say the following. Perhaps some, being infants, are dragged to such discipline even against their will. These are the ones of whom the Prophet says: "If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will punish their transgressions with the rod and their sins with whips; but I will not take my mercy away from him." But perhaps others become aware of their own failings and hand themselves over to the most painful remedies, the ones able to make them better. They do this as people who need to be treated by someone who has this skill. I think those spoken of in Isaiah belong to this group: "They will wish they had been burned with fire." So do those who pray in Jeremiah's words, saying: "Discipline us, Lord, but with justice and not in anger, so that you do not make us few." For in what they say, they plead to be spared the painful and more severe punishments, but they do not refuse punishment altogether. Let us consider whether the voice that says, "I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause," belongs to those who are punished willingly. Perhaps, then, those who judge the earth will not be disciplined unless they hand themselves over to discipline. But we have preferred the view that the kings called to understanding are the saints. So come, let us look at those who judge the earth in the same way. We find that this is proper to the saints: by the good they have done, they judge those who have not tried to do the same. For the Savior says: "The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment and condemn the people of this generation, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here." And also: "The queen of the south will rise up at the judgment and condemn the people of this generation, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here." So the Ninevites and the queen of the south are among those who judge the people who heard the Savior and did not change, and who despised the teaching of Jesus. Perhaps the apostles of Christ will judge the twelve tribes of Israel in this way too, for not believing in Christ. And those who have believed throughout the whole earth will judge the whole earth, each judging the unbelievers in his own region. So the text urges those who judge the earth to be disciplined by receiving knowledge as it is handed down. Solomon says the same in Proverbs: "Receive discipline and not silver, and knowledge rather than refined gold."

By the same. Or he is calling them to repentance, and he calls them kings to persuade them to return to the dignity they once had. Understand, then, O kings, why the nations have been given to me as an inheritance.

Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling, etc. Some (79) will think that whoever serves is certainly a slave, especially here, since "with fear" is added, and one who has received a spirit of slavery is "in fear." And they will not be wrong to think so. But a son too can serve. Fear is not the only reason for serving; love is another. At any rate, the Apostle teaches us to serve one another through love. Indeed, our Savior and Lord himself was among his disciples not as one reclining at table but as one who serves, serving them and washing their feet. And it would be wrong to say that he ever did these things out of fear, for it is clear that he did them out of perfect love. If, then, the kings who were named "kings of the earth" in the preceding verses are also the ones meant here, the command to serve the Lord in fear can be given to them as to people who were slaves from the beginning and unable to receive the spirit of adoption. In their case "in fear" must be taken of the fear that [?] has punishment, the fear of one who has not been made perfect. What follows, "rejoice in him with trembling," must be understood in the same way. But if the kings are the saints, and "those who judge the earth" are those interpreted in the exposition, then, since sons too can serve the Lord, the fear must be understood as what some call reverence, which has no punishment at all. That Scripture speaks of a fear that has no punishment, and that this fear is an accomplishment of the perfect, is clear from the verse "Those who fear him lack nothing." We may seem to be forcing the text, because "with trembling" is added. But perhaps the perfect are the kings, while the others, who are still being trained by fear, are the judges of the earth. The Savior commands them to rejoice, but not loosely or without restraint, so that they do not fall into slackness and conceit. They are to rejoice "with trembling," with a kind of restraint, keeping in view that they could fall if God's care were to abandon someone who has reached a state in which he might reasonably be proud. "To rejoice" belongs to the usage of Scripture. We take it to mean a joy of the mind, in which the soul has communion with the Holy Spirit, who rejoices together with the saint.

Lay hold of instruction, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the righteous way, etc. With "be instructed" he describes progress (80), and with "lay hold of instruction" he describes perfection. Anyone who observes carefully will see that a person who is still imperfect in instruction and not yet making progress may share in the Lord's anger, while the perfect cannot share in it. If someone is ordered to lay hold of instruction so that the Lord will not be angry with him, he may share in the anger if he does not lay hold of it, even if he is making progress in instruction. It is grasping instruction that sets a person wholly free from the sufferings that anger brings, not merely being introduced to instruction and beginning it. Whoever is still being instructed is certainly imperfect, and an imperfect person can experience God's anger. But "righteous" does not appear in the Hebrew or in the other versions. So we suspect that either the translators added it by way of accommodation or the copies are corrupt. If it was added by accommodation, we should understand it like this: "If you do not lay hold of instruction, you will perish from the righteous way and fall away from it, because the Lord is angry with you." But strictly speaking, if God's anger is meant to instruct, how will anyone perish from the righteous way because the Lord is angry? It will not be because of the anger at all that you perish from the righteous way; that will come upon you because of your sins. If "righteous" is not in the text, then, since those who have not laid hold of instruction are certainly on a way that is not good, the verse may be quietly saying this: if you do not lay hold of instruction, the Lord will be angry, and as a result you will perish from the way you are now living in, so that you are no longer on it.

When his wrath is quickly kindled, blessed are all who trust in him, etc. Wrath (81) is mentioned after anger, but anyone who pays attention to the way Scripture puts things will see that the wrath is kindled first, and that once God has become angry a person perishes from the way. The wrath is kindled "quickly," that is, after a little while, or it subsides after a short time. This points to the punishment that comes after one departs from this life.

Blessed are all who trust in him, etc. We must hear "those who trust" as meaning a faith joined with untroubled hope, a faith that is utterly firm, settled and unshaken. The one who trusts in this way never despairs of the Lord's coming to him, not even in what seem the hardest times, and nothing draws him away.
PSALM 3.

A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son, etc. The psalm seems (82) to have been spoken by David when he fled from the face of Absalom his son. But it is not possible to make everything in the psalm fit the history. What does this contribute to the subject at hand: “I fell asleep and slept; I awoke, for the Lord will help me”? And if anyone wishes to be a slave to the letter and look for nothing more in it, let him show how the Prophet speaks truly when he says, “You have broken the teeth of sinners.” We must ask who David is and who Absalom is. We must also ask what Absalom's attack on his father signifies, and the flight of the king, who bore meekly the rebellion of the son who coveted his kingdom and commanded those under him to spare the young man Absalom. In many places in Scripture we have found that David is Christ. One is the eighty-eighth psalm: “I have found David my servant; with holy oil I have anointed him. For my hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him. The enemy shall gain no advantage over him, and the son of lawlessness shall not again afflict him. I will cut down his enemies before his face, and put to flight those who hate him. My truth and my mercy shall be with him, and in my name his horn shall be exalted. I will set his hand on the sea, and his right hand on the rivers. He shall call upon me, ‘You are my Father,’ and I will make him firstborn, high above the kings of the earth. For ever I will keep my mercy for him, and my covenant shall be faithful to him.
