I will establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven.” Another is Isaiah, who says: “A throne shall be set right with mercy, and one shall sit on it in truth in the tent of David, judging and seeking justice and hastening righteousness.” David the man lived long before Isaiah, so it is not he who is prophesied as the one who will judge. It is Christ, to whom the Father has given authority “to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” And in Ezekiel Christ is clearly said to be David, in the vision addressed to the shepherds whom the word rebukes for not having tended the sheep well. Next let us see who Absalom the son of David is. Some will suppose him to be an image of Judas the traitor, others of the devil. Melito of Asia, at any rate, says that he is a type of the devil, who rose up against the kingdom of Christ. But Melito mentioned only this and did not work out the passage.

Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Many rise up against me; many say to my soul, “There is no salvation for him in his God,” etc. As far as the letter goes (83), these words are spoken by David as he fled from Absalom, who had risen up against him. At that time two hundred invited men went with Absalom from Jerusalem, going in their simplicity and knowing nothing of the matter, and all of them were afflicting David. But we have chosen rather to take these words as spoken in the person of David, as we showed in our remarks on the title. As far as the history goes, David was afflicted by the many who joined Absalom as their numbers grew. Those who rose up against him were Ahithophel, Shimei, Thekon [?], and any other of the powerful. Those who say there is no salvation for him in God may be other people, distinct from those who afflicted him and rose up against him. They need not have followed Absalom at all, but may have said this because they had given David up as defeated. Those who afflicted the Savior in the flesh were the Jews, who cried out, “Away, away with such a one from the earth.” Judas the traitor and Caiaphas rose up against him. Those who said to his soul that there was no salvation were the passers-by at the time of the passion, who said, “Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe in him.” At a higher level, one can distinguish among the people who afflict him, rise up against him, and deny that there is salvation in him, as follows. All the leaders and teachers of doctrines other than the teachings of Christ would be those who rise up against him. Those who approve of their teaching and become their disciples would be those who afflict him. Then there are those who disbelieve that divinity is present in Christ's teaching, without teaching the contrary and without being taught falsehoods. These could be said to say to his soul that there is no salvation for him in God. They mean either that there is none for him according to the narrative that reports the wonders of his coming, or that the word of his teaching does not contain the salvation it promises. In another sense, however, all sinners can be among those who afflict him. A wicked son does not afflict the one who begot him with the intent of harming his father. Rather, because of the father's love, it inevitably follows that he is afflicted by his son's sins. In the same way the wickedness of each sinner afflicts the Son of God. And the more a person abounds in good works and sound doctrines, the greater he is, and so the more people afflict him and the more rise up against him. Many in turn then say, “There is no salvation for him in God,” having despaired of his cause, even though none of these things will harm him in regard to salvation. God allows many to afflict the righteous man in order to give him an occasion for a weight of glory, which comes from surpassing afflictions. And if ever the righteous man, in perplexity, should say to God, “Why have those who afflict me multiplied?”, then while he is still speaking God will say, “Here I am, so that the momentary lightness of affliction may work for you a weight of glory beyond all measure.” That is why “many are the afflictions of the righteous.” If there is salvation, it is God's [?].

But you, Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head, etc. If David is speaking (84), the words befit the faith of the Prophet. He bore such great calamities unshaken. He was confident that he would not be forsaken, and that besides being helped he would also be glorified in God and exalted by being restored to the kingdom. If Christ is the speaker, he is equally confident that he will rise again and that he will be plotted against by men. He is confident too that he will not be forsaken, because the Father would help him and restore him to his original glory, and would exalt him, or even exalt him above all. As the Apostle also says: “Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” Those who think they have glory place it in different things. One might say that his glory is his homeland, another his family, another his beauty. Some have considered bodily strength and skill in physical contests to be their own glory, priding themselves on having thrown so many opponents in wrestling. But why list all the things in which those who do not know God take pride? As the Apostle says, “their glory is often in their shame.” The glory of the saint, by contrast, is God, in whom he trusts. This is no casual trust, but faith reckoned as righteousness, and through it one can see signs of God's presence and of fellowship with his power. For example, God was the glory of Moses. He bore witness to his friendship with the prophet even on his face, and did so openly before the whole Hebrew people and before the Egyptians. God was the glory of Elijah the prophet when he raised the widow's son and when he prayed for rain and obtained his request as soon as he asked. So God speaks truly when he says, “Those who glorify me I will glorify.” God is plainly the glory of those who minister wondrous powers. One can understand him to be no less the glory of those who are glorified for their virtue. That glory has been begotten by none other than the Father, in the souls of those who have presented themselves [?] to receive him.

With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain, etc. It is worth asking (85) why these two half-verses were not placed before what was said earlier. It would be quite natural for the prayer to come before the thanksgiving for the benefits received. The difficulty can be resolved in this way. What is said here is not a prayer but a report that the prayer was made. The prayer was made in silence, and at the very moment of praying he succeeded: the one who brought his petition to God received what he wished. Having succeeded, he rightly puts his thanksgiving to God before his account to men of what he prayed for. If it had happened the other way round, then on obtaining what he asked he would first have told how he prayed and only afterward given thanks. In that case he would have weakened the prompt address owed to God in thanksgiving by first reporting to us, his readers, how he prayed. But it is better to resolve the difficulty in this way. The beginning of the psalm contains a prayer. Then, after the prayer, from the diapsalma onward, there is thanksgiving for having obtained what he asked. When the thanksgiving is complete, the Prophet turns his face toward us and tells how he was heard when he prayed. Let us consider word by word “With my voice I cried to the Lord” and what follows, according to the usage of Scripture. Let us also consider what it means that the saints have often prayed to God with a cry. In this connection one should also note that Jesus stood and cried out, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” The Apostle gives us a starting point when he says in general terms that the Spirit cries out in the hearts of the saints, “Abba, Father.” There is, then, an intense intelligible cry, which is the voice of the soul. Perhaps the soul uses it after it has laid aside the instrument through which it utters such things. We think that the rational reasoning that goes on in the ruling faculty is itself the voice of the soul. If that reasoning is more substantial and concerns greater things, not things that lie below and are lowly, it would be the intelligible cry. Those who cry to God with this cry are heard. The exception is when, by God's dispensation, they are left unanswered so that they may carry off greater crowns in greater contests, as is said in Habakkuk: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? Shall I shout to you when I am wronged, and you will not save me? Why have you shown me toils and troubles, so that I look upon misery and ungodliness?” The Savior also always utters this cry in great doctrines. In this way the Word of God has always stood crying out, as Wisdom does in Solomon. Wisdom is the same as the Word of God in subsistence, and she calls with a lofty proclamation to her mixing bowl, saying: “Whoever among you is foolish, let him turn aside to me. To those who lack sense I give this command: Come, eat of my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you.” So the intense voice of the one who speaks to the Lord in the psalm is heard from nowhere else than from the holy mountain, that is, from heaven. Elsewhere it is also said, “He will hear him from his holy heaven.” And he hears from on high, for it is written, “He will hear him from on high and from his holy temple.”

I fell asleep and slept; I awoke, for the Lord will help me, etc. In our view (86), if we wanted to keep David as the speaker because of the letter, nothing in these words would fit, in human terms, the history of David's flight from the face of Absalom. For this reason we could press even the unwilling, compelling them to raise the history to a higher sense and fully accept that what is declared is spoken in the person of Christ. But so that we do not seem to abandon the interpretation that can be kept according to the letter, we must say this too. We say, then, that David is accusing himself when he says this. He had not been watchful over his kingdom or paid it due attention, and so there was an opportunity to attack him, and he suffered these things through Absalom's attack. “For while I had fallen asleep,” he says, “and was sleeping, these things happened to me. But I rose up, since the Lord will help me, and having risen I will not fear the myriads of people attacking me.” Taken this way, what follows will also seem to fit without forcing. This, we think, is the interpretation according to the letter. By anagogy, as we said before, these words are spoken in the person of the Lord, who is now describing his own falling asleep and the sleep of his passion. First let us consider the difference between falling asleep and sleep as the words are understood. Falling asleep has to do with stillness, and Paul speaks of it when he says, “We shall all fall asleep, but we shall not all be changed.” Sleep, on the other hand, is a relaxation of the soul as it slackens its hold on the body and lets go its tension, because it cannot bear unremitting strain. We think the difference is shown most clearly in Job, in these words: “Now I would have fallen asleep and been still; having slept I would have rested with kings, counselors of the earth.” We needed the difference between falling asleep and sleeping in order to understand how it might be shown in the case of the Savior. It is customary to call departure from this life falling asleep, and we remember that it is sometimes also called sleep. Scripture says, “He fell asleep with his fathers”; and, “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised, and they entered the holy city and appeared to many”; and, “But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep”; and, “We shall all fall asleep.” It is also called sleep, since slumbering is the same as sleeping: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall rise.” This should be compared with the words “of the saints who had fallen asleep.” Apart from departure from this life, however, sleep also signifies the soul's inattention, since attention is called wakefulness. The divine word, wishing us to guard against inattention, says: “Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, so that you may save yourself like a gazelle from the snares and like a bird from the trap.” And the Prophet, wishing to show the slackness and laxity of sinners, says, “They slept their sleep and found nothing.” Scripture also says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” Corresponding to the sleep of inattention is the drowsiness of the soul, which Solomon forbids when he teaches us to give our eyes not only no sleep but also no drowsiness. And the Psalmist himself puts the word “drowsiness” in a context of blame when he says, “All who mounted horses grew drowsy.” We say, then, that our Savior Jesus Christ fell asleep in the common death that he died for us, and slept when his soul was separated from his body. Sleepers are active in soul while the body lies still. They follow certain images that come upon them and do things without needing the body at all. In the same way, “I slept” is said after “I fell asleep” to refer to his soul, separated from the body and in this sense sleeping. The image is not like its original in every respect; the point is to show the soul's activity apart from the body. And is it any wonder if in the Savior's case such sleep is not total inactivity of the soul, but inactivity only as regards using the body as an instrument? The soul acts on its own and by itself, as is also shown when Job says the same thing: “Why was I not carried from the womb to the grave? Now I would have fallen asleep and been still; having slept I would have rested with kings, counselors of the earth, who gloried in swords, and with rulers who had much gold.” If he had not understood that there is some activity of the soul in which it rested while enjoying certain good things in such company, he would not have said, “Having slept I would have rested with kings, counselors of the earth, who gloried in swords.” These would be holy soldiers of godliness, who use the word that is sharper than any two-edged sword against every word opposed to the truth. And the rulers who had much gold could be taken to mean those who surpass the many and in this respect are rulers. They trade and grow rich in thoughts and in contemplations of the truth. It is no wonder, then, that the Savior too says, “I fell asleep and slept.” Even at the time of his separation from the body he was far more active for the salvation of souls. This is what is said in Peter's Catholic Epistle: “In which he also went and preached to the spirits in prison, who had once been disobedient, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah while the ark was being built, in which a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water.” After this falling asleep, the Father came to his help and raised him up.

I will not be afraid of the myriads of people who surround me and attack me together, etc. These words befit a saint (87) who has attained a very great virtue, fearlessness, through confidence in God. They are like these: “If an army encamps against me, my heart shall not fear.” The Savior might also say these words. In spirit he knew the myriads of the people of the mutilation who were demanding that he be crucified, and he saw his own calm (I say this with reference to the flesh). And if anyone perceives the multitude of missiles hurled by the enemies, which attack the soul, trouble it and toss it like waves, he might fittingly take refuge in God and say, “I will not be afraid of the myriads of people who surround me and attack me together.”

Arise, O Lord, save me, my God, for you have struck all who are hostile to me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners, etc. When we consulted the Hebrew (88), we found that it could in no way mean “without cause.” What does the word “without cause” have in common with “jaw”? The other translators have also rendered it as the Hebrew has it. It is likely, then, as some of the Hebrews say, that the ancient copies had a different reading. Alternatively, the Seventy, avoiding the crudeness of the expression, ventured to put “without cause” instead of “jaw.” Let us, then, understand the text according to the Seventy. Let us go through how we must take the more human expressions used of God, and from these it is easy to see how it can be said, “Arise, O Lord, save me, my God.” When God handed us over to the opposing powers to be tested, it was as though he had fallen asleep toward us, and the psalmist rouses him. Perhaps also, when the Father handed over the Savior for all of us, he was as though asleep toward him. But he rises, saving him and striking his enemies, whether those of the circumcision or the invisible powers hostile to the truth. The saint, however, takes no account of anyone as an enemy. With those who hate peace he is peaceable, for he loves his enemies. Someone might seem to be hostile to another not “without cause,” when we look at the enemy either in a more human way or in a more pious way. In a more human way, this happens when he turns on the one who first started doing him harm and wants to retaliate. In that case he might be thought to be hostile not “without cause” to the one who wronged him first. In a more pious way, it happens if someone becomes an enemy for the sake of the truth, as the Apostle says, “I have become your enemy by telling you the truth.” Scripture also says, “Did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord?” We must ask whether there are any who hate God. No one would admit to this, not even the utterly unjust and godless. Who, then, are those who hate the Lord? Who openly hate Jesus and anathematize him? Whatever is done to him is certainly referred to the Father. And everyone who sins hates God, either by despising wisdom, that is, Christ, or by hating righteousness and working lawlessness. Since Christ is righteousness, whoever hates Christ, who is righteousness, hates God. It is now clear who hates God. But unless we examine precisely what is meant by “Did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord?”, we shall hate all people except a few, since those whose works mark them out as loving God are very rare. What could be more absurd than turning away from everyone, and even, if one may say so, from oneself? For anyone who honestly examines his own state will be found to hate God. Perhaps, then, we should not think of the person as the one who hates God, but rather the evils that have befallen rational beings. For example, injustice hates God, and the unjust man hates God insofar as he is unjust, because the injustice in him is what does this. So we must hate such accidental qualities, which are our enemies first of all, with a perfect hatred, that is, a hatred that comes from perfection. Just as justice and self-control come from perfection, so does such hatred. We have said these things in examining “You have struck those who are hostile to me without cause,” since all who are hostile to anyone are hostile without cause. Such also is the verse “They hated me for nothing.” The teeth of sinners that are broken are like those of which it is said, “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” The teeth of sinners are irrational thoughts that come upon us contrary to nature. The adversaries often use them as teeth as they draw near to us to eat our flesh, that is, the things that spring from the flesh. “Now the works of the flesh are manifest,” says the divine Apostle.

Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people, etc. Whoever is convinced (89) that salvation belongs to the Lord also knows what it means to trust in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation. Salvation belongs to the Lord, and that is why our God is the God of salvation, for to the Lord belong the ways of escape from death. His blessing upon his people is spiritual, in the heavenly places in Christ.
PSALM 4.

"For the end, among the psalms, a song of David," etc. Many psalms bear the heading "For the end" in the Septuagint, and in these places the other translators give equivalents of "For the end." So it is worth tracing out, as far as we can, the meaning this expression points to. We should know that every art and every science has an end, which the person who truly pursues that art or science hastens toward. In the same way the rational nature must also have an end, and according to the Apostle this end is to be made alive in Christ. We think, then, that the psalms headed "For the end" announce some meaning of the end and call those who understand their words toward it. For everyone who competes, the end is victory. Now, as we showed earlier, Christ is called David. So the psalms headed "For the end" and "of David" announce the end and the victory of Christ. Following Aquila, he could be called "the victory-maker," since he has won victory for everyone he has conquered. The one whom Christ conquers has himself conquered the wickedness that had befallen him, and he wipes it out by submitting to Christ. Christ conquers no one against his will but wins by persuasion, because he is the Word of God. Theodotion says that the hymns or psalms headed "For the end" in the Septuagint are inscribed "for the victory," and Symmachus would call these psalms or songs Christ's "songs of victory." Some of these psalms are said to be "for the end" not only of David but also of Asaph or of the sons of Korah. In those cases it is not absurd for us to apply what is said here to all the saints who have taken on the image of Christ. The phrase "among the psalms," used by the Septuagint and Aquila, is I think rendered more clearly by Symmachus as "with psalteries." Together the three teach us that this song or melody was composed for the instruments called psalteries. For we must look for several instruments on which the "For the end," or "the song of victory," or "to the victory-maker" is sung. Theodotion's rendering, "for the victory in hymns," can also mean this. This song, then, or melody, or psalm, which has the theme just described, proclaims what we have set out above. In a more general sense it speaks in the person of the prophet David. In a more mystical sense it speaks in the person of Christ, who takes on the person of the saints. At times he regards their afflictions as his own, along with the room they are given in those afflictions, since the saying "Afflicted in every way, but not hemmed in" is the voice of the saints. At other times he turns back the heavy-hearted and those who love vain things. The difference between the words "song" and "melody" does not call for much inquiry. "Song" indicates the inflection of the speaker's voice, while "melody" perhaps also indicates the artistry of a mystical tune sung in rhythm. According to the rules of anagogy, however, the melody would be a well-ordered life, examined by reason and lived for the glory of God, with sound doctrines and words that also benefit others.

"When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me," etc. The person speaking is either the Prophet or Christ, in the role he took on for our sake in the economy of salvation. The words show that he is heard not after he has called but while he is calling. For to the saints, who obey the divine commands in every respect, a promise has been proclaimed through the prophet Isaiah: "While you are still speaking, I will say, Here I am." It is also worth considering what calling upon God is. Those who have not examined Scripture think it is the act of anyone at all who is inclined to pray. But the Prophet establishes very clearly that calling upon God belongs to saints and to those who will certainly be saved. "Everyone," he says, "who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved." If everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved, then whoever is not saved has not called upon the name of the Lord, even if he has often seemed to do so. Calling upon the name of the Lord is judged not by the voice but by the disposition of the speaker and by firm faith. So in Psalm 98 calling upon the Lord is attributed not to ordinary people but to Samuel. God honored him so highly that he is counted alongside Moses, God's friend, as Jeremiah says: "Even if Moses and Samuel stood before my face praying for some of these ungodly people, I would not listen even to them, says the Lord." So it is written of him: "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name. They called upon the Lord, and he heard them; he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the ordinances that he gave them. O Lord our God, you listened to them; O God, you were gracious to them." Because they kept his testimonies and the ordinances he gave them, they were counted among those who call upon him when they prayed. In Psalm 144 we are taught more precisely who it is that calls upon him: "The Lord is near to those who call upon him in truth." This implies that some do not call upon him in truth. "For not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father in heaven." A person says "Lord" perfectly when his works also speak and say "Lord, Lord." Here, then, it is clear that whoever calls upon the Lord has righteousness, and true righteousness. And if Christ is righteousness, the righteous person shares in righteousness, that is, in Christ. So that "God of my righteousness" may not sound like a boast, we can draw on the verse "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and redemption." Then the phrase will be equivalent to "the God of my Lord."

"In affliction you made room for me; have pity on me and hear my prayer," etc. Divine Scripture seems to have its own usage here, one that does not pry into a person's choices. It uses "affliction" for a hardship that befalls the saint for the sake of training, but it calls what happens to the sinner a "scourge." "Many," it says, "are the afflictions of the righteous," and "Many are the scourges of the sinner." To give examples: what Job suffered, and Joseph in Egypt, we shall call afflictions, but what David suffered because of Uriah's wife and because he numbered the people we shall call scourges. Still, we must watch that nothing in Scripture escapes our notice, in case "affliction" is somewhere applied to sinners and "scourge" to those already righteous. That the trial given to the saints as they compete is called affliction we are persuaded by many texts besides those already cited. Nor is it surprising if the scourge touches sons who have sinned, as Solomon says: "He scourges every son whom he receives." Again, we must consider whether what befell the Egyptians because of Israel should be called scourges, since being scourged belongs to sons. For Psalm 88 says: "If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod." With this said, being afflicted is not among the things in our power. But being discontented and giving in are among the things in our power, and they are blameworthy. The Scriptures call this being "hemmed in." To go beyond not giving in, and even to rejoice in afflictions as occasions for greater prizes and promises, is the work of saints, as the Apostle says: "Afflicted in every way, but not hemmed in." When he rebukes the Corinthians, he says they are subject to being hemmed in: "You are not hemmed in by us, but you are hemmed in within your own hearts." Then he urges them on by pointing to the saint's own condition and says: "You too, open wide." So here too the Prophet thanks God, who helped him and gave his will room in a time of affliction. God makes room not by stopping the evils but by granting greatness of soul.

"Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?" etc. Some will think "sons of men" is a periphrasis, as is also customary among the Greeks, who say "sons of the Achaeans." Others will start from the Savior, who is often called the Son of Man. They will try to trace why human beings are often called "sons of men" rather than simply "men." In the Savior's case, his being called Son of Man could never be a periphrasis, since it is said: "He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man." As a general rule, then, we should know this: when the saints are called gods, the name "man" is used as a reproach, but when sinners are called cattle and beasts, it is used as praise. An example of the first: "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you will die like men and fall like one of the princes." Also: "For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly and walking like men?" An example of the second: "Men and beasts you will save, O Lord." We find that the first particular person in Scripture addressed by God [?] with the title now under discussion, "son of man," is Daniel, and after him Ezekiel. Both were prophets during the captivity. Before the captivity, as far as we can learn from the undisputed inspired books that have come down to us, no one is given this title. And what need is there to speak of the Savior, when the Gospels are full of this expression? We think that, because those in the captivity had become sinners, Daniel, who alone had kept the dignity of human nature made according to the image and likeness, was addressed as "son of man" as a reproach to them. The same must be said of Ezekiel. For "man" was the name first given to the one God made according to the image and likeness, and so he would be man in the proper sense. In the Savior's case we must also consider whether his humanity is the "Son of Man," the father of that humanity being the "man" who is the image of the invisible God. The saying "both earthborn and sons of men" also shows that the sons of men are superior to the earthborn. But to return to the text: those addressed here are rebuked when they hear "How long will you be heavy-hearted?" and what follows. So the rebukes will not seem fittingly addressed to sons of men, unless we must take "man" in two senses, as the Apostle understood it when he said: "The first man was from the earth, made of dust; the second man is the Lord from heaven. As was the man of dust, so are those who are of dust; and as is the heavenly man, so are those who are heavenly." There is a further question. The sons of men are commanded to know that the Lord "has made his holy one wonderful." It will be asked how sons of men in the worse sense can be commanded to do the work of the holiest. For to know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful is an achievement of the holiest. This is easy to resolve. While in a worse state, the same person can be a son of man after the man of dust. Then, once changed, which is not impossible, he can become a son of man after the heavenly man. These sons of men of the second kind, being sons of the man of dust from the earth, could reasonably be called heavy-hearted, lovers of vanity and seekers of falsehood. For they have the mind of the flesh, a bodily love, and a quest for the enemy of truth, that is, falsehood. The heavy-hearted are those who have in their heart the lawlessness that sits upon a talent of lead. Because it tends downward, it will sink with the Egyptians like lead in the mighty water of life's waves. The opposite of the heavy-hearted are those who are under Jesus' light yoke. There may be another sense. Disciples are sons of the one who made them disciples, and teachers are themselves made according to the image and likeness of God. So those who have been taught but have not proved worthy of their teachers might be reproached as heavy-hearted sons of man, because they did not follow through on the opportunities given them to make their hearts pure. For teachers commonly call heavy-hearted those learners who do not follow what is being said, because their hearts are dull. That is also why they seek falsehood: they do not see the truth. In a deeper sense, since the Savior is truth, his enemy would clearly be a false word that claims to be true, which John often calls antichrist. If someone takes "sons of men" as a periphrasis for "men," the verse blames the heavy-heartedness that is found among most people. The aim is that they should cast off their hardness of hearing, so to speak, and develop quickness of mind. The power of seeking in the soul should be withdrawn from the things it ought not to seek, which are all false, and turned toward the things it ought to seek, so that they seek the truth.

"The Lord will hear me when I cry to him," etc. A loud voice that reaches God is not one that sounds loud and strained to human ears because it strikes the air more forcefully. It is the pure and untroubled flow of words sent up to God from the ruling part of the soul. We should know that the hidden heart of a person also has a voice that makes no use of the body. A person sometimes sends this voice up to the only one who hears such a voice. He does so when he has gathered himself into himself, "entered your inner room," shut the door of the senses, and come to be wholly outside the body. That is why, although Scripture records no audible sound from Moses, God says to him, as we learn from Exodus: "Why do you cry out to me?" But every voice is small that sets forth earthly, small and lowly things and asks God for them. The Savior forbids us to offer such requests to the Father and says: "Ask for the great things, and the small will be added to you; ask for the heavenly things, and the earthly will be added to you."

"Be angry, and do not sin," etc. The word "be angry" signifies the imperative mood, but it also signifies the indicative, which some call the declarative, as in "we are angry, you are angry, they are angry." Again, in a different way, the noun "anger," from which "be angry" is formed, signifies something deliberately chosen. Some have defined it as a desire to retaliate against those who seem to have done wrong. It also signifies something not chosen, which some call a pre-passion. This arises in us, and certain provocations draw it toward the anger defined above. If, then, we take "be angry" in the other sense, I mean the unchosen one, [?] the passage about Elijah and Ahab: "And the Lord said, Have you seen how Ahab was pierced with compunction before my face? I will not bring the evil in his days." And in Psalm 59: "You shook the earth and threw it into turmoil. Heal its breaches, for it has been shaken. You showed your people hard things; you made us drink the wine of compunction. You gave those who fear you a signal to flee from before the bow." Here the Prophet confesses that he has been made to drink the wine of compunction. He digested the words of reproof, so to speak, and felt compunction from them. Therefore he confesses that, along with those who fear God, he received a signal to flee the arrows shot from God's bow. These are aimed at the ungodly who persisted in their sins and did not repent. And in Genesis: "Esau said to his father, Have you only one blessing, father? And when Isaac was pierced with compunction, Esau cried aloud and wept." Instead of "be pierced with compunction," Aquila and Theodotion have "be silent," which Symmachus translated "be still," setting out more clearly what the words mean. Their sense is this: speak with yourselves in secret upon your beds. That is, examine what you have done during the day and what concerns you, and in this way be still.

"Offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord," etc. Whoever makes an offering from unjust income does not offer a sacrifice of righteousness. Neither does someone who shares with the needy less than his means allow, nor someone who gives grudgingly or under compulsion. The text teaches very clearly that the divine word did not give its command about sacrifices in the sense that readers of the books have taken it. For in Psalm 40 it said: "God, your God, am I. I will not reprove you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are before me continually. I will not accept bulls from your house, nor goats from your flocks; for all the beasts of the field are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. I know all the birds of the sky, and the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world and all that fills it are mine. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of affliction, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me." And in Psalm 50: "For if you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings. A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise." And elsewhere: "Your burnt offerings and sacrifices are not pleasing to me." Further, in Jeremiah: "These are not the things," he says, "that I commanded your fathers about burnt offerings and sacrifice on the day I brought them up out of the land of Egypt. Rather, this is the word I commanded them: Let none of you harbor malice in his heart against his neighbor, and do not love a false oath. For I have hated all these things, says the Lord Almighty." Through all these passages, then, he clearly teaches us to examine what the subject of sacrifices really is. The oracles themselves give us starting points when they say, "A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit," just as here: "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord." Our Savior and Lord himself also corrects those who did not understand the prophetic words and were therefore excited about bodily sacrifices. He says: "If you had known what this means, I desire mercy and not sacrifice, you would not have condemned the guiltless." The passage stands in one of the Twelve Prophets as follows: "For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings." That this is what the legislation about sacrifices amounts to, Paul taught when he said: "who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things." Whoever reads the laws about sacrifices must therefore strive to expound them in both ways, examining them in their symbolic sense and in their more hidden, mystical sense. We have noted these points in brief because we wish to expound "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness" and, following from it, "hope in the Lord." For no one can reasonably hope before acting justly, but someone who acts justly can hope with confidence and expect the good things of the Lord, since hope is the expectation of good things. Many have asked whether the noble and good person will hope for anything. Their reasoning is that the perfect person already has the good things in full and lacks nothing, and so hopes for nothing, since hope is for things that are absent. Having good hopes is another matter, since for the noble and good their good things are continually followed by further good things. So let us too discuss the problem briefly, following the intent of the Scriptures. The sacred oracles very clearly urge us to hope in the Lord. "Let Israel hope in the Lord," it says, and "The house of Israel has hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and their protector." In Psalm 90, among the other promises, the perfect person is told: "With his shoulders he will overshadow you, and under his wings you will hope; his truth will surround you like a shield." Paul wishes to show what kind of thing it is on which the law and the prophets hang; I mean love. So he says: "Love believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; love never fails." Never failing is the work of the perfect person, since it belongs to love. Enduring all things belongs to one who, through love, has risen above every hardship. Believing all things means, clearly, believing what exists and is true, for false things are not to be counted among "all things," since they do not even exist in the first place. Whoever has achieved love is perfect and firm in the saving faith concerning each of the things that must be believed. Clearly, then, hoping all things too, and despairing of none of the things that can be laid up for a saint, could rightly be called the work of no one but the person adorned with perfect love. So if we wish to expound "hoping all things" by breaking it down into its parts, we shall say that it means hoping to inherit the kingdom of heaven and to be comforted. It means hoping to be called sons of God, to see God, and to be filled with the righteousness one hungers and thirsts for. It means hoping to receive perfect mercy and, in short, to share in all the things promised by God, who does not lie, and by our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. "For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him."

"Many say, 'Who will show us good things?'" and so on. The simpler will take this to mean that, when the things laid up in promise are proclaimed, the many say, "Who will show us these things and bring us to be in them?" Clearly they are struck by them as true and long for them. Yet because of human weakness, and their many sins, they have hardly allowed themselves to see these things and live in them. Others will explain the saying this way. The things recorded in the promise as to be given to the elect cannot be understood at all clearly and distinctly except by those who have become wise. For example: what is the land that the meek will inherit, and what should we understand by inheriting it? What does it mean to see God through purity of heart, when he is invisible and no one has ever seen him? What will happen, and what sort of events will take place, so that those who mourn now will later be comforted? And what is the kingdom of heaven, and of what sort? So many people, hearing of the good things recorded and wishing to behold and understand them with the mind, say, "Who will be the one to show us good things?" For truly rare is the one able to show the good things in the sense we have explained. Paul was such a man, able to set them forth in words, as he says somewhere: "But we have the mind of Christ, so that we may see the things freely given to us by God, which we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual." We have often observed that in Scripture "who" is used of what is rare, as in "Who is the faithful and wise steward?" and "Who is wise, and will understand these things?" and "Lord, who will dwell on your holy mountain?" So too here it is said, "Who will show us good things?"
From the volume on Psalm 4, on the verse: "Many say, 'Who will show us good things?'"

People have inquired a great deal about which things are good and which are evil. Some say that goods and evils do not depend on choice, and so they declare pleasure a good and what is painful an evil. Others confine goods and evils to matters of choice alone, calling only the virtues and the actions that accord with them goods, and only the vices and the activities that accord with vice evils. A third group mixes the two and says that goods and evils lie both in matters of choice and in things that do not depend on choice. Naturally, then, many believers who love learning are pulled this way and that by the plausible arguments, and on the subject of goods they might say, "Who will show us good things?" Now anyone at all who accepts the teaching about the judgment would admit, without needing to be taught, that the nature of goods lies in matters of choice. For Scripture says that good is that for which a person will hear: "Well done, good and faithful servant. You were faithful over a few things; I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your master." And good is what the good man brings out of his heart, as the Savior says: "The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart." In short, every fruit of a good tree is good, since it is a matter of choice: love, peace, joy, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control. And their opposites are evil. We must still ask whether, after the teaching of Christ, there is any good and evil among things that do not depend on choice. But even if there is some evil or good among such things, as we shall perhaps show after examining the matter later, the things called goods and evils by those who mix the unchosen with the chosen would not be such. For they think that some goods concern the soul, some the body, and some are external, and likewise with evils. Concerning the soul there is virtue and the actions that accord with it, or vice and the actions that accord with it. Concerning the body there is health, good condition and beauty, or disease, poor condition and ugliness. Among external things there are wealth and poverty, fame and obscurity, noble birth and low birth.

Some will think that according to the Scriptures too there are likewise three kinds of goods and three of evils. They accept that virtues and vices are goods and evils, as we too agree about virtue and vice and the actions that accord with them. Beyond this, they will use texts that supposedly declare bodily and external things to be good or evil. As for virtues and vices, what need is there to say anything? Moral teaching itself instructs us to choose justice, prudence, temperance and courage, and the actions that accord with them, and to turn away from their opposites. So there is no need of examples for the goods that lie in matters of choice. But they will show bodily and external goods from many places by taking the text literally. For the present it is enough to cite some passages from Exodus, Leviticus and Deuteronomy, given as promises to those who keep the commandments and as threats and curses against those who break them. For instance, to show that health is a good and disease [an evil], someone will point out that Exodus foretells this: "If you keep my commandments and my ordinances, I will not bring upon you any of the diseases that I brought upon the Egyptians, for I am the Lord who heals you." And what is said to sinners in Deuteronomy might be taken as presenting bodily plagues and diseases as evil, and so, plainly, health and bodily strength as good. The passage runs as follows: "If you will not listen and do all the words of this law that are written in this book, so as to fear this honored and wonderful name, the Lord your God, then the Lord will make your plagues extraordinary, and the plagues of your offspring: great and wonderful plagues, and evil and very many diseases. And he will bring back upon you all the evil plague of Egypt, which you dreaded before them, and it will cling to you. And every sickness and every plague that is not written in the book of this law the Lord will bring upon you until he destroys you." And again it is said to those who break the commandments: "I will send upon you fever and jaundice, and your eyes will waste away and your soul will melt away." Besides these, in Deuteronomy the word threatens those who depart from godliness with an incurable spasm that bends the back.

As for external goods, those who want them to be promised by the divine word will use these words from Leviticus: "If you walk in my ordinances and keep my commandments and do them, I will give you rain in its season, and the earth will yield its produce, and the trees of the plains will yield their fruit. Your threshing will reach to the vintage, and the vintage will reach to the sowing; and you will eat your bread to the full, and you will dwell securely in your land," and what follows. And from Deuteronomy they will use these: "And when you cross the Jordan into the land that the Lord God is giving you, and you take care to do all his commandments that I command you today, the Lord your God will set you above all, and all these blessings will come upon you and find you, if you listen to the voice of the Lord your God. Blessed are you in the city, and blessed are you in the field. Blessed are the offspring of your womb and the produce of your land, the herds of your cattle and the flocks of your sheep. Blessed are your storehouses and your stores," and what follows. And again, conversely, it is said to the ungodly: "Cursed are you in the city, and cursed are you in the field. Cursed are your storehouses and your stores. Cursed are the children of your womb and the produce of your land. Cursed are the herds of your cattle and the flocks of your sheep." And those who want goods and evils to lie in bodily and external things will bring forward countless other passages. They will also seize on the Gospels and say that the Savior came and removed from people, as evils, bodily blindness, deafness and paralysis of the limbs, and that he healed every disease and every sickness, giving goods in place of what had afflicted them before: bodily sight and hearing, and health and strength in general. And they will try to shame you by asking whether we will not admit that being possessed by a demon and being moonstruck are evils, and so, conversely, that being freed from them is good. The apostles too, by exercising gifts of healing and working miracles, did good to people by that very activity and freed them from evils. Those who say these things will go on to the age to come as well, saying that pain is evil, that is, the handing over of sinners to eternal fire. And if pain is evil, pleasure must be good. From what has been said, then, it is clear what arguments can thoroughly put to shame those who cannot refute the case made for three kinds of goods and three of evils according to Scripture. This deception has deceived not only believers who are admittedly simple, but also some who profess the wisdom that is according to Christ. They think the Creator's promises are of this sort, and that nothing is meant by the threats beyond what the letter shows.

To all who understand such things from the Scriptures in this way we must put a question: did the prophets keep the law, those against whom no sins are charged? Take Elijah, who owned so little that he did not even have bread of his own to eat, and for that reason was sent to a woman in Zarephath of Sidon. Or Elisha, who received from the Shunammite woman a very small lodging, a couch and a cheap lampstand, and who fell sick and died. Or Isaiah, who went naked and barefoot for three years. Or Jeremiah, who was thrown into a pit of mire and was mocked continually, so that he even prayed to live in a desert. Or John, who spent his time in the wilderness, ate nothing but locusts and wild honey, wore a leather belt around his waist, and was clothed in camel's hair. They will admit that these men kept the law. Then we will ask whether the things they consider goods belonged to these men who kept it. Since they cannot show this, they will be forced to say one of two things: either the promises said to be given to the godly are false, or, being true, they need a higher interpretation. And if they are forced to resort to allegory, their belief will be overturned that the law threatens the ungodly with bodily disease and what are thought to be external evils, or that it promises healthy bodies and abundance to those who have followed God. And how is it not foolish for people to take pride and boast in evils when they are in them? If afflictions are evils, and the Apostle says to boast in them, that would be foolish. But the Apostle is not foolish. So such trials, which exercise the saint, are not evils. Afflicted in every way, he is not crushed; perplexed, he is not forsaken; tried, he is not put to death; thought to be poor, he makes many rich; supposed to own nothing, he possesses all things. For the whole world of wealth belongs to the believer, but to the unbeliever not even an obol.

Furthermore, those who suppose that according to Scripture there are three kinds of goods, and clearly of evils too, must conclude that the righteous are always in many evils, since the prophecy is true that says, "Many are the afflictions of the righteous." [?] It is also worth reminding those who think such things are evils of what happened to Job. After he had borne most nobly the contests that beset him, the divine oracle says, "Do you think I dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?" If Job is shown to be righteous in no other way than through such things, how could we say that these were evils for him, when they were the causes of his righteousness being revealed? It would follow from this that not even the devil is an evil for the saint. At any rate, the devil was not an evil for Job, "since God works all things together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose." Moreover, we say it is against all evidence that the righteous will enjoy the literal blessings, the supposed goods found in the Scriptures. Much of what we learn on examining the history of the saints contradicts such interpretations. And it is senseless to suppose that the saint will be a lender to many nations, opening banks in every city, distracted with giving and receiving, and doing forbidden things. For "he did not lend his money at interest, and did not take bribes against the innocent; whoever does these things will never be shaken." And according to Ezekiel: "The saint did not lend his money at interest and for profit." To think that fever comes because of sins is a doctrine of extremely ignorant people, since the causes of such disease are often obvious: the surrounding air, or certain waters, or certain foods. And if health and wealth were prizes for the righteous, none of the ungodly ought to be healthy or rich. Rather, we must seek health as a certain condition of the soul, and wealth as that which, according to Solomon, is the ransom of the soul, when he says, "A man's own wealth is the ransom of his soul." And the poverty to be avoided is the kind of which it is written, "But the poor man does not withstand a threat." Further, we must understand wounds, bruises and diseases as what comes upon careless souls through vice. The prophet rebukes those who are in this state, saying, "From the feet to the head there is neither wound nor bruise nor festering sore; it is not possible to apply ointment, or oil, or bandages."

This is enough for those who are not wholly careless. Using it, they can gather for themselves the texts of Scripture that trouble them and apply themselves to an understanding worthy of the working of the Holy Spirit. But to silence those who think that these are the goods to be given to the saints and these the evils to be given to sinners, we must add this as well. Everything that exists for the sake of something else is lesser than that for whose sake it exists. For example, incisions, cauteries and plasters are used for the sake of health, and so they are lesser than health. Even if they are called goods as medical aids, we must understand that they are not the final goods of medicine but the means of producing them; the final good in medicine is the health of the body. So too, if these commandments are to be kept in order to obtain these goods, and the prizes are bodily and external, then good actions will be good not as ends but only as means of producing goods. Then the wealth they think Scripture promises, and bodily health, will be superior to justice, and even to holiness, piety and godliness, those great achievements of virtue. To accept this belongs to people who do not know the worth of virtue but prefer its material rewards. For of all things it is the most absurd to say that being rich and being healthy in body are superior to virtuous achievements. Because of these wretched doctrines, some have consistently accepted that after the resurrection, among the first promises, we shall eat foods of this kind and drink, and some even that we shall beget children. When these teachings reach the Gentiles as well, they will give Christianity a reputation for great simple-mindedness, since some who are strangers to the faith hold much better doctrines.

But we will now set out what appears to us from examining the sacred oracles. We were saying that we are content to say that goods and evils lie both in matters of choice and in things that do not depend on choice. Yet we did not count health, beauty, noble birth, good reputation and wealth among the goods that do not depend on choice, and as far as possible we tried to resolve, in summary, the points that cause difficulty. Now we must say what the goods are that do not depend on choice. For it is true that "Unless the Lord builds a house, those who build it labor in vain," and "Unless the Lord guards a city, the watchman stays awake in vain." Everyone who makes progress builds a house, and everyone who is perfect guards a city. But the work of the builder is in vain, and the guarding of the watchman is in vain, unless the Lord builds and the Lord guards. So there is a good outside our choice: the power of the Lord, which takes hold of the builder's work and builds together with one who cannot finish what is being built by himself. The same must be understood of the city that is guarded. Suppose I were to say that the good of farming, which produces the fruit, is a mixture of what is chosen, namely the farmer's skill, and what is not chosen, namely what comes from Providence through mild weather and a sufficient supply of rain. In the same way, the good of a rational being is a mixture of his own choice and the divine power that breathes together with the one who has chosen what is best. There is need both of our choice and of this divine co-breathing, which, as far as we are concerned, does not depend on choice, not only for becoming noble and good, but also for remaining in virtue once one has become noble and good. For even one who has been made perfect will fall if he becomes puffed up over his goodness and credits himself as its cause, rather than giving due glory to the one who has contributed far more to the acquiring and preserving of virtue. We consider some such cause to lie behind what Ezekiel says of the one who walked blameless in all his ways until iniquity was found in him, and behind what Isaiah says, that he fell from heaven: once he was the morning star, rising at dawn, but afterward he was crushed to the earth. For it is not only among the sons of men that, if someone is perfect but the wisdom that comes from God is absent, it is true that he will be counted as nothing. It is true also of the angelic order, of the principalities, and of every order that is divine insofar as God is present to it. Perhaps it was because the holy Apostle saw that our power of choice is far less than God's power in acquiring goods that he says the outcome "is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy." He does not mean that God shows mercy without our willing and running, but that willing and running are nothing compared with God's mercy. For that reason the credit for what is good should be given to God's mercy rather than to human willing and running.

We may seem to have digressed at length in examining these matters, but we are convinced that they are necessary for the verse "Many say, 'Who will show us good things?'" For, as far as possible, our discussion has set out and shown to the many who say "Who will show us good things?" what the goods are, and clearly also what the evils are, so that through ascetic practice and prayer we may acquire the goods and cast the evils out of our souls. But since in speech words are sometimes used in their proper sense and sometimes loosely, it is no wonder if we sometimes find the names "goods" and "evils" applied to the things that those who do not hold sound doctrines call bodily and external. For example, in Job: "If we received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear evil things?" And in Jeremiah: "Evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem." [?] For instead of saying, "If we have received from Providence such things as came to us kind and pleasant, shall we not readily bear what is bitter and painful?", it says, "If we received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear evil things?" And instead of saying, "By Providence such things happened to Jerusalem [?] so that its inhabitants might be disciplined," it is written, "Evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem." So those who understand the realities must not be fussy about names. Rather, they must grasp when these names are applied to things in their proper sense, and when they are used loosely because words are in short supply. And if the Savior healed such conditions and gave people health, sight and hearing, we must first of all seek the higher meaning of these accounts, since through these historical events the Word is shown to heal the passions of the soul. Yet in such cases it is not absurd to understand that what is reported as history also really happened. It happened to astonish the people of that time, so that those who were not persuaded by arguments of proof and teaching might be put to shame by the wondrous miracles and give their assent to the teacher.

"The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord," and so on. That God is light, John says in the Catholic Epistle: "God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all." He is also called fire, as Paul says in Hebrews: "For our God is a consuming fire." There Paul shows that he is the God of the Law and of the Gospel, that is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and for that reason our God. Even so, we must not think that the consuming fire is something other than the light, differing from it except in concept. The same thing happens with bodily light. One and the same substance is light insofar as it illuminates, and is a consuming fire insofar as it overpowers certain materials, burning and consuming them. In the same way God destroys what is worse and consumes wickedness, but he is light to those who are fit and pure in heart. Bodily light works together with those whose eyes are healthy, helping them to see both the light itself and the things perceived by the senses. In the same way God reaches the mind of each person by a certain power. If the mind he reaches is not veiled in any way, and its own keen sight has not been hindered by passions, God becomes the cause both of his being understood and of the mind he enlightens reaching the other intelligible things. It is no wonder if some people who are perceptive in certain arts or sciences, or very sharp at understanding certain ethical and logical problems, do not know God. We compare their intellect to an eye that gazes at anything rather than the sun and is never lifted up to contemplate its rays. But the sun's ray reaches the face of anyone who looks at it, and a person turned toward the sun cannot fail to share in it. In the same way we must understand that whoever contemplates the law of the divine word, having given his mind to understanding God, certainly participates in God. I think the Prophet shows this here when he says, "The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord." He means that a sign of the light in your countenance has reached us and been imprinted on us, and the very light of your countenance has been engraved on us. So whoever knows how to see the sign of God's light marked on us understands that it has then come to be in us. I think this secret is also shown in Exodus. As Moses spoke with God at greater length and was with him, his face was glorified, so that the children of Israel could not gaze at its glory, and for this reason the servant put on a veil to speak with the people. Every soul that is devoted to God, that has entered into his truth, which the many do not see, and has partaken of divinity, becomes more than the many can take in. So it is veiled when it guides those of lesser capacity, telling them what is suited to them. What is called the face of God enlightens the ruling faculty that is able to receive its rays and becomes the cause of knowledge. This is shown in the sixty-sixth psalm, which runs: "May God have pity on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us, so that your way may be known on earth, your salvation among all nations," and so on. Those who share in the light in this way, and can say in deed, "The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord," have the light in which they have shared. Because of it they suffer nothing at the time when those who need such remedies are punished. I think this is shown in the Psalms and in Ezekiel. In the Psalms it runs: "You have given those who fear you a sign, to flee from before the bow, so that your beloved ones may be delivered." In Ezekiel: "And the glory of the God of Israel, which was upon the cherubim, went up from them to the court of the house. And he called the man clothed in the long robe, who had the belt on his waist. And he said to him: Go through the middle of Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who groan and are grieved over all the iniquities committed in her midst. And to the others he said, while I listened: Go after him through the city and strike; let your eyes not spare, and have no pity. Kill old men and young men, virgins, infants and women, to utter destruction; but do not come near anyone who has the mark on him; and begin from my holy places." What is the sign that God has given to the devout? What is the mark placed on the foreheads of those who are zealous for the truth and groan over the transgressions committed among the people? Is it not the participation in divinity that reaches those who understand [?] soundly?

"You have put gladness in my heart," and so on. The sense of this verse agrees with what we said about the verse before it. When the light of the Lord's face is marked upon the saints, what else is there but a heart made glad? We take the heart to be the intellect, which is given gladness as it contemplates God and shares in his divinity. It is not the same thing for the heart to be gladdened and for the flesh to be gladdened. The heart is gladdened in contemplation, but the flesh is gladdened by material food and drink and by sexual union, while the heart grows dull and is hindered from its own good. So when it is said in these same Psalms, "Wine gladdens the heart of man, and bread strengthens the heart of man," we must understand the true bread, which gives the mind the richest nourishment, and the fruit of the true vine, which intoxicates as the best of drinks.

"From the fruit of their grain, wine and oil they have been multiplied," and so on. The Hebrew had "from the time." The Seventy also rendered it this way, so that the sense of the whole phrase is: "At the time when the crops of wheat and barley and all these pulses are harvested, they were multiplied." Those who receive their ration of grain in due season have been multiplied from the time of grain, because its timeliness helps them to increase. The same must be said about the wine that gladdens the heart of man.

"In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you, Lord, have made me dwell alone in hope," and so on. The psalm may be spoken in the person of Christ. In that case it refers to the majesty given him by the Father, which is beyond comparison, so that no one can share in the whole of his greatness, and it fits that he says, "You have made me dwell alone." If it is spoken in the person of the prophet, I think it shows how rare holiness is, especially in generations of sinners. So it was in the days of Elijah, who said: "Lord, they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars, and I alone am left." Perhaps whoever wins the prize and rises above those of his own generation will also say this phrase of the psalm. As for "in hope," if the Savior says it with reference to his incarnate dispensation, it is no wonder that, hoping for his own restoration, he says that God has made him dwell in hope. This fits the words: "Glorify me, Father, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed." The Savior can also say "alone" because of the time when all his disciples took offense and abandoned him. And even if it is a prophet who speaks, the meaning of "in hope" is clear, since every saint, because of love, hopes all things.
PSALM 5

"Give ear to my words, O Lord; understand my cry. Attend to the voice of my supplication, my King and my God," and so on. We must consider how great a spiritual voice one needs in order to call upon God's understanding, and words fitting to be addressed to the Lord, and a voice of supplication that is confident even of the Master's attention. No one ruled by sin will say to God, "My King"; and those whose god is the belly will not say "My God" to God.
"In the morning you will hear my voice," and so on. Let the one who has put off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light say these words.

"In the morning I will stand before you and will look; for you are not a God who wills lawlessness, nor shall an evildoer dwell beside you, nor shall the lawless abide before your eyes," and so on. As soon as the sun rises I will stand before you and will be in contemplation "that you are not a God who wills lawlessness, nor shall an evil man dwell beside you, nor shall the lawless abide before your eyes." For just as a sick man does not remain sick under the eyes of a physician who is able to heal him, so the lawless do not abide before the eyes of God.

"You have hated all who work lawlessness; you will destroy all who speak falsehood," and so on. Those who stumble in their way of life he has called workers of lawlessness, and these God hates; those who have fallen away from the truth, the heterodox, he has called speakers of falsehood, and these God will destroy. Note the difference between "you have hated" and "you will destroy": first, whether "you have hated" is worse than "you will destroy"; second, why he put the one in the past tense and the other in the future. "You will destroy all who speak falsehood": not those who have spoken, but those who speak falsehood. But if the Lord destroys these, and every man is a liar, then God destroys all, so that, having put off being men, they may become gods; for though they had become gods, and all sons of the Most High, they have become men. So God will destroy the heterodox in the age to come.
"The Lord abhors a man of blood and deceit," and so on. A man of blood is one born of blood, or one who is murderous.

"But I, in the abundance of your mercy, will enter your house; I will worship toward your holy temple in fear of you," and so on. Since the wicked and the lawless do not dwell beside you nor abide under your gaze, I, by your mercy, will enter your house. For so I will also be able to say: "In the morning I will stand before you, and you will look upon me." And since it is by no other means than your mercy that I will enter your house, I will worship you in spirit and in truth with great reverence, which is called fear of you, having come toward your holy temple. The temple and house of God is the holy and virtuous state, of which those who possess it speak with boldness: "But Christ as a son over his house, whose house we are." And they also address other believers in writing: "You are a holy temple, and your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God." For how is the one who keeps the word of Jesus, with whom the Son and the Father make their dwelling, not a house and temple of God? It is also possible to call the Church's mind and teaching the house of the Lord and his temple. This is shown from what is written to Timothy: "That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the living God." According to both interpretations, one enters the house and worships toward the holy temple of the Lord by the mercy of God rather than by one's own way of life and wisdom.

"Judge them, O God; let them fall from their counsels. According to the multitude of their ungodly deeds cast them out, for they have embittered you, O Lord," and so on. For one who sins it is more profitable to be judged by God than to be outside judgment. And to fall away from wicked counsels is no harm to the one who falls away, since he does not reach their wicked end; just as it is not good to fail to bring better counsels to their end. It is very gracefully done that he has not said from where God cast them out, so that it might not be clear to the many. But I think it is from their ungodly deeds, according to their multitude. For God does not drive anyone away from himself: "For those who remove themselves far from you," it says, "shall perish."

"Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies; make my way straight before you," and so on. Whoever resolves to think and act rightly has many opponents. For there are both men and demons who are envious, grieved at the good fortune of those who do well. Seeing this, the speaker here did not entrust to his own strength the fighting off of those who assail him, but besought God to stretch out a hand to him that would shelter him unharmed from so many and such great enemies, saying: You yourself, O Master, lead me in your righteousness; for so would my way be made straight before you.

"For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain. Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully," and so on. Since enemies hinder your way from being revealed before my eyes, make it straight before me yourself. For I know that in what they profess about the way they do not speak the truth, because there is no truth in their mouth, and their heart is vain. And everything uttered from their throat is dead, because it is an open grave. Moreover, their words are a kind of calculated sophistry.

"They shall rejoice forever, and you will dwell among them," and so on. An age is a natural system, comprising rational distinctions among bodies of various kinds, for the sake of the knowledge of God. "They shall rejoice forever," he says, because their dwelling too is eternal. "And all who love your name shall boast in you; for you will bless the righteous, O Lord," and so on. If those who love are better than those who fear, boasting belongs rather to those who love. And if there is some reasonable boasting also in the fear of the Lord, it is less than "they shall boast in you." Noah blesses Shem and Japheth; Melchizedek blesses Abraham, and Isaac Jacob, and Jacob the twelve, and Moses the tribes; but above all these, and after them, the Lord himself will bless the righteous, in keeping with "I myself who speak am here" and "Will you not go with us yourself?" "You have crowned us as with a shield of good pleasure," and so on. The shield and the crown of the righteous are one and the same, so that the one who is armed is crowned, and the one who is crowned is armed. This has something in common with "He will shield you with a crown of delight." The knowledge of God, then, insofar as it wards off enemies, is a shield of good pleasure; insofar as it makes one reign over the passions, it is called a crown. The knowledge of God is divided into two, practice and contemplation: the shield of good pleasure belongs to practice, the crown to contemplation. And the order has been kept: the shield comes before the crown, since practice also comes before contemplation.
PSALM 6

"For the end, in hymns, concerning the eighth; a psalm of David," and so on. The eleventh psalm is also "concerning the eighth." But the titles of this psalm and the eleventh differ, in that this one is "For the end, in hymns, concerning the eighth; a psalm of David," while that one is "For the end, concerning the eighth; a psalm of David." On the eighth, I think, wrath reproves and anger chastens.

"Lord, do not reprove me in your wrath, nor chasten me in your anger," and so on. Wrath is an impulse of the desire of a gentle soul, chiefly toward retribution [?]. So he says: Even if wrath reproves more sharply and anger chastens more swiftly, I, because of my weakness, beg your mercy, to be reproved and chastened by some other treatment that does not bring so much pain.

"Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled," and so on. Heal me, for I am sick in soul; for the joints of its bones are troubled, and the soul itself is greatly troubled.

"And you, Lord, how long?" and so on. This is said elliptically, in place of: How long will you not deliver my soul, nor save me according to your mercy, nor turn me back? The one who has no confidence of being saved by works will say: "Save me for your mercy's sake." After hearing that the Lord had taken away his sin, David, wrestling with temptations and afflictions and tasting the medicines, appeals to the physician to be released from the medicines.

"Turn, Lord, deliver my soul; save me for your mercy's sake," and so on. He puts two things here: turning, and delivering his soul. For this was what the righteous most earnestly sought. "Turn," that is: Restore me to intimacy with you. But also deliver my soul, since it is among enemies. You turned away because of my sins; turn back because of your love for mankind, having also handed me over to temptations for my chastening.

"For in death there is no one who remembers you; and in Hades who will confess to you?" and so on. The one who remembers God, who says, "I am the life," is not in death. It is not possible for one who is in death, God's last enemy, to remember you; therefore deliver me from it, so that I may remember you again. For this reason also those who sin before death do not remember God. Either no one in Hades will confess, or very few; for this is what is implied by this [?], and perhaps because of: "Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into Hades." Those who go down alive into Hades can remember God, since they are not in death, and can confess to him.

"I am weary with my groaning," and so on. The sons of Israel, groaning such a groan in Egypt, were heard. And Paul, saying, "We who are in this tent groan," does the same. Of the same kind is "I roared from the groaning of my heart." And it is not enough to groan; one must groan to the point of weariness. We may gracefully use this saying to exhort to chastity: "Every night I will wash my bed," declaring that "Every night I will wash my bed" is rightly said only by those who always keep themselves pure from intercourse; and these, devoting themselves to prayer, drench their couch with tears over sins committed long ago. That is why he said: "Blessed are those who weep now."

"My eye is troubled by wrath; I have grown old among all my enemies," and so on. Nothing so blinds the mind as wrath when it is stirred up. Because of this trouble of the eye, even one who thinks he sees the things of the mind sees not clearly but confusedly.
