"I have grown old" means: I have become old and full of years, spending my time among them in the life where they are; or: Among them I took on the old man with his deeds, "who is corrupted according to the desires of deceit."
"Depart from me, all you who work lawlessness," and so on. To work lawlessness always belongs to demons; to work it but not always, to men; never to work it, to angels.

"For the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer," and so on. The one who understands the blessedness of those who weep, and who weeps, will say these things to all who work lawlessness and are present with him, visible and invisible. First God hears the voice and the weeping, then the supplication, and then he receives the prayer.

"Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled," and so on. Shame brings the sinner to awareness of himself. Stop, he says, heaping reproaches on me; consider your own evils and be filled with shame and trouble. For the divine tribunal is just and fearsome.

"Let them be turned back and be greatly ashamed, and quickly," and so on. If we conquer, the powers that wrestle against us are put to shame, especially when a man is found to be stronger than they are and confounds and troubles them by his own wisdom. And perhaps he also turns them back in their shame, and the saint does this quickly.

By the same. You will understand these words as said also to the invisible enemies who contrived the plot against him, envious of his progress according to God, and who assailed him after his sin, in that they said: "There is no salvation for him in his God."
PSALM 7

"O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all who pursue me, and deliver me, lest like a lion he seize my soul," and so on. With each provocation to sin we are pursued by the one who works the provocation. Hence understand from this how many pursue man, from whom the Prophet prays to be delivered, since if he were not delivered his soul would be seized as by a lion. "O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is injustice in my hands," and so on. Toward forgiveness of wrongs [?]
By the same. "When I am lifted up," he says, "I will draw all to myself."
"Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end," and so on. When someone no longer sins, his wickedness is brought to an end; or else the wickedness of sinners is the devil.

"If you do not turn back," as far as "will come down," and so on. Perhaps these things are said about the devil without his being named. For besides these things he also travailed with injustice, and what follows, since he is wrath. But the Father of the one who said, "I am the life," does not prepare vessels of death in his bow; indeed he sets his bow in the cloud, so as not to bring a flood of water upon the earth. Therefore these things must be taken as said about the devil. And the fiery arrows belong to the evil one, which he has wrought for those who are burning and inflamed by passions.

By the same, on: "And in it he has prepared vessels of death," and so on. Vessels of death are unclean rational beings, or souls that have death in them; just as vessels of life are souls that have life. For so the Lord also called Paul a vessel of election. "Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived toil, and brought forth lawlessness," and so on. The one who is a lover not of God but of pleasure, in proportion to the pleasures he serves, conceives a single toil, continuous and without any interval, and travails with injustice and brings forth lawlessness. Conversely, the one who is a lover not of pleasure but of God, in proportion to the toils he takes on for the sake of virtue, conceives a good affection, joy, single and continuous and without any interval, and travails with righteousness and brings forth good order; and so he becomes a child of good order, hating every kind of lawlessness.

By the same, on the same. He brought forth lawlessness because he conceived toil and travailed with injustice. For this is the sequence of nature. Ahithophel travailed when he proposed his wicked counsel.

"He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the ditch he made. His toil will return upon his own head, and his injustice will come down upon his crown," and so on. Perhaps the pit is a place of punishment, into which, by God's providence, he who dug it will himself fall. The crown of his head is level with the rest of his body, for no part of him is above; that is why he is somewhere called a dragon. Fittingly, then, his injustice, which was lifted up and exalted against the knowledge of God, will be brought down and descend upon his crown.
PSALM 8

"For the end, concerning the winepresses; a psalm of David," and so on. In Psalms 80 and 83 too you will find the title "Concerning the winepresses." Alongside these let us take the passages about Noah planting a vine, and Jacob's blessing of Judah, "binding his colt to the vine"; and that of Issachar, who, seeing that rest was good and that the land was rich, put his shoulder to labor and became a farmer. And indeed Uzziah was a farmer, with vinedressers in the hill country. And the wife of every righteous man "is like a fruitful vine on the sides of his house," and becomes wine that gladdens the heart of man. And the Preacher planted vineyards and dug a winepress. And Solomon says: "And let your winepresses overflow with wine."
By the same. Winepresses are rational natures that have received the fruits of the spiritual vine.

"Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise," and so on. In Matthew, first those who went before the Savior, and also those who followed him, "cried out, saying: Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest." A little later it is written that when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things he did, and the children crying out in the temple and saying, "Hosanna to the Son of David," they were indignant and said to him: "Do you hear what these are saying? And Jesus says to them: Yes. Have you never read, Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes," and the rest. It seems, then, that Matthew calls these same crowds children, and the Savior calls them not simply children but infants and nursing babes, teaching us, through the words of the psalm that he cited allegorically, to interpret the psalm allegorically as well. You will inquire whether "house of David" and "Son of David" are the same. And if they are not the same, the text of Matthew has suffered a scribal error, since it ought to read either "to the house of David" both times or "to the Son of David" both times.

"Because of your enemies, to put down the enemy and avenger," and so on. By "enemy and avenger" understand the true Nebuchadnezzar. Christ put down the devil through fishermen, men without learning, infants in malice.

"For I will behold the heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded," and so on. "For I will behold the heavens." We know this thing clearly when we know its rationale and its cause as well. "The works of your fingers." You will inquire whether the works of God's fingers are different from the works of his whole hands, and whether the former are a part of the latter. "The moon and the stars, which you have founded." Why did he not name the sun? Perhaps because when someone is first being instructed, he understands the things of the night first, and only later, at some point, the things of the day.

"What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" and so on. If he says this marveling that the Lord remembers man and visits the son of man, it is clear that he visits by doing good. Note this because of "I will visit their lawless deeds with a rod, and their injustices with scourges," and because of "I will not visit your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery," and the like.

"You made him a little lower than the angels," and so on. For he too, being by nature capable of knowing you, does not fall very far short. For he is made like you, as far as is possible, by taking on holiness and virtue. And because of the image and likeness you assigned him rule over the mortal living creatures. Paul tells the Hebrews that these words were spoken about Christ. For he says: "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death."

"You crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands," and so on. It was from here that the Apostle too spoke of "the unfading crown of glory." And sometimes one who has been crowned with honor has not understood, as in "Man, being in honor, did not understand." He did not say "over your works," which I think are the things that are not seen. We, then, are first among the works of God's hands, that is, among the things that are not seen. These things are also understood of the time after the incarnation of our God and Savior; for man has been crowned with glory and honor: "For he raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places," as the Apostle says.

"You have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea," and so on. Where there are clean animals, sheep and oxen, he added "all"; but where unclean ones may also be included, as with the beasts of the field, "all" is not said. The same holds for the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea.
PSALM 9
"For the end, concerning the hidden things of the son, a psalm of David," etc. The hidden things are the ineffable knowledge of the mysteries concerning Christ, the true God.

"I will confess you, Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders. I will be glad and rejoice in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High," etc. Whoever loves with his whole heart can confess with his whole heart. "I will recount all your wonders," and what follows. Someone who can explain the marvels recorded in Scripture, which are truly wonderful, showing by what principle each came about and what it symbolizes, has done what the verse says. But to see this is the work of the Savior alone. And if creation, and everything that God has made, are also his wonders, it will appear all the more that this prayer is the Savior's. For who will recount all the wonders of the Father except the Lord? He recounts them to the perfect, who can understand such great wonders, and of whom it will rather be said: "Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect." — "I will be glad and rejoice": he asks those who are glad about certain things whether their gladness is in God, so that they may either continue in that gladness or give it up. And whoever has gone up the high mountain, Zion, and exalts him, sings praise to the name of the Most High.

"When my enemy is turned back, they will grow weak and perish from your presence," etc. He has not said beforehand who it is that will grow weak and perish from the face of God (since "the face of the Lord is against those who do evil"), but has left it to us to understand. When the enemy who advances in wickedness is brought to nothing and backs away because he is being hindered, then those who are strong in wickedness will grow weak. Then, insofar as they sin, they will perish, and it is the face of God that works this in them. For once it is perceived, it does away with earthly things.
"You have sat upon a throne, you who judge righteousness," etc. The throne of God is Christ, and the throne of Christ is the incorporeal nature.

"You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly perished; you blotted out their name," etc. "You rebuked" signifies correction, as is clear from: "Reprove, exhort, rebuke." — "You blotted out his name." God blotted out the name of Abram by making him Abraham, and that of Sarai by calling her Sarah, and that of Simon by naming him Peter. So it follows that the name of those whom he rebuked should be blotted out, especially since there follows: "Proclaim among the nations his doings, for he who requires their blood has remembered." Note also that it does not say, "You blotted out their name from the book of the living" (for the nations had not been written in the book of the living). Rather, in keeping with the bonds of debt held against them, it means the book of debtors, or the book of the dead, kept by the steward of injustice, who presumably registers the dead and writes them down in the earth. For the Savior writes the names of the disciples in heaven.
By the same. If "name" here signifies an evil condition, and he blotted out the sinner's name, then he blotted out his very worst condition.
"And let those who know your name hope in you, for you have not forsaken those who seek you, Lord," etc. Those who seek the Lord, and not those who have been forsaken by him, have known his name.

"Sing praise to the Lord who dwells in Zion," etc. He sings praise who has Christ within himself. The prophet said this according to the ancient belief of the Jews. Yet there is also an intelligible and heavenly Zion. And God dwells in every soul that is a Zion (the name means "watchtower"), one that continually watches for divine things and pictures them to itself. He also requires the blood of the nations from those who killed them, and he remembers them by raising them up. So the verse "their memorial perished with a noise" will be applied to the swords. But he remembers those for whom he became a refuge.

"Proclaim among the nations his doings," etc. What doings? All that Christ told the disciples of John the Baptist: "Go and tell what you have seen: the blind see again, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised." These, then, are the doings worthy of God, and the apostles proclaimed them to the nations. They also proclaimed that immortality comes through death, salvation through the cross, and resurrection through burial, and that the devil, who put us to death, has himself been put to death.

"You who lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion," etc. The gates of death are the sins that lead to death. Whoever does not even consider committing them is lifted up from them, and he alone can proclaim all the praises of the Lord in the gates of the daughter of Zion, which are the virtues.

"The nations are stuck fast in the corruption they made; in this very snare that they hid their foot was caught. The Lord is known by executing judgments," etc. The nations are stuck fast, clearly as in mud, that is, in the body, because of the corruption they made. And their foot was caught, meaning, of course, the spiritual foot. And the Lord is known, since when judgment comes upon them they will know him who judges in righteousness.

"Let sinners be turned back into Hades," etc. As paradise is the dwelling of the righteous, so Hades is the place of punishment for sinners. Let them be shut in, he says, so that they may not see the soul of Jesus descending and ascending, since they are turned back inside. For those who awaited it were confined in Hades, yet looked outward, as it were. First came the prophets, then all the rest of the righteous; or else first the sinners among us, then the nations.

"The endurance of the poor shall not perish forever," etc. Just as the Spirit is not quenched, so endurance does not perish. For "the Lord is the Spirit," and "the Lord is my endurance." So too Christ is formed in the Galatians, though he himself is without form. In the same way he is said here to sleep: "Awake, why do you sleep?"

"Arise, Lord, let not man prevail," etc. So to the one who says, "My strength," you will say that it is now God who is made strong in the holy one [?], once that person's human thoughts and impulses have been removed.
PSALM 10.
(According to the Hebrew.)

"Why, Lord, have you stood far off?" etc. One might answer the person who is perplexed by this: "Behold, those who remove themselves far from you will perish"; and "I am a God near at hand, and not a God far off," says the Lord in the prophets. When you do not help those who are wronged, you seem not to be present to what is happening; you seem rather to stand far off and not even see. This increases the wickedness of the wicked, but it inflames your poor one and casts him into despondency.

"For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul," etc. Some people who sin often prosper in the world. The Apostle said this too: "Evil people and impostors will go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived." And in another psalm we sing: "These are sinners, and, prospering forever, they have taken hold of riches." So sinners and the unjust are praised both by themselves and by their flatterers and hangers-on, and being blessed in this way they are moved further into sin.

"According to the greatness of his wrath he will not seek," etc. Who? The Lord, or the sinner? Perhaps the sinner. For he does not inquire about the wrath of God, nor consider that he has a multitude of sins. That is why he sins in multitude.
"His ways are profaned at all times," etc. The righteous man blesses the Lord at all times, but the sinner profanes his ways at all times. "Are profaned" means "are sunk in wickedness."

"He will gain mastery over all his enemies," etc. Some temptations are brought on through the body, some through the soul, and some through external things. Some cause blows, tortures, persecutions and imprisonments. Others are impure thoughts that give birth to sin, and false doctrines. Others involve loss of property, bereavement of children, and the taking away of wives. From these it is clear that Satan has gained mastery over every righteous person. For if Satan will gain mastery over all his enemies, and all the righteous are his enemies, then he will gain mastery over them all. Clearly, though, he will not master them in everything, but only in some respect; for Christ alone committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. Perhaps divine Scripture is stating his intention, which is to accomplish what is impossible, since "they devised plans which they cannot establish." For in Job too the devil says falsely, "Having gone around the earth and walked about under heaven, I am here," even though he had not persuaded Job to do anything wrong.

By the same. If those who make progress do so by lessening their vice, then those who have acquired a perfect habit of righteousness are called righteous, and so are those who progress without hindrance. For "the righteous man," it says, "is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech." Yet if he is righteous, how is he an accuser? And if he is an accuser, he is certainly not perfectly righteous. "Instruct a righteous man, and he will increase in receiving." So it is rightly said that the devil gains mastery over all his enemies. This clearly does not mean the perfect, but those who are striving toward perfection. For if hatred toward Satan were not both imperfect and perfect, David would not have said, "I hated them with a perfect hatred; they became my enemies."

"His mouth is full of cursing, and of bitterness and deceit," etc. The mouth of the wicked offers nothing useful, only what brings toil and trouble to those who receive it. And the mouths of other kinds of people are full as well: of cursing in those who speak evil of the Creator, of reviling in revilers, of bitterness in the hot-tempered, and of deceit in the deceitful.

By the same. He who has fallen from holiness and led himself far away from truth and blessing has a mouth full of cursing, because of what he says as he tries to bring those he deceives under punishment and curse. His speech is not only deceitful but also very clever; therefore, along with cursing, it is full of bitterness and deceit.

"He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places," etc. The devil sits within those who have the wealth of ignorance and injustice. But in those who possess knowledge and virtue the holy powers find rest. These powers are symbolized by the birds of the air nesting in the branches of the mustard plant, which signifies the kingdom of heaven that is present in us potentially.
but the wrongdoers too will cease from doing evil, and those who are wronged will cease from suffering.
PSALM 10.

"For behold, the sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready arrows in the quiver, to shoot down the upright in heart in the moonless dark," etc. The sinners, he says, are not content with their own destruction. Drawing their sins along as with a long rope, they make war on the people of God and try to shoot them down with the venom of their wickedness. Envying such great purity in their ruling faculty, they cast darkness at them, as cuttlefish do their ink. And they do this after removing from themselves the natural and rightly ordered notions that God had established.

By the same. The bow is an impure mind. "I," he says, "trust in the Lord." Those waging war are sinners. Who, then, with God as his helper and only sinners as his enemies, would be afraid and run away? "They have made ready arrows in the quiver." An arrow is a passionate thought, and the quiver is a thoroughly wicked habit filled with impure thoughts. These are understood spiritually of demons waging war, but they could also be understood literally of visible enemies. "In the moonless dark." The moonless dark is the ignorance of a rational soul. He says that they lie in ambush on a moonless night to show how secret their plot is. He calls himself and those with him upright in heart. He is not boasting, but showing his own intention, and that he had done nothing to harm Saul.

"The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his throne is in heaven. His eyes look upon the poor, his eyelids examine the sons of men," etc. God dwells in a holy and heavenly understanding and reigns there in a heavenly and divine way. His watchful powers guard the poor. Being good, he examines our affairs with his eyelids, not with his eyes, so as not to scrutinize all our sins, for that would be unbearable for human beings. But with his eyes he looks on the poor, bestowing his kindness generously even if there is only one poor person. Meanwhile he holds back the punishments of the many, whose sins contain much that is hidden. In God's examination the good deeds that have been done will be openly displayed. For "we must all appear before his judgment seat, so that each may receive what is due for the things done in the body, whether good or evil."

By the same. Let us become poor, so that the eyes of the Lord may look upon us. If the rich are not poor, the Lord does not look upon the rich. With his eyes he looks on the poor, bestowing his kindness generously even if there is only one person in poverty.
"Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?" etc. Pharaoh also says, "I do not know the Lord," just like the one who says, "Who is lord over us?"

"Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says the Lord," etc. Paul spoke in the same way: "Wretched man that I am"; and "as poor, yet making many rich"; and "to this very hour we hunger," and what follows; and "we who are in this tent groan."

By the same. In another sense too, the poor groan because they cannot bear the tyranny of the arrogant. Therefore the Lord says: "I will arise, so as to set my counsel in salvation. I will speak boldly in it" against the proud, and I will free the needy from misery. He rises at the time of his coming and arrives among us, so that salvation might be revealed for those who have been set free from misery and groaning. So Paul, after saying, "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" adds, "I thank God through Jesus Christ." For he showed that it is the Lord who delivers the one in misery. That is why the one who now says, "Now I will arise," had a body of death. They say that the "poor" man is one who has fallen from wealth, and the "needy" man is one who earns his living by toil. Scripture says, "The rich have become poor," and "We have become very poor"; and of the Savior, "who though he was rich became poor for our sake, so that" we "might become rich by his poverty." It speaks of the groaning of the needy because they are always groaning over their toil. "I will set in salvation" means "I will appoint and make." Compare "whom he appointed heir of all things"; and likewise "God has set in the Church first apostles," and what follows; and the words to the elders of the Church: "The Holy Spirit has set you as overseers to shepherd the Church." In each case it signifies being appointed and made.

"I will set in salvation, I will speak boldly in it," etc. One who lays up treasure in heaven, having been set in salvation, says this: "I will speak boldly in it"; for his conscience does not condemn him.

"The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried in the fire, tested for the earth, purified seven times," etc. Even if those who are not of Christ's portion have fine words, those words are not pure, since they are mixed up with countless falsehoods. Only the words of the Lord are pure, with no falsehood mixed into them. They are pure as silver is pure when it has been tested and refined by smelting. Therefore one must not doubt what they signify.
PSALM 12.

"How long, Lord, will you forget me—to the end?" etc. Perhaps he is saying that God has forgotten him only until the end, and not simply forgotten him. And in another psalm she [?] is called forgotten. "How long will you turn your face away from me?" This face the angels behold continually. For when God reveals himself to one who is able to receive the sight of his face, he will stop turning it away from him and hiding his face. He once did this in the case of Moses too, sparing him for as long as he was a man. God turns his face away out of care for us when we act unworthily of his commandments. He does this in order to draw us to himself. Since the Son is the face of the Father, the psalmist asks that his incarnation come about more quickly, and that is why he used such an expression.

"How long shall I take counsels in my soul?" etc. A person first forms many counsels in his soul, and then at last the great counsel above them all, the counsel of God, whose spirit rested upon the rod from Jesse.

"Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death," etc. "Kindle for yourselves the light of knowledge." Calamities surround me like darkness. If you do not drive away the darkness of my despondency, but put off your help, my sleep will be turned into death, because grief will have completely overpowered my reason.

"Lest my enemy ever say, 'I have prevailed against him.'" As often as we sin, the enemy says this: "I have prevailed against him. Those who afflict me will exult if I am shaken." The angels rejoice over those who repent, while the demons exult over those who sin. For the angels love virtue, and the demons love vice. They will be full of exultation and gladness if they only see me fallen from my hope in you and in despair.

By the same. Even if I do not fall altogether but am only shaken, those who afflict me will exult, says the prophet. And as the prophet says in the seventy-second psalm: "But as for me, my feet were almost shaken."

By the same. For they gloat over those who fall, when they ought to grieve. But I shall not suffer this, by your mercy. For I await your salvation, and anyone who has experienced God's salvation rejoices in it. This can also be a prophecy about Christ. For when he came to save the world, he both brought light and overthrew the one who arrogantly gloated over those who were tottering. He looked upon us and came to dwell among us. And the one who has received such blessings offers a hymn of victory, saying: "I will sing to the Lord who has dealt bountifully with me, and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High." He has learned by experience what the Lord says to those who pray rightly: "While you are still speaking I will say, Here I am." He tells those with him that he has obtained what he wanted, and so he sings hymns. We too must sing for each benefit by contemplating it, and must add action to our psalm-singing.
"But I have hoped in your mercy; my heart shall exult in your salvation," etc. They gloat over my fall and expect to exult, but I have hoped in you and in your mercy.

"I will sing to the Lord who has dealt bountifully with me, and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High," etc. Let the one who has been blessed sing, and let the one who is cheerful sing praise. For it says: "Is anyone among you cheerful? Let him sing praise." In the time to come, too, I will keep the greatness of this blessing unforgotten in my soul.
PSALM 13.

"The fool has said in his heart, 'There is no God.' They are corrupt and have become abominable in their practices," etc. If they are corrupted in their practices, then it is not the bad thought that corrupts a person, but what it produces, which is wickedness. Having said from the disposition of their heart that there is no God, they went on to live as godless people, and their life was corrupt and full of every kind of uncleanness.
"All have turned aside, together they have become useless," etc. Those who say, "We are useless servants," are in effect saying, "We have become useless."

"Who will give the salvation of Israel out of Zion?" etc. "The deliverer will come out of Zion, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob." If the Savior comes out of Zion, and he came forth from the Father and arrived, then Zion here is a symbol of the Father. The psalmist speaks not only of the salvation that came to the people in the time of Hezekiah, but also of the saving appearance of our Savior from there, which came about many ages later. For since all had turned aside, the one who could forgive sins and save had to come. "Out of Zion," because he is of the seed of Israel, and because the one who was to come came out of Zion, as it is written. "When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people." Captivity is the involuntary passage from knowledge and virtue to ignorance and vice. "Jacob will exult, and Israel will be glad." The one who has acquired practical dispassion exults, and the one who has been counted worthy of gnostic contemplation is glad.

By the same. Countless evils held sway over the world, and the Holy Spirit, aware of the only one who could bring help, says: "Who will give the salvation of Israel out of Zion?" For neither Moses, nor Elijah, nor Isaiah, nor the rest of the prophets had given it; all the works of the law were too weak for such a task. A physician was needed, one able to heal all things, not by skill or by any work, but by the power of the word. So the Holy Spirit prays that he may come.

By the same. In the books of the Old Testament we are taught that our Lord Jesus Christ is called "the salvation," and he was announced to the nations by promise under the very name of "the salvation." For Isaiah says: "And the Lord will reveal his holy arm before all the nations, and all the ends of the earth will see the salvation that comes from our God." And again in the Psalms it is said: "The Lord has made known his salvation; before the nations he has revealed his righteousness." And again: "Show us your mercy, Lord, and grant us your salvation."
PSALM 14.

"Lord, who shall sojourn in your tent, and who shall dwell on your holy mountain?" and so on. "My soul has long been a sojourner (21)," he says elsewhere, teaching that one sojourns through many places until one comes to the holy mountain of God.

Of the same. The holy mountain (22) is the knowledge of Christ, which is the contemplation of the things that have come to be. He calls Jerusalem the holy mountain. And so, having asked, he also receives the answer.

"He who walks blameless and works righteousness, who speaks truth in his heart," and so on. "Walking (23) blameless": you will strive after this once you have understood what is said of Abraham, that he went "as the Lord had spoken to him." For he has spoken the same things to us too in the holy Scriptures, and if we understand them and do them, we have heard God and have gone as he spoke to us. "And works righteousness." Applying this pattern, you will say: working temperance, likewise courage, likewise prudence, likewise piety, likewise wisdom, and the remaining virtues. This is also what it means to work one's own land, so as to be filled with bread. But Cain, when he ought to have worked righteousness, or one of the virtues, or his own land, worked the land that was not his own.
Of the same. He means the one who, in the inner (24) man and in the outer, is free of all wickedness and every blemish, and pursues every virtue.

"Who has not deceived with his tongue, nor done evil to his neighbor," and so on. As the servants (25) of Satan do, when they disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. "And has not done evil to his neighbor." If not all men are neighbors, the wording does not forbid doing evil to those who are not neighbors. The same holds for "He who swears to his neighbor and does not break his word." "And has not taken up a reproach against those nearest him." One who lives blamelessly does not take up reproaches against those nearest him; this is the one who has not mocked his neighbor in misfortune, nor rejoiced at another's fall, but has grieved with him; or the one who has not reproached the one nearest him, as the Pharisee did the tax collector; or the one who has not been reproached on account of those nearest him, as Eli was on account of his children; or simply the one who lives blamelessly.
PSALM 15

"Keep me, Lord, for in you I have hoped. I said to the Lord, You are my Lord, for you have no need of my goods," and so on. He says "Keep me" as though enemies (26) were pressing upon him. And Jesus says in the prophet: He who hopes in the Lord and in nothing else is kept by him. But no one who sins can make these words true. For being a slave of the sin he commits, he cannot serve God. But the one who has set up a monument to the practical and contemplative life cries out: "I said to the Lord, You are my Lord," and from your own gifts I bring you gifts, not as to one in need. For none of the heretics will speak truly in saying this. And these words are to be offered not only of things brought in a bodily way, but also of things offered spiritually. For even if we offer virtues in sacred service, even if we offer our own bodies through complete chastity, we know that God accepts this not for his own benefit, but so that he may give us the goods of heaven when we ask for them.

Of the same. If all virtues (27) are goods, and knowledge has need of the virtues, then knowledge has need of all goods. And perhaps the indifferent things are here called "goods," whose right use makes us good, and not God. "For if," says Job, "we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear the evil?" For there he called possessions "goods," which become good through right use.

"For the saints who are in his land he has made all his wills wonderful among them. Their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they made haste," and so on. The sinner (28) is outside the land of God, and to him he has not shown his wonders. Christ will say of the perfect who are formed after his likeness: All my wills are in them. The infirmities of those from the Gentiles were indeed multiplied, but they made haste, changing through repentance. You will inquire whether these were in some sense once saints dwelling in the land of God, before their iniquities were multiplied; or whether some of them are Israel, in whom the wills of God once were; or whether the saints, having their citizenship in heaven, thus dwell in his land even while they are still in this land. The wills of God are the virtues in their several kinds, as in: "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my wills." These God makes wonderful in his saints, who practice the virtues better than other men; for apostles, prophets and martyrs excelled beyond comparison in courage, Joseph and Susanna in chastity, and likewise in the other virtues. And one who is thus made wonderful is ashamed of his own weakness, falling far short of the divine strength. And the infirmities, lasting only until they are recognized, quickly depart, because the saints are strengthened by Christ and say: "In God we shall do valiantly."

"I will not gather their assemblies out of blood, nor will I remember their names with my lips," and so on. These words (29) plainly belong to one greater than the many, and to none other than Christ; for when he gathers, he does not gather assemblies out of blood, nor does he any longer remember names out of blood. Or thus: Not like the Greeks and the Jews will I too pour libations of blood. For another translator rendered it this way: "I will not pour their libations of blood"; rather, I will hand on new mysteries to all, and a bloodless sacrifice; nor will I remember their old names, for they were called profane and idol-worshippers; but I will grant them to be called the pious and the holy. Or thus as well: He does not say absolutely that he will not gather their assemblies, but "out of blood"; nor that he will not remember their names absolutely, but "with my lips." Perhaps, then, since there are some who gather assemblies out of blood, shedding it by harming those who are gathered, he, by benefiting—or rather, by giving life to—those who are called, gathers them not out of blood but out of immortality, remembering their names not superficially but from a disposition that has depth, not by speech but by deep understanding. Or: Even though many saints were killed, the assemblies are not in their blood, but in the one blood of Christ the Lamb.

"The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are the one who restores my inheritance to me," and so on. The inheritance of rational (30) nature is the contemplation of the ages that have been and that will be; the inheritance of Christ is the knowledge of God. Christ says these things as high priest, whose portion is the Lord. If the Lord is the portion of the cup, or of him whose [?] the Lord is, then the portion of Christ's inheritance is the Father, which remained to him, while the rest of the inheritance is the people restored to him from God. Both things can also be said of the Father, including that he restores the inheritance to himself after the self-emptying. Or: Having risen above the world in your disposition, what portion would you have except the Lord? For it belongs to one who renounces everything to say: "God is my portion forever." The Lord also becomes bread, providing teaching and strengthening the heart of the one who eats; and a cup, in the contemplation of the truth, providing the gladness of knowledge to the one who drinks by giving his assent. This the true vine supplies, so that the one who has drunk says in thanksgiving: "You have put gladness in my heart."

"The measuring lines have fallen for me in the finest places; for indeed my inheritance is most excellent to me," and so on. If the line (31) is a measure, how is it written in the Gospel according to John, "For God does not give the Spirit by measure," and, "I will pour out of my Spirit"? Perhaps the measure is not named with reference to the knowledge itself, but with reference to the one who receives it, since he cannot take in more. For rain itself is without measure, but it is measured in the vessels that receive it. And there was allotted to me, he says, a land as if by measure, with which I am content, and that through the finest of my men, Joshua and Caleb.
Of the same. Thus Israel became (32) the measured portion of his inheritance. And he says these things because he is well pleased with his own inheritance as the best.

"I will bless the Lord who gave me understanding; moreover, even until night my kidneys instructed me," and so on. One blesses the Lord (33) when an insight has arisen in the mind. For from his face come knowledge and understanding. In this way the Lord gives understanding to one who keeps the commandments. He speaks of the kidneys that are named together with the heart in: "God who tests hearts and kidneys." These, perfected through understanding, instruct the one who attends to them, providing the light of knowledge until the night of ignorance is dispelled. And if night also signifies the deeper meanings, inasmuch as the mystical word is called dark, it is clear that the kidneys instruct until this night, making plain what is hidden and enigmatic. The term is borrowed from the kidneys, in which seed and seminal powers are formed, supplying the generative passages. So in the soul too there are certain thoughts analogous to seeds, corresponding to the inner offspring in good deeds and true contemplations. And the bodily kidneys also instruct the one who has perfect chastity, being restrained by temperate reason, even into the night, from emitting bodily seed.

"Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced," and so on. That is, my mind (34). For it is the custom of divine Scripture to use "heart" for the mind, as in: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation." It is the mind that believes, and it also discerns words, according to Job. Here he calls the gift of the Holy Spirit "tongue." For he says to the Lord, "my glory, and the one who lifts up my head." And "the Lord is the Spirit," according to the Apostle. I was glad, he says, in the hope of the resurrection after the third day. For the tongue exults as though it were alive, and rejoices as it speaks, and makes others exult. "And moreover my flesh will dwell in hope." "My flesh" means my living, ensouled being. So too Job says: "You clothed me with flesh and meat."

"Nor will you let your holy one see decay," and so on. Peter in the Acts (35) of the Apostles applies this to Christ. Christ accepted corruption in his body, as the Melodist also says: "Having accepted the corruption of death, you kept your body untouched by decay." Yet he did not undergo decay or rotting. Corruption is blows and wounds; decay is for the body to [?] flow apart and be sent back into each of the elements of which it is composed; rotting is for one nature to suffer at the hands of another nature, as wool from the moth, and flesh, grain and wood from worms.
PSALM 16

"Hear, Lord, my righteousness; attend to my plea; give ear to my prayer, which comes not from deceitful lips," and so on. Every righteous (37) person is a servant of righteousness; but God alone is the righteous Master of righteousness. David, then, conscious that he was pure of all deceit, says these things in prayer with boldness toward God.

"Let my judgment come forth from your face," and so on. If the Father has given all judgment (38) to the Son, and judgment comes forth from his face, then it comes from the Son; for Christ is the image of the Father. Of the same. Since "he who believes (39) in me," says the Lord, "is not judged," the judgment of the believer comes forth from the face of God.
"Let my eyes behold what is upright," and so on. He prays for the restoration (40) of all things, that there may no longer be any crookedness, with God walking contrary to those who sin.

"You have tested my heart, you have visited me by night; you have tried me by fire, and no injustice was found in me. That my mouth may not speak the works of men; because of the words of your lips I have kept to hard ways," and so on. Note (41) that "you have visited" is not used here of punishments. Again, one should know that the devil tries by fire in the opposite way to God. But when God tries by fire, either he finds the injustice already present, or, since it is not already present, he does not find it. "The works of men" stands for "about the works of men." Or the works of men are the words that are not divine, which men have produced by their own devising.

Of the same. By night he means affliction (42), in which the soul is darkened. One is tested by enduring hardships nobly. And he called the hardships night because of the darkness that comes from despondency. Or he mentioned night because it was at night that, having caught Saul asleep and in his power, he spared him, not only refraining from killing him himself, but also stopping those who wanted to kill him.

Of the same. "Enter through the narrow (43) gate and the hard way," that is, the practical life, which, though for now it seems to bring pain and not joy, afterward yields the fruits of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

"I cried out, for you heard me, O God. Incline your ear to me, and hear my words. Make your mercies wonderful, you who save those who hope in you," and so on. As though heard (44) before we prayed, we have cried out as we prayed. Or, if crying out well means not saying small and contemptible things, then having prayed for great things and obtained them, we have cried out, since we have cried out in this way. Many mercies come from God which happen through some ordinary human sequence of events, and are not made wonderful by the one who performs them. Few are those that are made wonderful, when they happen unexpectedly and miraculously. For example, let those who receive mercy be people freed from fevers and from leprosy. If they are healed by way of medicine, they have received mercy from God, but not as though God were making his mercies wonderful for them; but if they are freed from fever at the touch of Jesus as he rebukes it (so that they can at once take up the activities of those who are healthy and strong), or from leprosy as he touches them and says, "I will; be clean," then it is as though God were making his mercies wonderful toward such people.

"From those who resist your right hand, keep me as the apple of the eye," and so on. Whoever resists (45) Christ resists the right hand of God. You will inquire whether it is good to resist the left. The most clear-sighted person, being like the pupil of the eye in the whole body of Christ, will say this; to touch him is to touch the pupil of the eye. And whoever sees the multitude of those resisting the eye of the soul, let him run to God, asking to be rescued by the divine shelter, as by a shield, from what are, as it were, arrows being shot at him, so that they may not make him wretched. And since the right hand of the Lord is the only-begotten Son of God, and intelligible and invisible enemies resist it, he asks that his own mind remain unharmed by them; and these are the words of a man enlightened in the eyes of the soul.

"In the shelter of your wings you will shelter me, from the face of the ungodly who have made me wretched," and so on. The righteous man is made wretched by the (46) ungodly and is pitied as wretched, sometimes even pitied as a fool; but then the one who is worthy is sheltered in the shelter of God's wings, so that he is not shaken by being called wretched.

"My enemies have surrounded my soul. They have shut in their fat; their mouth has spoken arrogance," and so on. When we perceive (47) worse thoughts surrounding our soul, then we say: "My enemies have surrounded my soul"; and if they make our mind dull and gross, "they have shut in their fat." It depicts a siege and the savagery of the enemies, who have shut in their fat because of their attachment to matter. For they are wholly fleshly through and through.

Of the same. Fat in the intelligible sense (48) is the grossness that comes upon the ruling faculty from wickedness. By fat he seems to me to mean goodwill and brotherly love; and he says that they shut out all natural compassion, giving no room to thoughts of brotherly love. Some, however, have taken fat to mean prosperity and good health.

"Having cast me out, they have now surrounded me; they have set their eyes to bend down to the earth," and so on. The enemies do not surround (49) those who are inside, for they cannot, but only once they have cast them out from within. And they set their own eyes, he says, on turning me aside from heaven to the earth, that is, to matter. Those who seek to destroy surround to do harm—those who look toward the earth and consider only temporal things; and by their lawlessness they turn aside from the straight way, having no wish for it.

Of the same. The demons surround (50) the one whom they cast out of virtue; therefore it is well said: "If the spirit of the ruler rises up against you, do not leave your place"; and, "Give no place to the evil one"; as if he were saying: If a spirit of fornication rises up against you, do not leave your chastity; and if a spirit of hatred rises up against you, do not leave your love. But one must consider whether it is the one who has fallen from all the virtues who is surrounded, or from many, or from one. If the vices entail one another, as the virtues do, then the one who has fallen from one virtue is surrounded; but if the vices do not entail one another, it is not the one cast out of one virtue who is surrounded, but the one cast out of all. Or perhaps, from whatever virtue one falls, one is surrounded by the vice opposed to it.

"They seized me like a lion ready for prey, and like a young lion lurking in hiding places," and so on. For in hidden (51) places, unforeseen by us, the enemies lay their ambushes against us like a young lion.

Of the same. Through the impure (52) thought the lion who opposes us seizes our mind. Having cast off the rational part of their nature, they imitate beasts that crave food, look about for it, and spring upon it suddenly.

"Arise, Lord, go before them and trip them up; rescue my soul from the ungodly, your sword from the enemies of your hand," and so on. The enemies of God's hand sometimes take up (53) his sword against us. So he prays to God that this sword be rescued and taken away from the enemies.

Of the same. Just as Job (54) calls the power that struck him the hand of God—for he says, "Let not your hand toss me about"—so also David calls the enemies of God's beneficent hand the sword of God. The beneficent hand is the holy angels, through whom God exercises providence over the world; opposed to them are the demons, who do not want every man to come to the knowledge of the truth. The hand of God is the only-begotten Son; the sword is the strength, the power, the authority. Every righteous soul that draws sinners from ungodliness to godliness is a sword of God sharpened against the spirits of wickedness. This sword of yours, then, rescue from your enemies who oppose faith in the Only-begotten.

"Lord, from the few, from the earth, divide them in their life; and their belly was filled with your hidden things," and so on. Divide them, so that (55) they may not be of one mind. "And their belly was filled with your hidden things." When the enemies of the Gospel, in their philosophizing, at times state great and well-aimed doctrines, you will say to God: "Their belly was filled with your hidden things"—things they perhaps bring up because they knew them; and having only dim outlines of them, they made them brilliant by their disciplined study and inquiry. Another translator says: "Their portion is among the living." For the whole inheritance of God's enemies is in the present life, in which they have also been filled with every luxury.

"They were satisfied with sons, and left what remained to their infants," and so on. They were filled with their own offspring (56), and have left the remnants of them to their own infants. For this is also included among the curses of Leviticus: "You shall eat the flesh of your sons."

Of the same. "Of sons" stands for (57) "of uncleanness." Not only did they themselves become unclean, but they also passed their uncleanness on to their children. For it is not the mark of the perfect to prefer unclean things to clean.

"But I shall appear in righteousness before your face; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears," and so on. In righteousness (58) and every virtue the saint will appear before the face of God, but no unrighteous person will appear there. And the blessed satisfaction will come when the glory of God appears and is made clear. For this is the food that fills every [?] of the soul; whoever hungers and has a healthy appetite will be satisfied, being filled with it.
PSALM 17

I will love you, O Lord, my strength. The Lord is my firmament, my refuge and my deliverer; my God is my helper, and I will hope in him. He is my protector, the horn of my salvation and my defender, etc. The Lord is the very strength and the very firmness of the saints. So no one who is not in the Lord is strong or firm. But firm is not the same as hard, nor is strength the same as the convulsive strainings of frenzy.

By the same. We recognize like through like: love through love, and righteousness through the righteous. For this is the great and first commandment. And one who loves also serves the one he loves. He calls God his strength because God rescued him from all his enemies, both visible and spiritual.
By the same. He called God his firmament because God strengthened him against his enemies; his refuge because God became a wall for him; his deliverer because God redeemed him.
By the same. He called God his helper because God came to his aid.

By the same. He called God his protector because God fought in front of him. He called him the horn of salvation because through God he gored his enemies, so to speak, and was kept safe by God's providence. Christ too is a horn of salvation, as Zechariah says: "And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us." The kingdom is also a horn, as in: "He will exalt the horn of his anointed."

With praise I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies, etc. Whoever prays while singing hymns calls upon the Lord with praise. But no one who resents what happens to him prays in this way. So even when enemies surround us, this is how we should pray.

The pangs of death surrounded me, and torrents of lawlessness threw me into turmoil. The pangs of Hades encircled me; the snares of death came upon me first, etc. Christ says these things as man. For death went into labour against him, and the torrents of lawlessness troubled him when he said, "My soul is troubled"; yet they did not hold him fast. The pangs of Hades encircled him, thinking they would seize him, yet he never became a son of Hades. And sins unto death, that is, snares, came before him, which means they went ahead of him; but they did not capture him. So by torrents of lawlessness you should understand the streams of wickedness, and by snares of death the sins committed in deed.
By the same. The pangs of death are either those that give birth to death or those conceived by death, which Paul has proclaimed as the last enemy to be destroyed.
By the same. The torrents of lawlessness are lawless thoughts. When they linger in us they are called pangs, and they are called snares when they kill us through sin carried out in act.

And in my affliction I called upon the Lord, and I cried to my God. He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will come into his ears, etc. In the very midst of afflictions, when they are at their height, we must call upon the Lord and cry out to God. For in this way he will hear us from his temple [?]. And when we pray in such a frame of mind, our prayer will enter with confidence into what are called his ears, as into its proper place. Perhaps we are also armed against our enemies by the very act of praising and calling upon the Lord.
By the same. Christ is the temple of God, and the spiritual and holy powers are the temple of Christ. This is why Christ is now said to sit upon the throne of David his father.

And the earth was shaken and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because God was angry with them. Smoke went up in his wrath, and fire blazed from his face; coals were kindled by it, etc. God stands for the one who stands, and is shaken for the one who is shaken. So it is said to Moses: "Stand before Pharaoh." But when Adam disobeyed God, or rather listened to the woman, he heard the Lord God walking. God no longer stood for him, and because God is good, the Judge did not stand. When God is shaken, it is not heaven that trembles but the earth. The foundations of the mountains are troubled too, and it is the fire kindled from God's wrath that will trouble them. "The face of the Lord is against those who do evil"; but it gives light to the saints, as in:

"The light of your face has been stamped upon us." By the same. "And fire blazed from his face," burning up wood, hay and straw, that is, consuming evil habits. In this way it once burned up Matthew when he was a tax collector, and Paul when he was a persecutor and a violent man.

By the same. Because God is good he is shaken, so that his earth may no longer despise him but may fear him as a father, and so that the foundations of the mountains may no longer stay unmoved but be thrown into turmoil. And because God is good, as a burning and consuming fire he first rises and sends out smoke, then kindles coals, then comes down after bowing the heavens, and after this he shows the darkness under his feet. Then he mounts the cherubim and flies, and he flies on the wings of the winds. But his ascent and descent must be understood as his various dispensations, since God is present to all things and everywhere.

By the same. God dwells and walks among holy people, but he flies among the cherubim. And if you take the winds to be the physical ones, he rides upon them by the rule of his providence and steers them as he wills.

And he made darkness his hiding place; his tent was all around him: dark water in the clouds of the air, etc. Since he made darkness his hiding place, and his tent is all around him, there is dark water in the clouds of the air. This is what the prophets mean: "For I will command the clouds," he says, "not to rain upon them, and there will be a famine, not a famine of bread, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord." If our God is light, how is he covered with darkness? I think darkness covers him in the same way that ignorance leaves what can be known unrevealed. Ignorance is said with reference to the knower, not to what is known. He called the flesh in which Christ dwelt his tent. He also says "tent" because the incarnation was for a time: "For even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer." Or perhaps he called the body a tent because of the vine that God brought out of Egypt, to guard it until the grapes ripened, so that the boar from the forest would not ravage it. He may also be calling bodily nature a tent, since God is seen in it through the Word. For the Maker is contemplated through the beauty of his creatures, and is clearly seen when he is understood through the things that he has made.

And he sent out arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and threw them into confusion. And the springs of the waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare, at your rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the breath of your anger, etc. All those grim things serve this good end. He rebukes and breathes out a breath of anger so that the springs of the waters may be seen and the foundations of the world laid bare. It is good for the springs of the waters to be seen and revealed, since they are led by the one who said, "They have forsaken me, the spring of living water." It is also good for the foundations of the world to be laid bare, so that the Holy Trinity, which rules over created things, may be contemplated. So how could anyone reasonably blame the things that bring these about, even if they seem grim? These are the hail, the coals of fire, the arrows, the lightnings, God's rebukes and the blast of the breath of his anger. Notice too that a rebuke is a kind of treatment for the one rebuked, who is reproved so that he may stop doing what is worse. So when you hear that Jesus rebuked a fever, the winds and the sea, understand it in a way worthy of Jesus' goodness. Or take it this way: thoughts, words and deeds make up a world that is built upon habits and dispositions. He scatters the wicked with arrows and throws them into confusion with lightnings, when the hidden things of men are revealed and God brings to light the hidden things of darkness. Then he will also lay bare the foundations of the world, rebuking the ungodly with punishments. Holy men are also foundations of the world because of their strength, and those who live according to Christ are built upon them. They too are laid bare when the rebuke falls upon the wicked, while the punishment does not touch them at all. God does not punish sinners at once. Instead he announces in advance the punishments of his wrath, and this is what it means for him to breathe out the breath of his anger.

By the same. When we compare spiritual things with spiritual, we produce lightnings by revealing the knowledge that comes from them. You may also take the lightnings to be the brilliance of the divine preaching, which has lit up the obscure words of the prophets.
By the same. He calls the virtues springs, because knowledge flows from them. "For blessed," he says, "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

He sent from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters. He will rescue me from my mighty enemies and from those who hate me, because they grew stronger than I, etc. He took me from on high. He received the one who had come down, drew him out of the many waters of human life, and rescued him from enemies mighty in their hostility. Notice that the enemies are said to be mighty. Perhaps the doctrines of godlessness are also much water, which cannot quench love. The mighty enemies are both the invisible ones and the men who practise deceit through knowledge falsely so called.

By the same. From this we learn that before the Saviour came the demons were stronger than we were, but now we are stronger than they are. For Christ has given us power "to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy."

They came upon me in the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my support. And he brought me out into a broad place; he will rescue me, because he took pleasure in me, etc. Those who are afflicted but not crushed should know that they will be brought out of their affliction and led into God's holy broad place. For in the day of affliction God supports the one who flees to him, so that he does not totter and fall. And while supporting the one hemmed in by afflictions, he brings him out into an open space, as in: "In affliction you have enlarged me." This happens not necessarily when someone is set free from affliction, but when he bears it nobly.

And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands he will repay me, because I have kept the ways of the Lord, etc. Someone who lifts up holy hands and dares to say, "The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice," will also declare that his hands are clean. These are the words of one who sees how each thing is judged. God has certain judgments concerning each kind of sin. So when someone keeps before his eyes all the judgments concerning all sins, he will say, "All his judgments are before me." Besides, whoever says these things finds himself guilty of nothing. So these words must be applied to the Saviour, "who was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin."

By the same. Purity of soul is freedom from passion, given by God's grace together with human effort. By the cleanness of the hands he means the prophetic activities, which are kept undefiled by the best disposition.

And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my lawlessness, etc. No one can be blameless without God. So a little later he says, "And he made my way blameless." Someone who says "The Lord will repay me according to my righteousness," and what follows, cannot be guilty of lawlessness. And "I shall keep myself from my lawlessness" can be taken to refer to what is called the darkness within us, as in: "If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!"

By the same. The blameless one is the person who has within himself the way of God, which is Christ. "For I am the way," he says. David himself called this way blameless when he said, "My God, your way is blameless."

And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, etc. "The measure you give will be the measure you get." These are the words of saints whose great confidence allows them to say, "Repay your servant." He means the righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus Christ, which has been revealed to all who believe. For to those who believe rightly, faith is counted as righteousness.

With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent, and with the elect you will be elect, and with the crooked you will twist, etc. Just as I shall be blameless with God himself, so God will be holy with the holy, innocent with the innocent, and elect with the elect. But with the crooked he will not be crooked, for that would not be right. Instead "you will twist," as he did with Pharaoh.

By the same. Among the holy God is holy, among the innocent innocent, and among the elect elect. Among the crooked he is not crooked, but he is twisted along with them, out of reverence in speaking. For the psalmist was careful not to call God crooked. Simpler readers often take these verses to be about men. God is twisted along with them in the sense of what he says in Deuteronomy: "If you come to me crookedly, I too will come to you in crooked wrath."

By the same. You fit your rewards to the dispositions of men, O Master. To the holy you give what is worthy of holiness, to the blameless and just what suits them, and to the elect and perfect what is perfect. But for those who have turned aside and travel the opposite road, you prepare an end that matches their road. And how? "For you will save a humble people."

For you will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, you will light up my darkness, etc. The lamp of the body is the eye, and the Lord will light it. There is also a kind of darkness in our human makeup, and in the righteous man the Lord will light it up. Or the lamp of the soul is the mind, since it can receive light. The soul's darkness is its irascible and desiring parts, and the mind lights these up once it has received the divine rays. Perhaps also those whom the Lord has surrounded with the light of truth have a lamp that has been lit. Since their mind has been enlightened, they conduct their actions by reason, as in the light of dawn, and they have their darkness lit up as well. For in you I shall be rescued from trial, and in my God I shall leap over a wall, etc.

Life, I think, is a trial, as in Job. No one can be rescued from bitter circumstances unless he has come to be in God. A person comes to be in God by sharing in him, just as a person is rescued from ignorance by coming to be in knowledge. Such a person does not enter into temptation, not because he is never tempted, but because he is not caught in the snares of temptation. So he leaps over the wall of sin and puts sins behind him.

My God, his way is blameless; the words of the Lord are tried by fire; he is a shield to all who hope in him, etc. The blameless way is Christ, who said, "I am the way." And since the words of the Lord are fiery, those who hear them say, "Was not our heart burning within us?" They are also "fervent in spirit" and do not accept a fire foreign to God, such as the fire in the arrows of the evil one. But the one who said, "I came to cast fire upon the earth," had fiery words. So he says, "And what do I wish, if it is already kindled?" Perhaps this is why Jesus baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire; but the fire burns up wood, hay and straw.

For who is God but the Lord? And who is God but our God? It is God who girds me with power and has made my way blameless; who makes my feet like a deer's and sets me on the heights, etc. In this sense the only true God is the God and Father, unless we take the "who," which often refers to something rare, as applying to the Only-begotten. Here the belt is power, but in Paul it is truth. The feet of one who runs well and finishes the race are made like those of deer. "And sets me on the heights." Each person has his own particular heights, from which he has fallen or come down.
By the same. A person's feet are made like a deer's through the practical life, and they are raised up through contemplation. For the deer kills snakes.

He trains my hands for war; and you have made my arms a bow of bronze, etc. Bronze is a symbol of the practical life. "For he has ruined your bronze," Ezekiel says to Jerusalem. Since our arms send out the arrows, he says, "You have made my arms ready as a bow." He adds "of bronze" to show its toughness and unbreakability, as if to say, "You have made me invincible in my struggles against my enemies."

And you have given me the shield of my salvation; and your right hand has upheld me, and your discipline has set me upright to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me, etc. The one who sits at the right hand of the Father is himself called the right hand. Through the first discipline he sets "us" upright, and through the second he teaches. For a right way of life raises up the soul, while true knowledge enlarges it. The right hand is the Son, who created all things. Of him it is said elsewhere: "The right hand of the Lord has done mighty things; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me."

You have enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footsteps did not falter, etc. This is the voice of one who bears afflictions easily. The Word gives him room even in such circumstances, so that not even the slightest weakness shows in his steps.

I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they are gone. I will crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet, etc. God has made someone competent to be a minister of a new covenant, so that he can tear down every height raised against the knowledge of God. He pursues the hostile arguments with the salvation that comes from God, and he will keep pursuing them. He will not turn back from fighting them until they are gone. When they are crushed, the arguments hostile to the truth will not be able to stand before the one whom God has made competent.

By the same. The one who pursues his enemies is the one who does not let passionate thoughts arise within him, for it is from these that our sins arise. By the same. Freedom from passion brings about the end of the enemies.

By the same. Those who have fallen from their stand in evil receive a benefit. And the arguments hostile to the truth will not be able to stand before the one who is strong of hand, which is the meaning of the name David.
And you made my enemies turn their backs to me, and you destroyed those who hate me, etc. The enemies turn their backs when they can no longer cast passionate thoughts into the soul.
By the same. You have made my enemies change and follow me without ever leaving me, so that they have become my back; or else, so that they flee.

Rescue me from the disputes of the people; you will make me head of the nations, etc. Christ, who became a sign that is spoken against, says these things, and God has made him head of the nations. For Christ is the head of the Church.

A people whom I did not know served me; as soon as they heard me they obeyed me, etc. The Scriptures use "I did not know" particularly of worse things. Here Christ applied "I did not know" to the people from the nations, for there was a time when they were not known. You will also find God saying such things.
By the same. While they did not know, they were not known; once they knew, they were acknowledged.
Foreign sons have grown old and have gone lame off their paths, etc. Virtue makes new, but vice makes old. And limping belongs to those who are growing old.
By the same. "How long will you limp on both your legs?" The paths of men are practice and contemplation.
It is God who grants me vengeance and has subjected peoples under me, etc. Christ has received vengeance from God and says, "Vengeance is mine; I will repay."

By the same. "Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions," and so on. He grants the people that was once unknown the privilege of being placed under him. "My deliverer from wrathful enemies." Where rage holds sway, wrath is present too. If my enemies are wrathful, they are also full of rage. "For they have rage," it says, "like that of the serpent."
PSALM 18

"The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands," etc. If the heavens declare the glory of God, and yet the heavens will perish (for it says, "The heavens will perish, but you remain"), will those that declare the glory of God perish, then? But surely no one who declares the glory of God will perish, for God says, "Those who glorify me I will glorify." So the heavens will not perish. Rather, the heavens that declare the glory of God belong to the intellectual nature, and they are called heavens because they have within themselves the Sun of righteousness. The heavens that perish are of bodily substance.

By the same. For neither the earth nor the earthy one who comes from the earth can declare the glory of God: "For he who is from the earth speaks from the earth." But perhaps the heavens are those who bear the image of the heavenly one, and it is they who declare the glory of God. And there are also heavens that are the work of God's hands. Note the difference: "declaring" is applied to the heavens, while "proclaiming" is said of the firmament.

"Day pours forth speech to day, and night proclaims knowledge to night," etc. Those who embrace the contemplative life also lay up treasure in heaven. Since their heart is there, they are heavens, declaring the glory of God already mentioned through their contemplation of intelligible things. Those who lead the practical life are the firmament, because they are steadfast. They proclaim the work of God's hands by doing the works of God and by being his works. The luminous understanding is day, and in harmony with another luminous understanding it pours forth speech. In the same way the Old Scripture, filled with spiritual nourishment, pours forth out of its fullness and offers words to the New Testament. Night is the deepest apprehension of mystical matters, and it leads us on to another obscurity. The Spirit of God gives this apprehension to those who have the Spirit, which searches even the depths of God. Speech prepares the way for words, and words bring knowledge by supplying proofs. God has spoken both so that they may be heard, and this is why the disobedient have no excuse. Those who are earth fit for sowing receive the sound, that is, the wording of Scripture in its sensible sense. But those who have gone beyond these and are called "ends" receive the words, being clearly instructed. For Peter was not hearing a mere sound when he said, "You have the words of eternal life." And the Saviour said, "The words that I have spoken to you are spirit." He was speaking to the apostles, who are the ends of the inhabited world.

"There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard," etc. Speech and word are not the same thing, just as a chatterer is not the same as an eloquent man. Or perhaps the sound belongs to speeches, while the words belong to words of reason.

"In the sun he has set his tabernacle," etc. Our Lord is the Sun of righteousness, and the Father dwells in him, as it says: "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me." And again: "The Father who dwells in me does the works himself." And the Apostle says, "God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself."

"And he is like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber," etc. Christ is like a bridegroom, for it says, "He who has the bride is the bridegroom." In his beauty he resembles a bridegroom coming out of the bridal chamber in great splendour.

"The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is sure, making infants wise; the ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening the heart; the commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is pure," etc. The spiritual law purifies those who are spiritual and converts the soul. The testimony of the Lord may be Christ's witness on the cross, the sure testimony of the Lord that makes infants wise. The ordinances of the Lord are those that contain the justice of rendering to each according to his desert. There are ordinances in his law, or else the ordinances are what concerns his dispensation toward each person, for when these are understood they gladden the heart. The commandment of the Lord is a commandment in the form of a general law. It is not spoken obscurely but radiantly, and when it is kept it enlightens the eyes of the soul. "The fear of the Lord is pure." Among those who seem to fear the Lord in their soul, some know what ought to be feared, and they turn away from evils, for by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil. Others do not have the true fear of the Lord. For this fear is pure, and its fruits endure for ever and ever.

By the same. "The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls." Does it convert them from vice to virtue, or from sensible things to intelligible ones? Perhaps the latter, since the former is the natural work of the commandment. The law of Moses is called by various names. It is called law because it regulates the conduct of life. It is called testimony because it bears solemn witness about transgression and points to the punishment. It is called ordinances because it urges toward the good and forbids what is unjust. It is called commandment because it orders with authority and prescribes what must be done. It is called judgments because it shows what good things the one who keeps it will obtain, and to what punishments the transgressor will be handed over. So the law of the Lord, he says, is blameless, and it converts the souls of human beings.

By the same. "The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring for ever and ever." Purity is abstaining from sins, and this fear is pure because it makes people pure, for by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil. Being eternal, this fear also makes eternal those in whom it arises. Reverence and the fear of God bring about the enjoyment of eternal goods. The fear of God is rightly called pure, because human fear is blamed and goes by the name of cowardice.

"For indeed your servant keeps them," etc. If the servant keeps them, then whoever does not keep them is not a servant. The one who desires nothing other than the desirable things of God is the one who keeps them. Therefore his reward is to obtain what he desires. Having set right what is manifest, he prays about what is hidden.

"If they do not gain dominion over me, then I shall be blameless," etc. If strangers do not gain dominion over us, then we shall be blameless, though we were not so before. We shall be blameless once we have been cleansed even of the greatest sin.
