If a person brings forth nothing from his own mouth but what is pure [?], his words will be acceptable, since he opens his mouth only for the word of God. Because of his boldness, the meditation of such a person's heart is before God, not sometimes yes and sometimes no, but always. When no one lets go of the meditation of his own heart and so becomes defiled by evil thoughts, the meditation of the heart can be before God always.
PSALM 19

"May the Lord hear you in the day of affliction; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you; may he send you help from the sanctuary, and support you out of Zion," etc. The person who is on the narrow and afflicted way that leads to life is certainly afflicted in everything and is in a day of affliction. He therefore receives the blessing of being heard, which the person on the broad way does not receive. So let us rather choose to be in a day of affliction. The name of the God of Jacob will protect us if we put on his full armour and stand against the wiles of the devil. Let us therefore pray at every turn in the day of affliction, so that we may be heard and help may be sent to us, whether from angels or some such source, or the help of Christ.

By the same. The person who walks the narrow and afflicted way is always in afflictions, and when he prays he is heard. The person who walks the broad way is neither afflicted nor heard. Let us pray in our afflictions, then, so that we may be heard. Hezekiah, too, received Sennacherib's letter and spread it out before God in the temple, and while the people prayed for him, he was heard.

"May he remember all your sacrifice, and may your whole burnt offering be made fat," etc. Irrational animals are fattened and then sacrificed and wholly burnt. Rational beings are fattened after they have been wholly burnt, that is, if after the cleansing of holy fire such a being is found worthy of knowledge, having been entirely sanctified by fire. God fattens a person's burnt offerings so that the fat may feed the fire on the altar. Perhaps the sacrifice consists of inanimate things, while the burnt offerings consist of living ones.
By the same. The word "all" indicates a great number, implying that what he remembers is no small amount.

"May the Lord grant you according to your heart," etc. This means whatever it befits God to give and the one who asks to receive, as one who knows what he should pray for and how he should pray. Or it means: may the Lord grant you as much as your heart can hold, namely your counsel, since it is good.

"We will rejoice in your salvation," etc. People rejoice in wealth, in glory, or in noble birth, but the saint rejoices in the salvation of God. The Father's salvation in the world is the Son, and the Son's salvation in the world is the cross. It is the salvation of which it is said, "Today a Saviour, the Lord, has been born for us," and of which Simeon said, "For my eyes have seen your salvation."
By the same. God's salvation is being saved in him, and this salvation is not found among the sons of men. The requests of the one who asks are fulfilled, and they are great and heavenly.

"May the Lord fulfil all your requests," etc. But not evil requests. May he to whom you have offered the sacrifices fulfil whatever you have asked in your mind, since the things of your counsel are not foreign to him.
"He will hear him from his holy heaven," etc. For the Lord hears every king who is ruled by the King of those who reign.

"They were fettered and fell," etc. Our adversaries rush upon us with wickedness, but we meet them with the knowledge of Christ. For the opposing powers will fall when the salvation spoken of appears.
PSALM 20

"O Lord, the king will be glad in your power, and he will rejoice exceedingly in your salvation," etc. If Christ is the power of God, perhaps it is in him that the king will be glad. And just as Christ is power and wisdom, so he is also salvation.

"You have given him the desire of his heart, and you have not deprived him of the wish of his lips," etc. The desire of the heart concerns intelligible things, and the contemplation of the eyes concerns visible things and sights. The wish of the lips concerns professing what has been understood and contemplated.

"You have set on his head a crown of precious stone," etc. God is the crown of Christ, and Christ is the crown of the rational nature. The precious stones are the words that are pearls, of which it is said, "Do not throw your pearls before swine." They are also the merchant's very precious pearl. And they are Christ's disciples, who will be woven together like a crown and set on Christ's head.

By the same. A person is crowned with the things he practises. For the righteous man who has pursued righteousness will receive the crown of righteousness. The one who has delighted in the Lord is shielded with a crown of delight. The one saved by grace receives a crown of graces on his head. And the one who has stored up precious stones along with gold and silver will be crowned with the stones he has wrought. And the Lord crowns those who hope in him with mercy and compassion.

"He asked you for life, and you gave him length of days for ever and ever," etc. Inquire whether one kind of life is given by God and another comes from matter. Compare "He breathed into his face the breath of life" with "Let the earth bring forth a living soul." "He asked you for life": that is, the life he had before his illness.

By the same. The king asked the Lord for life as a good thing, and he received it. And Life is good, he who said, "I am the life." Perhaps Hezekiah, who seemed to love life, wanted that life which his love of life symbolized.

"Great is his glory in your salvation," etc. Salvation gains great glory for the king who rose from the dead. He already had glory, and salvation added another glory, the glory of the resurrection, as it says: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again."

By the same. The king's glory is great in the salvation of the Lord, and not in any of the things lower than it. "You will lay glory and majesty upon him." Christ had glory and majesty while he was in the form of God. But when he also became man, God highly exalted him.

"May your hand be found by all your enemies," etc. The Lord's enemies find him, while those who hate him are found by him. Through the law we find God, but through the Gospels we are found by him, though we were formerly enemies and "strangers to the covenants" of God, "having no hope and without God in the world." Or else: through the practical life we find God, but through knowledge we are found by him.
By the same. It will overtake the swiftest and destroy the mightiest. The hand that punishes will be found waging war, as it says: "The Lord wages war with a hidden hand against Amalek."

"You will make them like a furnace of fire," etc. He says this about evildoers. They are a furnace of fire, since their hearts have been heated like a furnace. And somewhere it is said, "They are all adulterers; their hearts are like a furnace."

"The Lord in his wrath will throw them into confusion," etc. They are thrown into confusion as they await punishment. This does not mean everyone without distinction, but those who are wicked for the sake of pleasure and who hold false opinions. "And fire will devour them," since they are wood, hay and straw.

"You will destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from among the sons of men," etc. He will not destroy their substance, for that is indestructible, but the quality by which they sprouted wood, hay and straw, that is, their evil works. Or else it means the seed that the wicked and impious have sown, which God wipes out from among the sons of men. To be rid of sins and evil thoughts is a kindness, for an evil thought is the seed of sin.

"For they directed evils against you; they devised a plan that they cannot carry out," etc. The wicked, perverted in everything, attempt what is impossible. For they plot treacherously against one who cannot be harmed.
By the same. Each of the wicked directs his evils against the one he wants to harm, or the one he wrongs, or the one against whom he acts impiously.
By the same. We are turned aside when we are moved contrary to nature.

"For you will make them turn their backs; among your remnants you will prepare their face," etc. First those who hate the Lord are made like a furnace of fire at the time of his presence. They are thrown into confusion by the Lord in his wrath. Fire devours them, and the Lord destroys their fruit from the earth, since it was not the fruit of the Spirit. He destroys their seed from among the sons of men, for those who hate the Lord directed evils against him and devised plans that they cannot carry out. After all this he makes them turn their backs in flight. Then he will prepare their face among the remnants, so that even among these, after so many punishments, they may find relief and contemplate.

"Be exalted, O Lord, in your power; we will sing and make music to your mighty deeds," etc. If Christ is the power of God, then when the Lord is exalted in his own power, he is exalted in Christ. A person sings when he contemplates, and he makes music when he acts according to virtue. We must both contemplate his mighty deeds and act in accordance with them.
PSALM 21

"O God, my God, attend to me; why have you forsaken me?" and so on. This cry of the Lord Christ, nailed to the cross, also prefigures our own suffering in another way. For we were the ones who had been forsaken and overlooked before. Now we have been taken up and saved by the sufferings of the one who cannot suffer, and, as though making our folly and our wrongdoing his own, he says in the verses that follow in the psalm: "Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions." It is as if he said: My sins put me far from salvation.
"But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel," and so on. From this we learn that the Lord is praise itself, and a praise far from Israel.

"But I am a worm and not a man," and so on. The worm is not born from mating but from wood, and it devours wood, hay and straw. Perhaps our God too is a fire that consumes wicked and easily kindled matter. Rational natures are also called trees, for "all the trees of paradise," it says, "envied you," and it is in them that Christ is by nature born as wisdom and righteousness. So Christ is fittingly called a worm, since he has come to be in such trees. As a worm he also became bait for the devil and his angels. To the wise he is found straight, but to the fool crooked. And when we sin he becomes a worm for us too, convicting our conscience and gnawing at it.

"For you are the one who drew me out of the womb, my hope from my mother's breasts," and so on. For when he was born, the Father himself acted as midwife. I think he did so for him alone of all who have come into being, since he alone was from the Holy Spirit. But if he had to hope in perfection [?] while he was still being nursed with milk, then with regard to "who drew me out" it might be said that plots were laid against him and he was hindered from coming out of the womb, so that God was needed to draw him out of the womb. Perhaps some invisible power also draws everyone who is born out of the womb. It is a holy power in the case of Paul, who was set apart from his mother's womb, but a worse one in the case of the sinners who are estranged from the womb. But the Father himself drew out of the womb the Savior alone, so that the Savior, aware of this special privilege, said: "For you are the one who drew me out of the womb." Other human beings are not drawn out but come out: "Esau came out," it says, "like a hairy hide." This is why he alone did not share in the folly and condition of infants. While he was still sucking at his mother's breasts because of his body, he knew how to hope in the one who drew him out of the womb. For all human beings, once born, turn first to evil. But our Lord, as Isaiah says, "before he knows good or evil, refuses wickedness so as to choose the good." Examine alongside these passages what is said of John "leaping for joy," of Jacob "supplanting his brother in the womb," and of Jeremiah, "sanctified before he came out of the womb."

"My hope from my mother's breasts; upon you I was cast from the womb," and so on. Enosh hoped to call on God, but not from his mother's breasts. Christ, however, chose the good before he knew good or evil, so he is rightly said to have hoped from his mother's breasts. "For there is no man," it says, "who will live and not sin."

"From my mother's womb you are my God," and so on. He prayed as soon as he was born, and perhaps even before he was born. For he had more understanding than Jonah, who prayed in the belly of the sea monster.

"Do not stand far from me, for affliction is near, for there is no one to help," and so on. Perhaps he said "affliction is near" while hanging on the cross, referring to the struggles in Hades against the powers there. He says this as though none of the angels were helping him, for none of them dared to go down with him that far.

"Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls encircled me," and so on. You may also apply these words to the spiritual demons. By the calves you will understand the evil powers that bring about earthly things, since that animal tills the earth. The fat bulls, so called because of their great learning in evil, are the powers that preside over deceitful words and gore human beings by means of them. The lion is the devil, who roars against us and snatches away many. From this lion the good shepherd snatched back two legs and the lobe of an ear: the lion swallows the ear of the human soul through disobedience, and through the legs its course.

By the same. Starting from "Many calves surrounded me," you will ask whether some of these things are said about what came before the departure and others about what came after it, or whether all of them concern what came after the departure. It is likely that he saw powers standing around him, wishing to seize his soul and bring it down to gloomier places.

"I was poured out like water, and all my bones were scattered," and so on. The bones of wisdom are the holy doctrines of the Church, which the Jews were commanded by law not to break at the Passover: "You shall not break a bone of it." The Word is poured out by those who champion it in a watered-down way, and by those who speak it into unsuitable vessels and so pour it out. All the bones of the Word are scattered by those who do not preserve its loftiness but break up its harmony in the Scriptures, so that one person has this bone of it, another has another, and someone else yet another. But at the consummation God gathers bone to bone and joint to joint from the true Israel. Or else, in keeping with "Have mercy on me, Lord, for my bones are troubled," there are certain spiritual bones of the soul.

"And you brought me down into the dust of death," and so on. Christ was brought down not into death but into the dust of death. For his soul was not held fast in Hades, and his flesh did not know corruption.

"They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots," and so on. The Jews keep the written law, and so they divide the perceptible garments of the Word. We guard the spirit of the Word, and so we divide the spiritual garments of our Savior, being baptized into Christ and putting him on as wisdom, truth and righteousness.

"Rescue my soul from the sword," and so on. The sword that can strike the soul must be a spiritual one, the sword of which it is said: "And a sword will pierce your own soul too." A spiritual sword, then, is a temptation that summons the soul to unbelief in God, or knowledge falsely so called, or an impure thought that drags the soul into sin. This happens to those who wish to succeed in the practical life.

"And my only one from the hand of the dog," and so on. Those born of this dog are themselves also called little dogs, and of them it is said: "It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs."
"I will tell your name to my brothers," and so on. These words are spoken as by one who has risen from the dead and been heard in what he prayed for.
"From you is my praise in the great assembly," and so on. "In the Lord my soul shall be praised": that is, not in noble birth or in wealth, but in wisdom and righteousness.
"The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him shall praise the Lord," and so on. "I am the bread that came down from heaven."

"All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord," and so on. After knowledge comes forgetting, and after forgetting comes remembrance. He was right to put "shall remember." For they received their being from God, so they will remember the one who created them, and having remembered they will turn. As has been said, this is not one nation, nor two, but all the ends of the earth, illuminated by the light of the knowledge of God.

"For the kingdom is the Lord's, and he rules over the nations," and so on. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. It is as if he said that all the unrighteous become righteous and cease to become earthly and corruptible.
"And my soul lives for him," and so on. The soul that is God's lives for God alone, since it has knowledge not only of the things that have come into being but also of God himself.

"The generation to come shall be proclaimed to the Lord," and so on. "A generation goes, and a generation comes." And according to the wise Solomon, "the generation of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and wealth, and glory, and life."
PSALM 22
"The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing," and so on. Just as a sheep is fed by green grass and water, so a human being is given life by practice and knowledge.

"He restored my soul; he led me in paths of righteousness," and so on. If there is a path of righteousness, there are also paths of moderation, love and self-control, by which one enters the kingdom of heaven.

"For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me," and so on. From this point on he is not speaking about God but to God himself. To walk in the midst of the shadow of death is not the same as to sit in the shadow of death. The one who sits is settled in it and fixed in evil and in the shadow of death. That is why he is in darkness and needs mercy, so that a light may rise for him. But the one who does not sit does not walk alone. He travels through the midst of the shadow of death, not standing still but hurrying on through it, and the Lord travels with him. And where is it written about sitting in the shadow of death? "For those who sit in the region and shadow of death, a light has dawned."

"Your rod and your staff, these comforted me," and so on. Scripture itself will testify that "rod" is used of scourges and punishments, when it says: "If my sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will punish their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges, but I will not scatter my mercy from them." So if you have sinned and see the rod of God laid upon you, know that God's mercy has not been scattered from you. But if you have sinned and there is no rod or scourge anywhere, be afraid. God, "who scourges every son whom he receives," is not receiving you. Words like these are spoken about sinners when they are not scourged: "But my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped. For there is no refusal at their death, and no firmness in their scourge. They do not share the troubles of other people, and they will not be scourged along with other people. That is why pride has taken hold of them; they have clothed themselves with their injustice and ungodliness." "Your rod and your staff." A rod is enough, so what is the staff for? If you are a sinful sheep, you will be struck with a rod; if you are a sinful human being, with a staff. That is why, when Solomon speaks of such people in Proverbs, he names not a rod but a staff: "He who spares the staff hates his own son." These things, then, comfort the one who is beaten and punished, for he is convinced that God scourges every son whom he receives.

By the same. As a rod disciplines, so the practical life teaches moderation of the passions. As a staff gives rest, so knowledge gives joy. The staff signifies strength. So he means: Your mighty kingdom has supplied me with this comfort.

"You prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict me," and so on. What does "in the presence of those who afflict me" mean? It contains an unspeakable mystery: that one should pray to be afflicted. Consider this with me. In great games, prizes are set out for each event. In the same way, in each affliction, whenever the affliction is present along with the opposing powers that afflict us, think of a spiritual and intellectual table prepared because of that affliction. However often you are afflicted, a spiritual table is set before you just as often. Only have eyes that see my tables, so that in giving thanks you may say with the Apostle: "And not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions." At the beginning we said that the one who is making progress encamps in a place of green grass. The one who progresses may reach the end. Then he no longer remains a sheep but has been raised up [?] as a rational being, and he has a table of rational foods prepared for him by the Lord. For Wisdom will prepare her own table for one who has attained the Lord, and on it her own sacrifices are set out [?]. So he says in thanksgiving: "You prepared a table before me." This is no longer introductory and moral teaching as before, but mystical teaching and the contemplation of truth. Consider whether, as long as someone is in this life and sees through a mirror and in a riddle, he is a sheep led by a shepherd; but when he passes over into the age to come and meets the truth face to face, he will come to a spiritual table, as it says: "And I will appoint a covenant for you, to eat and drink at my Father's table in truth." Hence also the saying: "God has prepared what eye has not seen," and what follows. The words "before me" show that my table has been made manifest and known in the presence of those who afflict me, the many who wish to be my enemies. The Lord wanted me to rise up strongly against them by means of those who afflict me, and so he prepared a table before me with solid food laid on it. When I have filled myself with this food like an athlete, I will be able to stand bravely against those who afflict me. And the one whose head is anointed with oil by the Lord will say: "But let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head," just as Christ was anointed by God with the oil of gladness. I think that when he fasts, too, he anoints his head in this way and washes his face. Wisdom has not only prepared a table but has also mixed her wine in a bowl, a wine born from the true vine itself. She mixed this wine by blending divine thoughts with human words. From such a bowl she draws a portion and gives each person a cup. That cup is most excellent, that is, precious and exceptional, and it is said to belong to the one who receives it.

By the same. At first Christ tends the sheep as a shepherd; but now he calls his friends to the table as a friend. "No longer," he says, "do I call you servants, but friends." The fear of God makes servants, but knowledge of the mysteries of God makes friends. Here he calls immortality a table. "In the presence of those who afflict me" means "against the will of those who plot against me." The Babylonians presumably did not want them to be released, but Cyrus, who had become more powerful, set them free from captivity.

"And your mercy shall pursue me all the days of my life," and so on. Who is this pursuing mercy, if not the one of whom the Apostle says: "He became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption"? The living Mercy that pursues you overtakes some people but not others. It does not overtake those who flee hard, but it seizes those who flee less, so as to show them mercy. And mercy not only pursues; it also brings it about "that I dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days." For length of time, and of life as well, is in Wisdom's right hand, and the days of life are the various illuminations of the truth.
PSALM 23

"The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it," and so on. Consider also, in this connection, whether all human beings are the Lord's portion. Perhaps the statement that all who inhabit the world belong to the Lord should not be taken simply, unless this is a prophecy about the calling from all the nations.

By the same. Before Christ came, God was known only in Judea; but since Christ came, the whole earth is the Lord's. Before Christ came, no fullness could be found anywhere on earth; most of the earth was, if one may put it this way, emptiness. But when Christ came, many of those from the nations who believed could say: "From his fullness we have all received." For this reason they are his fullness, since those who are empty of the gospel way of life could not be Christ's fullness. And not only the earth and its fullness, but also the inhabited world is the Lord's. The sinner dwells in a desert. But whoever is in the Church, which is filled with the Holy Trinity, dwells in the inhabited world, and that world is the Church. The Lord has founded it upon the seas of temptations, and it conquers in them, so that afterward, watered, it may be made ready upon the river.

"Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place?" and so on. Compare these words with "Lord, who shall sojourn in your tent?" and what follows. Notice that there such a person first sojourns in the Lord's tent and then dwells on his holy mountain. Here, however, such a person first ascends the mountain of the Lord and second stands in his holy place. By the mountain of the Lord he means the final good and God the Word, for rare is the person who can climb to its summit by making progress. But one who has been made perfect, and can go no further, stands firm and is called the holy place of God. Walking behind the Lord, he ascends, "forgetting what lies behind and straining toward what lies ahead," and his good end is to stand with God in his holy place. If you want an example from the sacred writings: Moses stood in the place of God's sanctuary, and God said to him, "But you, stand here with me." But since you are asking which sanctuary of God one must stand in: the prophets say, "And he set my feet upon a rock," and "the rock was Christ." Let us learn, then, who it is that will obtain these promises.
"Innocent in hands and pure in heart," and so on.

In answer to the question he replies that this person is both practical and contemplative. Many people have pure actions, but because they act for human praise they are not pure in heart. And vain is the soul that is rational yet does not flee what is harmful and choose the good. The one who keeps his "yes" and "no" swears his oath without deceit, and blessing is his prize, and God will save him by mercy and grace. For whatever kind of person someone may be, he needs mercy from God.

By the same. Judas ascended the mountain of the Lord but did not stand in his holy place. He was neither innocent in hands nor pure in heart, but was a thief who carried off what was put in the purse. By the same. Some people have pure actions but are not pure in heart, so he added "pure in heart." For the one who does what is right in his actions must also be pure in knowledge.

"This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob." But no one who seeks the face of God will see God's face here. "For no one," it says, "who is human shall see my face and live." You must be changed, so that you who seek the face of God may see it. You must put off everything human; you must already become an angel and a god. "For do not despise," says the Savior, "one of these little ones in the Church. For truly I tell you that their angels continually behold the face of my Father in heaven." This, then, is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.

By the same. Seeing the face of God continually belongs to angels, and human beings also seek to see this face. So human beings too seek the knowledge that belongs to angels, if indeed it is possible for a human being to eat the bread of angels.

"Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts," and so on. By gates he means the virtues, for it says: "Open to me the gates of righteousness." As the gates of righteousness are opened, so too are those of moderation, courage, love and patience. Through them the knowledge of God naturally enters, as though God were leading the way, having broken up the captivity and made the captives victors. And as they enter a splendid city with a display of trophies, the crowds cry out: "Lift up your gates, O rulers."

By the same. He did not say, "Open the gates that you rule and guard," but "Lift them up." When he came down, he bent the heavens and descended without opening them. In the same way, when he was taken up, he entered not by the gates being opened but by their being lifted away.

By the same. "And be lifted up, eternal gates." He says "be lifted up" to these gates as to rational beings. They are spiritual, and they are not temporary, because they are immaterial and incorruptible.
"The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in battle," and so on. "Take courage," says the Savior, "I have overcome the world. Now the ruler of this world will be cast out."

"The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory," and so on. They called him Lord of hosts as commander of armies. It should be noted that those who have studied Hebrew matters closely say this: when the Seventy rendered into Greek the word "Sabaoth" found in the Hebrew, they sometimes put "Lord of hosts," sometimes "Lord mighty," and sometimes "Almighty." They say, then, that here too the "Sabaoth" in the text has been rendered as "Lord of hosts." But when "Sabaoth" is used of the Savior, it is translated as "Almighty." The word "Almighty" may fittingly be applied to the Savior. For if "all things came into being through him," and he is before all things, it follows that he is called Almighty.
PSALM 24

"Let those who act lawlessly without cause be put to shame," etc. It is also possible to act lawlessly not without cause. "To those without the law I became as one without the law": this lawlessness is not without cause. Turn the shame, Master, upon those who act lawlessly against us, who have done no wrong. For this is what "without cause" means.

"Make your ways known to me, Lord, and teach me your paths," etc. Whoever wishes to know the ways of the Lord, let him become meek; for "he will teach the meek his ways," it says. The meek are those who have brought to rest the ceaseless battle in the soul between anger and desire and the passions subordinate to them. "Make known to me, and teach" refers to realities. For he means to say: "Establish me in the enjoyment of your works," that is, "Lead me into what is your own." Hence he adds: "Guide me into your truth."

"Do not remember the sins of my youth and of my ignorance," etc. For a person does not confess in repentance the things in which he is still offending; so too the sins and ignorances of youth are no longer at work in one who has passed beyond youth. One might also call the instability of character "youth," when someone sins in ignorance until God grants such a person perception. For it is said, "to give shrewdness to the innocent." These words, however, do not fit David, of whom no sin of youth is recorded. Rather, he teaches all who have fallen into youthful sins to show them, like old wounds, to the one who is able to heal them through confession.

"According to your mercy remember me, for the sake of your goodness, Lord," etc. When human beings remember someone, they stir up within themselves the images of what they knew before. But when God remembers rational nature, he comes to be in it. For he is said to remember that in which he finds room. And he finds room first through the contemplation of the things that have come into being, and then also through the knowledge of himself.

"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he will give law to those who sin in the way. He will guide the meek in judgment, he will teach the meek his ways," etc. "For the law is not laid down for the righteous." For this reason, it says, since justice also belongs to him, he gives law to those who sin in the way; that is, he turns sinners back to godliness. Toward sinners, it says, he displays his justice, but toward others his goodness. Hence he adds: "He will guide the meek in judgment, he will teach the meek his ways."

"Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor," etc. The one who does and says everything for the sake of the knowledge of God keeps the eyes of his soul continually turned toward the Lord. If anyone has not received the spirit of adoption, and has not become a brother of the holy powers and of Christ himself, let him say that he is alone and poor, deprived of the riches of knowledge. But I think that David sings these words out of modesty; for God had revealed to him the unseen and hidden things of his wisdom.

"The afflictions of my heart have multiplied; bring me out of my distresses. See my humiliation and my toil, and forgive all my sins," etc. Not every toil takes away sins, but only the toil that is added to the practical life for the Lord's sake. "Be content, Master," he says, "with the afflictions that have been brought upon me, and cut short the penalty I am undergoing for the multitude of my offenses." A person is humbled when he is without boldness because of his awareness of his sins, and he toils for the fruits of repentance.

"Let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you," etc. Hope does not put to shame. For it is the daughter of proven character, and proven character is the offspring of endurance; and endurance comes from afflictions, which are brought about by the virtues, and the knowledge of God follows upon the virtues.
PSALM 25.
"Try my kidneys with fire," etc. The kidneys are a symbol of the passionate part of the soul, that is, of anger and desire; the heart is a symbol of the rational part.

"For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been well pleasing in your truth," etc. The one who understands what concerns mercy will say this, remembering the contemplation of mercy: "Your mercy, which I have contemplated, by being before my eyes, helps me to be well pleasing in your truth." For the mercy of God makes a person well pleasing in truth and not in pretense. This is the voice of one who is wise and contemplates the truth. Then he goes through the kinds of being well pleasing.

By the same. If the truth is Christ our God, as he said, "I am the truth," and David was well pleasing to God in the truth, then David was well pleasing to God in God. Therefore, he says, "I hastened to be well pleasing to your truth," that is, to you. For by periphrasis he calls God himself the truth of God.

"I have not sat with a council of vanity, and I will not go in with transgressors. I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly," etc. The council of vanity is heretical presbyters; the transgressors are lawless lay people. The assembly of evildoers is a heretical congregation, and the ungodly are heretical presbyters. "With these," he says, "I did not come together, nor did I mingle with those who transgress the divine law. Most of all I turned away from those who insult divine worship while supposedly gathering in a church; and besides these, from the ungodliness of idolaters, with whom I considered even spending time to be dangerous."

By the same. These words are to be addressed to [?] and to heretics. He set all this down wishing to show that he never took part in the festivals of idols, nor loved the splendors of the ungodly, nor was dazzled by the wealth of Babylon, but that piety and humility were his way of life.

"I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, Lord," etc. The rational altar of God is our mind, on which, with the fire cast upon the earth by the Father, we burn every irrational thought that strays from the Master's flock. When, then, the soul does not incline outward but looks toward itself and its own center, it goes around the altar of God, producing no corner that admits corruption; for "folly lurks in corners," says the wise Solomon. The altar is also the contemplation of bodies and of incorporeal things, in which the mind is purified; whoever goes around it, that is, has come to know it, recounts all the wonders of God.

"Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells. Do not destroy my soul together with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood, in whose hands are lawless deeds; their right hand is full of bribes," etc. I have kept my soul free from passion.

By the same. He says this as though even a righteous person could perish together with the ungodly. Abraham too says to God, "Will you destroy the righteous together with the ungodly? And shall the righteous be as the ungodly?" This text should be used with devout men or women who live with wicked people.
By the same. "Their right hand is full of bribes." Because they worked lawlessness, for this reason they filled their right hand with bribes.
PSALM 26.

"The Lord is my light and my savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" etc. The courageous person will say this, one enlightened by knowledge, such as the one who said, "Who will separate us from the love of Christ?" For if Christ is truly for us, everyone against us is brought to nothing. But if we do not take "my life" as referring to the one who said, "I am the life," but to life understood in the simpler sense, then the Lord will not be the protector of the martyrs' life. Paul too, when he said, "so that we despaired even of living," was speaking of the divine life. The one who says these things has not suffered cowardice out of his disposition. For "the cowardly, [?] the Lord, have their portion in the lake of fire." A blinded soul stumbles and fears everything, and will deny its confession of God; but when it is enlightened by God, it first beholds its champion and Savior, and after this takes courage against its enemies, whether men who do not know God or invisible powers, since it has the Son himself as its helper. For in this Hebrew word "my savior" the name of our Savior Jesus Christ is written, by means of the letters with which one would write "Jesus" in Hebrew characters.

"When evildoers drew near to me to eat my flesh, those who oppress me and my enemies, they themselves grew weak and fell," etc. When the tempters draw near to us to do us harm, wishing to eat the flesh that cannot inherit the kingdom of God, and to feed on the works of the flesh that we do when we sin—this flesh being different from the flesh that will see the salvation of God—and when they draw near to the righteous one to do him harm, then first they grow weak, and then they fall, since the very virtue [?] of the righteous one which they lay hold of punishes them and makes them grow weak and fall.

By the same. If we eat the flesh of Christ (for he says, "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood"), and the demons eat ours, then perhaps the demons also eat the flesh of Christ, striving to corrupt the virtues and true doctrines within us. For "to eat" is also used to mean "to destroy." "If you are willing," it says, "and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land; but if you are not willing and do not listen to me, a sword will devour you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." Here "will devour" stands for "destroys," since a sword does not by nature eat. Or else the demons are said to eat our flesh in the sense of eating what grows from the flesh. "Now the works of the flesh are evident," says the holy Apostle, "which are adulteries, fornications, licentiousness, idolatries," and so on.

"If an army is drawn up against me, my heart will not fear," etc. The army is of the same kind as the Legion that dwelt among the tombs. And perhaps the army of the adversaries is light [?]. But the heart, that is, the governing faculty, will not fear; since its mind is enmity toward God, as it is not subject to the law of God. "If war rises against me," and so on. In this respect it has been granted to hope irrevocably in the heart.

By the same. Let the practical person fight the foreigners by means of the virtues; the contemplative person, by means of true doctrines, tears down every height raised up against the knowledge of God. By "heart" he means the governing faculty, which will not fear. For perhaps it is the flesh, having grown weak, that will fear, since its mind is hostile toward God, as it is not subject to the law of God.

By the same. "If war rises against me, in this I hope"—that is, in the heart. "For I was enlightened in this help, of which I have had experience; hence I do not dread even another, greater battle line, since such help shelters me."

"One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his temple; for he hid me in his tent in the day of my troubles, he sheltered me in the hidden place of his tent; he lifted me up on a rock." We have learned that the house of the Lord is the name given to the Church of the living God, built of living stones. Since there is both the goodness and the severity of God, those who dwell in the house of the Lord will see the delight that is in God's goodness, while those who are outside the house will experience his severity. You will consider whether the temple of the Lord and the house of the Lord differ, and whether the house is the Church, by analogy with the Levites and the priests [?]. First one is hidden in the tent of God from the Lord in the day of troubles, then one is sheltered in the hidden place of his tent, and third one is lifted up on a rock. He asks, then, to dwell in the Church, by holding the mind of the Church, all the days of his enlightened life. "While I am on earth," he says, "even though I need many good things, for now I make one request. For it is not possible to come into all good things at once; only let this great and excellent thing not be lacking: 'to behold,'" and so on. The one who loves the beauty of the house of the Lord wishes to take delight in the sight, and after the contemplation to visit his temple. One beholds the delight of the Lord when one sees the lower doctrines of the Church; but when one approaches the teachings about the Trinity, one will gaze upon his temple. The beauty of the Lord is also the whole virtuous life of those who excel in godliness. "For he hid me," and so on. "My enemies," he says, "grew weak and fell; but I was hidden by his right hand, dwelling in a tent, because I was living in deserts and did not then have the house of God nor his temple. And in that time of persecutions he sheltered me." The hidden place of the tent is the innermost and inaccessible part, which they called the Holy of Holies. He does not say that the tent was in a place at all, but in a sanctified state of the soul, freed from all association with the many. "But he did not let me," he says, "remain hidden to the end; rather, wishing me to become useful to others as well, he lifted me up on the rock, Christ." It has also often been said elsewhere that the tent signifies progress, and the house perfection. No one, then, while the day of evils is upon him, can be in the house of God; but he is hidden in the shade, because progress shelters the one who is being freed from vice. For those who are still repenting cannot have perfection. Here too "evils" can be understood as adversities; the hidden place of his tent refers to discipline, and there we make progress. Some things are manifest, others mystical. So God does not [?] the one who is making progress in superficial things. He said "his" tent, since not all progress is according to God; and the rock of perfection succeeds progress. "He hid" fits progress, and "he lifted up" fits perfection. You might also call the tent the training given through the Law and the Prophets, in which God hides the one being trained in the mystical sense, lifting him up on the rock, Christ.

"For he hid me in his tent in the day of my troubles," etc. He calls Christ the tent, in whom God also dwelt; for "In the sun," it says, "he set his tent." And the Lord is the Sun of righteousness. For he also speaks from the temple [?]. "This," he says, "I had as a tent: shelter and help." For after he prayed in the tent of God and received the blessing of the loaves, he escaped the hands of those who were making war on him, at the time when Doeg, who tended the royal mules, informed Saul of his flight. "He sheltered me in the hidden place of his tent": that is, as if in a hidden place. "So," he says, "though my enemies searched for me a great deal, they did not find me, because God was sheltering me." And this is how "He hid me" is meant.

"And now he has lifted up my head above my enemies; I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of jubilation," etc. If the one who goes around offers sacrifice, and a sacrifice is a broken spirit, then the one who has broken his own soul has made it a circle, a shape having no corner that admits corruption, and [has removed] folly itself, which, says Solomon, "lurks in corners" [?]; and there is the saying, "Fire came down upon the children of Job and struck the four corners of the house."

"My heart said to you: I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will seek," etc. When someone's face seeks the face of the Lord, then with unveiled face he reflects the glory of the Lord, and having become equal to the angels, he will continually see the face of the Father in heaven. By the same. Through the things by which a person purifies himself, he shows that he is seeking the face of God, which the angels are said to behold continually.

"For my father and my mother have forsaken me," etc. Blessed is the one who has been forsaken by the devil and by his consort, wickedness, from whom he begets his lawless sons. Just as Paul through the Gospel begets the Galatians, so too the devil through wickedness begets the wicked. "Now that calamity has come upon me," he says, "and such an onslaught of so many enemies, neither father nor mother could have helped me; but you yourself, in place of all, have appeared as my helper."

"Give me your way as a law, Lord, and guide me on a straight path," etc. See how one who is in the law of Moses and in the letter, as not being on the way of the Lord, prays to be given the way of the Lord as his law.

"Be courageous, and let your heart be strong," etc. "Be courageous," that is, take up courage, not in bodily strength, but with your heart being strengthened; for in this way you will be able to wait for the Lord.
By the same. A courageous heart and soul is one that has no impure thoughts and no false doctrine.
PSALM 27.

"To you, Lord, I will cry; my God, do not be silent toward me," and so on. Among those who cry out to God and offer up their prayers, if someone asks for earthly things, his voice is small; but if someone asks for heavenly things, he cries aloud. That is why the Scriptures often say of the saints that they cried out to God. So let each of us try to pray to God crying out. I will say something even more paradoxical about how to cry out: he goes into his inner room, shuts the door, and in this way cries out to God. "Do not be silent toward me." God is recorded as having spoken to Moses, to Aaron, and to Joshua son of Nun, for they were the kind of people God would speak to. And through the prophets, while there was a people of God, he was not silent. Let us not suppose that God speaks to us from outside. Rather, the holy things that rise [?] in our heart are what God speaks to us. This is how to understand "God spoke … to so-and-so." [?] That this is so, hear Scripture itself bearing witness: "Blessed is the man whose help is from you, Lord, in his heart." We have another hearing, one that hears the word of God. The perception that Solomon calls "divine" is the one that hears the word of God, mingled and united with it. "My God, then," he says, "do not be silent toward me, or I shall become like those who go down into the pit." We know of none of the saints who dug a pit. Whenever a saint needed water, he dug a well. Solomon commands us to drink from wells, while the prophet threatens those who drink from pits, saying in the person of God: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken pits." "Never, then, be silent toward me, or I shall become like those who go down into the pit." But to see who those are who go down into the pit: holy Scripture says that divine things are hot, but the things of sin and of matter are cold. There too dwells the enemy of humankind, the dragon, who was called cold. For nothing on earth is as cold as the dragon. Every sin, then, is cold, but divine things, it seems, are hot: "He who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire"; and "I came to cast fire upon the earth"; and "fervent in spirit." Hear now how sinners are found by pits. In Exodus it is written: "God killed every firstborn, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on the throne to the firstborn of the captive woman in the pit." So those who go down into the pit are sinners and captives. But the good God [?] also proclaims release to them: "For the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind."

"Hear, Lord, my supplication when I pray to you, when I lift up my hands toward your holy temple," and so on. If a temple is that which holds God, and God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, then Christ is the holy temple. Toward him a person lifts and raises up his own soul through the virtues.

By the same. It seems to me that prayer differs from supplication, and the Apostle seems to me to set out several names for this difference when he says: "I urge first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made." As I see it, he means that prayer is greater than supplication, intercession greater than these, and thanksgiving greatest of all. I would say, then, that supplication belongs to someone who is still in need and still lacks something. But when I have understood the dignity of God and ask something from God, then I pray. And when I have become more fully his friend, then I give thanks to God. "When I lift up my hands toward your holy temple." We have often spoken about lifting up the hands. Moses lifted up his hands and Israel prevailed; when he let his hands down, Amalek prevailed. There is also "lifting up holy hands without anger or dispute," and "the lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice." I would say, then, that our hands are our godly actions. If we store up treasure in heaven, our hands are lifted toward God and we conquer the enemy. But when our hands come down, we are bound to be conquered. So when I lift up my hands to God, and through the hands of the soul am raised toward him, Amalek is conquered by me and is nowhere to be found. We must therefore lift up our hands toward God's holy temple. And the temple of God is the glory of God.

"Do not drag me away with sinners, and do not destroy me with those who work injustice," and so on. If either course is in our power, why did he ascribe the cause of good things to God? Or is it rather that God draws toward such people someone who is able to save them? That is why the Savior was called a friend of tax collectors, though he was in no way harmed by them. So he asks to acquire such a disposition. Or perhaps he refuses the company of the utterly sinful, such as those who say what they do not think [?]. For although the Savior was with a prostitute, she spoke peaceable words and did not think the opposite.

By the same. What need is there to say these things? Either you commit iniquity, and he destroys you along with them, and you say these things to God in vain; or you do nothing lawless, and God does not destroy you, for God is not so unjust. So let us venture an answer from the Gospel and say that God draws the righteous along with sinners. He draws the righteous man along for the sake of the sinners and those who work iniquity, so that they may be saved. Those who did not know this mystery accused Jesus, saying, "You eat and drink with sinners." Yet he was far from being harmed by them; indeed he benefited them. So too with anyone who imitates Christ and does this. But if someone who is not prepared and lacks the strength throws himself into such danger as to be with sinners and workers of iniquity, he will not benefit them and will destroy himself as well. Therefore here too the prophet wants to prepare himself so that he can be with sinners and workers of iniquity without being dragged away with them. Perhaps by saying this he also refuses the company of those who commit incurable sins. For he added: "who speak peace with their neighbors, but evil is in their hearts." They are utterly impious, for they are neither disposed as friends nor speak as enemies: they keep their enmity within themselves while feigning friendship with peaceable words. Nothing is more abominable than such people, and these the righteous man refuses. For you see that our Savior too was with sinners and with a prostitute, but not with one who spoke peaceably while having evil in her heart. Or else he prays, saying: Since destruction surely follows whoever does injustice, grant me righteousness and do not let me fall into injustice, so that I may not perish with those who practice it.

"Give to them, Lord, according to their works and according to the wickedness of their practices," and so on. He asks that they be afflicted by way of discipline, so that they may stop offending. By "works" he means their hidden works, for they spoke evil in their hearts.

By the same. We are taught by the word to put away all sins; for if we are not pure, we must be punished so that we may be disciplined. "According to the works of their hands," he says, "give to them," as if he were saying: render them their recompense according to the hidden part of their works. The discerning person, approaching things with knowledge, turns away from what is base as harmful and chooses what is good as beneficial. But the base person, charmed by pleasure, does evil without seeing the harm in it. Since, then, he does not perceive harmful things by reason, the saint prays that painful things be repaid to him according to his works, so that through these pains he may turn away from the evils that have become the causes of his punishment.

"Because they did not understand the works of the Lord and the works of his hands," and so on. The works of the Lord are perhaps the intelligible realities, while the works of his hands, I think, are the things perceived by the senses: "Did not my hand," he says, "make all these things?" Or perhaps the works of the Lord are the virtues, and the works of his hands are the principles of created things. "You will tear them down and not build them up." The Lord will tear down wicked habits and will no longer allow those who build them to build them up.

"And my flesh has flourished again," and so on. He called the soul "flesh" because it is joined to the flesh, as in "All flesh shall see the salvation of our God." Or perhaps it is the visible flesh that flourishes once it has put off the passions.

"Save your people and bless your inheritance; shepherd them and lift them up for ever," and so on. Here by "inheritance" he means the rational nature that inherits him. By the same. Christ himself will shepherd us who have believed in him, having sent in his place, and as himself, the Paraclete, who is the Spirit of truth. Moreover, he lifts us up from earthly things, that is, he makes us exalted for the ages to come that have no end.
PSALM 28

"Bring to the Lord, you sons of God," and so on. Saint Paul became a son of God through the Gospel. He too begot sons and brought them to God. He calls "sons" those who received great care from God and were wondrously saved, whom God spared as he would spare sons.

"Bring to the Lord the young of rams," and so on. Whoever gathers the scattered sheep of Christ, turns back those that have strayed, and finds those that were lost, brings the young of rams to the Lord; so does whoever acts so that people see his good works and glorify the Father in heaven. And whoever speaks of God in a word of wisdom brings glory to the Lord. Whoever has mercy on the poor, not out of grief or compulsion, brings honor to the Lord and thereby lends to God. For in Scripture "to honor" is used specifically in such cases too, as is clear from "Honor widows who are truly widows," and "Honor your father and mother." The holy court is the Church.

"The voice of the Lord is upon the waters," and so on. The voice of the Lord is simply upon the waters, but the Lord himself is upon many waters. Here the waters signify rational natures: "Let there be a firmament," he says, "in the midst of the water, and let it divide."

"And he will crush them like the calf of Lebanon," and so on. The calf of Lebanon is the evil one, who stiffened his neck against the Lord Almighty, threw off the yoke of the Gospel, and strove by force to be a god. "The voice of the Lord, who cuts through the flame of fire," and so on. The voice of the Lord quenches the fiery darts of the evil one. It is spiritual teaching [?], calling whoever has believed in Christ to a wise way of life.

"The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness; the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh," and so on. "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord." The wilderness is the rational soul deprived of God.
PSALM 29

"For the end: a psalm of a song for the dedication of the house of David," and so on. An upright life builds the house, and the knowledge of God dedicates it. "I will exalt you, Lord, for you have taken me up," and so on. That the psalm is spoken in the person of Christ is clear from "And you brought up my soul from Hades." But these things can also be said, more figuratively, in the person of the saint, indeed of every saint: he was, as it were, in Hades during the time of wickedness and was brought up from there by God when, helped by the Word and following him, he was made perfect. For no one can exalt the Lord unless the Lord has first [?] taken him up. When we are lifted from the earth, raised aloft and lifted up by the cross of Christ, who said, "When I am lifted up, I will draw all to myself," we exalt the Lord. He himself exalted the Father and, as far as lay in him, handed on the loftiest conception of him to those who believe in God. The psalm also teaches that certain invisible enemies of the human soul begrudge its salvation in God, lie in wait and plot against it, and then watch for any slip, stumble or fall that might befall it. If any of these happens to it, the enemies, as those who delight in evil, gloat over it; but they suffer the opposite when it shines out through its progress in God. So he gives thanks to God that he did not allow the enemies to gloat over his misfortunes, but honored him by raising him up from his fall [?]. And whoever speaks of God [?] and holds teachings befitting God also greatly exalts the Lord; and whoever raises up his own soul in every virtue and in a philosophical life exalts [?] it. "For you have taken me up." In place of "you have taken me up," Aquila says "you have saved." The sense is clear, since everyone who is taken up by God is saved from wickedness.

"Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me," and so on. These words are spoken in the person of the saint. But if the Savior says them, this too can receive a fitting interpretation. Believers are the body of Christ and members in part. If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, and if one member is glorified, all the members are glorified with it. Christ's body suffers in this way and needs healing. So with respect to our healing, there is nothing absurd in his saying: "Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me." For he confesses our sins as his own, as when he says in the twenty-first psalm, "Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions," and in the sixty-eighth, "Lord, you know my folly, and my offenses are not hidden from you." Both psalms are spoken in the person of Christ.

"Sing to the Lord, you his holy ones, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness," and so on. Since praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner, it is not just anyone who is commanded to sing to the Lord, but his holy ones, who can sing with the spirit and sing with the mind as well. But why was the Prophet not content to say, "Sing to the Lord, you holy ones," but added "his," as though there were holy ones who are not his? We answer that just as God alone is good without any qualification, so the Lord alone is holy without any qualification, as we find in the Song of Deuteronomy: "Just and holy is the Lord." But just as, with a qualification, there is a good servant, as in "Well done, good and faithful servant," and a good man, as in "The good man out of the good treasure of his heart," and what follows, so, with a qualification, there are the holy ones of the Lord.
By the same. Perhaps he is also urging to thanksgiving those who formerly lived among unclean things and afterwards came to remember his holiness.
By the same. Everyone who remembers God's love for humankind gives thanks to him.

"For wrath is in his anger, and life in his will," and so on. Just as wrath comes forth from what is called the anger of the Lord, so life is born from his will. And if life signifies knowledge (for "I am," says Christ, "the life"), wrath signifies ignorance. Death is the opposite of life; so wrath signifies death, indicating the loss of contemplation.
So it is well said: "Life and death are in the power of the tongue."
By the same. In anger that is stirred up there is readiness and wrath for retribution, but life is in God's will in the primary sense.

"But I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved," and so on. Whether it is Christ or a righteous man who says "I said," and then, after a pause at this point, "in my prosperity I shall never be moved," it is fitting for someone in prosperity to say that he will not be moved. In the Savior's case, however, as we have often said, it is his humanity that says this. But if, according to Symmachus, the reading is "in my tranquility," it can indicate the calm and untroubled state of the perfected soul; whoever comes to be in that state will never again be overturned. For whoever prospers spiritually will never be moved.

"Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty; but you turned away your face, and I was troubled," and so on. Another says: this is a voice of thanksgiving belonging both to Christ and to the righteous man. For besides the beauty of the Godhead already mentioned, the humanity of Christ and every saint have also shared in power, and they partake of these things by the will of God and by their own prior free choice. But if, as Aquila wrote, it is "to my mountain," Christ's mountain must be understood as his Church, which is most lofty and exalted. To this mountain might has been securely given by the Father in his good pleasure. The Church holds power, reigning over all else on earth and reigning together with Christ. And if, according to Symmachus, it is "to the forefather," who could be called the forefather of Christ or of the righteous man but Abraham? Might can be established for him, for his descendants, and for all the nations blessed in him, as the divine promises are fulfilled.

By the same. It is not absurd for Christ too, when the time of his passion had come, to say, "You turned away your face, and I was troubled," just as in the Gospel he says in one place, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" and in another, "Now my soul is troubled."

By the same. The angels continually behold this face. And if, as the wise woman of Tekoa says, the angels know all things on earth, then the face of God is the principles of things on earth, which bear the stamp of his creative Word.

"To you, Lord, I will cry, and to my God I will make supplication. What profit is there in my blood if I go down to corruption?" and so on. The person who longs only for heavenly things also cries out these words. What need have I, he says, for my body to thrive with an abundance of blood, when the corruption of death awaits me? Should I not rather discipline my body, so that the blood does not boil over and stir it to sin?

By the same. The Savior says these things when he sees us doing nothing worthy of the precious blood by which we were bought. For since some of those for whom he died persist in wickedness and impiety, the Savior's descent into corruption and the shedding of his blood seemed to have been in vain. By "corruption" he means the nature of the flesh that he put on, or the death he came to. You will say that he did go down to corruption, but did not receive from God to see corruption. "Will dust give thanks to you, or declare your truth?" Whoever has become dust by doing material things and minding earthly things, and persists in sin, will neither give thanks to God nor declare his truth, since he has gone astray both in conduct and in knowledge. For whoever bears the image of the man of dust, by being in the flesh and not in the spirit, is dust and is in Hades; that is why he will not give thanks to God. But whoever declares God's truth, having been appointed a teacher by him, cannot be dust; for whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. But if someone is dust and bears the image of the man of dust, he could not declare the truth of God.
By the same. The man of dust will not give glory. Christ is the truth; or perhaps he means the truth found in deeds.

"The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper," and so on. The Savior too might say these things, having been heard concerning those who share in him, since through him they were going to give thanks to God. Rejoicing over them, he says: I shall not be grieved (for that is what "I shall not be pierced" means), now that I have received back my glory. He says he has been shown mercy because we have been shown mercy [?], and because he has turned his mourning and lamentation over us into gladness. And at the salvation of those who are saved he says, "Lord my God, I will give thanks to you for ever."
"You have turned my mourning into dancing for me," and so on. Just as joy follows toil, so too the knowledge of God follows the practical life.
PSALM 30

In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me and rescue me, etc. It is as if he were saying: "May I not be put to shame for any part of the age, but may I be free of shame throughout the whole of it"; for some will rise to reproach and shame. What follows is the voice of one who is confident in himself. To be delivered by mercy is not the same as to be delivered "in righteousness": the latter shows boldness, while the former is not according to merit. Who, then, would boldly call God to hear his own words, as the one saying these things does? We should ask, and ask very quickly, not so much to be rescued from toils as from wickedness, so that God may rescue us from it before we are steeped any further in it.

By the same. God delivers us not only in righteousness but also in temperance, courage and love. Here, however, he has named righteousness, since it encompasses all the virtues. Or perhaps by "righteousness" he means Christ, for he "became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption."
Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge, to save me, etc. If God protects us, who is against us? We need God as our protector when the alliance of the angels is not enough for us.
By the same. The house of refuge is the knowledge of God.

For you are my strength and my refuge, and for your name's sake you will guide me and nourish me, etc. He guides through right faith and through the practical life, and he nourishes through knowledge of himself.

Into your hands I will commit my spirit, etc. He speaks as one under attack in his soul, for the saints take little thought for the body. Fearing to be wounded by the deceivers, he commits his spirit to God, calling God's providential powers "hands." The Savior too used this very saying when he was fixed to the cross. Scripture sometimes calls the mind "spirit," as when the virgin strives to be holy in body and spirit; sometimes the soul, as in "For just as the body without the spirit is dead"; and sometimes the conscience joined to the soul, as in "No one knows the things of a man except the spirit that dwells in him." The present passage may be understood in all three ways. As one taken captive by the enemy and redeemed by God, he called [?] of his way of life [?].
My eye was troubled by anger, etc. Nothing so darkens the mind as anger when it is stirred up.

My lots are in your hands; rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from those who pursue me, etc. The lots of righteous people are the contemplations known by the holy angels. By the same. "Flee fornication," says Paul. If fornication pursues, then clearly so do adultery, greed, anger, wrath and the rest.

Let the deceitful lips be struck dumb, which speak lawlessness against the righteous in arrogance and contempt, etc. The one who speaks deceit is done a kindness if he is struck dumb, for then he clearly casts off his deceit.

You will hide them in the hiding place of your face, etc. Just as the face of God hides the soul from the turmoil of men, granting it dispassion through the practical life, so too the tent guards the mind through true knowledge from contrary arguments and false doctrines.

Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful in a fortified city, etc. The dispassionate soul is a walled city. When the enemies tore down this wall, they came in to David along with Bathsheba; that is why in the psalm he also prays that the walls of Jerusalem be built.

For the Lord seeks out truth, etc. "Truth" stands for "the truthful." For he will fill the truthful mouth, that is, the mind, with laughter, meaning with knowledge. "And he repays abundantly those who act arrogantly." The Lord is patient with the arrogant, but those who act exceedingly arrogantly he also repays.
Psalm 31
Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered, etc. Iniquities are forgiven through holy baptism, but sins are covered through bitter repentance for sin.

Because I kept silent, my bones grew old, from my crying out all day long, etc. My bones grew old because I kept silent. Through crying out continually to God, the powers of the soul do not grow old but are always renewed, day after day. But when people keep silent, these powers grow old, taking on the old man, who is corrupted by deceitful desires.
I made my sin known and did not hide my iniquity. I said: I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord, etc. "The righteous man is his own accuser at the outset."
Do not be like horse and mule, which have no understanding, etc. By "horse and mule" he means the irrational movement of the soul. Understanding is rational discernment.
Many are the scourges of the sinner, etc. The many afflictions of the righteous are called the many scourges of sinners.
And boast, all you upright in heart, etc. If those who boast are upright in heart, then boasting in the Lord does not belong to everyone, since not everyone is upright in heart.
By the same. The upright in heart will have good reason to boast. It is also reasonable to boast in afflictions. Perhaps the one who boasts in afflictions is upright in heart.
Psalm 32
Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, etc. If our Lord is wisdom, and the righteous rejoice in the Lord, then the righteous rejoice in wisdom.

Give praise to the Lord with the lyre; sing psalms to him on a ten-stringed harp, etc. The lyre is the practical soul moved by the commandments of God; the harp is the pure mind moved by spiritual knowledge. The musical instruments of the Old Testament, understood spiritually, suit us as well: the lyre is figuratively called the body, and the harp the spirit. These are tuned in harmony for the wise man, who uses the members of the body and the powers of the spirit as strings, as is fitting. He sings well who sings with the mind, speaking spiritual psalms and singing to God in his heart. Or "ten-stringed" stands for "ten-sinewed," for a string is a sinew. So the body too is called a ten-stringed harp, as having five senses and five activities of the soul, each activity taking place through its own sense.

Sing to him a new song, etc. The one who is being renewed in the inner man would sing the new song, since he has put off the old man and put on the new, which is renewed according to the image of its creator.
He loves mercy and judgment, etc. That is, he is merciful and discerning.

By the same. He loves "mercy": both the mercy by which he shows mercy and that of those who show mercy. Likewise he loves "judgment": the judgment by which he judges, for the judgments of God are true, a great deep, and unsearchable. He also loves the judgment of the righteous, whose thoughts are judgments, and of whom it is said: "Judge righteous judgment." When he "makes the sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous," we see how the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.

He puts the deeps in storehouses, etc. The principles of the deep are in the storehouses of God. Let all the earth fear the Lord, and let all who inhabit the world be shaken by him, etc. This was fulfilled at the coming of God, when the whole earth was filled with the churches of Christ. Perhaps one might say: "You men, love; but let the earth fear." Those who inhabit the world, the churches of God, are not insensible to the Lord, and they are shaken by him, fulfilling the present command. Those who are moved by the word of God are shaken by him, since Christ lives in them.
By the same. Praiseworthy shaking is the transfer of a rational soul from wickedness and ignorance to virtue and knowledge.

For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created, etc. "Coming to be" signifies the bringing into being of rational creatures, while "creation" signifies the change from the better to the worse. For "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation": he is renewed.

The Lord scatters the counsels of nations, sets aside the thoughts of peoples, and sets aside the counsels of rulers, etc. The counsels of the nations, the thoughts of the peoples and the counsels of the rulers are set aside by the Lord, since they oppose his will. For he "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth."
He who alone fashioned their hearts, who understands all their works, etc. He who alone fashioned them alone also knows them. That is why God is rightly said to be the only one who knows hearts.

To deliver their souls from death and to nourish them in famine, etc. A person must first be delivered from death and only then be nourished. Through the practical life the Lord delivers a person from death, and through knowledge he nourishes him.
Our soul waits for the Lord, for he is our helper and protector, etc. The heart of the righteous does not rejoice in food or drink, but in righteousness, knowledge and wisdom.
Psalm 33

Of David, when he changed his face before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed, etc. He who showed his fleeing face not as fleeing but as sent away is the one who changed his face. Here "face" means the state of the soul, for it is one thing when fleeing and another when sent away. Scripture also often calls a man's word his "face," as when the angel says to Lot: "Behold, I have regarded your face, and because of this word I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken."
I will bless the Lord, etc. It is Christ, who lives at every time and is unchangeable, who says these things.
In the Lord my soul shall be praised, etc. I shall be praised in nothing else but in wisdom, for our Lord is wisdom.
I sought the Lord, and he heard me, etc. "For everyone who seeks finds"; but the one who seeks wrongly does not find.
Come to him and be enlightened, etc. We draw near through right conduct, and we are enlightened through knowledge. "Kindle for yourselves," he says, "the light of knowledge."
This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him, etc. The Lord does not hear everyone who cries out, but only those who cry out for the sake of the knowledge of God.
The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, etc. The angel of the Lord, though he is one, serves as a whole camp.
Taste and see that the Lord is good, etc. If the Lord can be tasted, he is tasted through faith; and if he is good, he is good through knowledge.

For those who fear him lack nothing, etc. If those who fear him lack nothing, how were the saints "destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, of whom the world was not worthy"? But even if they lacked food and drink, they certainly did not lack knowledge.
Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord, etc. From holy David we are taught what the one who fears God must do and say.
Turn away from evil and do good, etc. Fear teaches us to turn away from evil, and love to do good. That is why the one who loves is greater than the one who fears.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and he will save the humble in spirit, etc. If "the sacrifice to God is a broken spirit," and "the Lord draws near to the brokenhearted," then it is through this sacrifice and no other that the Lord draws near.
The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them will be broken, etc. Here "bones" means the powers of the soul, or the true doctrines that hold the life of the soul together.
The death of sinners is evil, etc. "Evil" means painful, bitter. He seems to call "death" the punishment that separates the soul from wickedness.
The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants, etc. A ransom is a gift given to the enemy by the defeated, or by one who cares for the defeated, for the deliverance and release of the captives.
Psalm 34

Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me; fight against those who fight me, etc. He knew that through the trespass of the Jews who wronged him, and the sin of the Israelites who fought against him, salvation would come to the Gentiles. So in effect he prays on behalf of the Gentiles when he asks that those people be judged and fought against.
