Perhaps, too, those who are judged and fought against here are made lighter in view of the judgment. All who do wrong wrong Christ, who is righteousness; and those who have no peace within themselves have wars and fight against Christ, who is our peace. The Lord judges those who do wrong by destroying the wrongdoing in them. In the same way he fights against those who fight the righteous man, and does so for the good of those he fights against, so that they may at last stop doing what is hostile to righteousness.
By the same. Nothing resists the demons so much as righteousness and knowledge.

Take hold of weapon and shield, and rise up to help me, etc. "He will take his zeal as his full armor, and will arm creation to repel his enemies. He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, and wear impartial judgment as a helmet; he will take holiness as an invincible shield, and sharpen stern wrath into a sword." It is these he means when he says, "Take hold of weapon and shield." And just as the righteous, once made perfect, beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles, so after the punishments God will refashion his full armor: his zeal into garments of peace, the breastplate into the long robe and the oracle, the helmet into the priestly turban, the shield into holiness in peace, and wrath into kindness. And it is a mark of goodness that the sword is not only drawn but also shut away. Or he means this: Take hold of the fitting shield and the weapon of truth, and "rise up to help me"; that is, become my champion. "Draw the sword" means "Bare it"; and "Close in against those who pursue me" means "Meet them and shut off their path, holding back their onrush with the sword."

By the same. If the victor in war enslaves his enemies, and Christ has conquered the world ("Take courage," he says, "I have conquered the world"), then Christ has enslaved the world, so that all may become servants of Christ.
Say to my soul: I am your salvation, etc. This very thing is the salvation of the soul: that the Lord should say to it, "I am your salvation." It could not be understood in this way of anyone else.

Let them be turned back, etc. Those who are traveling from virtue toward wickedness are done a kindness if they are turned back. "And let those who devise evil against me be put to shame." This shame is a praiseworthy passion, for it brings the sinner to awareness of himself.

Let their way be darkness, etc. By "the way of the ungodly" he means the wicked life along which they have made their journey. Let it become "darkness" for them, deprived of all light, and "slippery," so that they cannot even stand, while an angel of God pursues them. You see that the angelic powers are God's weapons.

Let a snare come upon him which he does not know, etc. Note that in these verses he has used imperative verbs instead of optatives, for each person is punished according to what he has done. Or rather, he has used them instead of futures.

And let the net that he hid catch him, and he will fall into the very snare, etc. I think he is speaking of the cross, into which the devil fell without knowing it. For if he had known, he would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
Rescuing the poor man from the hand of those stronger than he, etc. From this we learn that without the Lord we are not able to fight our enemies, for they are stronger than we are.
They repaid me evil for good, and childlessness to my soul, etc. A childless soul is one that has begotten nothing good, or has done good to no one.
And I humbled my soul with fasting, etc. Nothing humbles the soul so much as fasting. "And my prayer will return into my bosom." Here he calls the mind his "bosom."

They tempted me, they mocked me with mockery, etc. Unable to seize me by their temptations, they at least consoled themselves by jeering at me, and like wild beasts they gnashed their teeth at me, that is, their wrathful and irascible power. They wanted to devour me, but they failed.
Let not those who are my enemies without cause rejoice over me, etc. Those who are hostile to the righteous man because of his righteousness are hostile unjustly.
For to me they spoke peaceably, but in anger they devised deceits, etc. "For you will be," it says, "like gods, knowing good and evil"; this was a peaceable word.
Nor let them say: We have swallowed him up, etc. Paul too says of the man in Corinth who had committed fornication: "lest such a one be swallowed up by excessive sorrow."

Let those who boast against me be clothed with shame and disgrace, etc. Those who are baptized into Christ put on Christ, that is, righteousness and wisdom; but those who are baptized into Satan put on shame and disgrace.

And let those who desire the peace of his servant say continually: Let the Lord be magnified, etc. To magnify the Lord continually belongs to angels; to magnify him but not continually, to men; and to magnify him neither continually nor at all, to demons.
Psalm 35
There is no fear of God before his eyes, etc. For by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil.

For he dealt deceitfully before him, so as to find out his iniquity and hate it, etc. "Find out" stands for "recognize." But we must ask whether everyone who recognizes iniquity as iniquity necessarily hates it as well.

The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit, etc. Another translator says: "The words of his mouth are iniquity and toil," that is, burdensome, so that they cause weariness to those who listen to them. "He did not wish to understand." It is clear from what has been said that the lawless man is not such by his constitution; for not wishing to have the understanding to do good is a matter of free will. Besides this, "he devised iniquity," and what follows. This is like the saying: "Woe to those who work evil on their beds, and at daybreak they carried it out." In the same way, the one who devised iniquity while lying on his bed sets himself on every way that is not good, that is, on every wicked deed, not loathing his wickedness. Accepting it, though it is the worst of states, he begins in practice to walk every way that is not good.
O Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds, etc. Misled by this verse, some have declared that the things beneath the moon are not under providence; among them is also [?].

They will be drunk with the richness of your house, etc. This is a good drunkenness: "and your cup that inebriates, how excellent it is!" Since temptations are winter storms, the winter torrent of God's delight would be the reward for endurance in temptations, flowing like a river for those who are more than conquerors in them through Jesus Christ.

By the same. The one who does not sober up from this drunkenness does not act rightly; that is why it is said of the blameworthy drunkenness: "Sober up rightly, and do not sin." For with you is the fountain of life, etc. If the fountain is life, and life is Christ, then the fountain is Christ. "In your light we shall see light." In the contemplation of the things that have come to be we shall see Christ; or in the knowledge of Christ we shall see God.
Let not the foot of arrogance come against me, etc. If arrogance is the worst of states, how does it have feet? Perhaps he is speaking of the living being that works arrogance.
Psalm 3[?]
Do not be zealous over those who do evil, etc. Here by "zeal" he means imitation.

Reveal your way to the Lord, etc. "Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light"; he does not reveal his way to the Lord. First, "hope in the Lord and do good," and what follows; and when you have done this, again "hope in him, and he will act." And God, who sees in secret the righteousness done in secret, will bring it forth, at the time when he discloses the counsels of hearts; and the one who shines out at the judgment will have his judgment like the noonday.

Submit to the Lord and implore him, etc. This submission is the willing assent of rational nature to the knowledge of God. "Do not be zealous over the one who prospers in his way, over a man who commits transgressions." Here by "prospering" he means progress toward the worse; as also in the saying, "But evil men and impostors will progress toward the worse."

Cease from anger and forsake wrath, etc. Wrath is an anger of the soul's desire [?], above all for retaliation [?]; anger is an appetite for vengeance; and vengeance is the repaying of evil. "Do not be zealous so as to do evil." Do not look at their prosperity, but wait for the end, and you will see their destruction. For those who do evil will be utterly destroyed, etc. To be utterly destroyed is nothing other than to fall away from God.

And yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more, etc. The expression is ambiguous: either the sinner will cease to exist altogether (as those suppose who say, unsoundly, that the wicked are wholly destroyed), or he will cease to exist insofar as he is a sinner.

And you will seek his place, and you will not find it, etc. The sinner's place is wickedness. But the meek will inherit the earth, etc. Here the earth signifies knowledge; for the mind is said to be in contemplation as in a place. "And they will delight in abundance of peace." The delight of the righteous is abundance of peace, and abundance of peace is the soul's freedom from passion together with true knowledge of the things that are.
Better is a little to the righteous than the great wealth of sinners, etc. Better a little spiritual knowledge than an abundance of the wisdom of the Gentiles.

But the Lord upholds the righteous, etc. Nothing upholds the righteous man so much as a spiritual gift: "That I may impart to you some spiritual gift, so that you may be strengthened," says the Apostle.

The Lord knows the ways of the blameless, etc. Another translator has: "The Lord foresaw the days of the blameless." He not only upholds their life but also knows their coming days and the inheritance prepared for them. So a brief time of grief will do them no harm; for they are trained in endurance as they travel the narrow and hard-pressed way, and they are not put to shame in the evil time, when he brings wrath upon sinners. Even now the one group perishes for lack of rational food, while those who are God's will delight in him to the full.
And their inheritance will be forever, etc. The inheritance of rational nature is the knowledge of God.
They will not be put to shame in an evil time, etc. By "an evil time" he means the time of judgment. "And in days of famine they will be satisfied."

He calls "days of famine" those in which many of the impure are deprived of the bread who said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." Vanishing like smoke, they vanished, etc. This smoke is driven out of the rational logs by the fire that Christ came to cast upon the earth.

By the same. Smoke is the sign of a fire that has gone out. These too blazed up like fire and were quenched. Such are those who flared up against us. Sinners perish, not by the complete dissolution of their being, but by no longer being sinners.
PSALM 39

He brought me up out of the pit of misery, etc. The pit of misery is wickedness and ignorance. "And he set my feet upon a rock." The rock is faith in Christ. "And he directed my steps": through the practical life and through true doctrines.
And he put a new song into my mouth, etc. After we attain freedom from passion we sing a new song, since our house has been renewed.

Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, etc. The Epistle to the Hebrews says that these lines were spoken in the person of the Saviour, and so gives us grounds for understanding the whole psalm as spoken in his person.
Whole burnt offering and sin offering you did not require, etc. God does not seek burnt offerings that can be perceived by the senses; "for the sacrifice to God is a broken spirit."
In the head of the book it is written of me, etc. By "the head of the book" he means the whole Scripture of the Law; for all of it is summed up under one head: the prophecy concerning Christ.

To do your will, etc. He means the will of the Father, according to which he took away the sin of the world. "For I did not come," he says, "to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." And he was offered up for the sin of all, so that, once forgiveness had been granted, there would no longer be any need of a sacrifice for sin.

I proclaimed righteousness in the great congregation, etc. The great Church is the one made up of great and perfect members, in which he proclaimed the righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus. He knew this righteousness as his own [?], accepting it and making it his own, and proclaiming it without interruption. And he said, "I will not restrain my lips." Nor has he restrained them; he speaks even now through the evangelists and through the teachers of each age, whom one might call the lips of Christ. And concerning his righteousness, as being better than that of the Law, he charged them, saying, "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees."

My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was not able to see, etc. The memory of old failings naturally darkens our mind. "They have multiplied more than the hairs of my head." That is, the evils around us that go unnoticed multiply, and when many of them have come about, we lose the power of thinking rightly and are forsaken by our heart. The speaker begs to be guarded by mercy, remembering his former evils so as not to fall into the same ones again. And the remembrance of one's change for the better makes one grateful and attentive. Let those who seek my soul, to take it away, be put to shame and confounded together, etc. They do not take it away in its substance; rather, through wickedness they take it away from virtue and knowledge.
But I am poor, etc. Being weak in acquiring good things, he confesses himself poor and needy, and entrusts the care of himself to God, casting his anxiety on the Lord as on a guardian.
PSALM 40

Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy, etc. What is "he who considers"? He who understands. What is "the needy"? [?] Grasping his affliction. For the one who has learned of his affliction will surely and immediately have mercy on him. The one who considers the person poor in reason, in wisdom and in the good can be called blessed for helping him — whether the one who is poor in the ordinary sense, or the poor man who is called blessed. "In the evil day the Lord will deliver him": either the whole of the present age, as being one evil day, or the day of judgment. For that day is darkness for sinners and not light, according to the prophet. And the Apostle says, "Because the days are evil"; and again, "That he might deliver us from the present evil age." So he exhorts us to be kind to the needy, or to understand the one who has voluntarily become poor.

May the Lord help him on his bed of pain, etc. The bed of pain is the body of our humiliation. "You have turned his whole bed in his sickness." He will be brought over to better things, he says, and will undergo a change to good health. For it is Scripture's custom to use "turning" in place of "change," as in: "You have turned my mourning into joy for me."

My enemies spoke evil against me, etc. The invisible enemies of our Saviour wanted him to die, so as to extinguish the glory of his name; but besides its not perishing, at the name of Jesus every knee will bow and every tongue will confess. You might also say that he made this prayer on behalf of his disciples, who were, as it were, his soul, and who happened at that time to fall sick and to sin, when they all forsook him and went away, and Peter even denied him three times.

And if he came in to see, he spoke vain things, etc. The hidden and the visible enemies of Christ were contriving his death. Judas came in to see what was being done and what was said in parables, but he spoke in vain, since he was unable to grasp their meaning because of the wickedness that blinded him. The saying also fits all the heterodox who promise secret teachings. Or else, having already come to be outside the Saviour and the company of the apostles, he spoke in vain when he addressed the Lord as Teacher, while his heart gathered iniquity. And going out — that is, leaving the discipleship of Jesus — he spoke together with the Pharisees against the Saviour and secretly set the betrayal in motion. But the heart of anyone who reasons evil things and devises heretical ideas also gathers iniquity for him; and such a one, even if he receives [?], goes outside. Concerning such it is said: "But to those outside, in parables"; and, "God judges those outside."
Will not he who sleeps rise again? etc. He says that resurrection necessarily follows sleep. And sleep is death. Resurrection, then, will necessarily follow death.

But you, O Lord, have mercy on me, etc. He asks for mercy and resurrection not for himself but for us. "Raise me up" is said in a manner befitting a human being; "I will repay them" — that is, the enemies — in a manner befitting God. The enemy rejoices over those who are defeated. Then again he spoke in a more human way: "By this I knew that you have taken pleasure in me" — that is, in having mercy on me and raising me up; in other words, you loved me, for whatever is wanted is wanted in love. Once I have risen, the enemy of humanity, the devil, who brought in death through sin, will not rejoice over me. Or perhaps he is also hinting at the Jews. And "because of my innocence" — that is, my being undefiled — is also said in a more human way. We have been established in Christ, and this has been done before the Father forever.
PSALM 41

My soul has thirsted for God, etc. Those who are called blessed in the Gospel for thirsting thirst for God. He did not say, "My soul has thirsted God," for the soul does not drink God, but "for God." For the saint thirsts for the things that lead to God, just as the sinner thirsts for the things that do not lead to God but to worldly life, or to the devil. And the Saviour stood and cried out, saying, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." And he says this because only the saints will appear before the face of God, since God turns it away from sinners. Or else, since God had turned his overseeing power away from the people, they lamented the life here and wished to come to God himself. They said this having been cleansed of every blemish; for the one who is stained says, "Turn your face away from my sins."
By the same. If the angels continually see the face of God, then David desires to become an angel and to see the face of God.

My tears have become bread for me, etc. Those whose tears are bread are the ones who are blessed for weeping now. To be able to say this belongs to the perfect; for the imperfect person is troubled by external things and keeps his soul outside himself, unseemly and exposed to everyone's reproach, laying his soul bare through his words. But the saint gathers his soul in from external things. And the one who weeps from a genuine disposition will be fed by his tears as by bread, not only in times of ease, which he calls day, but also in times of hardship, which he calls night.
By the same. Most nourishing is the weeping that nourishes the soul. Blessed are those who weep now, for they will laugh.

While it is said to me every day, Where is your God? etc. God, as creator, is in all things that have come into being; as virtue and wisdom, he is in all the holy powers; and if virtue and wisdom are taken in the sense of potentiality, he is also in the opposing powers; and if partly in potentiality and partly in actuality, God is also in human beings. For always to act according to God belongs to angels; never to do so, to demons; sometimes to act well and sometimes not rightly, to human beings. To the question "Where is God?" one might reasonably answer: Everywhere except in your soul.

For I will pass into the place of the tabernacle, etc. The tabernacle of Moses in Exodus was, I think, a type of this one, and Solomon's temple a type of the true house of God. "For," he says, "I am still making progress and am not yet perfect." The tabernacle, a symbol of progress, wonderfully leads to the house of God itself, that is, to perfection, in which God dwells there. Those who keep the feast spiritually make their sound heard, exulting and giving thanks. Or he is saying this: I was comforting myself with such hopes, saying, "Why are you deeply grieved, my soul?" For I expected that the blessed end would receive me — the wonderful tabernacle of God and his innermost house, into which the saints will be brought, carried up by angelic powers. And if "there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents," is it not fitting that, when a soul is brought into the heavenly sanctuary after its training, there should be a joyful shout from a multitude celebrating the salvation of the one being saved? He gives thanks for these things as though they were already real. "Why are you deeply grieved," and the rest. So let us rebuke ourselves in this way when we are grieved and troubled. Since our God is the salvation of our face, "beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face as in a mirror, we are transformed into the same image."

Therefore I will remember you from the land of the Jordan, and of Hermonim, from a little mountain, etc. "Jordan" means descent; "Hermonim," anathema. He seems to be vexed and pained within himself as he recalls the miracle that took place at the Jordan under Joshua son of Nun, when the water was divided until the people had crossed the river, and what took place at the very small mountain nearby, because he does not now meet with the same providence as was shown then. Perhaps it is also a kind of characterization of the soul conversing with itself.

By day the Lord will command his mercy, and by night he will make it known, etc. Once, when Rabshakeh was besieging Jerusalem and blaspheming the God of the universe as unable to save them, 185,000 of the Assyrians with him were slain by a single blow in one night. Now God had said to Hezekiah on the day before that night, "I will defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant." Because the promise was given by day and the deed done by night, he says, "By day the Lord will command," and so on. And "a prayer to the God of my life" means that nothing comes between your command and my enjoyment of it; rather, he says, at once there is found in me thanksgiving sent up to God who has granted me life. And by night and by day, he says, knowing the mercy you supply, I sing and hymn.

By the same. He teaches that the good things belong to the age to come, calling it "day," in which, he says, God has promised his mercy for gladness; and that converse with God through hymns, and the earnest effort of prayer, belong to night and darkness [?].

I will say to God, You are my helper; why have you forgotten me? Why do I go about gloomy while my enemy oppresses me? etc. He does not ask not to be oppressed by the enemy, but, when oppressed, not to be gloomy. For this befits an athlete who is well-pleasing to God in hardships. And in the next psalm, by placing "Why have you cast me off?" before "Why do I go about gloomy?", he seems to show that what is characteristic of one cast off by God is not being oppressed by an enemy, but being gloomy while oppressed. If, however, it is Christ who speaks the words of the next psalm, he says similar things in the Spirit, thus: "But you have cast off and despised; you have put off your anointed." And he goes about gloomy, saying, "My soul is deeply grieved." Or else Christ speaks in perplexity, as if expressing something like this: What worthy end is achieved by my going about gloomy, cast off by you for the salvation of human beings, while the enemy oppresses me? While they say to me every day, Where is your God? etc. Perhaps what grieves the saint is the word "where" being used of God, since it signifies place. And it is the height of ignorance to think that God is in a place; for place goes together with bulk, and the Divine is free of bulk.
PSALM 42

Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an unholy nation, etc. Christ too asks to be judged by God; and to him, I think, refers the saying, "You will prevail when you are judged." One who is confident in himself and persuaded that, though wronged, he has never done wrong but has given place to wrath, says these words: "Against an unholy nation," and the rest. If it is the Saviour speaking, the unholy nation is the Jews; if it is the righteous man, he is speaking of the opposing powers. God delivers from an unjust and deceitful man when one suffers no harm from such people. "Deliver me from an unjust and deceitful man" refers to everyone who adulterates the word of God, and to the unjust man who makes a pretence of the things of faith.

Send out your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles, etc. "I am the light of the world," says the Saviour; and again, "I am the truth." Here the Seventy changed the tense and spoke of things that were to come as though they had happened. The other translators put it more clearly: "Send out your light and your truth, which will lead and bring us to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles." By "tabernacles" he means the temple, and by "mountain" he means Zion, to which he asks to return once he has obtained God's favour. By "light and truth" he means God's just and saving manifestation, just as by "darkness" he means calamities.

By the same. The light of God sent forth upon the soul of Jesus, and his truth, is the Only-begotten. For the light of God sent forth upon him will show that we have a great high priest, Jesus Christ the Son of God, clothed with it; and the present expression teaches truth, not type. These, having guided him, brought him to the spiritual holy mountain of God and to his true tabernacles, so that as high priest he might go in to the altar of God. Perhaps the "holy mountain" of God is the Father's house, and his "tabernacles" are the many dwelling places in it. Or his "tabernacles" are the eternal tents. You will ask whether the tabernacles are on the holy mountain, and what they are; whether they are those that lead to God himself, who gladdens his youth [?]. For he had no oldness. And the words "having put on the new self" are said on account of this youth. And the feast belongs to such as are young in this way.
By the same. The holy mountain of God is Christ; and his tabernacles are the holy powers in which he dwells.

To God who gladdens my youth; I will give thanks to you on the lyre, O God, my God, etc. In the eighty-third psalm too he says to the soul: "Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's." These words are narrative, addressed to us in between. Then he turns again to God, beginning with "I will give thanks to you on the lyre" — perhaps meaning on the body tuned by the Spirit.

Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him, the salvation of my face, my God, etc. The soul needs the reminder, "Hope in God." And he is the salvation of the face of everyone whose face is unveiled and who reflects the glory of the Lord, being transformed into the same image — that is, one that remains always alike — and above all of Jesus.
PSALM 43

"O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have told us," etc. The psalm is spoken in the person of those in the dispersion, or in the person of those from the Gentiles who believed, having received the word by hearing from Israel, to whom God appeared. What follows is said because of "Ask your father, and he will tell you." Yet whoever tells is a father.

"Your hand destroyed nations," etc. God destroys vice and ignorance, but he plants virtue and knowledge. "For every plant that God has not planted will be uprooted." By "nations" he means the five satrapies in Palestine: the Gittites, the Ashdodites, the Ekronites, the Gazites, and the Ashkelonites.

By the same. Then this is fulfilled: "Bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance." The nations of vice are destroyed before we are planted. The hand and the right hand destroyed, but neither the hand nor the right hand planted, for it was not a part but the whole that planted. And it was not the hand but the right hand that saved. Once Israel had been cast out, those from the Gentiles were planted in the divine Scriptures. Different names are given to a single subject: he calls the Savior hand, right hand, arm, and light. He is also the face of the Father, as the imprint of his substance. And the light sent from him into the minds of those called to redemption is the understanding given through the Spirit, which brings those who are enlightened to God. The meek inherit the earth without fighting; they do not inherit it by the sword either.

"For it was not by their sword that they inherited the land," etc. It is up to us to achieve virtue, with the power of God, but it is not up to us to be deemed worthy of spiritual knowledge. "You yourself are my King and my God, who commands the deliverances of Jacob," etc. These words would suit those among the people and the prophets, who confess that they are not saved by their own power. Jacob is the one by whom base things are supplanted. God gives commands to the holy spirits sent out for service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. There are many salvations, just as there are many lives.

"Through you we will gore our enemies with the horn, and in your name we will bring to nothing those who rise up against us," etc. The saints have been given horns by God, who is their horn. Indeed, Zechariah says, "He has raised up a horn of salvation for us." And merely by speaking your name, he says, we shall have the strength to bring them to nothing.

By the same. The horn of the soul is a pure mind. Through the practical life it gores its enemies, and through knowledge it brings to nothing those who rise up against it and oppose spiritual contemplation.

"In God we shall be praised all day long," etc. The blessed person is praised all day long in God, that is, for his own life, which consists of impassibility and the knowledge of God. But a person praised for some indifferent skill, as one who excels at it, or for progress among heretics, or for words of some other falsehood, will not be praised as blessed, and perhaps not all day long either.
"You have turned us back," etc. The virtues are said to be in front of us and the vices behind us. This is why we are commanded to flee fornication but to pursue hospitality.

"You have given us up like sheep for food," etc. For not all sheep are for food. And since you have given us up like sheep for food, "when men rose up against us, they would then have swallowed us alive." God thrusts people away from himself not always because of sin, but also for other reasons that he knows. Not everyone who is turned back suffers this blameworthily, but only someone who has fled from evil and then wishes to return to it. If someone has left Zion, that is, virtue, and is hurrying toward vice, which is called Babylon, then being turned back is a blessed thing for him. But those who are speaking here, since they have been turned and have come to be among enemies, have fallen backward in a blameworthy way.
"You sold your people for no price," etc. For we were sold by our sins, from which Christ redeemed us.

"You made us a reproach to our neighbors," etc. Those who hold doctrines close to ours are neighbors; the others are those round about. "You made us a parable among the nations" (for those from the Gentiles hold Israel as a parable, and as in a parable they look in it for the solution to their own affairs) "and a shaking of the head," that is, of Christ. Those people came to be "among the peoples."
"And the shame of my face has covered me," etc. When we sin in thought we are ashamed before ourselves, but when we offend in deed we are ashamed before other people.
"At the voice of the one who reproaches and slanders," etc. This should be said with reference to those who endured in persecutions.
"And we have not dealt unjustly with your covenant," etc. Whoever sins knowingly deals unjustly with God's covenant.
"And our heart has not turned back," like Lot's wife's, or that of the one who put his hand to the plough, or rather that of those who turned back in their hearts to Egypt.

By the same. Everyone who does not live according to God's covenant wrongs it. We have come, he says, by the opposite path from the others. They were tripped up even before the terrors came, but we stand firm even after the terrors, keeping our resolve unshaken. What does "We have not dealt unjustly with your covenant" mean? That is, we have not acted unjustly in what was entrusted to us, but have kept it with care.

"For you humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us," etc. The place of affliction is the human body and the world that is akin to it. You have made us live in a foreign land, he says, and this did not allow our acts of worship to be performed.
By the same. The mind is covered by the shadow of death when it does not see. Or the body of humiliation is the shadow of death, since it is born in death's shadow.
"If we had spread out our hands to a foreign god," etc. If someone is not essential knowledge, or does not have this knowledge in himself, he is a foreign god.

"For your sake we are being killed all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter," etc. Paul says: "I die every day, I swear it by my boasting in you, which I have in Christ Jesus." Why does he say "for your sake"? Because we could have changed sides, abandoned our ancestral way of life, and been safe. But we choose to suffer harm and keep our ancestral ways rather than enjoy peace and lose our ancestral heritage. God's strength is worth marveling at, since he preserved those who were exposed like this as sheep for slaughter, and did not let those who were dying every day fall into death. "Awake, why do you sleep, O Lord?" etc. Christ was once sleeping in the disciples' boat, but when a storm arose the disciples woke him. The passage shows that when a storm of thoughts arises in the soul, whether of anger, injustice, gluttony, or pride, we should awaken love, justice, temperance, self-control, humility, knowledge, and wisdom.

"Arise, O Lord, help us, and redeem us for your name's sake," etc. They might say such things to the Savior while he remained in the heart of the earth at the time of his passion. He gave his life as a ransom for many and does these things for the glory of his name.
PSALM 44

"My heart has poured forth a good word; I tell my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe," etc. He said "poured forth" in place of "uttered." He does not mean to call the Son an outpouring, but the account of him. The person speaking would be David. For if the Father were the one telling his works to the Son, the Son would turn out to be ignorant, and later than the works.
By the same. A good word is one that signifies virtue and knowledge of God.

By the same. The tongue of everyone who tells his works to the king is the pen of a swift-writing scribe. A person with a good conscience declares his own brave deeds. But someone who is conscious of the opposite in himself is slow of tongue when he tells his works to the king.

"You are fairer in beauty than the sons of men," etc. These words are spoken in the person of the prophet, whose tongue was the pen of a swift-writing scribe. Grace was poured out on the lips of the imitator of Christ and of Christ himself. This was not only because of the words of grace that came from his mouth, but also because of the grace of the forgiveness of sins, when he said: "Your sins are forgiven."
By the same. He compares spiritual wisdom and the Word of God with worldly wisdom and human speech.

"Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one," etc. This sword separates the soul from vice and the mind from ignorance. It destroys what is called the old man and makes a new one in Christ according to the image of the Creator.

By the same. Perhaps "the thigh" is a symbol of birth. Then what is said amounts to this: "Join to your birth what destroys [?] the enemies." And clearly the birth of Jesus became a sword against his enemies. Or the word that dwells in a life of purity and destroys the passions is said to gird a sword on its thigh. Jesus was the first to do this, since in Christ there is nothing slack or loose. This is how you will understand "draw taut." And his right hand guides the Savior and his saints.

"For the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness," etc. The truthful, the meek, and the righteous are ruled as king by Christ. "And your right hand will guide you wonderfully." The right hand of God is God the Word who is in him.

"Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you, in the heart of the king's enemies," etc. Christ's arrows are the practical virtues. With justice he shoots the unjust, with prudence the foolish, with courage the coward, with self-control the licentious, with patience the irascible, and with faith the unbeliever. The arrow of faith is sent ahead of the others, for one must first believe that God exists.

By the same. Whoever ably pleads for the truth and powerfully pulls down falsehood has sharpened rational arrows. Those who fall beneath Christ are in the heart and the thoughts of the enemies of Christ, who is king. Christ is clearly God. Perhaps it is possible to do righteousness and abstain from lawlessness out of fear of God, without doing so out of love for God and what is right [?] or out of hatred of lawlessness. But Christ is not like that.

"A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom," etc. The rod of Christ, which he uses to punish sinners, is called a rod of uprightness because it straightens those under his rule and frees them from all crookedness. And since he punishes with it by royal authority, it is the rod of his kingdom.

"Daughters of kings are among your honored ones. The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in garments woven with gold, adorned in many colors," etc. The holy disciples received the kingdom of heaven and became kings. This is why the souls begotten by them in virtue are called daughters of kings. All these souls, united in faith and virtue, together make up one queen standing at the right hand of Christ God. For now the Church of God has garments interwoven with gold, since she knows in part and prophesies in part. But when the perfect comes and the partial is done away with, then she will have garments of pure gold. For the garment of a rational nature is the manifold wisdom of God.

"And incline your ear," etc. The Father says "Incline your ear" to the Church. Forgetting is praiseworthy here, since it is what makes the king desire the beauty of the one who forgot. Further, the source of the Church's glory lies in the hidden part of the heart. Her glory is within, in true garments that accord with the wisdom of God, and in a conscience full of boldness. This is why it is said of her: "All the glory of the king's daughter is within." Her glory is the kind of glory a king's daughter would have. Here "king" refers to God. Her garments too are many-colored, according to the virtues. "All the glory of the king's daughter is within," etc. All the glory of our Church is in the inner man, and it is seen in virtue and knowledge.

"Virgins will be brought to the king after her; her companions will be brought to you," etc. The undefiled and pure souls, who are virgins for that reason, will go forth and be brought to Christ in gladness and rejoicing. The chamber of the king, that is, of Christ, is also his temple, since he is also God. And in place of the patriarchs, the apostles have come to be.
By the same. Our neighbors are either all human beings, or those who do not fully agree with us in doctrine.

"In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you," etc. In place of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others who pleased him under the Old Covenant, the disciples were born, and so were we who believed through them and inherited that faith and knowledge. For the inheritance of a rational nature is the knowledge of God.
PSALM 45

"God is our refuge and strength," etc. God alone is a refuge, so let us flee to no one else. If whoever is able is able by power, and God is the power of the saints, then the saint is able by God. God is also a helper in afflictions, so that we may boast in them as we endure them. Note the words "Many are the afflictions of the righteous": these are different from the scourges of sinners. And because the way that leads to life is narrow and hard, and few find it, perhaps it is afflictions that find the righteous. "Therefore we will not fear," and what follows. At the consummation, sinners, who are earth, will be troubled, but the saints, who are mountains, will be carried away as Enoch was carried away. Israel too, being a mountain, has been removed because of the Gentiles. "In his might" applies to both clauses, so that it reads: "Therefore we will not fear when the earth is troubled and the mountains are removed" in his might.

By the same. When we flee fornication, we take refuge in chastity; when we fight against gluttony, we fight alongside self-control. If we flee to it, it is called a refuge; if we make war together with it, it is called strength.
"Therefore we will not fear when the earth is troubled," etc. Here by seas and mountains he means rational natures that exalt and lift themselves up against the knowledge of God.

"The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God," etc. The rushing streams of the river correspond to the varieties of gifts and the varieties of ministries. The city of God is helped as day draws near. Another reading is "He will help her countenance," for he keeps her beauty unharmed when she is troubled by her adversaries.
By the same. The city of God is either the Church or the rational soul itself. The rushing streams of the river are the gifts of the Spirit.

"Nations were troubled, kingdoms bowed down," etc. At Christ's coming the kingdoms bowed down. "Christ uttered his voice, the earth was shaken." This means those on the earth, as Churches were established everywhere.

By the same. If a rational soul hears the voice of the Lord, it is shaken, moving from vice to virtue and from ignorance to the knowledge of God. When divine help appeared, he says, the enemies turned their backs. The kingdoms that had long held contrary views bowed their necks to the divine and saving yoke. For God used, as if it were a voice, the truth, the testimony of events, and miracles of every kind, and so showed human beings his own loftiness.

"Making wars cease to the ends of the earth, he will break the bow and shatter the weapon, and burn the shields with fire," etc. "Making wars cease" can be said because the wars that had previously been continual were stopped by the Romans. After the Savior's birth, they brought the many kingdoms that had existed before under a single kingdom. For there came "glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men." So the Lord Jesus worked wonders on the earth, making the wars that people had been waging cease to the ends of the earth. In making the wars cease, he broke the bow from which the devil's fiery arrows were shot, shattered his weapon, and burned up his shields. And "I will be exalted" is the voice of God saying these things after the wars to the ends of the earth have been made to cease, the bow broken, and the weapon shattered.
By the same. Here by bow, weapon, and shield he means a most wicked condition and evil thoughts.
"Be still, and know that I am God," etc. Stillness is needed for [?].
PSALM 46

"All you nations, clap your hands," etc. Let our hands, as it were, send out a voice of exultation from good works. For whether we are shouting or doing anything else, we do it either for God, when it is in accord with God, or for the devil, when we practice vice. In the same way we sing both to God and to Christ the king. "With a voice of exultation" applies to both, so that it reads: "Clap your hands to God with a voice of exultation." This can mean any action in accord with God, which is followed by exultation; the opposite is followed by weeping. In former times he was not Lord over all the earth. He was most high to few, terrible to a small number of the devout, king to not many, and great to rare individuals such as the great Isaac and the great Moses. But now he is all these things to far more people, and in the end he will be all in all without qualification. Formerly his name was great over Israel alone, but since the coming of Christ he is great over all the earth. For God is now king of all the earth, since God has come to reign over the nations.

By the same. People naturally clap their hands at victories. So let us too clap at the victory of the one who said: "Take courage, I have conquered the world." A shout is a song of victory. So he urges the nations to shout at the downfall of the opposing powers.

"He subjected peoples to us," etc. "He subjected peoples" means those who are being instructed in the mysteries of Israel. The apostles will say this about those who are being made disciples, who are many. Since we did not know how to choose for ourselves what we would inherit, our Lord himself chose for us a portion to inherit: the beauty of Jacob, which the Lord loved.
By the same. He gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.

"God went up with a shout," etc. Just as the Lord will come "with the voice of an angel, and will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God," so God went up with a shout. The Lord also went up "with the sound of a trumpet," and perhaps with the shout of all the nations, who clapped their hands and shouted to God with a voice of exultation. I think that God goes up through these as well. And if anyone praises him with the sound of a trumpet, then the one who goes up with the sound of a trumpet will go up in that person too.

"Sing praises to our God," etc. Praises are sung to God in both cases, because "God is king of all the earth." "With understanding" is the same as "sing praises with the mind." It is also an exhortation to knowledge. And he began to reign at the coming of Christ. The holy throne of God is those whom he rules, in whom God is seated.
By the same. Singing praises belongs to one who is cheerful in a godly way, as it says: "Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praises."
"God sits on his holy throne," etc. The throne of God is Christ, and the throne of Christ is rational nature.

"The rulers of the peoples were gathered with the God of Abraham, for the mighty ones of the earth belong to God; they were greatly exalted," etc. All who are gathered with Abraham have the knowledge of Abraham. "Were gathered" stands for "will be gathered." For on the basis of what has already happened, he says, the rulers of all the nations will be gathered together with us to sing hymns to God, and they will praise him.

By the same. If anyone is mighty on the earth, he belongs to God, for the weak person is not yet his. One who is mighty on the earth is one who has grown strong against the mind of the flesh. Among the mighty on earth there are some who belong to God, who were exalted not simply but greatly. But surely they were not exalted beyond measure?
PSALM 47

"Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised," etc. Where the majesty of the Lord is contemplated, there above all the Lord is great and praiseworthy in the city of God, praised by those enrolled as its citizens. If, then, the Lord is above all great and praiseworthy in the city of God, what else could the holy mountain of the Lord be, "well-rooted, the joy" not only of part of the earth but of the whole of it, than Christ, rooted in the Father, at whose coming the whole earth rejoiced because of the churches of God established everywhere in his name? Perhaps the reading is not "well rooting" (for that makes no sense) but "well-rooted," meaning having a good root that matches the branch.

"Well-rooted, the joy of the whole earth, the mountains of Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King," etc. The well-rooted joy is Christ. For "My joy," he says, "deliver me from those who surround me." And his root is God the Word, who is in him.

By the same. The mountains of Zion, the sides of the north, are the city of the great King. In this sense it can be said in the Gospel that Jerusalem belongs to the great King, as here: "The mountains of Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King." And just as the high priest is called "great" to distinguish him from the priesthood under him, so too the King is called great; for he is King of those who reign.
"For behold, the kings of the earth were gathered together," etc. So that all may say the same thing, and there may be no divisions among them.
"With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish," etc. Tarshish means "of the sea." Tarshish is also said to be a part of Ethiopia, and in Jonah the city of Tarsus is called Tarshish.

"As we have heard, so have we also seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God," etc. Outside the city we heard; having come into the city, we saw what we had heard before. And having come into the midst of your temple, we received your name at the coming of Christ. Their praise was worthy of the name of God.
By the same. Whatever we hear about God through faith, we come to know through a pure life, receiving through freedom from passion the proofs of what we have believed.
"Your right hand is full of righteousness," etc. Christ is the right hand of God, filled with righteousness. Therefore "from his fullness we have all received."

"Let Mount Zion be glad," etc. Mount Zion is glad, and the daughters of Judea rejoice because of the judgments of God, as they contemplate their reasons and the works done according to those reasons. And those who have understood Zion encircle her and embrace her; and having climbed her towers, they tell from above those who have not yet been able to climb her towers, saying: "Set your hearts to perceive her power," so that each one, by the life he leads in what he does, may receive a memory worthy of the division of the city. Or it may be taken thus: since the mind of the Church keeps watch for the truth, and is for this reason called Zion, we must embrace her doctrines in our thought. Having therefore understood her teaching with true knowledge, examine each part one by one. For her palaces are the particular contemplations in which the doctrines of piety dwell. And since the former generation, which received the city and its power, was shown to be wicked, by giving heed to the power of the city and dividing up her palaces you will come to know about the calling of the saints, which is another generation besides the former one, if indeed you will also tell that this is God, who did the wonders described above, casting off the former generation, since he is eternal and always remains the same. And he will shepherd us, according to the saying: "The Lord will stand and see, and will shepherd his flock in strength."
"And divide her palaces," etc. These words are fulfilled in the disciples, who divided the inhabited world among themselves in order to proclaim that Christ is our God, who shepherds us.
PSALM 48

"For the end; a psalm for the sons of Korah. Hear these things, all you nations," etc. The title can refer to the victory of each of those who are victorious in the contest. The word "Hear" is the voice of Christ calling all the nations, who said, "Come to me, all you who labor." And since from the letter of the Scriptures the simpler person, someone earthborn and poor, is built up, while the one who can pass over to spiritual things, being a son of man and rich, benefits more, for this reason he calls all of them together at once to hear, as to a banquet. The calling of rich and poor alike summons us to equality and humility [?]. He named three things in opposing pairs: nations and earthborn, rich and poor, world and sons of men. Those who are strangers to the faith are referred to by the word "nations." Those in the Church are the ones who inhabit the world.

"My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding. I will incline my ear to a parable; I will open my riddle on the harp," etc. The mouth of Christ speaks wisdom. The mouth of Christ is those who serve his word, and the others are the rest of his body. And if the meditation is understanding, what is promised? When the meditation of the heart is understanding, evil thoughts do not come out from within the heart, nor are there the things that defile a person, nor is any room given to the devil. Clearly the Savior calls those who listen with understanding his own ears. Another might say that he speaks wisdom in the New Testament, but hears it as a parable in the Old. Christ opens his riddle, which is shut up in obscurity, when he finds a well-tuned instrument and a chosen vessel, which he calls a harp; for through such a one he opens and makes clear what is shut up in obscurity for those who are not such. The apostles too could say these things.

By the same. The one who is cheerful sings psalms, and through the harp he opens the riddle. Through cheerfulness he discerns the riddle. And cheerfulness is the freedom from passion [?] of a rational soul.

"Why should I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me," etc. He says these things not about himself but about the Jews, out of concern for them, since they are to be judged and most of them have done things deserving punishment. And if the speaker is Christ, you will find that his heel is Judas, the lowest member of the body and the nearest to the earth; for the apostles are the body of the Lord. So: I do not fear the betrayal of Judas at the time of the cross; just as no one fears the disobedience of Adam (for this is what we suggested the heel of iniquity to be). For no one is condemned for another's wickedness. He called Adam's disobedience the iniquity of the heel because the serpent has power against his heel. Or else: since the apostles were not such, nor the prophet who says these things, that it could be said of him, "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth," it is likely that he had sinned only in the least and lowest things. That is why Symmachus rendered it "the iniquity of his footprints." For only faint traces, as it were, of iniquity were left in them; and therefore he says, "I do not fear the day of judgment." And the heel of Christ is the lowliest of all the faithful.
By the same. By "the evil day" he means the day of judgment; and by "heel," one's way and life.
"Those who trust in their power," etc. "A man will not give God a ransom for himself, nor the price of the redemption of his soul"; for Jesus gave himself up for all.
"A brother does not redeem; will a man redeem?" etc. It should be read as a question: "Will a man redeem?"

"And he labored forever," etc. The one who toils through his whole age and through life here will at the end live the true life, [not] seeing corruption. When the wise die, the foolish and the senseless will perish together.

By the same. The one who labors in the practical life will live to the end in knowledge. Having attacked the unrepentant, he turns also to those who repent, and consoles the toil of repentance with the hopes of what is to come. He labored here, he says, in repenting, and from now on he will live forever. For that is what "to the end" means. By "life" he means life in the proper sense, life without toil; for life here is called life only loosely. By "end" you should understand the age to come, which is the end of the present one. Symmachus puts it this way: "Having rested in this age, he will go on living forever"; and Aquila: "And he rested forever, and he will live to victory." For whoever has led a toilsome and laborious life here will be counted worthy of the promised life in the age to come, and will not see corruption when the wise die.

"For he will not see corruption when he sees the wise dying; the foolish and the senseless will perish together," etc. We shall see the wise of this world, in the age to come, deprived of the Life that said, "I am the life." And who are these wise who die, if not those of whom it is said, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise," from whom God hid the mysteries that he revealed to infants? He calls "wise" the crafty, according to the saying, "They are wise in doing evil," and the disciples of the rulers of this age. Their death will not be seen by the one who has been redeemed by him who was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching. The one who is fully convinced about the coming judgment, when he sees the wise dying, will not consider what happens to be the corruption of soul and body together, as they defined death while they lived, but a migration to another world.

"And their graves are their houses forever," etc. "Those who are like whitewashed tombs, full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness": these the Savior accuses; and those who build tombs, even of prophets; and those who adorn monuments, even of the righteous. He does not allow a disciple to bury a dead man, even his father. And in Isaiah he says, "Why have you built yourself a tomb, and hewn yourself a monument?" And those in the tombs, if they hear the voice of the Son of Man, will live. The names of the senseless and the foolish are upon the lands.

By the same. The tomb of the mind is an impure soul; and the tomb of the soul is the body. "They called their names upon their lands." They are named not after virtues but after earthly things. For they are not called just and temperate, but orators, grammarians, philosophers, tribunes and counts.

"And man, being in honor, did not understand," etc. The man who does not understand while he is in honor has compared himself to the beasts and become like them, and sometimes even like those that differ from them. By what he does, each person makes himself like something. And it is good to become like God. "This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them": that is, the way of the foolish and the senseless. And Christ is a stumbling block, being a rock of offense. "They will be well pleased with their mouth." I think this points to a good end for the foolish and the senseless.
"And afterwards they will be well pleased with their mouth," etc. That afterwards they will be well pleased is a good hope.

"They are laid in Hades like sheep; death will shepherd them," etc. Death will shepherd the foolish and the senseless, or rather the man who does not understand his own honor. Clearly the one who said, "You will not abandon my soul to Hades," also says this: "But God will redeem my soul," and what follows.

By the same. Life shepherds the angels; death and life shepherd human beings; but death alone shepherds the demons. "And the upright will have dominion over them in the morning." For in the age to come the upright will be over five cities and over ten cities. Solomon too says the same thing in Proverbs: "For an envious man hastens to be rich, and does not know that the merciful man will rule over him."

"Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich," etc. Woe to those who are rich with this kind of wealth; for no one will take it with him when he dies. "Nor will the glory of his house go down with him." Unbelievers seek this glory, which will not go down with them. The one who dies will not take with him the increased glory of his house. Rather, the virtuous man who ascends will have his glory, that is, his virtue, ascend with him; and the one who descends will have it descend with him. And the soul of the holy one will be blessed in his life, which is Christ. Whoever is holy will give thanks to God, who does him good.

"And man, being in honor," etc. We must ask what nature belongs to the man who is in honor and does not understand. If he is spiritual, how is he made like the beasts? If he is earthy, how is he in honor? And if he is of the soul, then if he is in honor, in what is the spiritual man?
PSALM 49

"The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken," etc. "The God of gods," having "spoken" through Christ, "called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting": from the rising, Israel; from the setting, the most lowly-born.

"Out of Zion comes the splendor of his beauty," etc. If the splendor and beauty of the Lord is wisdom, this wisdom is in Zion. He is the one at whose birth we say "Emmanuel"; he came openly and does not keep silent, but speaks through whomever he wills, since he is our God. Here, he says, "he will not keep silent"; but further on, "These things you did, and I kept silent." "A fire before him": "For I came," he says, "to cast fire upon the earth." And in Daniel: "A river of fire flowed before him." Fire and storm are upon those who do not heed his appearing and the Word, who will come from the heavenly Zion, being equal in power to the Father; for he was the heavenly God even when he came openly, that is, when he became flesh. For then he became visible; having come, he will not keep silent, but will convict the world of its sin, that is, he will announce the will of the Father. For he is called "the angel of great counsel." The fire signifies the light that comes from him; for the spiritual light that comes through faith leads the way to the knowledge of Christ. You may also understand it this way: being in the authority and power of the Godhead, even though he had come in the flesh, he fell like a fire and a storm upon those opposed to him, the devil and the demons.
"God will come openly, our God, and he will not keep silent," etc. Our God will come openly; and our God is Christ; so Christ will come openly.
By the same. Christ has come in the flesh. So "openly" refers to the flesh; for the flesh of Christ could be perceived by the senses.

"He will call to the heaven above," etc. In Deuteronomy, when the law was given, Moses called heaven and earth to witness; likewise, at the beginning of his song he calls upon them; and they are invoked in Isaiah too. For this reason, when the people is judged, God will summon heaven and earth. Here "to judge" means to separate his own, who are his people, from those who are alien to him and graze together with his own, so that he may give his own to heaven and the aliens to the earth. He will summon the angels in heaven, and those chosen on earth for the apostolate, to separate his people. For the apostles brought to God those who obeyed, but handed over to Satan those who did not.

"Gather to him his holy ones, who make his covenant with sacrifices. And the heavens will declare his righteousness, for God is judge," etc. Either the heavens are those who bear "the image of the heavenly one." Or this clearly refers to the separating of the Lord's people by the rational powers and by those who serve as priests of the saving proclamation, who also gather his holy ones to Christ: "those whom he foreknew," he says, "he also predestined; and those whom he called, he also justified"; and these fulfill the covenant not with blood but with spiritual sacrifices.
By the same. Here he plainly calls Christ God. "For the Father has given all judgment to the Son."

"I will not reprove you for your sacrifices," etc. These things may fittingly be taken as a prophecy about the sacrifices set aside among the Jews after the coming of Christ. Or: Do not offer with an evil disposition, he says, for which I reproved Cain.

"For all the beasts of the field are mine," etc. He says that all things are under the providence of God. "Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall without my Father in heaven."
"Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?" etc. He abolishes material sacrifices; for "a sacrifice to God is a broken spirit."

"But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my ordinances?" etc. I think God said these things not only to the sinner understood in the simpler sense, but also to the people of the mutilation. The sinner takes up the covenant of God with his mouth alone; at any rate, by sinning he hates instruction and what follows. Or else, since "this people," he says, "honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me": those of the circumcision hated instruction at the coming of Christ, and cast behind them the words of God spoken through Jesus Christ. They ran along with Judas, the thief and traitor, and with the adulterers made wood and stones their portion. To others they slander their brother, the people from the Gentiles; and they even set stumbling blocks against their own mother's sons, those of the circumcision who believe, wishing to turn them aside. For these reasons God kept silent toward them. Though the words ought to be before his eyes, he casts them behind him.
By the same. That one who sins ought not to preside in the rank of a teacher.
"But you hated instruction," etc. Instruction is moderation of the passions.

"And you made your portion with adulterers," etc. Our portion is the knowledge of God. We make it one with adulterers when we take up theirs. Here he calls the fornicator and every kind of licentious person an adulterer.
"You thought, in iniquity, that I would be like you," etc. Likeness is imitation through good deeds. That is why the Lord is made like not those who sin but those who do what is right.
"Lest he seize you, and there be no one to deliver," etc. The soul that has fallen away from God entirely is seized.

"A sacrifice of praise will glorify me," etc. In the sacrifice of praise, he says, is the way to salvation from God. A sacrifice of praise will glorify our God, because those who see our good works will glorify our Father in heaven. And when we are engaged in these things, there is the way by which God will show us his salvation.
PSALM 50
(12) From the exegetical comments on Psalm 50. After partly allegorizing the beginning of the story of Uriah, he adds:

If anyone thinks it forced to allegorize a story in part without making the whole of it consistent, then clearly what has been said here is said in vain, and another explanation of the passage must be sought. That is, unless someone examines the details of the passage more thoroughly and finds a way to account for everything: both what concerns the man who was killed and his apparent goodness, since he was unwilling to go to his house and rest while the people were in camp and fighting. But I do not know how those who shun allegory here, and think that the letter was written down for its own sake, will show that it was the Holy Spirit's will to judge worthy of record things in which David is accused not only of licentiousness but also of cruelty and inhumanity. For he dared to do to Uriah a deed foreign even to an ordinary character that has been only moderately improved. I would say this. The judgments of God are great and hard to explain, and they seem to cause uninstructed souls to go astray. In the same way his Scriptures are great and full of meanings that are ineffable, mystical and hard to contemplate. They are also exceedingly hard to explain, and they seem to cause the uninstructed souls of the heterodox to go astray. These people rashly and recklessly accuse God on the basis of Scriptures they do not understand, and so they fall into fabricating another God. It is safe, therefore, to wait for the interpretation of the Word who makes things clear, and of "the wisdom hidden in a mystery, which none of the rulers of this age has known, according to the revelation of the mystery kept silent for eternal ages." This wisdom has been made manifest to the apostles and to those like them, both through the prophetic Scriptures and through the appearing to them of our Savior, the Word who was "in the beginning with God."

Have mercy on me, O God, etc. He who fashioned our nature (13) has mercy on it, for it is sick in many ways with weakness. The inventor of sin shakes the mind, and his accomplice is the law that rages in the members of the flesh. We must therefore approach God, for all strength comes from him. Perhaps he also foresaw that in due time Christ would shine upon those on earth to blot out all the sin of the world, and so he fittingly calls such splendid grace "great mercy." For it is written that "all sin shall stop its mouth." And according to the Apostle, "It is God who justifies; who is it that condemns?"

Wash me thoroughly, etc. The lawless deed (14) of one who no longer acts lawlessly is blotted out, and one who has been washed thoroughly is cleansed from his sin. So a single operation is conceived in different ways. One term denotes sin apart from the law, the other transgression of the law. He asks the one who is able to cleanse him from his worse habit to wash it away. And see again the mystery of Christ: the power of baptism, which surpasses the cleansing under the law, also brings about the cleansing of this soul.

Against you alone have I sinned, etc. This "so that" (15) does not express purpose. They did not sin so that God might be justified in his words. Rather, God was rightly justified because they were ungrateful even while receiving his benefits. God had spoken at length about repentance, saying that he does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live. So the psalmist wisely recalled the words just quoted, and drew this conclusion: "If you forgive me when I repent, and are merciful to me when I turn back, you will be justified in your words, shown to be true to your promises. And at the time of recompense you will bring me forward as one who obtained mercy through repentance, and you will justly judge those who did not repent."
Of the same. When we sin (16) in deed, we sin against both people and God. But when we offend in thought, we sin against God alone. Or it means: "To you alone is my sin known."

Restore to me the joy, etc. To "restore" is to give back (17) what is owed to someone. So the joy of God's salvation is restored to the rational nature, and one who is established by the guiding spirit will not be a slave to sin. "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain." In the same way, unless God creates a pure heart in someone, human choice and power are not enough for this. First a pure heart is created. Then a right spirit is renewed upon it in the inward parts, and all this while the Holy Spirit is not taken away. Then, after these two spirits, a person is established by God with a guiding spirit, so as to be steadfast and unshaken.
PSALM 51.
Why do you vaunt yourself in wickedness, you who are mighty in lawlessness? etc. "Let the one who boasts," (18) says the Apostle, "boast in the Lord."

Of the same. He did not use (19) a neutral word, but one that indicates something base. He did not say "Why do you boast?" but "Why do you vaunt yourself?" "To vaunt oneself" is never used in a good sense; rather, when someone sins, he vaunts himself. The words could also have been addressed to Saul.

Of the same. If one can be mighty (20) in lawlessness, one can also be powerless in lawlessness. The one who is mighty in lawlessness is powerless in righteousness, while the one who is powerless in lawlessness is mighty in righteousness.

Of the same. "Vaunting oneself" is (21) base, while "boasting" is neutral. Take the one who is weak, feeble and slight in wickedness, because the better way abounds in him. Since he is weaker in wickedness, he would be ashamed when he sins, and, stung by his conscience, he would repent. But the one who is mighty in wickedness is puffed up by it and vaunts himself, priding himself on it as on a great achievement. And if someone is taught the divine word every day and still sins, he too "devises all the day." Or "day" signifies manifestation, or the whole time during which he acts lawlessly.

All the day your tongue devised injustice; like a sharpened razor you worked deceit, etc. What devises (22) is the governing faculty and the heart; it was not Doeg's tongue that devised injustice. "Devised" means that he conceived unjust thoughts. Since "the heart of fools is in their mouth," Doeg's tongue spoke them out. The tongue is not what devises, but what serves the thoughts.

You loved evil more than goodness, etc. There are some (23) who love opposites, as it were, because they are never wholly devoted to virtue and are not willing to give themselves wholly to vice either. The baser among them love vice more than virtue, and the others the reverse.
You loved all words of drowning, etc. Doeg loved words (24) of drowning when he slandered David.

Therefore may God tear you down to the end; may he pluck you out and remove you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living, etc. God, who tears down (25) wicked buildings, tears Doeg down, and there are two ways of understanding this. Either he does not leave even the wall of his building standing, because the whole of it was badly built from top to bottom. Or, since the worse are torn down [?] last and Doeg is the worst, he will be torn down at the end, close to the time when the last enemy, death, is abolished. And if the root of Doeg the Idumean is plucked out of the land of the living, then it had been planted there.
Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the abundance of his wealth, etc. Perhaps (26) he grew rich from the mules, a hybrid animal, over which Saul had appointed him.

But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, etc. "The fruit (27) of the Spirit is joy, peace, love, patience," etc. Having this fruit in himself, the saint said: "But I am like a fruitful olive tree." He likens himself to a fruitful olive tree because mercy prevailed in him, and the other virtues followed from it. In the same way we call Job brave and Joseph temperate, and we name the others after the virtue that prevails in them.

I will wait for your name, for it is good before your holy ones, etc. What is good (28) by nature appears as it truly is to a healthy nature, and in the same way the name of God appears good to the holy.
PSALM 52.

The fool said in his heart, etc. The fool (29) thinks that there is no God, and that is why he said it in his heart. He does not confess it with his mouth because he fears people. Or the fool is the people that denies that Christ is God. According to the first interpretation of the fool, he is presented as saying that there is no God, not with his mouth but in his heart.

There is none who does good, etc. The Savior too (30) admonished the man who said, "What must I do to inherit eternal life?" He said to him, "Why do you call me good?" For he knew that there is none who does good. And perhaps, since the law has a shadow of the good things to come, there is no one in this life who does good, but at most a shadow of good. And since there is none who does good, the man is rebuked with the words, "Why do you call me good?"

Those who devour my people as they eat bread have not called upon God, etc. If anyone devours (31) any of God's people, he is shown not to be calling upon God, even if he says he does. "For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved."

For God has scattered the bones of people-pleasers, etc. Not everyone who pleases (32) people is a people-pleaser. A person may sometimes set out to please people and do it fittingly, and he will not be a people-pleaser. Paul, at any rate, says: "Give no offense to Jews or to the church of God, just as I too please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, so that they may be saved." One ought to aim at pleasing God alone, so that even pleasing people is done for his sake, whenever reason chooses to do it. So if someone aims at nothing but pleasing people, or at pleasing people more than God, or people and God equally, he will be a people-pleaser. And in some cases one sees that no particular deed or word can please both God and people. Then one must disregard pleasing people and choose to please God.

Who will give out of Zion (33) the salvation of Israel? etc. "The deliverer will come from Zion, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob." He will also give salvation and return to the ten tribes already taken into captivity. But who will grant us to see Christ, the salvation of the spiritual Israel?
PSALM 53.

Save me, O God, by your name, etc. He prays (34) as far as "before them." Then, perceiving that help is present to him, he points to it, as it were, in "Behold, God helps me," and in the next verse and the one after it. Then he prays, making petition about certain things and promising a freewill sacrifice in return. Then he gives thanks, answering point by point what was said in the prayer and petition. In answer to "In your truth destroy them," he replies: "My eye has looked upon my enemies."

For behold, God helps me, etc. Perceiving that he has been heard (35), he says these words in the middle of the petitions joined together and addressed to God, so that the sense runs [?]: "Mighty men have sought my soul and have not set God before them; in your truth destroy them." Perhaps he confesses that he has the Father as his helper, and as Lord the upholder of his soul, meaning the Son, who "will turn back the evils upon my enemies." For the harm they wanted to bring on me he will turn back upon them, since this is how God judges. With this agrees the saying, "Do to her as you did to the rich man." And when these things have happened, he says, I will come to give thanks of my own free will and will sacrifice to you willingly.

I will give thanks to your name, O Lord, etc. He gives thanks (36), answering "Save me by your name" with "I will give thanks to your name." And he answers "Strangers have risen up against me" with "You have delivered me from every affliction, and my eye has looked upon my enemies." Some things are hostile to us that we have not yet seen, and they may still escape our notice. It is good that they should at last be perceived as hostile. What eye does this work, if not the discerning eye that is able to see what is friendly? But the eye that is not discerning is deceived and overlooks things. It will see the hostile as friendly and the friendly as hostile.
PSALM 54.

Give ear, O God, to my prayer, etc. No one (37) who sins, especially at the moment of sinning, would want a venerable man to pay attention to him, much less God. If you understand "Give ear, all you who inhabit the world," then you have left the desolate regions of the word of wickedness and come to the inhabited world, and having come you have settled in it. Once you have given ear to the words of God, say: "Give ear, O God, to my prayer," and he will give ear. He will also not disregard you when you make your supplication. Take courage, as one who will not be disregarded, to say: "And do not disregard my supplication." And if you attend to God, trusting in him, say: "Attend to me." Further, if you have heard him, he will hear you. And if, like the Apostle grieving out of love for humankind, you weep with those who weep and groan in this tent, being burdened, say "I was grieved" and what follows.
