I was grieved in my musing, etc. Either (38) "musing" here signifies prayer, as also in Hannah's case: "Out of the abundance of my musing I have wasted away." Or it means idle talk: whatever we do or say contrary to right reason is idle talk, as is whatever we speak at random. So he condemned himself for having been troubled and for having lost the calm of his soul "at the voice of the enemy and from the affliction of the sinner." So the prophet makes confession, taking on our person in order to teach us to confess.

And I was troubled at the voice of the enemy and at the affliction of the sinner; for they turned lawlessness upon me, and in wrath they bore a grudge against me, etc. Christ (39) was drawing people away from the opposing powers. The voice of the sinful devil stirred up the powers under him against the Savior, and it caused them to turn lawlessness upon him and to bear a grudge against him in wrath. As a result, Jesus' heart was troubled within him and the fear of death fell upon him. Fear and trembling came upon him, and darkness covered him.

My heart was troubled within me, etc. "My heart was troubled within me" has (40) something in common with "My soul is troubled within myself." When death is expected, fear also arises from some wicked power at work. This power fell upon the one speaking the psalm because it wanted to work in him, but it did not necessarily accomplish what it wanted. You will say the same about the fear and trembling that came upon him: since they found him watchful, they had no effect. He said "And darkness covered me" because the body darkens the soul when the sinner and the enemy turn lawless action upon me. For sin provokes sin, while a righteous man in the company of a righteous man becomes more righteous. "And in wrath they bore a grudge against me." This too is typical of sinners, who do not simply act with enmity but also in darkness [?]. "To bear a grudge" means to keep anger stored up within. Every earnest person knows that sinning in thought is one thing, and tolerable, while sinning in deed and word is another, and dangerous and grave. So if agitation and harm ever arise in his thoughts, he keeps them within himself. He does not utter a word, in keeping with what is said about hidden sin, nor does he carry them into effect, for he knows that a thought can be cured. But what is in deed and word is hard to cure, and sometimes incurable. That is why he says: "My heart was troubled within me." It is as if he said: "I did not express the agitation or act on it. Even when the fear of the death that follows sin fell upon me, I kept it within myself." For fear can show outwardly, and then the one in whom it shows becomes a stumbling block to others. As for "Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me," this belongs to human nature, which has the passions, the spirited part and the desiring part. Even if someone advances in virtue, the passions are not abolished, and so it happens that he comes to experience what is called sympathetic feeling. So the person speaking here, pressed by the voices of enemies and the affliction of the sinner, felt the passions within him fanned into flame. As a result, he was afraid and fell into trembling from the darkness of perplexity. By "darkness" he meant dizziness.

And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove's? etc. The wings (41) of the holy dove are the contemplation of bodies and of incorporeal beings. Raised aloft by this, the mind comes to rest in the knowledge of the Holy Trinity.

Behold, I went far off in flight and lodged in the wilderness, etc. The word translated "in flight" (42) means to pursue and put to flight those who are being driven out. So the one speaking the psalm says, "Behold, I went far off," that is, I put the enemy and the sinner to flight a long way, so that once they were driven off I lodged in the wilderness, that is, I rested in a state of peace. But the word may here properly mean "to flee." In that case the righteous man flees those of the circumcision and goes far from them because of their arrogance toward him, and he will say: "I lodged in the Church, which was a wilderness as far as the law and the prophets were concerned." It also fits Christ in his incarnate state.

I waited for him who saves me from faintheartedness and from the tempest, etc. The tempest is (43) great temptation, which blows hard against the soul and can even wreck it if the soul does not keep watch over itself.

Drown, O Lord, and divide their tongues, for I have seen lawlessness and contradiction in the city, etc. Some people build a city (44) out of wickedness and false doctrines. Ignorance and confusion of tongues come upon them and stop their evil activity, as happened to those who built the tower in Calneh. "Drowning" signifies disappearance, because everything that sinks into the deep disappears. The deep, then, is sin, and destruction is the breaking up of what holds wickedness together. That is why he says that God drowns the evil by dividing the tongues of those who agree together in evil.

Of the same. "Drown (45), O Lord." Whose tongues? Those of the enemy and the sinner? Or else wisdom is an abyss, in which are the depths of God. It floods the tongues and voices of the enemy, and of those who champion him, with the truth of the word, and so it drowns them. It also divides them by exposing their discord and fragmentation. The reason for saying this follows. For there is also the contradiction of the truth by those who quarrel about words. It is useful for nothing except to ruin those who listen. Christ might speak what follows about the city of Jerusalem, having seen the lawlessness in it and the contradiction about him among those who said various things about him. "And it did not depart from its streets." This would rightly be applied to the person of the betrayer.

Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive to Hades; for wickedness is in their sojournings, in their midst, etc. Let death (46) indeed come upon them: the death that separates the soul from wickedness.

Of the same. Those who go down (47) to Hades alive are those who have [?] instruction in the divine teachings. Someone who has not tasted the words of life is dead, and it is not possible for anyone who is alive only with ordinary life to go down to Hades alive. Judas and the Jewish people had instruction in the law and the prophets. So when the death that follows sin comes upon them, they go down to Hades alive. The next verse follows on consistently: "For wickedness is in their sojournings, in their midst." Even if they had experience of the life-giving Scriptures, they did not dwell in them but only sojourned there. "Wickedness in their midst" means in the governing faculty, which is said to be in the middle of the whole living being. And "alive to Hades" means that one should die suddenly. He calls each person's life "sojournings" because it is short. So he says that their life and existence are full of every kind of wickedness and evil, because they do not consider how short life is.

Evening and morning and noon I will tell and declare, and he will hear my voice, etc. Noon is (48) midway between morning and evening. Jacob rose early and wrestled with an angel; Abraham saw the angels at noon; Lot saw them in the evening.

Of the same. "Evening" (49) means the eleventh hour, near the end of the world, when the Savior suffered. "Morning" is when he rose. "Noon" is when they were more firmly persuaded and believed. Or else he begins the account in the evening, it reaches its height in him in the morning, and he completes it at noon, when the day is at its height.

God will hear, and he who exists before the ages will humble them; for there is no change for them, and they did not fear God, etc. If all things came into being (50) through him, he is rightly said to exist before the ages. From this we also learn that the ages came into being out of nothing.
Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you, etc. He nourished (51) Jacob in the same way, who said: "God, who has nourished me from my youth."
PSALM 55.

"Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me; all day long he has fought and afflicted me," etc. Christ says to the Father, "Have mercy on me." For though I am God, a man has trampled me. And this, I think, is where the saying "He who has trampled the Son of God" was taken from.

By the same. The earthly demons trample us, but if the ones beneath the earth come up, they cover us. That is why it is said: "You set a boundary which they shall not pass, nor shall they return to cover the earth."

"I will not fear what flesh shall do to me," etc. He who took the form of a slave and came in the likeness of sinful flesh, he who knew no sin, made himself sin for our sake by taking on flesh. Since he alone of all who have lived in the flesh committed no sin, he could boldly say: "What shall flesh do to me?"
"They will dwell nearby and hide; they will watch my heel," etc. They watch to learn from what we do, for the demons do not know hearts.

By the same. Like the serpent, the wicked will watch the heel of Christ or of the righteous man, as it is said: "And you shall watch his heel." "That I may be pleasing before God in the light of the living," etc. The light of the living is the knowledge of the angels.
PSALM 5[?]
"And in the shadow of your wings I will hope, until iniquity passes away," etc. He is speaking to the Holy Spirit, for the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove.

By the same. Until iniquity passes away, the righteous man hopes in the shadow of God's wings. But once it has passed away and ceased to exist, he will no longer hope in a shadow, but in God himself. These words can also be divided like this: "I will hope in the shadow of your wings; and until iniquity passes away, I will cry to God Most High."
"He sent from heaven and saved me," etc. From heaven he sent either the Savior or an angel to save.
"God sent forth his mercy and his truth," etc. Perhaps he who said, "I am the truth," is also mercy itself, so that we should seek no mercy other than him.
"I slept, troubled," etc. For after he had said, "My soul is troubled," he fell asleep not long afterward.
"Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword," etc. The teeth of the demons are the wicked thoughts with which they devour our soul.
By the same. The tongue of slanderers is a sharp sword, and so is the tongue of those who teach the doctrines of knowledge falsely so called.
"Be exalted above the heavens, O God," etc. "If I am lifted up," says the Savior, "I will draw all to myself."
"Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and lyre," etc. By "glory" he means the gift of the mind. The mind itself is the psaltery, and what surrounds the mind, namely the soul, is the lyre.
"I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing to you among the nations," etc. This can be an exhortation to confess one's sins in the Church.
"For your mercy is magnified to the heavens, and your truth to the clouds," etc. Since the one who receives mercy rises as far as the kingdom of heaven, God's mercy is magnified to the heavens.
"Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth," etc. These two verses are said twice in this psalm.
PSALM 57

"If you truly speak righteousness," etc. Let us see what it means to truly speak righteousness, and in how many ways this can come about. In one way, a person speaks righteousness when he holds sound doctrines about righteousness and discusses them. In a second way, a person speaks righteousness when everything he says comes from the righteousness that dwells in his soul. Put both together and you will find the one who truly speaks righteousness. For those who outwardly appear righteous to others but inwardly are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness do not speak righteousness truly, even if they do speak it. And I think that no one can speak righteousness without sharing in Christ, "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." Judging uprightly follows from truly speaking righteousness, so that there is nothing crooked in the judgments and reasonings of the one who truly speaks righteousness.

"For indeed in your heart iniquities," etc. The passage wants to show that the ruling faculty of the wicked man, filled with iniquities, is the source and beginning of every sin, like a stream welling up from the earth, and that action, symbolized by the hands, is the practice that the ruling faculty brings forth. So it names first what belongs to the heart and second what belongs to the hands. Sin begins in the heart and ends in deeds. But for those who turn to God, the beginning is abstaining from evil deeds, and the end is purity of heart. That is why here, where the blameworthy are being rebuked, the iniquities of the heart are named first, and only then the injustices that the hands weave together. Instead of "weave together," Theodotion and the fifth edition have "weigh out," and Aquila has "is weighed out." They do not weave injustice at random, he says. Because of these vices, when an army came against the city, lawlessness and contradiction reached [?] even the holy angels who guarded it on its walls. For they too abandoned it when they saw it acting lawlessly and contradicting. For "lawlessness and toil," the opposite of praiseworthy pleasure, "have come to be in its midst along with injustice," so that "usury and deceit do not depart from its streets." Its inhabitants deal deceitfully through their wicked thoughts, and they toil to lift onto themselves the burden of wickedness, which is compared to lead. Its "streets," or broad places, should be taken to be those who broaden themselves through love of pleasure by walking the broad and spacious road, that is, the life of pleasure and passion. Toil over evil things and deceit in fraud always remain in them, and so the saying is fulfilled: "Usury and deceit have not departed from its streets." For those who are ready for injustice weigh out each of their unjust acts to weave wickedness together, and they carry out what they choose without ceasing, while the deeds of their injustice are recorded on a pillar that cannot be erased.

"The sinners were estranged from the womb; they went astray from the belly; they spoke lies," etc. Those who from childhood walk the road not of virtue but of vice are estranged from the womb and go astray from the belly.
"Their anger is like the serpent's, like a deaf asp that stops its ears," etc. Every soul that has not listened to the words that save it is an asp stopping its ears.

By the same. Because sinners have anger like a serpent's, it is said to them: "Serpents, brood of vipers," since they have taken on the likeness not of God but of the serpent. The saint stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed, and like a deaf man he does not hear what is worse. But the sinner does not hear what is good, like a deaf asp that stops its ears so as not to hear the voice of the charmers. The people this passage speaks of also stop their ears, not the ears of sense but those of understanding, so as not to hear those who offer the wise charms of the prophets and apostles. For each of these is a wise man preparing a remedy, that is, making a rational medicine that wards off the asp's attack.

"God will shatter their teeth," etc. "He crushed" stands for "he will crush," by a change of tense. God does this to them as a kindness, so that they do not devour the people they deceive and become liable to an even greater punishment. He also crushed their molars, so that they would not bite or devour. Note that Scripture distinguishes molars from teeth: the teeth cut and divide the food, while the molars chew it and grind it smooth. Water flowing through a channel does not stay but is scattered and comes to nothing; in the same way these people too will be brought low, for they have nothing firm or lasting. Hence he adds: "He will bend his bow." He has pictured God's punishment as a bow that keeps sending arrows and slays everyone. For he goes on releasing arrows, he says, until he has shot them all down and made them weak.
"Like melted wax they will be taken away; fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun," etc. As wax comes along with honey, so vice comes along with the rational soul.
By the same. He whom they did not see as the sun they will come to know as fire.
"The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance," etc. The punishment of the sinner makes the righteous man more secure and purer.
By the same. The righteous man will rejoice when he sees the wisdom of God's judgment in punishing the unjust.
PSALM 58

"Deliver me from my enemies, my God," etc. Because of "Without iniquity I ran and went straight," and "I will keep my strength for you," and also because of "Attend, to visit all the nations," it is the Savior who speaks this psalm.

"For behold, they have hunted my soul," etc. The mighty have hunted my soul and set upon me. They do not take up the fight against me in passing, he says. They press hard, giving no moment's respite, and wage war on us in every way. He called them "mighty" so that their strength would show how much greater the plot against him was.

"Without iniquity I ran and went straight," etc. He who says, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith," will say, "Without iniquity I ran and went straight." Or rather, the Savior will say this.
By the same. No one can go straight along the way that said, "I am the way," unless he has run without iniquity.
"Rise up to meet me, and see," etc. Who then is worthy to say to God, "Rise up to meet me, and see"?
By the same. God rises up to meet the one who climbs toward God by a sound life. In the Gospel too, the father goes out to meet the son who is coming back to him.
"And a sword is on their lips," etc. A sword is on the lips of the heterodox, who teach blasphemous and impious things.

"Do not kill them, lest they forget your law," etc. The Lord kills those whom he allows to go on sinning for a long time, because this leads them to forget God: "For in Hades who will give thanks to you?"

"And from cursing and lying will their endings be proclaimed, in the wrath of the end, and they shall be no more," etc. Cursing and lying are the cause of the end. If they did not exist, there would be neither wrath nor end.
PSALM 59

"O God, you have cast us off," etc. Speaking as if in the person of the Jews, he shows their rejection by saying, "O God, you have cast us off and torn us down," or, as Symmachus has it, "you have rejected us and cut us to pieces," which shows that they were cut off. Then he adds, "You were angry, and you had compassion on us"; but according to Aquila, "In your anger you overturned us." The way events turned out supports this reading rather than the other, since they suffered these things after the coming of the Savior. For when the wrath came upon them in full, they were cast off and torn down and rejected, cut to pieces and driven about, scattered among all the nations.

"Heal its breaches," etc. The land just mentioned was moved and shaken from its proper place and stability, and it came to have breaches and wounds. That is why the next words are: "You showed your people hard things."

"You showed your people hard things," etc. God shows someone hard things when that person falls into hardships. If someone accepts these and comes to regret his former sins, he drinks the wine of compunction, taking them as a reason to be stung into repentance. In many places Scripture calls hard circumstances by the same name as unmixed wine, as in "A cup of unmixed wine in the hand of the Lord." "Hard things" also shares its name with the "hard ways" mentioned in the sixteenth psalm: "Because of the words of your lips I kept to hard ways." There the virtues are called hard ways because they are achieved with much sweat and toil. Here, however, the people saw hard things because they were tried by afflictions.

"You gave a sign to those who fear you," etc. We, he says, have been punished for the impiety we committed, but those who fear you received a sign (clearly the one with which we were sealed), so that they might escape all punishment. The type of this sign was the blood of the sheep smeared on the doorposts in Egypt.
PSALM 60

"From the ends of the earth I have cried to you," etc. A person who perceives how far he falls short of perfection, by understanding who the perfect one is, and brings this up in his prayers, saying about it, "Hear, O God, my supplication," will be heard. But when the imperfect person is unaware of what he lacks, his supplication is silent; whereas the one who perceives it and offers himself to God to be made perfect has cried out.

"When my heart was weary," etc. For in truth every soul that loves God grows weary and distressed while it lingers in this mortal life. It also grows weary and distressed out of love for humanity, when it sees the multitude of those who are perishing. It also mourns for the many who sinned in the past and did not repent of the sin, lawlessness, and impiety they committed. David did the same: he fled from the middle of the land, and from its ends he cried out to God. And grieving in soul over the destruction of the many, and of Saul himself, he wept bitterly.

"You lifted me up on a rock," etc. We will take the rock to mean the one that pours out spiritual drink, Christ, I mean. Whoever comes to stand on this rock, by sharing in it (for it is "wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification"), is lifted on high in mind, exalted by God. Those who have resolved to follow the Savior, as he urges when he says, "Come after me," take him as their guide and share in the same exaltation. They do not hope to find any other leader on the road that leads to the cause of all things. David too received this gift and says to the Lord in a hymn: "You guided me, for you became my hope." And not only a guide: you also became a tower for me against the face of the enemy. Because I had you as my strength and a tower of strength, I remained unharmed, though the enemy stood facing me and chose to make war. "You guided me" can also be connected with "from the face of the enemy," in a sequence like this: You guided me away from the face of the enemy, having become my hope; and you also became for me a tower of strength against the face of the enemy, so as to guide me. The true and unfailing hope of the saints is the Savior. Paul says of him, "and of Jesus Christ our hope," and the prophecy says, "In him the nations will hope." For he is the one who was foretold to be the expectation of the nations. One who has been perfected in holiness sojourns forever in that tabernacle, which is what "Who shall dwell on your holy mountain?" shows. For this is eternal, being the same as the tabernacle which the Lord pitched, and not man. Yet even though such a tabernacle is so perfect that it is the Holy of Holies, there is still beyond it a state of rational beings that surpasses it, in which they will be in the Father and the Son, or rather in the Trinity. That is why it speaks of sojourning in the tabernacle forever, but [?] of dwelling there. Whoever has come to be in this house will be sheltered under the shelter of God's wings.

"You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name," etc. Because you are rich, he says, you also give great gifts. Or rather, by graciously granting perfect people to become your sons, you have given them an inheritance. Even if it is expected to be given after the resurrection in the age to come, it has already been given, in the sense that it has already been prepared for those who will be brought into it at the proper time. Moreover, God has given an inheritance to those who fear his name. There may be some difference between those who fear God and those who fear his name, and between those who believe in him and those who believe in his name, since it has often been said that those who have come close to God's name are inferior to those who are united to God himself. If so, see how the inheritance has been given even to those who fear God. For if this grace has been granted to the inferior, it has been granted much more to those who have risen above them.
By the same. Perhaps the Lord gave those who fear him an inheritance like that of Israel, but to those who love him he gave an inheritance like that of the Levites.

"So will I sing to your name," etc. Since I have received what I asked of you, he says, I have become thankful, and so "I will sing to your name." I will praise your name, which has been bestowed upon me, through deeds, thoughts, and good words. And besides this, day after day I will pay what I vowed. As Jacob says: "If God gives me bread to eat," and so on, "of all that you give me I will give a tenth to you." For before these words Scripture says: "Jacob made a vow, saying, If the Lord is with me," up to "I will give a tenth to you." It is also well said that one pays one's vows day after day but sings to God's name for ever and ever. Singing to the name of the one being praised stretches on into the age to come, while paying vows is fulfilled only as long as there is still time made up of days, and that is the time measured out by each person's life. So while we are in this life, let us pay our vows, so that we may also be able to sing to God's name for ever and ever.
PSALM 61

"For the end, for Jeduthun, a psalm of David," etc. Jeduthun means "of a judge who is coming"; David means "strong of hand." The psalm is about the Son of God, the eternal judge who is coming, who is strong of hand.

"Shall not my soul be subject to God?" etc. Everyone who is subject to someone has the same mind as that person. And if, as Paul says, we shall all be subjected to Christ, let us all have the same mind as Christ.

By the same. Since it is the Savior who speaks, "shall be subject" refers to "then the Son himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him." That he means the Father is clear from "But they plotted to thrust away my honor; I ran in thirst." At the same time we learn that what will be subjected is the soul, and that the soul's salvation, salvation itself, comes from God. This is why God himself is the Savior of the one who says these things. Nor can one who is subject receive salvation from anyone except God. So let us be subject to God. He helps those who are subject to him alone and saves them, so that because of their subjection to God they stand all the firmer, shaken by nothing. "My helper; I shall not be shaken any more." He may say this because he was shaken from the time he emptied himself and took the form of a slave, and so was shaken only a little, during his brief time in the body. Or else, when he became very sorrowful in soul, he only began to grieve and to be troubled a little, and so he says, "I shall not be shaken any more." For he did not commit sin, as those do who are shaken further.
"How long will you set upon a man?" etc. This is like "Now you seek to kill me." They seek to kill a man, and in setting upon him they set upon a man.
"But they plotted to thrust away my honor," etc. The honor of the rational soul is virtue and knowledge.

"But be subject to God, my soul," etc. The first subjection brings salvation; the second brings patient endurance from God. For many are the evils these men bring upon me, he says, but I look to God himself and have him as my expectation and hope. That is why I endure what happens. He usually helps me, and he will help me now too. He will not allow these men to accomplish their aim, so as to overpower us, remove us and drive us from what is ours, and put us to flight.

"Hope in him, all you congregation of the people," etc. It is as if he were saying: not only the remnant chosen by grace. This will happen when all Israel is saved. "Pour out your hearts before him." Whoever has put away every evil thought and repented so completely that he no longer even remembers worse things has poured out his heart before him. "For you will render to each according to his works." God will render to each according to his works, whether good or evil, many or few, according to the quality or quantity of whatever measures he renders.

"But the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are false in the scales, so as to do wrong together out of vanity," etc. Vain are those who devote themselves to the vain and perishable affairs of this age. All human things are vain and change quickly.

By the same. I do not lie about righteousness, for righteousness is the scale of the virtues. False are the sons born of their father the devil. For they disregard equality, he says, and hold the scales of their minds unevenly. They despise what is just and rejoice in injustice.

By the same. This is how the Seventy have it. But according to Theodotion: "The sons of men are a vapor; the sons of man are false, like the tipping of a scale." Nothing human is lasting, he says. It is like vapor that rises and is at once dispersed, and like the tipping of a scale, now sinking, now rising. The question is asked whether the saints are not vain. The saints are not sons of men, for their birth according to man has been abolished.
"God has spoken once; these two things I have heard," etc. God spoke the word once, the word about providence and judgment. This is shown by the words that follow.
PSALM 62

"O God, my God, I rise early to seek you. My soul has thirsted for you; how many times over has my flesh thirsted for you, in a desert land, trackless and waterless! So in the holy place I appeared before you, to see your power and your glory," etc. Everyone who has put off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light rises early to seek God.

By the same. Whoever thirsts for the good thirsts for God, but whoever thirsts for the shameful thirsts for the devil. Moreover, whoever is to see God's power and glory must appear before him in the holy place. Christ is the power of God and the radiance of his glory. The unmarried man, who is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God, so as to be holy in body and in spirit, might say to the Lord about his own flesh, "My flesh is yours." But the fornicator might say to the devil, "My flesh is yours." The one who lives in purity might say that his flesh is "in the desert," since his flesh is in solitude; and "trackless," since not even an evil thought treads upon it; "and waterless," for the body of the debauched is moist, but that of the one who keeps himself pure is dry. Hence the eunuch says, "For I am a dry tree." Further, the one who says, "In the holy place I appeared before you," rises early to seek God, and thirsts for him with his soul many times over, and his flesh is in a desert land, trackless and waterless.

"For your mercy is better than lives; my lips will praise you," etc. A human being's life is holy knowledge, and the Lord's mercy is the contemplation of the things that have come into being. Many have promised us the kinds of knowledge of this age; but the Lord's mercy is better than lives.
By the same. My lips, he says, commend; the soul praises; and spirit and mind sing psalms.

"So I will bless you in my life; in your name I will lift up my hands," etc. The holy man raises and lifts up his hands when he does heavenly things. The righteous man also raises his hands in the name of the Lord when, through sound doctrines about God and the reverence due to him, he lifts his practical life up from earthly things. But when he does so through some alien teaching, he does raise his hands, but not in the name of the Lord.

"May my soul be filled as with fat and richness," etc. A sleek and well-nourished soul. The verse "All the fat ones of the earth ate and worshipped" is useful for this passage. With bodily food, the fat and well-fed animals seem better to enjoy than those that are not, and the same holds by analogy for spiritual food. The prophet says this because he knows the soul's surpassing food. Perhaps the fatted calf in the parable in the Gospels was of this kind too. "And my mouth will praise with lips of rejoicing." The phrase is ambiguous: either my mouth will be praised by lips of rejoicing, or the lips of rejoicing will be praised by my mouth. When, he says, I come to remember your name, then, yes then, my lips are filled with joy.

"If I remembered you on my bed," etc. A persuasive exhortation to chastity, since whoever remembers the things of God on his bed is certainly keeping himself pure. Similarly also the verse "With my tears I will drench my bed." For those who give themselves to prayer deprive one another.

"My soul has clung close behind you," etc. If whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit, and David clung to the Lord, then he became one spirit. Scripture calls the spiritual man "spirit," just as "love that does not boast" means the one who has love. And when Moses saw God's back, then his soul clung close behind God.

"They will go into the lowest parts," etc. The more someone's wickedness is poured out, the lower he sinks, and he enters the lower parts of the earth. "Hands of the sword" is figurative, like "hands of the tongue." "They will be portions for foxes." They say that when lions seize an animal, they suck up its blood and greedily devour what falls to them, especially the choicest parts, but leave the rest behind; then the foxes find these remains and eat them. Since foxes eat what the lions have already killed, he means this: various punishments will come upon them one after another, and falling from these into others, they will be encompassed by a different punishment each time.
By the same. So that, believing in him who descended into the lower parts of the earth, they may be saved.
By the same. Here he calls the subterranean demons "foxes"; to them the earthly demons are also handed over for punishment.
PSALM 63

"Hear my voice, O God," etc. There is a voice of the heart that only God can hear. "From fear of the enemy," that is, from fearing the enemy, "deliver my soul"; or "from fear" that is not a friend but an enemy. The knowing fear of God is a friend, but fear of any other kind is an enemy, such as the fear of the heterodox, or of those who fear anything at all other than God. Of these the Spirit in Isaiah may be said to have spoken pointedly: "Do not fear their fear, nor be troubled." "From the gathering of evildoers": the heterodox in faith. For "gathering" Aquila said "secret council," and Symmachus "scheming." "From the multitude of those who work iniquity": those who travel the broad and spacious road.
By the same. A hostile fear is either one instilled in us by the enemy, or one opposed to the courage that comes from Christ. "Take courage," he says; "it is I; do not be afraid."

"Who sharpened their tongues like a sword," etc. Those who are skilled at defending false doctrines "bent a bow, a bitter thing"; but the bow of those who stand up for the truth is sweet. For "thing" Aquila said "word." "To shoot in secret at the blameless": Aquila has "the simple." The arrows with which those who have sharpened their tongues like a sword shoot at the blameless or simple are their secret, mystery-laden discourses.

"They strengthened for themselves an evil word," etc. God strengthens a good word, but man an evil one. So God strengthened his own word by divine power, but men strengthened theirs for themselves by so-called dialectical philosophy and empty deceit. "They talked of hiding a snare": these are the ones who deceive with plausible sophistries and deceptive arguments, in which the snare lies hidden and unnoticed. "They said, 'Who will see them?'" Priding themselves on the obscure things they think they discover, and strengthening an evil word for themselves, they searched out lawlessness. They ought to search the law, so that its spiritual sense might be found; but by seeking outside the law they searched out lawlessness.

"They searched out lawlessness; they failed, searching with searching," etc. The counterfeiters of the truth do this too. They ought to search the law, so that the spiritual sense in it might be found; but by seeking outside the law they searched. Here he signifies how wickedness intensifies.
"A man will draw near, and a deep heart," etc. A deep heart is one that has contemplated the depth of the riches and knowledge of God.

"Their blows became an arrow of infants," etc. And all proclaimed that this was your work, and they ascribed what happened to you, recognizing that it was no one else's doing. Thus the divine eye willed to bring all their efforts to nothing, and chose instead to punish them as well.

"The righteous will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart will be praised," etc. Perishable wealth gladdens the unrighteous man, but knowledge of God gladdens the righteous.
By the same. The Lord praises an upright heart, but he will thrust a perverse soul away from him.

By the same. The upright in heart are those from the nations who have believed. The same people are also righteous, because they have been justified by faith, and upright, because they never mixed the error of idols with the teaching that comes from God, as the children of the Jews evidently often did. These, then, will rejoice, because they kept watch and won the inheritance of those who grew negligent.
PSALM 64

"A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion," etc. "In Zion": clearly the heavenly Zion, that is, the intelligible watchtower; for a hymn to God is not fitting among the things of the senses. Therefore we will sing psalms not with the body or the letter but with the spirit, not with sense but with mind. "And to you a vow will be paid in Jerusalem": "in Zion" is understood here as well. The vow is the kind that the Nazirite makes.
"Hear my prayer," etc. "Hear my prayer" in Zion. "To you," God, who make spirit, "all flesh will come." For the soul that became flesh through sin will be changed and will become spirit.

"Words of the lawless overpowered us," etc. Words of the lawless entered us and overpowered us, and because of them we became flesh. "And you will be merciful to our impieties." We were overpowered by words of the lawless and became flesh. But because you are merciful to our impieties, so that we who became flesh may come to you, we believe that "to you all flesh will come."

"Blessed is he whom you have chosen," etc. If he whom you have chosen and taken to yourself is blessed, then the blessed are the chosen few, not the many who are only called. For the chosen few will find eternal life, having traveled the narrow and hard way that leads to it. But the many who are only called have traveled the wide way that leads to destruction; they will not dwell in your courts, in you, nor will they flourish as those planted in the house of the Lord. These courts are the many dwelling places in the Father's house. "We shall be filled with the good things of your house." Those planted in the house of the Lord, filled with his good things, will flourish in the courts where they will dwell. "Holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness." Christ, being the temple of the Father who is in him, is both holy and wonderful in righteousness. The second phrase cannot properly be said of the visible temple. "The hope of all the ends of the earth," and so on. He who says this, being far from the sea, prophesies about those tossed by the waves at sea far from him, or about those who are in the deepest troubles and say, "I came into the depths of the sea."
"He will dwell in your courts," etc. The Lord's court is knowledge of God; whoever dwells in it will be filled with good things.

"Hear us, O God our Savior," etc. Here again, foretelling the salvation of the world, he recalls the prophecy of Jacob, who said: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is reserved, and he is the expectation of the nations." Here he calls him the hope of the ends of the earth. Then he also points to the islands and to those at sea. Hear us, then, he says, you who will shortly light up the whole of human nature with the light of righteousness. Then he describes the power of God, as far as that is possible.
"Preparing mountains by his strength," etc. "Preparing mountains" means that God prepares those on earth who are greatest in piety by giving them a share of divine strength.
"Who stirs up the hold of the sea," etc. The Lord rebukes the wind and the sea, and makes a great calm.
By the same. By "hold" he means hollow or depth.
"The nations will be troubled," etc. At the signs worked by Jesus Christ even those at the ends of the earth were afraid, and the Jews still more, hearing of this, and still more seeing it.
"You multiplied it to enrich it," etc. By wealth he means knowledge: "For in everything you were enriched, in all knowledge," says the Apostle.

"You prepared their food," etc. By food he means spiritual food. He says it was prepared because the mystery of Christ was determined before the foundation of the world; Christ is the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world. And by your providence you will supply them with food ready to hand, so that they lack nothing. "For so is your preparation" means this: since it is your work to arrange and prepare such things for human beings, through all of which you supply them in abundance. Just as he uses "prepare" to mean "establish," because things made ready are at hand and secure for use, so here he calls the provision itself "preparation." It is as if he said: They will lack nothing, for everything is ready and prepared for them, so that they need not worry about anything; and such provision is also secure.

"In its drops," etc. As the divine gifts are given to it little by little, he says, he makes it rejoice and spring up, that is, with intelligible fruit. You will understand "its drops" from what is said about Christ: "He will come down like rain upon a fleece, and like a drop dripping on the earth."

"You will bless the crown of the year," etc. In Isaiah he says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." So he calls the time after the Savior's incarnation the year of goodness, because it brings him one single harvest. The prophet prayed that this year would be blessed.

"The beautiful places of the wilderness will grow rich," etc. When goodness appears, the wilderness will bear fruit. The hills on which they sacrificed to demons will receive those who pursue the life of the Gospel, and they will become renowned because of them. And even now everyone hurries to those who have settled on the mountain ridges. "And the valleys will abound," etc. The valleys, he says, will change for the better and, filled with intelligible fruits, will fervently send up hymns to you.
PSALM 65

"Shout to God," etc. Since resurrection after repentance is set before everyone, let everyone shout. To each person it is said, "Does not the one who falls rise again?" And to the whole Church from the nations the Lord says, "Arise, come, my beloved." For whoever has risen through repentance is not far from Christ. Once the shout of triumph over the defeated has gone up, those who have been set free are commanded to sing psalms to God, the cause of the victory. Whoever lives in a way that matches his praise gives glory to God's praise, "for praise befits the upright." The wicked man is therefore prevented from doing this, "since praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner."

"Say to God, How awesome," etc. Consider the difference between one who has proclaimed the works of God and the words "and they understood his handiwork," said in the sixty-third psalm. Consider also how it is said in the hundred and sixth: "Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business on many waters, saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep." Whoever has seen these things will see why one must say to God, "How awesome are your works," and not "Awesome is your handiwork." For those who go down to the sea in ships saw the works of the Lord, being fitted in this respect to see the Lord's awesome works. His wonders in the deep, which correspond to the Lord's handiwork, are not awesome.

"Let all the earth worship," etc. In the Apostle too, first comes "I will pray," and second "I will sing psalms." Consider whether "Let them sing psalms to you" is one thing and "Let them sing psalms to your name" another. Symmachus rendered it: "All on earth will worship you; making melody, they will sing to your name." Sing hymns, he says, as those who remember the Most High.
By the same. "Is anyone among you cheerful? Let him sing psalms," says the Apostle.

"Come and see the works of God," etc. Whoever understands how good the works of God are sees them, and whoever has come to the Spirit who says "Come" understands. Whatever a man may say about the works of God after deliberating, the works of God are far greater, so that whoever saw them would be struck with awe and filled with fear at how awesome God is in his counsels, beyond the sons of men.
"Who turns the sea," etc. First, through Moses, the sea is dried up; then, through Joshua, they will cross the river on foot.

By the same. He did not say "who turned" but "who turns." In the history it happened once, at the entry into Judea; but in the spiritual sense it always happens, as God by his teaching carries over to virtue and knowledge souls that are troubled by the briny waves of life and carried about by every wind. Symmachus renders it this way: "He changed the sea into dry land; they crossed the river on foot."

"There we shall rejoice in him," etc. "There" clearly means in the river, where we shall rejoice in the Lord after crossing the river on foot. This will be when the things have come to pass of which the miracle under Joshua was a type, when the waters coming down from above stood still.
"His eyes look upon the nations," etc. Through Israel's trespass his eyes look upon the nations.
"Let those who embitter not be exalted," etc. Those who embitter are the ones from Israel. So let these not exalt themselves, knowing that God's eyes look upon the nations.

By the same. Those who embitter are the ones who put gall in his food and gave him vinegar to drink in his thirst. Theodotion called them "those who turn aside," and Aquila "those who fall away"; Symmachus put it more clearly: "Let the disobedient not exalt themselves." So let the arrogant people of Israel not think highly of themselves, nor raise a lofty brow against the multitude of the nations, nor say to themselves, "I am the firstborn among the children of God."

"Who has set my soul in life," etc. Who has set it in him who said, "I am the life." Cain's feet were given to tottering when, going out from the presence of God, he dwelt in the land of Nod, which means "tottering." But Moses' feet were not, for to him it was said, "But you, stand here with me"; his legs were pillars of marble set on bases of gold, as is said in the Song of Songs.

"For you have tested us, O God," etc. You will see this clearly from Ezekiel, where it is written: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, behold, the house of Israel has become to me all mixed with bronze and tin and lead and iron; in the midst of a furnace it is mixed with silver."

"You brought us into the snare," etc. For we must enter the kingdom of heaven through many afflictions. Even if you have set men to ride over our heads, we are still confident that through endurance we will lift our heads up, as the hostile men pressing on them are dragged off.

"I will go into your house," etc. What I vowed when I was afflicted, he says, I will pay you. I vowed that, once I was rescued from my present affliction, I would continually send up praises to you. These are either the sacrifices under the law before the Savior's coming, or the spiritual ones, when one enters the house of God, the Church, with whole burnt offerings, offering wholeheartedly complete and entire virtues, and paying the vows that correspond to them.

"Burnt offerings full of marrow," etc. If "May your burnt offering be made rich" is a prayer, then in keeping with it we will say "burnt offerings full of marrow." This happens when the offering does not belong to another but is offered up to God, just as incense must be offered before him. The prayer, or rather the offering, is also made with rams. Rams are movements and impulses that originate in the irascible part of the soul. Besides these, he says, I will offer oxen with goats. Perhaps this is when someone performs the sacred rite by presenting his own body as a living sacrifice to God. For the ox, being an animal that tills the soil, corresponds to the body, which was formed from earth. And goats are works of repentance, for they were offered for sin.
By the same. Everyone who has a pure ruling faculty and prays to God offers God incense with rams.

"Come, hear, and I will tell," etc. He does not recall ancient stories, nor even how Israel was redeemed from Egypt in former times. He teaches, he says, not according to the letter of the law; rather, as a herald of the New Covenant, he marvels at the new achievements of our Savior, all that he has graciously bestowed on the souls of us all.
By the same. Only those who fear God can hear spiritual narratives.

"If I kept looking on iniquity in my heart," etc. Not looking on iniquity in one's heart agrees with what the great Paul says: "I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified," since God can see what we do not see. Similar also is "Who will understand his transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults."
By the same. He did not say "If I had looked on" but "If I kept looking on." The first signifies an evil thought of short duration, the second one that lasts longer.

"Blessed be God, who has not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me," etc. Pure prayer departs from the one who does not have a pure heart; and if prayer departs, clearly mercy departs too, for it is through prayer that we ask God for mercy.
PSALM 66

God be merciful to us, etc. (69) The psalm proclaims in advance the appearing of God the Word and the salvation of all the nations; this is why it is entitled "For the end." And since the things accomplished are not human, the psalm is entitled not "among encomia" or "among praises" but "among hymns." Since it is a divine hymn, and since it also reveals the deeds of the Savior and the most sublime contemplation of them, it is placed at number 66, a number that is perfect both in its units and in its tens.
That your way may be known on the earth, etc. (70) While we are on the earth we have come to know the way that said, "I am the way."
And you will guide the nations on the earth, etc. (71) He guides us through the practical life and through true doctrines.

The earth has yielded its fruit, etc. (72) This refers to all who were earthly and became heavenly, clearly through repentance. "But the fruit of the Spirit is joy, love, peace, patience," and so on. Just as he twice roused the nations to sing hymns, so he twice asked a blessing for them. Those who bless God offer him words alone, since they cannot do him good by any deed. But when God blesses, he confirms his words by deed and grants those he blesses a harvest of every kind of good fruit. Then he teaches how it is possible to obtain the divine blessing.
PSALM 67
Let God arise, etc. (73) Moses says, "Rise up, Lord, let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee."

And let those who hate him flee from his face, etc. (74) Those who speak ill of Providence or of the old Scriptures hate the Creator, and so do those who do things hostile to love. "For God is love." Or else by those who hate God and flee from his face he means those given over to vice in their conduct. For if whoever loves him keeps his commandments, whoever does not keep them does not love him. Those who hate God are the ones who do what he hates.

As smoke vanishes, etc. (75) He wanted the comparisons to make the destruction of the adversaries more vivid, so he mentioned both smoke and wax. For it is the nature of wax to melt and perish when it comes near fire. "So," he says, "you will consume them all, as fire consumes wax."

By the same. (76) Those who hate him are not fire, like the angels, nor light, like the righteous, but smoke, and smoke harms the eyes. "As wax melts before the fire," and so on. Just as the righteous are wheat and the unrighteous are chaff, so the wise are honey and the heterodox are wax. The wax is melted by the fire in the righteous man, which destroys the system of those opposed to the true word. This fire is God, and the same face of God melts sinners but gladdens the righteous.
By the same. (77) This smoke is driven away by the fire that the Lord came to cast upon the earth.

But let the righteous be glad; let them exult before God; let them delight in gladness, etc. (78) The exultation of the righteous before God is a kind of joy, and so it is a fruit of the Spirit, for the fruit of the Spirit is joy and peace. Gladness is a good emotion that expands the thinking part of the soul.

Sing to God, sing psalms to his name; make a way for him who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name, etc. (79) He sings psalms to the name of God who does so for the sake of his name. He mounted upon our poverty and veiled his own glory, as though he were rising from the west; yet even so, "the Lord is his name." For when he became man he did not cast off being the Lord God.

They will be troubled before his face, the father of orphans and judge of widows, etc. (80) An orphan is someone who has been deprived of the heavenly Father through wickedness that he willingly brought on himself. "God is in his holy place." God's place is a pure soul, which is why he goes on to say, "God makes the single-minded dwell in a house." By "single-minded" he means those who have dedicated their own life to him alone and have estranged it from all double-mindedness and worldly desire. These, then, he promises to settle in his house, that is, in the heavenly city. Scripture also knows how to call ways of life a "place." So "in his holy place" means, as it were, in his choicest and purest ways of life. "Leading out those bound in fetters with courage; likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs." Just as he leads out those in fetters with courage, so he leads out the unjust with justice and the foolish with prudence.

O God, when you went out before your people, when you passed through the wilderness, etc. (81) These words seem to suit the events in the wilderness, but they happen always. In one place he stands, in another he passes through: he stood in his holy place, but he passes through the wilderness. "The earth shook, for the heavens dripped before the face of the God of Sinai," that is, of the one who appeared on Sinai.

A voluntary rain you will set apart, O God, for your inheritance, etc. (82) Whoever has not received the voluntary rain is in drought. The voluntary rain is Christ, who came down from heaven, as he says: "I am the living bread."

Your living creatures dwell in it. In your goodness you have prepared for the poor, etc. (83) The living creatures, the cherubim and seraphim, dwell in God's inheritance. I think it is about them that it is said, "In the midst of two living creatures you will be known."
By the same. (84) By "living creatures" he means rational natures whose condition has become rather like that of beasts.

If you lie down among the lots, the wings of a dove are covered with silver, and its back with the pale green of gold, etc. (85) Some have said that the lots and the wings are the Old and New Testaments; others, practice and contemplation; others, the knowledge of bodies and of incorporeal beings; and still others, the knowledge of God and of Christ, whom he sent.

When the heavenly one distinguishes kings upon it, etc. (86) The kings are either those who have brought the passions into subjection or those who have attained the contemplation of created things. The gifts of the Holy Spirit themselves are also called kingdoms, and those who share in them are said to reign by virtue of them.
The chariot of God is ten-thousandfold, etc. (87) God's chariot is pure souls, upon which he rides; for "He mounted upon the cherubim and flew."

You ascended on high, you led captivity captive; you received gifts in man, etc. (88) Christ's captivity is the return of rational nature from wickedness and ignorance to virtue and knowledge. Paul also says something different about Christ: "He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men," and by "gifts" he means the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Having thus shown the descent of the Savior and the overthrow of the demons, he shows him ascending and setting free those who had been captives. Or else by "height" he means the cross. On it he ascended and pulled down from their pride the demons in the air, the spirits of wickedness. The souls those demons had taken captive through wicked deeds and had led to fall away from God he drew up from the recesses of Hades, like a band of captives, and set free.

But God will crush the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those who go about in their trespasses, etc. (89) The heads of the enemies are their rulers, or their ruling faculties. These enemies, whose very being comes from trespassing, go about in their trespasses. Or else the enemies' heads are the thoughts that the demons first bring upon the soul.

The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back in the depths of the sea, so that your foot may be dipped in blood, etc. (90) Bashan is interpreted as "shame." The Lord went down into it for our sake, despising the shame. And his foot is dipped in the blood that flows from the head of each of his enemies. For "I trampled them," says Isaiah, "in my anger."
Your processions have been seen, O God, etc. (91) At Christ's coming the processions of God were seen by those adorned with the word of knowledge.

In the churches bless God, the Lord, from the fountains of Israel, etc. (92) Blessing God among those outside the Church is not the same as doing it in the Church. Whoever blesses God in accordance with the treasure of God's wisdom in the Scriptures blesses him from the fountains of Israel; whoever does not do so does not bless God from the fountains of Israel.
There is Benjamin the youngest, etc. (93) They say this is a prophecy about Paul.
Because of your temple at Jerusalem kings will bring you gifts, etc. (94) Paul not only brought himself to God but also offered others to God through his teaching.
So that those tested with silver may be shut in, etc. (95) That is, so that those tested like silver may be set apart.

Envoys will come out of Egypt; Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hand to God, etc. (96) Through the Egyptians he hinted at the disposition toward wickedness; through the Ethiopians he showed the settled state of it.

Sing psalms to God, who rides upon the heaven of heaven toward the east, etc. (97) Earlier it said, "Make a way for him who rides upon the west"; now it says, "Sing psalms to him who rides upon the heaven of heaven toward the east." For "he who descended is the same one who also ascended far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things."

Give glory to God; his majesty is over Israel, and his power is in the clouds, etc. (98) Here by "clouds" he means holy powers. "For I will command the clouds," he says, "not to rain rain upon them." And there will be "a famine, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord." I think he calls the angels clouds, for they are the ones who teach us.
PSALM 68
Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul, etc. (99) By "waters" he means the thoughts and temptations that come into the soul.

I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold. I have come into the depths of the sea, and a storm has overwhelmed me, etc. (1) We find nothing like this suffered by David in the historical books. And if the psalm is applied to the Savior because of the words "Zeal for your house has eaten me up," we do not know of anything like this happening to the Savior himself either.

By the same. (2) In the preceding psalm the speaker taught how he went down to Bashan and said, "I will bring back in the depths of the sea." If so, it follows that we should take the speaker of the present words to be the same. So God the Word himself sends up a prayer to the Father, making his own the sufferings that belong to the man he assumed. And he refers to the regions of Hades, where he alone went down and passed through.

I am weary with crying out; my throat has grown hoarse; my eyes have failed from hoping in my God, etc. (3) This is said with reference to the disobedience of those who would not be persuaded by his teaching. But if he said he had grown weary with crying out to show that one must not lose heart in prayer but must cry out to God day and night, then consider alongside it, as being in harmony with it, the words "with loud cries and tears."

Those who hate me without cause are more than the hairs of my head; my enemies who persecute me unjustly have grown strong. What I did not snatch, I then repaid, etc. (4) From this, I think, one can know how many the demons are.

By the same. (5) He repaid what he had not snatched, yet even so he redeemed us (and this is what "repaying" means), blotting out the handwriting that stood against us. What we were compelled to repay, the charges brought against us, has been blotted out and taken out of the way, since forgiveness of sins has been given.

By the same. (6) God snatches no human being against his will. If he did, he would not say, "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest," or, "If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land." Paul was snatched up to the third heaven when he had already given himself over to God.

O God, you know my folly, and my trespasses are not hidden from you, etc. (7) God does not know the folly of everyone. He knows the folly of the one who became foolish for the sake of the foolish, lawless for the sake of the lawless, and weak for the sake of the weak.

By the same. (8) "Since false witnesses have risen up against me, you know, O God, whether I have committed any trespass, for nothing would have been hidden from you." It can also be taken another way. Since he took on our sins and became a curse for our sake, he says, "You know these trespasses too, which I took on for the sake of humankind."

For zeal for your house has eaten me up, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me, etc. (9) In the Gospels this verse is applied to the money-changers and bankers who were driven out of the temple. Where we read "has eaten me up," Symmachus translated "has consumed."

By the same. (10) Anyone who speaks on behalf of the Creator might also say these things, addressing those who stumble at Providence or the heterodox who speak ill of the Creator. Above all, someone reproached for God's sake might say, "The reproaches," and so on.

And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me, etc. (11) The disciples remembered this, as is written in the Gospel according to John: "And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me; and I made sackcloth my garment, and I became a byword to them."
By the same. (12) Fasting is a covering for the soul. It hides the soul's passions, namely shameful desire and irrational anger. So whoever does not fast is stripped bare and exposed to shame.
By the same. (13) "Nothing strange has happened," he says. "Those who reproached and insulted you, God the Father, in the Old Testament have also come against me, your Son."
And those who drank wine sang songs about me, etc. (14) This wine is the rage of dragons.

Save me from the mire, so that I may not stick fast; let me be rescued from those who hate me and from the depth of the waters, etc. (15) It is no ordinary task to allegorize these writings as events that happened to our Savior. I think all these things should be understood of his journey into Hades.

By the same. (16) The depth of the waters is where those end up who do not bear trials nobly. God alone rescues from it those who are able to say, "Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord." (16) Note that the text reads "from the depth of the waters," not "from the depths of the waters."
Nor let the pit close its mouth over me, etc. (17) Here he has called a certain subterranean rational nature a "pit," and many souls have fallen into it.

For you know my reproach, and my shame, and my disgrace, etc. (18) The reproach of Christ, which he suffered for righteousness' sake, is worthy of the knowledge of God. In the same way the righteous man may also be reproached.
By the same. (19) Our high priest, Christ, who has passed through the heavens, suffers shame on our account when the opposing spirits reproach him.

I looked for someone to share grief, and there was no one, and for someone to give comfort, and I found none, etc. (20) It does not say "someone to share my grief" but simply "someone to share grief," meaning the one who weeps with those who weep. Nor does it say "someone to comfort me" but "someone to give comfort," meaning the one who is able to say, "We comfort those in affliction." Or perhaps whoever does these things for one of those in the Church shares Christ's grief and comforts him, as is also said in connection with "I was hungry."

And they gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink, etc. (21) All these things happened at the time of the cross. By the same. (22) Wine that turns produces vinegar, and virtue that is corrupted gives birth to vice.

Let their table before them become a snare, and a retribution, and a stumbling block, etc. (23) The table of the Jews is the Old Testament, at which they stumble because they do not understand what concerns Christ. For it proclaims Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles.

By the same. (24) Perhaps the table from which the people received their food for the mind is the law and the prophets. Because Scripture is not understood, this table has become a snare, a retribution and a stumbling block for the Jews. But the table cannot be called this for everyone. The Lord is Wisdom, who says, "Come, eat my bread." He is the bread of life who came down from heaven, whose flesh is true food and whose blood is true drink.
Let their homestead be made desolate, and let no one dwell in their tents, etc. (25) These words can be taken as a prophecy about the temple of the Jews and about their city.
By the same. (26) After the cross their homestead, the temple and Jerusalem, was made desolate.

Add lawlessness to their lawlessness, and let them not enter into your righteousness, etc. (27) When those who have sinned lawlessly perish lawlessly, the punishment that matches their lawlessness is added to the lawlessness of those who sinned. "For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you."
By the same. (28) For how can they enter into righteousness when their eyes have been darkened?

Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be enrolled with the righteous, etc. (29) The book of the living is the knowledge of God, from which those with impure hearts fall away. For "Blessed," he says, "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." To see God is to be found worthy of knowing him.
By the same. (30) An unrighteous man is enrolled with the righteous if he stops being unrighteous.
It will please God more than a young calf that puts forth horns and hooves, etc. (31) That is, more than the irrational sacrifice perceived by the senses.
For the Lord has heard the poor and has not despised his prisoners, etc. (32) Let us become poor, so that our Lord may hear us.

Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all that creeps in them, etc. (33) Here he means the heavenly and earthly beings, calling them by the same names as their worlds. The same is true of "The heavens declare the glory of God."

By the same. (34) Will the creeping animals really give praise when Zion is saved and Judea is built up? But if the creeping things are to be understood spiritually, then clearly what is being built must also be taken spiritually.
For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judea will be built, etc. (35) By the cities of Judea he means rational souls.
PSALM 69
Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and confounded, etc. (36) Our invisible enemies seek the soul. They want to get it into their power by urging it on toward wickedness.
PSALM 70

It is clear that Christ speaks the words in this psalm. He prays that God may be a strong place for him. He who says, "I am in the Father," also says, "Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my protector." The first he says because he alone was conscious of God from the moment of his birth, and leaned upon him. The second refers to Herod's plot against Christ after the magi had worshipped him; Christ suffered nothing from it, because he was sheltered by God when the children two years old and under in the region of Bethlehem were being killed. And who is "the one who adds to all the praise" of God found in the law and the prophets, if not the Son? Though he pronounced woes on the scribes, he did not know their scribal learning. For he knows how the letter that kills teaches the things of the Spirit that gives life. He it is who rose from the dead; he it is who proclaimed the arm of God to every generation, and he says to the Father: "You brought me up again from the depths of the earth."

In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame, etc. If we endure in afflictions, we will not be put to shame in the age to come: "For affliction produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame."

My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner, from the hand of the lawbreaker and the unjust, etc. He calls Satan sinner, lawbreaker and unjust: sinner because of his utterly wicked state; lawbreaker because he transgressed his natural law; unjust because he deprives himself of the knowledge of God.

On you I have leaned from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my protector, etc. Jesus says this, for he alone knew how to lean upon God from the womb. God became his protector when the magi were warned to return to their own country by another way, and Joseph, as he was commanded, took the child with his mother and went away to Egypt, so that Jesus would not be killed with the other children.

I became like a portent to many, etc. To those who travel the broad and spacious way that leads many to destruction (for many are those who go through it) Jesus became like a portent; but not to the few who find the narrow and hard way that leads to life.

Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may hymn your glory, your majesty all the day long, etc. Unless the mind is filled with the grace of God, it cannot hymn the glory of God. For he has called the mind the mouth of the soul, and the Son of God its glory.
Saying, "God has forsaken him," etc. He has presented these words as spoken by the demons.
O God, do not keep far from me, etc. "Do not keep far" stands for "Do not be far away from me."

By the same. God becomes far from a human being, not in his essence (for he is present everywhere and fills all things), but in the working of his providence and his help. He is separated from us because of the stench of our sins, as another prophet says: "Your sins stand between me and you."
Let those who seek evil for me be clothed with shame and disgrace, etc. The saying "Let him have your cloak as well" can be applied to the shame and disgrace with which such a person is clothed.

But I will hope continually, and will add to all your praise, etc. Many praises of God have been spoken in the law and the prophets, and to them the one who said, "I did not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfil them," adds more, as is pleasing to the Church that bears Christ's name.

For I did not know letters, etc. If there is a letter that kills and a spirit that gives life, then the Lord, who knows those who are his, did not know what takes its name from the letter, but he did know what takes its name from the spirit.
Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone, etc. Christ will remember the righteousness of the Father.
Until I proclaim your arm to every generation to come, etc. The arm of God is Christ.
O God, the great things you have done reach to the highest heavens, etc. "Having made peace through his blood, both for the things in heaven and for the things on earth."

How many afflictions, many and evil, you have shown me! And you turned and gave me life, and brought me up again from the depths of the earth, etc. These words are clearly spoken about the resurrection from the dead.
By the same. Here he has called the region of the demons beneath the earth an "abyss." Some also call the demons themselves abysses, because their wickedness has no limit.
For I too will give thanks to you for your truth with an instrument of psalmody, etc. The instrument of psalmody is a pure soul.
PSALM 71
For Solomon, etc. For Solomon, the son of David: "For the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David." For "Solomon" means "peaceable"; and he is our peace.

O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son, etc. Christ is king, Son of God the king. That is why he reigns until all his enemies are made subject to him. Then he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father.
To judge your people in righteousness and your poor with justice, etc. Not all the poor belong to God, but only those whom Jesus calls blessed because they are with him.
Let the mountains receive peace, etc. "For blessed are the peacemakers."

He will judge the poor of the people, and save the sons of the needy, and humble the false accuser, etc. If the one who believes is not judged, perhaps the one who is rich in all speech and knowledge, rich in good works, and has laid up treasure, "whose own wealth is the ransom of his soul," is not judged; while the one who is poor in the way the people are poor is judged. He has neither made such progress in faith as to attain to the words "Whoever believes in me is not judged," nor has he fallen away so as to be among those of whom it is said, "Whoever does not believe is already judged." I take "whoever does not believe" to mean "whoever disbelieves."
He will come down like rain on a fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth, etc. Like rain upon the nations, like drops upon Israel.

In his days righteousness will rise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away, etc. That is, until the consummation. For when the moon is taken away, time is taken away; and when time has been taken away, the world of the senses will come to an end. He can also mean by the moon the opposing power, since it rules the night.
Before him the Ethiopians will fall down, and his enemies will lick the dust. The kings of Tarshish and the islands, etc. I think these words point to a difference among those who come to Christ.

By the same. Tarshish is an Ethiopian nation. Tarshish also signifies the colour of hyacinth, as we find in the prophet: "Their appearance was like Tarshish." In Jonah it also signifies the city of Tarsus. Sheba is a city of India, from which the queen of the south came to Solomon. Tarshish is interpreted as "spies," "a watching-out for gladness and joy."

All the nations will serve him, etc. If all the nations will serve him, then surely those that wage wars will serve him too. And if so, then every rational nature will serve Christ; and this is what Paul says, that every knee will bow to him.

And he will live, and he will be given of the gold of Arabia, etc. Christ lives in those who receive him: "It is no longer I who live," he says, "but Christ lives in me." Another commentator says of Solomon that both the Arabs and the neighbouring peoples pay him tribute.
And they will pray for him continually; all the day long they will bless him, etc. Saying: "Give us each day our daily bread."

By the same. The saints, having learned that no one born of woman will redeem humankind from the misery that holds it fast, continually sent up prayer to the Father concerning the one who is able to rescue from the hand of the mighty.
His fruit will be exalted above Lebanon, etc. In many places he calls the mountain, the temple and the sons of Israel "Lebanon."
By the same. The fruit of Christ is the nations that have believed and have been exalted in godliness above Israel, which he figuratively calls Lebanon.
All the nations will call him blessed, etc. Paul says: "the blessed and only Sovereign."
PSALM 72

How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart, etc. As far as it rests with him, God is good to all: for "he is the Saviour of all people, especially of believers." But perhaps what is written may amount to this: To the upright in heart God is seen to be good. For how is a physician not good also to the sick, who need him?
For I was envious of the lawless, seeing the peace of sinners, etc. Here he has called the prosperity of life in this world of the senses "peace."
For there is no regard for their death, etc. By "regard" he means the remembrance of death; hence Symmachus has rendered it, "For they gave no thought to their own death."
They clothed themselves with their injustice and ungodliness, etc. Injustice is seen in a wicked life, ungodliness in false doctrines.
Their injustice will come forth as if from fat, etc. "Their eyes bulged out from fatness," according to Symmachus.

They set their mouth in heaven, and their tongue went through the earth, etc. The saying, "Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit." At the same time we also learn through these words the essence of the good God.
PSALM 73

Why, O God, have you rejected us to the end? etc. Taken literally, these are the words of those in captivity. The Lord rejects those whom he rejects according to the multitude of their ungodly deeds. Some he rejects, as it is written, "exceedingly"; others "to the end," to the uttermost.
Your anger was kindled against the sheep of your pasture, etc. The saying "He will go in and go out and find pasture" is useful here.

Remember your congregation, which you acquired from the beginning, etc. You will inquire from what beginning God acquired his congregation, and whether he did so by foreknowledge or in some other way. The "why," addressed to God as a question, asks for an answer that teaches the cause of the rejection and of the anger. "You were angry against the sheep" is said in order to appease the one who is angry: he asks pardon for those who are as senseless as sheep, for the sins they have committed in thought. And though you have forgotten the congregation because of its sins, remember that it became your possession from the beginning.
