How it was "from the beginning" is not made clear, not even if you understand that it became God's possession when it came out of Egypt.

You redeemed the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion, where you have dwelt, etc. You will inquire, whether God acquired Mount Zion or redeemed it, how he acquired it or redeemed it from the beginning. Inquire into this mystically.

All the evil the enemy has done in your holy place, and those who hate you have boasted in the midst of your feast, etc. God is the God not of a place but of virtue. The place is mentioned out of hope in his love for humankind, so that he says that those who trespass on places consecrated to God are repaid in this way: the evil word, the enemy, is in the holy places. And now too the enemy does evil in the holy place, that is, in the Church. And if anyone falls away from the feasts of God, those who hate Christ and kill him boast, whether they be the people or the opposing powers.
As in a forest of trees they hacked down its doors with axes, etc. All these things were fulfilled at the capture of Jerusalem, as Josephus records, recounting each of the deeds done.

They set your sanctuary on fire, burning it to the ground; they profaned the dwelling place of your name, etc. The dwelling place of God's name is the mind, which is profaned when it becomes earthly instead of heavenly.

Why do you turn away your hand, your right hand, from the midst of your bosom to the end? etc. If God's hand differs from his right hand, I wonder whether perhaps the hand does what is directed against the enemies of the people, and the right hand does good things for the people. An example of the hand is when God, on behalf of the Hebrews, sent out from the midst of his bosom upon the Egyptians wrath and anger and affliction, a mission of evil angels. It is as though formerly good things had been given from the midst of the bosom by the hand of God, but later the divine hand had turned away from taking good things from the midst of the bosom and giving them to the people. At the same time you will inquire whether the hand and the right hand of God are two.

But God, our King before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth, etc. This was when the Son of Man spent three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Perhaps "the midst of the earth" means its centre, since it is spherical.

By your power you made the sea firm; you crushed the heads of the dragons on the water, etc. So that the wind might no longer be against the disciples as they sailed, and, once a calm had come upon them, they might reach the land to which they were going.

Summer and spring, you made them, etc. Why did he leave out autumn and winter? They say, then, that summer is the opposite of autumn and winter the opposite of spring; and that spring is the season of coming into being, and summer the season of completion.

Remember this, etc. Remember this, meaning the creation. If, he says, you made the creation for the sake of human beings, then [?] grant your help to those for whose sake the creation came into being. Or else it means: this congregation which you acquired from the beginning; for it can also be referred back to that.

Do not hand over to the wild beasts a soul that confesses you, etc. If the demons are called wild beasts, and anger prevails in wild beasts, then anger prevails in the demons. And in Job it says: "The wild beasts will be at peace with you."
Look upon your covenant, etc. Remember your promises, which you made to Abraham, to give his offspring a land flowing with milk and honey.
For the darkened ones of the earth are filled with houses of lawlessness, etc. A darkened mind is filled with lawlessness; for darkness has to do with knowledge, and lawlessness with action.

Arise, O God, judge your cause; remember how you are reproached by the fool all the day long, etc. "Arise, O God" as far as "all the day long." He did not say "my cause" but "your cause." For I, he says, endure these things justly; but they have dared to utter many blasphemies against you. He rouses God to punish those who deceived the people. Or else it means this: Remember the covenant you granted them through Christ. For even if some have become utterly darkened in understanding, and those who did not receive your Christ are filled with houses of lawlessness, yet do you, at least, as God, not turn away from the supplications of your poor. Since it is not we who have been wronged but you (for the enemy reproached you, and a foolish people provoked you), for this reason "arise and judge your cause."
By the same. Here he calls the devil "the fool."
PSALM 74

For the end; "Do not destroy"; a psalm of a song, of Asaph, etc. It is written in 1 Samuel: "And David said to Abishai, Do not destroy him," that is, Saul. See whether this is useful for understanding the title.
We will give thanks to you, O God, we will give thanks, and we will call upon your name, etc. The Church in Christ speaks these two lines.

I will recount all your wonders. When I take the appointed time, etc. Symmachus has: "When I receive the congregation." When, he says, we return and are gathered into your holy temple, then we will hymn you as the law prescribes, and teach your benefits to those who do not know them; for that time will allow us to do this. Having thus taught what the captives in Babylon ought to do, he shows God answering [?] concerning the promises that had been made and saying, "I will judge uprightly." See, then, whether through these words the Saviour is not teaching his own works as he expounds the theology of the Father. At any rate he says, "I will recount your wonders, O God, when I receive the congregation"; for he promises that, when he has found a fitting time, he will recount all the wonders of the Father. And it is a work of righteousness and uprightness not to admit the Jews alone, but to choose those who are to be saved from all the nations.

The earth melted, and all who dwell in it, etc. By "earth" he means rational nature, which melted under the spiritual fire that the Saviour came to cast upon the earth. Melting is the separation of the soul from evil; and the spiritual fire is the Saviour's spiritual teaching, which destroys evil and ignorance.
I have made its pillars firm, etc. "And when James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars," says the Apostle, "recognized the grace that had been given to me."

For there is a cup in the hand of the Lord, full of a mixture of unmixed wine; and he has tilted it from this side to that, yet its dregs have not been emptied out. All the sinners of the earth will drink, etc. Now punishments are served to sinners diluted; but in the age to come they will be served undiluted and, as it were, full of dregs. Or else it means this: The cup, he says, is in the Lord's hand. Into it he presses, as it were, the fruits of each person, both the good and the evil, and by mixing the good with the evil he fills it. Then those whose dregs are not poured out, that is, those in whom their sins remain, will drink it down and be made drunk on their own evils; just as all the saints too will drink the cup of life in the kingdom of heaven with the Lord Jesus himself, according to the Lord's word.
PSALM 75

In Judea God is known; in Israel his name is great; and his place has come to be in peace, etc. The place of God that is in us by nature, which was not formerly at peace, has come to be peace. So at Christ's coming God was made known, as the Son revealed him in the Jerusalem above. Or else: God is known in the Judea above, where his true [?] is, and not a glory of his in figures; for now God is known through a mirror and in a riddle. Moreover, his name is great not in Israel according to the flesh but in Israel according to the spirit. And the "place" of God, which people give him within themselves, is in the Judea above, in which it "came to be in peace." Corresponding to this is God's "dwelling place in Zion," of which it is said: "But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." There is peace there for this reason: because in it the might of the bows was broken, and the shield and the sword and war.
By the same. The place of God is a pure soul; the dwelling place of God is a contemplative mind.

There he broke the might of the bows, the shield and the sword and war, etc. Here he calls the demons bows, from which the flaming arrows are shot. A flaming arrow is an impassioned thought; and the same thing is also called a shield and a sword.
You shine wondrously from the everlasting mountains, etc. That is, you teach us through the holy powers.
All the senseless in heart were troubled, etc. To be troubled is the mark of the senseless; for the wise are not troubled.

They slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands, etc. That is why the wise Solomon rightly urges: "Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, so that you may be saved like a gazelle from the snares and like a bird from the trap."
By the same. "Men of wealth" is said in the same way as "men of blood"; for those who have passions are named after those passions.

Those mounted on horses fell asleep, etc. The demons sit upon horses and mules, which have no understanding, and force them to act like irrational animals. The horses and mules are people ruled by passion, who are carried irrationally toward what they ought not, and neigh after their neighbours' wives.

All who are around him will bring gifts to the one who is fearsome, who takes away the spirits of rulers, who is fearsome among the kings of the earth, etc. The one who is fearsome to the kings of the earth takes away the spirits of rulers. The spirit of rulers is in those who are ruled by the rulers of this age. The spirit of the ruler of this age was also in Judas, who betrayed Jesus. The Saviour, becoming fearsome to these spirits, removes them from those in whom they are at work, at a time that he himself knows, so that they may repent. In this way he is also fearsome among the kings of the earth, of whom it is said: "The kings of the earth took their stand."
PSALM 7[?]

With my voice I cried to the Lord, and my voice was to God, and he gave heed to me, etc. When our whole voice accords with God, then, whenever our voice reaches him, he gives heed to us, since the voice we have is undefiled.
In the day of my affliction I sought out God, etc. Through the practical life we seek out God in the present age.
By the same. It is the mark of a saint not to be troubled in hard circumstances, but to seek out God.
My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God, etc. The soul that is not grieved at all by temptations refuses to be comforted, since it has no need of comfort.
By the same. Nothing comforts the soul so much as the remembrance of God.
My eyes anticipated the watches, etc. This is a sign of much wakefulness.

I was troubled, and did not speak, etc. One who has been stirred by anger, or grief, or the other passions, but has restrained himself and said nothing out of anger, or grief, or any of the passions, could say: "I was troubled, and did not speak."

I considered the days of old, and I remembered the eternal years, etc. The one who has come to know the unseen and hidden things of God also holds the memory of the ages gone by, and of the years within them, and of the ancient days of which these are made up.
By night I meditated with my heart, and I searched my spirit, etc. As if he were saying: I meditated with my mind and with my spirit.
Or will he cut off his mercy for ever? etc. Because he cuts off his mercy from some, it is said elsewhere: "Extend your mercy to those who know you."

And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High, etc. He had never yet begun, though he had cried out to God, and sought him in the day of affliction, and not been deceived, and rejoiced in remembering God, while his eyes anticipated the watches. The right hand of the Most High is the Saviour, who changed himself by taking the form of a servant. Through him we began in the New [Covenant], having first been made ready for the types to begin to cease and the truth to begin.
By the same. Here he calls "change" the return from vice and ignorance to virtue and knowledge.
O God, your way is in the holy place; what god is great like our God? etc. Either the way of God is in every holy one, or his Word is in Christ; for he who said, "I am the way," is in the holy one.

By the same. Consider whether by these words he rejoices that there are indeed some gods, but none great like our God, and whether one may use in this connection the saying: "As there are many gods," etc.
You made known your power among the peoples, etc. That is, Christ; for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
The depths were troubled, etc. The depths signify the subterranean powers, which were troubled at the coming of Christ.
The voice of your thunder was in the wheel, etc. The wheel signifies either this age, or the sensible world, or the pure and eternal soul, since vice lurks at a corner.
Your lightnings shone upon the world, etc. The thunder comes before the lightning, but the lightning is seen first.

Your way was in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps will not be known, etc. Above it was said: "O God, your way is in the holy place." The way of God was in the Red Sea, and his paths in many waters at the Jordan, in the time of Joshua and of Elijah. But also "his ways are past tracing out." Therefore "his footsteps will not be known" as he travels in the sea and has paths in many waters, by which he led his people through the Red Sea.
PSALM 77.
And that they might seek out his commandments, etc. Those who seek out the commandments of God do not become blameworthy as their fathers did.
They turned back in the day of battle, etc. The one who does not keep the law of God is the one who turns his back to the enemy.
And they went on sinning still more against him, etc. How grievous it is to sin after knowledge!

Will God be able to prepare a table in the wilderness? etc. The soul of Matthew the tax collector was formerly a wilderness, but our Saviour made it a table that feeds people's souls through the Gospel.
And fire was kindled in Jacob, and wrath went up against Israel, etc. Fire is kindled against the practical person, and wrath goes up against the contemplative.
And he opened the doors of heaven, etc. By the doors of heaven he means rational natures that have been moved to spiritual teaching.

Man ate the bread of angels, etc. The Saviour says: "I am the bread that came down from heaven." So this bread was eaten before by angels, but now by human beings as well. "To eat" here means "to know." For the mind eats what it also knows, and does not eat what it does not know.
And he rained flesh upon them like dust, etc. He called the quail "flesh."
And he remembered that they are flesh, etc. That is, fleshly.
He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them, etc. The Hebrews say that the dog-fly means various kinds of beasts mixed together.
The firstfruits of all their labour in the tents of Ham, etc. Having disciplined those people in this way, he led his own people into the wilderness, like a shepherd leading his flock.
And he brought them to the mountain of his sanctuary, etc. The mountain of the sanctuary is the knowledge of God.
And he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents, etc. "For I will dwell in them," he says, "and walk among them."
And they tempted and embittered God the Most High, etc. A sinning soul embitters knowledge, but the soul that does right sweetens it.
They were turned into a crooked bow, etc. The crooked bow is a perverted soul, and its arrows are evil thoughts.
And he rejected the tent of Shiloh, etc. That is, the one that stood at Shiloh.
And he disregarded his inheritance, etc. Here he has called "inheritance" that which inherits. Alternatively, God's inheritance is rational souls.
Fire devoured their young men, etc. Perhaps the fire is the flaming arrows of the evil one.
And he chose the tribe of Judah, etc. "For it is evident that our Lord sprang from Judah," says the Apostle.
PSALM 78.
For we have become exceedingly poor, etc. We have become poor because we have been deprived of the riches of knowledge.
PSALM 79.
Stir up your might, etc. Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
You will feed us with the bread of tears, etc. Through these words he depicts a most bitter repentance.
And make your face shine, and we shall be saved, etc. Here he has called Christ the face: "For he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation."
You brought a vine out of Egypt, etc. By the vine he here means the twelve tribes of Israel.
And its climbing branches [covered] the cedars of God, etc. The climbing branches are the contemplatives.
Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, etc. By the man of the right hand he means Christ, who is also the Son of Man.
You will give us life, and we will call upon your name, etc. No one can give us life except the one who said: "I am the life."
PSALM 80.
He heard a language that he did not know, etc. He heard a law that he did not understand.
There shall be no new god among you, etc. A new god is one who cannot bring anything into being, or one that has taken on the quality of vice.
Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it, etc. By the mouth he here means the mind, which is made radiant by upright conduct and true doctrines.
And I sent them away according to the pursuits of their hearts, etc. "For this reason," says Paul, "God gave them up to dishonourable passions."
PSALM 81.
But you die like men, and fall like one of the rulers, etc. "I planted," he says, "a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you turned to bitterness, you alien vine?"
PSALM 82.

They said: Come, let us destroy them so that they are no longer a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more, etc. From this we learn that the demons summon one another to the destruction of a soul.
Who said: Let us take the sanctuary of God as our inheritance, etc. An impure soul is the portion of demons, but a pure soul is the portion of God.
O my God, make them like a wheel, etc. A wheel touches the ground only a little.
Fill their faces with dishonour, etc. This face is that of the old man, who is being corrupted according to the lusts of deceit; once it is destroyed, the mind seeks out the name of the Lord.
Let them be put to shame and troubled for ever and ever, and let them be confounded and perish, etc. This perishing signifies the destruction of vice and ignorance.
PSALM 83.
Blessed are those who dwell in your house, etc. David himself longs to enter the courts of the Lord, but he calls blessed those who dwell in the house of the Lord.
PSALM 84.
You forgave the iniquities of your people, you covered all their sins, etc. Through holy baptism the Lord takes sins away, but through bitter repentance he covers sins.

Mercy and truth have met, righteousness and peace have kissed, etc. Peace cannot be joined to righteousness unless truth has met with mercy; for mercy begets righteousness, and truth begets peace. Righteousness and peace are understood with reference to practice and contemplation.
Righteousness will go before him, etc. Righteousness is the chief of the practical virtues, and from it people are also called righteous.
PSALM 85.
Save your servant, O my God, who hopes in you, etc. The knowledge of God is the salvation of the soul.
And a gathering of the mighty sought my soul, etc. He has called the rank of the demons a gathering of the mighty.
PSALM 86.

Mother Zion will say: A man, and a man was born in her, etc. The child Jesus is born in Bethlehem, but the man in Zion, because practice is brought forth in the soul, while wisdom is begotten in the mind.
The dwelling in you is as of all who rejoice, etc. All who rejoice in knowledge dwell in wisdom; and all who dwell in wisdom rejoice in knowledge, as wisdom does.
PSALM 87.
And my life drew near to Hades, etc. If you take Hades to mean death, you will understand how death destroys a person's life. But here he calls the devil Hades, and himself life.
Like the wounded sleeping in the grave, whom you remembered no more, etc. The Lord remembers the one in whom he comes to dwell, and does not remember the one in whom he does not.
And they were thrust away from your hand, etc. By the hand he here means the knowledge of God, whose nature is to help those who are under attack.

Your wrath bore down upon me, etc. Christ halted the wrath of God that had rushed out against all people. For "all have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is none who does good."
Will you work wonders for the dead? etc.
Those who are deprived of life cannot see the wonders of the life that said: "I am the life."
Will anyone tell of your mercy in the grave, and of your truth in destruction? etc. Just as there is no truth in those who have perished, so there are no wonders in those who have been darkened.
And your righteousness in a forgotten land? etc. A forgotten land is a rational soul deprived of the fruits of the Holy Spirit.
Your terrors have troubled me, etc. By terrors he means certain unclean and harsh powers.
PSALM 88.
I will sing of your mercies, O Lord, for ever. From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth, etc. Mercy builds up human beings, but truth makes ready the holy powers.
The heavens will confess your wonders, etc. "Will confess" stands for "will glorify."

Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name, etc. Tabor [?] "chosen." Tabor is the mountain in Galilee on which Christ was transfigured. Hermonim is the mountain on which lies the city of Nain, where Christ raised the widow's son.
And in your good pleasure our horn will be exalted, etc. By the horn he here means the mind, and the mind is exalted through the knowledge of God.
Then you spoke in a vision to your sons, etc. Then you spoke through the holy prophets.
With my holy oil I anointed him, etc. The holy oil signifies the knowledge of God, or rather it points to essential knowledge.
The enemy shall not profit by him, etc. If we profit our enemies whenever we sin, but Christ did not sin, then Christ gave his enemies no profit.

And I will set his hand in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers, etc. Christ's hand is set in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers. Yet the sea, if it wishes, becomes a river; and again the river, if it does not keep the river of living water flowing from its belly, becomes sea.
And his throne as the days of heaven, etc. When the will of God is done on earth as it is in heaven, then Christ's throne too will be as the days of heaven.

And do not keep my commandments, etc. The one who does not keep the commandments of God ceases to be a throne of God: "For wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, nor dwell in a body that is in debt to sin."
I will punish their iniquities with a rod, etc. "For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives."
You have dashed his throne to the ground, etc. A mind is dashed from heaven to earth when it has become earthly instead of heavenly.
You have shortened the days of his time, etc. When we are forsaken, our virtues and our knowledge dwindle; for these are the days of the rational nature.

Who is the man who will live and not see death, who will rescue his soul from the hand of Hades? etc. Virtue and knowledge grow as all the vices and ignorance gradually diminish. Vice and ignorance are the death of the rational soul, and virtue and knowledge are its life.

Which I bore in my bosom, of many nations, etc. By the bosom he here means the soul, because the knowledge of God is called "good things," and good things are naturally put into the bosom. "For I believe," he says, "that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living."
The exchange for your Christ, etc. Perhaps the Lord's man.
PSALM 89.
Their years will be things of naught, etc. Their life will be brought to nothing.
Our years were like a spider's; they were pondering, etc. "For our life on earth," says Job, "is a shadow."
And most of them is toil and trouble, etc. For the greater part of the years that have passed we are in toils and troubles.
So make your right hand known to me, etc. Let your right hand be made known not for punishment but for loving-kindness.

And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us, etc. Brightness is the knowledge of God, for those who share in it are also called brightnesses: "In the brightnesses of the saints," he says, "from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you."
And direct the work of our hands, etc. The works of the hands are practice in particular matters, but the work of the hands is the knowledge that results from them.
PSALM 90.
With his shoulders he will overshadow you, etc. The shoulders are a symbol of the heart.
His truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night, etc. Christ's shield is true knowledge, and the one it surrounds will not be terrified.
From the arrow that flies by day, etc.
Here he has called a certain unclean power an arrow. From mishap and the noonday demon, etc. They say that the noonday demon is the demon of acedia.
And no scourge will come near your dwelling, etc. If anyone wishes not to fall under the scourge, let him become a house of God.
To guard you in all your ways, etc. The one who stumbles in nothing is the one who is guarded in all his ways.
Lest you strike your foot against a stone, etc. The foot signifies the soul, and the stone signifies sin.
And I will show him my salvation, etc. The salvation of God is Christ.
PSALM 91.
On a ten-stringed psaltery, with song on the lyre, etc. The psaltery is a pure mind moved by spiritual knowledge, and the lyre is a practical soul moved by the commandments of Christ.
A foolish man will not know, etc. The offspring of folly is vice, and the offspring of vice is ignorance.
For behold, your enemies will perish, etc. An enemy who perishes becomes a friend, for God has abolished his enmity.
And my old age in rich oil, etc. The old age of the righteous man is true knowledge, and his youth is the soul's dispassion.

Planted in the house of the Lord, etc. The righteous, planted in the knowledge of the Lord, will make many people blossom in this world or in the churches, making them bear fruit through spiritual teaching.
And there is no unrighteousness in him, etc. There is no unrighteousness in God, because he cannot admit vice.
PSALM 92.
The rivers have lifted up their voices, etc. He calls holy rational natures rivers, because rivers of living water flow from their heart.
Wonderful are the swellings of the sea, etc. A soul becomes wonderful when it is lifted aloft and separated from the waves of this life.
PSALM 93.
Render recompense to the proud, etc. Pride is contempt for a good calling.

They have humbled your people, O Lord, etc. "Whom the Lord loves he disciplines," says the Apostle. And if he calls blessed the one he disciplines, then everyone he disciplines will become dispassionate, for that is the one the Lord loves. Discipline is the moderation of the passions.
To give him rest from evil days, etc. By evil days he means the days of judgment, in which the one he disciplines, having been purified of the passions, will enjoy knowledge and remain untroubled.
Until a pit is dug for the sinner, etc. He has called Gehenna a pit.

Until righteousness returns to judgment, etc. Until Christ judges the world; for he "became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption," and "the Father has given all judgment to him."

Your mercy, O Lord, helped me, etc. Here the mercy of Christ signifies his providence, by which a person is either helped or abandoned. A person is helped when it is at work, and abandoned when it withdraws.
Your comforts gladdened my soul, etc. Comfort is the soul's recovery from its toils.
Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with you? etc. He has called the devil the throne of iniquity, since Christ, who is opposed to the devil, is the throne of righteousness.
And according to their wickedness he will destroy them [?], etc. "For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith."

The rivers will clap their hands together, etc. If the gifts of the Holy Spirit are called rivers, according to the saying, "Rivers of living water will flow from his belly," then those who will share in these rivers are rightly called rivers themselves. Note also that the rivers are "together," so that all may say the same thing and there may be no divisions among them.
PSALM 98.
You have prepared uprightness, etc. Uprightness: either the upright, or the virtues.

And worship at the footstool of his feet, etc. Some have said that the footstool of his feet is the flesh of Christ, which is worthy of worship because of Christ; and Christ is worthy of worship because of the Word of God in him.
And Samuel among those who call upon his name, etc. The one who acts righteously calls upon righteousness, the one who does not lie calls upon truth, and the one who does not hate calls upon love.
In a pillar of cloud he spoke to them, etc. The pillar and the cloud are rational natures through which the Lord spoke to the saints.
Exalt the Lord our God, etc. It is by a pure mind that God is naturally exalted.
PSALM 99.
Enter his gates, etc. The gates of wisdom are the virtues, for through them we enter the kingdom of heaven.
PSALM 100.
Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord, etc. He wishes to sing the account of providence and judgment.
Whoever secretly slandered his neighbour, him I drove away, etc. The verse is useful against slanderers.
He who walked in a blameless way, he ministered to me, etc. The verse should be used against members of the priesthood who are served by thoroughly wicked servants.
To destroy from the city [of the Lord], etc. Here he calls his own soul the city of the Lord, in which he put to death all lawless thoughts.
PSALM 101.
I kept vigil and became like a sparrow alone on a housetop, etc. Nothing makes the mind so light as keeping vigil.
For I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping, etc. The verse is useful against those who delight in pipes and songs at their drinking.
And I withered like grass; but you, O Lord, remain for ever, etc. I am temporary and mortal, but you are everlasting and immortal.
Do not take me away in the midst of my days, etc. Of the days produced by the Sun of righteousness.
They will perish, but you will remain, etc.
The heavens will perish not in their substance but in their form: "For the form of this world is passing away," says the Apostle.
PSALM 102.

Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name, etc. The things within the inner man are the intellectual faculty, the discursive faculty, the attentive faculty, the interpretive faculty, the imaginative faculty, and the faculty of memory.
Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's, etc. The eagle strips off its old age, just as a person also strips off the old man, which is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit.

For as high as heaven is above the earth, so has the Lord made his mercy strong toward those who fear him, etc. Just as he has exalted those in heaven, so he has had mercy on those on earth who fear him.

As for man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so will he flourish, etc. Here "man" denotes human nature in general; for every human being is temporary and mortal, quick to wither and transient.
For the spirit has passed through him, and he will be no more, etc. After death the soul no longer exists in this life.
But the mercy of the Lord is from age to age upon those who fear him, etc. The life of the senses is not everlasting, but the mercy of the Lord is everlasting.
And his righteousness upon children's children, etc. Children's children are those who have been deemed worthy of his Spirit of adoption.
And to those who remember his commandments, etc. The one who remembers the commandments is the one who lives according to them.
And his kingdom rules over all, etc. His kingship as Creator rules over all; but his kingship by way of knowledge rules not over all those on earth, though it does rule over all those in heaven.
PSALM 103.
Who wraps himself in light as in a garment, etc. The Lord's garment is true knowledge, and whoever puts it on will be enlightened by it.

Stretching out the heaven like a tent-skin, etc. Why did he not say "having stretched out" but "stretching out"? Is it not because he stretched it out once as regards its substance, but is always stretching it out as regards his providence? Of the same kind is what is said in Job: "Who makes the Pleiades, and Hesperus, and Arcturus, and the chambers of the south."
Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire, etc. To Abraham the angels appeared as spirits, but to the Sodomites as blazing fire.
Who founded the earth on its firm foundation; it will not be moved for ever and ever, etc.
Job said, "Hanging the earth upon nothing"; but David, "on its firm foundation."
Both of them rule out the existence of some other body underneath that supports it. For the "firm foundation" is not a substance but the art of God, which keeps the earth unmoved within the sphere.
The deep, like a garment, is his covering, etc. By the deep he represents the incomprehensibility of the knowledge of God.
Mountains rise up and plains sink down to the place you founded for them, etc. By these words he hints at certain rational natures.
You set a boundary which they will not pass, etc. They say that these things are said about the demons under the earth.
Watering the mountains from his upper chambers, etc. God's upper chambers are pure natures that water those who are loftier in heart.
The trees of the plain will be satisfied, etc.

But the Hebrew and the other translators have put "of the Lord." Having gone through the fruit-bearing trees, he must also mention the fruitless ones, since these too supply people with something they need. That is why he called them "the Lord's": they grow of themselves and are not planted by hand, but sprang up by the divine word. And so he went on: "The cedars of Lebanon, which you planted."
By the same. Just as there are certain trees of paradise, so there are also trees of the plain.
The rock is a refuge for the rock-badgers, etc. Whoever is in the condition of a rock-badger, let him flee for refuge to the spiritual rock that followed them in the wilderness and gave Israel drink.
The sun knows its setting, etc. The sun of righteousness now knows those in whom it once set. The sun rose, and they were gathered together, etc.
In those in whom the sun of righteousness rises, the vices too exist only potentially.

Man will go out to his work, and to his labor until evening, etc. By "work" he here means the material itself on which the labor is performed, and by "labor" the craft itself that is exercised on the material.

There are creeping things without number, etc. Of the people who have become creeping things through wickedness there is no number; for, it says, "He numbers the multitudes of the stars and calls them all by name."
You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust, etc. Those who fall away from the spirit given them by God become earthy.
You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth, etc. What the holy Paul called the resurrection, David called a renewal.
Who touches the mountains, and they smoke, etc. The smoking mountains cast off wickedness when the spiritual fire that was cast upon the earth touches them.
Let sinners vanish from the earth, etc. Not that they should cease to exist, but that they should cease to be sinners.
PSALM 104.
Tell of all his wonders, etc. One who has acquired all the knowledge of God is able to tell of all his wonders.
Seek the Lord, etc. Whoever does God's commandments is the one who seeks him.
Seek his face continually, etc. He tells us to seek the face which the angels behold continually.
Seed of Abraham, his servants, etc. Those who are of the seed of Abraham are potentially elect.

He remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations, etc. Some have thought that by the thousand generations he means many generations; others, the generations comprised within this number.

Saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan, the measured portion of your inheritance," etc. Before the coming of Christ the Canaanites held our souls, not allowing us to bring forth spiritual fruit.
He did not allow anyone to wrong them, etc. From this we learn that those who are wronged by others are wronged because God has abandoned them.

Do not touch my anointed ones, etc. These anointed ones are called anointed because they share in Christ; but Christ is called Christ because he shares in the Father. And by "Christ" he means the Lord who came among us together with God the Word.
And he made him stronger than his enemies, etc. Without virtue and the knowledge of God no one could become stronger than the enemies.
He spoke, and the dog-fly came, etc. The Hebrews interpret the dog-fly as a mixed multitude of wild and flesh-eating beasts; but the Greeks call the dog-fly the fly of the barking dog.
And he struck their vines, etc. For their vines were of the vine of Sodom, and their tendrils of Gomorrah.
He spoke, and the locust came, etc. This locust devours the evil seed.
PSALM 105.
And he saved them for his name's sake, to make known his power, etc. The Lord saves us for this reason: to bestow on us the knowledge of his power.
Not one of them was left, etc. Blessed is the one of whose enemies none is left.
They did not wait for his counsel, and they lusted with lust in the wilderness, etc. They did not wait for his grace but forgot his works and lusted with an evil lust.

And they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass, etc. Those who glorify a creature rather than the Creator exchange their glory. "And they exchanged," says Paul, "the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things."
And he said he would destroy them, etc. Destruction here signifies removal from this life.

Had not Moses his chosen one stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath so that he would not destroy them, etc. Note that even one holy man, like Moses, is able to turn away wrath that is bearing down on a whole nation.
And they despised the desirable land, etc. The desirable land is the kingdom of heaven.
And he lifted up his hand against them, etc. By "hand" he means his powers of punishment.
And they were initiated into the rites of Baal-peor, etc. Baal-peor is an idol of Bel in the place called Peor.
And they ate sacrifices of the dead, etc. They performed rites for Baal-peor, making remembrance in his mysteries.
And Phinehas stood up and made atonement, etc. Earlier he says that Moses stood and turned the plague away; but now the plague ceased.
And they mingled among the nations, etc. A person mingles with the nations by serving carved images.
And they went whoring in their practices, etc. A soul commits fornication when it receives seeds from the hostile power and bears evil children.
And he abhorred his inheritance, etc. "The Lord's inheritance is rational souls."
And those who hated them ruled over them, etc. Those who hate us and afflict our souls are demons.
And he gave them over to compassion before all who had taken them captive, etc. From this we learn that it is the Lord who makes us worthy even of receiving mercy.
PSALM 106.
For he satisfied the empty soul, etc. The empty soul is the one deprived of virtues and knowledge.

And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, etc. Inasmuch as the Lord is light, he leads us out of the darkness; inasmuch as he is life, out of death; and again, as one who is mighty, he breaks bonds apart.
Their soul loathed all food, etc. Just as the sick loathe all food, so the impure push away all knowledge.

They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep, etc. All who fall into many and varied distractions for the sake of practicing virtue see the works of the Lord, that is, the inner principles of the things that have come to be and are coming to be.
And all their wisdom was swallowed up, etc. Wickedness swallows up the wisdom of God, but the righteousness of the Lord destroys wickedness.
And its waves fell silent, etc. By the silence of the waves he means the destruction of temptations.
And he made them wander in a trackless place, and not on a road, etc. He left them to wander and did not come to their aid, because of their wickedness.
PSALM 107.
My heart is ready, etc. The one who has put away the passions has made his heart ready for God.
Moab is the cauldron of my hope, etc. The cauldron is the one who is fervent in spirit and hopes in the Lord; and this hope does not put to shame the one who hopes.
Over Idumea I will cast my sandal, etc. The flesh is the sandal of Christ; making use of it, the Lord came to dwell in human life.
PSALM 108.

And let the devil stand at his right hand, etc. Satan stands at the right hand of those whose right-hand works he cuts off. In Zechariah it says: "And the Lord showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand" — not merely standing, but "to oppose him." But he does not oppose Judas.

Let his children be orphans and his wife a widow, etc. It seems to me that the righteous man is not cursing here but praying. For "Bless your enemies," says the Apostle; "bless and do not curse." The orphans, then, are evil thoughts that have buried their own father, Satan; and the widow is the soul that has not received seeds from the devil. The order too is fitting: first he removes the sins committed in act, and then also their base thoughts.
Let it be to him like the garment he wraps around himself, and like the belt with which he is always girded, etc. This belt signifies the irrational burning of the desiring part of the soul.
My knees have grown weak from fasting, etc. This text should be used against those who despise self-control.
They will curse, but you will bless, etc. The Lord blesses the one whom the adversaries curse.
PSALM 109.

With you is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints, etc. If the Father is the beginning of the Son, and the beginning was with Christ, then he rightly says in the Gospels: "I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me." By the day of power he meant the day of the cross, or of the incarnation.

From the womb, before the Morning Star, I begot you, etc. That is: before every rational nature I begot you. For to inquire more deeply into the generation of Christ and of the Morning Star is beyond our power, since the account of this is long and hard to contemplate.
He will judge among the nations; he will fill up the corpses, etc. He fills up the corpses of the old man, which is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit.
PSALM 110.
In the council of the upright and in the assembly: great are the works of the Lord, etc. He called the works of the Lord great because of the wisdom stored up in them.
He gave food to those who fear him, etc.
The food of those who fear the Lord is the wisdom of God; for "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom."

He declared to his people the strength of his works, etc. He calls the contemplation of created things the strength of his works; and knowledge is called strength because it puts strength into rational nature.

The works of his hands are truth and judgment, etc. Truth is contemplated in right doctrines, and judgment in the practical life. "All his commandments are faithful, established for ever and ever." He called the commandments faithful in the sense of worthy of faith; for what they promise, they also perform. And they promise purification of the rational soul to those who keep them sincerely.
PSALM 111.
He will delight greatly in his commandments, etc. The one who delights greatly in his commandments is the one who keeps them with all exactness.

Glory and wealth are in his house, etc. The wisdom of God is called wealth insofar as it supplies an abundance of contemplations, and it is named glory insofar as it prepares people to glorify the one who possesses it.
Light has dawned in darkness for the upright, etc. The Savior says to the disciples in the Gospels: "What you have heard in the darkness, speak in the light."

He will dispense his words with judgment, etc. This text should be used against those who carelessly and indiscriminately divulge the divine mysteries of the divine Scripture. For Paul too says: "Let a person regard us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God."

He will not be afraid of an evil hearing, etc. "Hearing" stands for "report," as it is also written in the Gospel: "The hearing of him went out into all Syria"; and again: "You will hear of wars and hearings of wars."
His horn will be exalted in glory, etc. Satan fears nothing so much as a mind exalted in the knowledge of God.
The desire of the sinner will perish, etc. If the desire of the sinner will perish, and the desire of the sinner is wickedness, then the wickedness of sinners will perish.
PSALM 112.

From the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord is to be praised, etc. The risings are the intelligent natures, in which the sun of righteousness rises; the settings are the souls of human beings, in which the spiritual and heavenly sun once set.

Who dwells on high and looks upon lowly things in heaven and on earth, etc. God dwells in the holy powers, but he takes care of lowly human beings, so that his will may be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Who raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dunghill, etc. God raises the soul from vice to virtue, and urges the mind on from ignorance to knowledge.

Who settles the barren woman in a home, a mother rejoicing over her children, etc. "Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the desolate woman are more than those of the one who has a husband." A soul becomes barren when God abandons it, and a mother when he is at work in it.
PSALM 113.

When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarian people, Judea became his sanctuary, etc. If Judea is God's sanctuary, and Judea is interpreted as "one who confesses," then every soul that confesses is a sanctuary of God.

The mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock, etc. The mountains and the hills are intelligent natures rejoicing at the salvation of Israel. For if those in heaven rejoice over one who repents, how much more over so many tens of thousands journeying from vice to virtue, and from ignorance to the knowledge of God!

Who turned the rock into pools of water, and the flint into springs of water, etc. As regards the history, he turned the rock once in the wilderness and gave Israel drink; but as regards the spirit, he is always turning the rock, which is Christ, and giving drink to the spiritual Israel.

He blessed those who fear the Lord, the small together with the great, etc. It is not the great who are blessed with the small, but the small with the great, so that they too may become great. Small and great here are to be understood not of what is outward but of what is inward.

The dead will not praise you, O Lord, nor all who go down to Hades. But we who are living will bless the Lord from now on and forever, etc. A dead person cannot praise the Life that said, "I am the life." — "Nor all": he did not say "who have gone down," but "who go down." — "But we who are living," as Paul too says: "Then we who are living, who are left."
PSALM 114.
For he inclined his ear to me, and in my days I will call upon him, etc. Since we cannot stretch ourselves up to God when we pray, he himself inclines his ear to us and draws near to us.
By the same. Let whoever calls upon the sun of righteousness call upon it while living in the days of this sun.

The pangs of death surrounded me, etc. One who has fallen into heavier temptations and in them has given proof of his own free choice, so that he was even in danger of being overcome, yet was not overcome, might say: "The pangs of death surrounded me; the dangers of Hades found me." But "Hades found me" is not the same as "The dangers of Hades found me." For Hades finds the one whom its gates overpower; but the dangers of Hades find only the one who, because of the magnitude of his temptations, was in danger of being held fast by the gates of Hades, yet was not actually held fast by them.

I found affliction and pain, etc. Affliction is a find for the one who endures it, who boasts in afflictions, and who travels the road that leads to life, a road that is narrow and hard pressed. So pain too is indeed a fine find, when someone is pained out of love, like Paul, who said: "I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart," and what follows.

And I called on the name of the Lord, etc. "For everyone," it says, "who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved." So let the merciful call on the Merciful One, and the righteous on Righteousness. For the righteousness in us comes to us like a kind of echo, by reflection from the first Righteousness.

The Lord is merciful and righteous, and our God shows mercy, etc. Since the Lord shows mercy with righteousness, he is merciful and righteous; but Saul was not righteous in showing mercy when he spared Agag. And if every act of mercy were righteous, the law would not have said concerning certain people, "You shall not have mercy on him." There is also the saying, "He who shows mercy with cheerfulness": such a one shows mercy with righteousness.

Return, O my soul, to your rest, etc. The rest of the soul is the cutting off of sins; for sin strains the soul and crushes all its powers. That is why David also called baptism "water of rest," since it brings release from sins. So he urges the soul, as one that has wandered away in sins, to return to its rest, either through baptism or through tears and repentance.

For he has rescued my soul, etc. That is, the soul of one who no longer sins; for "the soul that sins shall die." And the one who has attained freedom from grief will say that the Lord has rescued my eyes from tears. The one who has mourned with the mourning that is called blessed will also say it, when he obtains the "they shall laugh" and the "they shall be comforted." And the one who has heard, "But you, stand here with me," will say: The Lord has rescued my feet from slipping.
PSALM 115.

"I believed, therefore I spoke," etc. Unless someone has believed firmly and without distraction, let him not teach; for "I believed, therefore I spoke" is the voice of a genuine teacher. And the proof of this man's freedom from conceit and of his humility, in that he is in no way puffed up over his teaching, comes from the words "But I was greatly humbled."
By the same. Faith is the rational assent of a soul endowed with free will.

"But I said in my ecstasy, 'Every man is a liar,'" etc. If David too is a man, he is a liar. But if he is a liar, then in calling himself a liar he is not a liar but is telling the truth. And if he is telling the truth in calling himself a liar, then, though he is a man, he is not a liar. So the argument turns round both ways: to his being truthful, if he is a man, and to his being a liar. Among the dialecticians this argument is called insoluble.

By the same. Insofar as someone is a man, he is a liar; but if he puts off being a man, he is truthful. For the name "man" sometimes signifies a substance, as in "There was a man in the land of Uz," and sometimes the worst condition, as in "But you die like men, and fall like one of the rulers." The one signifies a substance, the other the worst state.

"What shall I render to the Lord," etc. As one who had been greatly benefited by the Lord in these things and wished to repay his benefactor, but was at a loss as to how to repay him, he says, "What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?" For he had come to perceive the countless gifts he had received from God: that he was brought from non-being into being; that, though formed from earth, he was honored with reason, through which he is able to bear the image of the heavenly one as well. Then, looking also to the dispensation on behalf of the human race, in which the Lord gave himself as a ransom for many of us, he is perplexed, and searches among all that he possesses for some gift worthy of the Master: not sacrifices, nor whole burnt offerings, but his whole life itself.

"You have burst my bonds," etc. In answer to "What shall I render to the Lord?" it seems to me that what is rendered is, first, "I will take the cup of salvation"; second, "I will pay my vows"; third, "I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise"; fourth, "I will pay my vows to the Lord." But the first "I will pay my vows" has only "in the presence of all his people," while the second also has "in the courts of the house of the Lord" and "in your midst, O Jerusalem." And the first "I will pay my vows to the Lord" is attached to the cup of salvation, while the second comes after all of them and is joined to "You have burst my bonds" and to "I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise"; and "You have burst my bonds" is joined to the death that is precious in the sight of the Lord. Glorifying God for his martyrdom, he says this because through martyrdom the former chains of his sins have been burst by God, so that he no longer has any bonds of sin. Or, if the bonds of the soul are the bodily masses of the various members, it might well be said in this way too that, released from his bonds in martyrdom, he is at peace, since no one but God has burst them. For God does not burst the bonds of those who are violently separated from the body for whatever cause. Sometimes, then, God kills a man without bursting his bonds; but the martyr he does not kill: he only bursts his bonds. For through martyrdom each martyr offers himself to God as an unblemished sacrifice, imitating Christ, and he says, "I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise." For in the heavenly Jerusalem, our mother above, the righteous man will pay his vows to the Lord before every witness of the people [?] of God and of Jerusalem, in a chosen place; and this place is "in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the midst of Jerusalem."

By the same. "You have burst my bonds." He did not say "you loosed" but "you burst," so that they have become useless. Here he calls afflictions bonds. For there is also a good bond, as when it says, "In the bond of love." The chains of sins that accrue to us are also bonds; and these are burst not only through divine baptism, but also through martyrdom for Christ and through tears of repentance.
PSALM 117

"Let the house of Israel now say," etc. "Let Israel now say" is said in this psalm, and also in "If it had not been that the Lord was among us, let Israel now say," which is the 126th psalm and the fifth of the Songs of Ascents; and in the 128th, the tenth of the Songs of Ascents, which begins: "Often have they fought against me, let Israel now say."

"Let the house of Aaron now say," etc. Unless one is Israel, or the house of Aaron, or one who fears the Lord, he does not taste the goodness of the Lord, whose mercy is forever. Therefore these alone will say, "His mercy is forever." And since these are three orders, I think there are three general kinds of mercy for them. Since a house is a community lawfully established for living, "the house" is here applied to the house of Aaron. And consider whether the temple, where the priests carry out the worship, can be the house of Aaron. So he called the priests to the singing of the hymn separately, because they also enjoyed greater honor, not only by reason of the priesthood but in every other respect as well. For when fire came down, it came down because of them; and the earth quaked, and the rod budded; and countless other miracles took place through them and on their behalf.

"Let all who fear the Lord now say," etc. Above too it is said that Israel hoped to call upon the Lord, then the house of Aaron, then those who fear the Lord; and we have already said that those who fear the Lord, the house of Aaron, and Israel are one. That is why he bade them raise a common song proclaiming the mercy of God. For the mercy of the Lord is upon all flesh, and neither circumcision nor uncircumcision can be saved without mercy.

"Out of affliction I called upon the Lord," etc. The one who travels the narrow and afflicted way calls upon the Lord out of affliction; but the one on the broad way does not even call upon him. "For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved."
"I will not fear what man will do to me," etc. Scripture calls the devil a man, as in "An enemy man has done this," that is, the sowing of the tares.

"All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I warded them off," etc. Of the demons, some fought against him as one engaged in the practical life, others as one engaged in contemplation; the former he warded off with righteousness, the latter with wisdom.

By the same. It is more fitting for Christ, warred against by all the nations, to say these things. There are many kinds of doctrines which the saint wards off by the wisdom of God, overturning them with sound reasoning.

"They surrounded me like bees," etc. Each of the doctrines of the nations produces something sweet, which sweetens and delights the hearer. That is why those who champion them are like bees, but are not bees. And according to Solomon, "honey drips from the lips of a harlot," and she is knowledge falsely so called. He who joins himself to her is one body with her, just as he who joins himself to the Lord and true Word is one spirit with him.

"The Lord is my strength and my praise," etc. The Word is strength to the one who has taken him up; that is why Paul says, "I can do all things in Christ Jesus who strengthens me." This Word is also praise, for in him is theology. These might also be the words of a martyr full of courage: "The Lord is my strength and my praise."
"I shall not die, but live, and recount the works of the Lord," etc. It belongs to the living to recount the works of the Lord.

"Open to me the gates of righteousness," etc. Just as the gates of righteousness, which is one of the virtues, are the actions done in accordance with it, so there might also be gates of prudence, of temperance, of courage and of the other virtues, open in the virtuous man but shut in the base. Yet there are also gates of the vices, opened to the base man through actions done in vice, but shut in the good man. Perhaps they may also be understood differently, on account of "Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates": each of the virtues has everlasting gates leading into the everlasting dwellings, through which the virtuous will enter in a manner corresponding to their own actions. But the Savior had to pass through all of them, as they were lifted up and enlarged in a way worthy of the greatness of Christ. For he took up all of them in a manner worthy of the subsistence of the Firstborn of all creation. And consider whether, just as they are lifted and raised up for the Savior, so for each person, according to his worth, they are either lifted and raised up, or are set in place and not raised up. These gates are also ensouled and living; that is why "Be lifted up" is said to them. And perhaps the rulers and the gates, marveling [?], say, "Who is this King of glory?" There are, however, gates of righteousness for many; but which is the gate of the Lord alone? So he calls the various forms of virtue gates of righteousness, for through them it is possible to praise the God of all worthily. And he showed this more clearly through what follows, for he gives a kind of answer, saying: "This is the gate of the Lord."
By the same. As the gates of righteousness are opened, so too are those of temperance, courage and love. For through these gates the mind enters the kingdom of heaven.

"This is the gate of the Lord," etc. After entering through the practical virtues, we shall find the gate of knowledge, which is the contemplation of created things, both bodies and incorporeal beings.

"The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner," etc. This text refers to Christ; for in the Gospels he himself cites this prophecy, saying: "Have you never read, 'The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner'?" By the builders he means the Jews, the scribes and the Pharisees, because they rejected him, saying, "You are a Samaritan and have a demon," and again, "This man is not from God, but leads the crowd astray."

"This came about from the Lord," etc. What took place was not a human thing. It was not the work of one of the many; it was not for angels, nor for archangels, to join together such a corner. For no one had the strength for it, not a righteous man, not a prophet, not an angel, not an archangel. The achievement was God's; this was his own particular work.
"This is the day which the Lord has made," etc. This day was made not by lawgivers nor by prophets, but by the Sun of righteousness himself. By "day" he means the knowledge of Christ.

By the same. By "day" here he does not mean the course of the sun, but the great deeds accomplished on it. For just as he speaks of an evil day, meaning not the course of the sun but the evils that happen on it, so too he calls a good day the great deeds done on it. What he says amounts to this: All the great deeds accomplished on that day God has done; for what took place was the work of that hand alone. For what could equal this day, on which God was reconciled with men, the long war was ended, earth was shown to be heaven, men unworthy of the earth were shown to be worthy of the kingdom, the firstfruits of our nature was carried up above the heavens, paradise was opened, we recovered our ancient homeland, the curse was abolished, and sin was undone? For although he made all the days, he made that one in a special way, since on it he fulfilled the greatest of his own mysteries. Therefore let us too rejoice and be glad in it, keeping a festival of twofold joy: first, because we have been rescued from captivity to the devil; and second, because we are also being led up to the kingdom of heaven.

"Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," etc. This saying too the evangelists have taken as a prophecy about Christ. For he truly is the one who comes with authority and in the name of the Lord, while all the men and angels sent by him came as servants of the Lord. Indeed, each of them said, "Thus says the Lord"; and each of the angels says to the one to whom he comes, "The Lord has sent me." But he himself, who comes in the name of the Lord, is blessed.

"The Lord is God, and he has appeared to us," etc. For his coming is not a change of place but an appearing, since he was not seen before. For, being invisible, in that he is the image of the invisible God, he took the form of a servant; and the Word, having become flesh, was seen, so that, appearing in this way, he might lead us by the hand through this understanding to behold his glory as well, "glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth."

"Keep the feast among those that cover thickly," etc. Those cover thickly who are luxuriant with leaves and fruit: with leaves, that is, fitting acts, and with fruit, that is, the virtues. For "their leaf shall not fall, and they will yield their fruit in their season," because they have become "trees planted by the streams of water."

By the same. By "those that cover thickly" he means the cherubim that overshadow the mercy seat; for this is what "cover thickly" means. To cover thickly is to shelter, and the cherubim sheltered the mercy seat with their wings.

"You are my God, and I will give thanks to you," etc. Here he shows that one ought to give thanks to God even apart from his benefits, and to glorify him for this reason: for the majesty of his being and for his ineffable glory. This, at any rate, is what he hints at here as well, after recounting the benefits he had received. Even apart from these, he says, I will both give thanks and confess, because I have such a Master, so lofty, so great, so invisible and incomprehensible. "I will exalt" means "I will glorify."

"Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good," etc. It is not without purpose that the Psalmist placed this verse a second time in the present psalm. He wishes us to rehearse the same song often, so that, remembering what our salvation was, we may never again run back to the enemy, who became the cause of our destruction.
PSALM 118

"Blessed are the blameless in the way," and so on. "The first elements of the words of God" are the divine subject. The hundred and eighteenth psalm treats of them. It is written according to the letters of the Hebrews: its first eight verses begin with Aleph, the first of their letters, the next eight with Beth, and so on in order. This psalm contains the whole field of ethics, together with a full treatment of the various terms that the Scriptures use in ethical passages. One must know that a law is one thing, an ordinance another, a command another, a testimony another, and a judgment another. The letters are set at the head of each section here to show readers that these elements are the knowledge of ethics. Psalms 111 and 112 are also ethical in a certain way, and they too began their verses with the Hebrew letters. There, however, the alphabetic arrangement is not drawn out but is given briefly. One must know, then, that these psalms, like the rest of Scripture, were written in the Holy Spirit and carry a meaning not to be despised. There is also a reason why, in the Hebrew, each of the letters occurs eight times in this psalm. Turn, then, to the number eight. Wherever Scripture mentions it, take note of it and of the connection in which it is used. The exercise will help you see that each letter, together with the number, signifies a perfecting. When we are being perfected in the elements, the number seven is to be preferred by us, since it is assigned to matter, if indeed seven is a sign of material grossness, while eight is the beginning of a more immaterial and higher state. Admittedly, we also say that six in a sense signifies the matter of the world. But we refer six to wholeness of quantity and eight to perfection of character, by which a person scrapes away the filth of the soul and is cleansed. Before the eighth day of the Lord Jesus Christ came, the whole world was unclean and uncircumcised. But when the eighth day, the day of Christ's resurrection, came, all of us together were cleansed in the circumcision of Christ, buried with him and raised with him, as the Apostle says. Our soul is cleansed through this elementary instruction as we learn ethics and are perfected in the knowledge of it. That is why the number eight was adopted for each of the letters in the present psalm. In this psalm, at any rate, he describes the life of the saints, their struggles, their afflictions, and so on. Whoever does not sin in any way at all would be blameless, and indeed blessed.

By the same author. A person is called blessed not because of blamelessness itself. He is called blessed because of the knowledge of God that he will gain through blamelessness: "For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

"For those who work lawlessness have not walked in his ways," and so on. If those who work lawlessness do not walk in the ways of God, then clearly those who work righteousness will walk in the ways of God. So the ways of God are the contemplations of created things, and we shall walk in them as we work righteousness. Christ is our righteousness: "for he became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." So Solomon rightly says in Proverbs that wisdom, which is Christ, is the beginning of the ways of the Lord. By Christ I mean the Lord who came to dwell among us together with God the Word.
By the same author. If anyone works lawlessness, he does not walk in the way of the Lord. Therefore he is not blameless in the way either.
"You have commanded that your commandments be kept strictly," and so on. Whoever does not sin even in thought keeps God's commandments strictly.

By the same author. One can keep God's commandments strictly, and one can keep them laxly. Or: God commanded that his commandments be kept strictly. "Would that my ways were directed to keep your ordinances," and so on. For I will not keep your ordinances unless my ways are directed by you. What, then, are the ordinances? [?] "These are the ordinances that you shall set before the children of Israel: if you acquire a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh you shall send him away free," and so on. "Would, then," he says, "that my ways were directed," so that whatever you have ordained, I may render to each according to [?].

"Then I shall not be put to shame, when I look upon all your commandments," and so on. Not upon [?], but upon all of them. For I shall be put to shame by those commandments that I do not [?] look upon. As for us, when we look toward the divine [?], we will not be put to shame if we see ourselves in harmony with it in every respect. We must never shift toward [?], nor come down as if falling from a height.

By the same author. Whoever keeps all the commandments but stumbles in one becomes guilty of all. So it is rightly written: "Then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments." For even one neglected commandment can become a cause of shame for us.
"I will confess to you in uprightness of heart," and so on. Whoever has never taken up uprightness of heart, but still keeps it crooked, has not yet confessed in a way that allows his [?]

confession to be accepted by God. How this comes about is shown by [?]. "Do not utterly forsake me," and so on. [?] my strength holds out when I am tempted. "Do not," he says, "subject me to temptations beyond my strength, nor forsake me utterly." "But God is faithful, who will not let us be tempted beyond what we are able," and so on.

"I have hidden your sayings in my heart, so that I might not sin against you," and so on. A person may be entrusted [?] with the more secret sayings and commanded to hide them from the many. If he does not hide them from those he should, he sins against God. There is danger not only in saying what is false, but also in saying what is true when it ought not to be told at all. For one must not throw one's pearls before swine, nor give what is holy to the dogs.

"Blessed are you, O Lord," and so on. A person may perceive the progress [?] that comes from seeking God with his whole heart. He then blesses God and gives thanks for what he has already been granted [?]. He has sayings that are secret and worthy to be hidden, and he blesses the Lord for them.

"In the way of your testimonies I have delighted, as in all riches," and so on. Blessed is the one who rejoices in the way of God's testimonies as in all the wealth of gold and silver, clothing, building plots and estates, cattle and servants.

"I will meditate on your ordinances," and so on. A person does not meditate on God's ordinances with trifling phrases and little words. He meditates on them by understanding them and doing them. It is not the hearers of God's ordinances who are righteous before God, but the doers of them, who meditate on them through their works. Because they meditate on them in this way, they will never forget the words of God.
"Reward your servant; I shall live and keep your words," and so on. Let the one who has done everything that leads to the knowledge of God also say to the Lord: "Reward your servant."
By the same author. He gives in return to the one who gives. So he gave Isaac to Abraham, and so the master who had graciously given the ten minas rewarded the servant who brought them back to him.

"Unveil my eyes, and I shall perceive the wonders of your law," and so on. The law needs unveiling, for the commandment of the Lord is radiant. Here he uses "law" for the history in Scripture when it is allegorized spiritually. Paul did the same in the Epistle to the Galatians, where he writes: "Tell me," he says, "you who want to be under the law, do you not read the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman." Allegorizing the history spiritually, he leads it up for everyone to the Jerusalem above.
"My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times," and so on. He does not say "has desired," but "has longed to desire," and to desire at all times.

"You have rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments," and so on. Whoever opposes the proud also rebukes the proud. Now the Lord opposes the proud. Therefore the Lord also rebukes the proud.

"For rulers sat and spoke against me, but your servant pondered your ordinances," and so on. In this way they gather against the righteous man and consider how they may plot against him. Yet he does not stop speaking of the ordinances of God, for he utters nothing merely human. By the same author. Continual discourse about something and constant occupation with it is called "pondering."

"My soul has cleaved to the ground; give me life according to your word," and so on. The souls of sinners cleave to the ground because they set their minds on earthly things. The souls of the righteous cleave to it either because they are bound to bodies or because they remain in them for a time by divine dispensation.

By the same author. Now the soul has cleaved to the ground and has become flesh. But in the resurrection the flesh will cleave to the soul. The soul that cleaves to the Lord in the general resurrection becomes one spirit, and the body becomes spiritual. Similar to this is [?] "You have brought me down into the dust of death"; and "[?] our soul has been humbled to the dust"; and "[?] the body of our humiliation"; and "Who will deliver [me] from the body of this death?" Through these passages he has shown the extremity of humiliation. So too in Psalm 43: "For our soul has been humbled to the dust; our belly has cleaved to the earth [?]"

"Make me understand the way of your ordinances, and I shall ponder your wonders," and so on. Once I have received knowledge [?] of the mysteries in them, I will have travelled this way. Then I shall be able to converse and speak about the wonders they contain. "My soul has slumbered from listlessness; strengthen me in your words," and so on. Listlessness is a prolonged movement of anger and desire at the same time: anger rages at what is present, while desire longs for what is absent. Slumber is the rational soul's neglect of the virtues and of the knowledge of God. Sleep is the rational soul's voluntary separation from true life. That is why our wise Solomon advises us not to give sleep to our eyes, nor slumber to our eyelids.

"Remove the way of injustice from me, and with your law have mercy on me," and so on. "Do not remove me from the way of injustice," he says, "but remove it from me," since it is already present within me. Its removal [?] requires our own effort, but above all the help of God, so that we may [?] by the law of God. It is like saying to a physician: "Restore me to health by your medical art, even if cutting and burning are needed, or anything else that causes pain." This law has not even begun for those whom God has not yet visited. They are still given over to dishonorable passions, or to a reprobate [mind], or to any of the things that bring about correction and healing [?]. As long as the way of injustice does not depart from us, we do not even begin to receive mercy by the law of God.
"I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart," and so on. The words of the commandments enlarge the heart and so make the way of the practical life easy for it.

By the same author. "Narrow and hard pressed is the way that leads to life." But the holy heart is broad and spacious, because the Word widens it. It will see [?] and runs the good race of [?] God's commandments. So the broad and spacious way leads to destruction. But the narrow heart has no room within itself for the dwelling of the Father and the Son. Because of its narrowness, it separates from God the person who has made it so by his own wickedness.

"Give me as law, O Lord, the way of your ordinances, and I shall seek it out continually," and so on. He asks one thing from God and promises to contribute the other himself. "You, O Lord," he says, "lay down for me as law the way of your ordinances, and I will devote the whole time of my life to seeking it out."

"Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law and keep it with my whole heart," and so on. We need understanding to grasp the law, for it is neither plain nor to be despised. It requires God's cooperation and our own effort. Then we can receive from it both the use and the comprehension of practical and contemplative matters. "In this way, doubting nothing, I shall keep it with my whole heart." If the search needs understanding, how much more does the goal, so that one may find?

"Behold, I have longed for your commandments; in your righteousness give me life," and so on. As his reward he asks for a life of righteousness and virtue. He has not only kept the commandments but is also disposed toward them with love. He fulfils them for no other reason than for themselves and for their own sake. And since the Son is the righteousness of the Father, the one who says this wishes to live in the Son.

"And I shall give an answer to those who reproach me, because I have hoped in your words," and so on. For I will say that one who holds such doctrines does not deserve reproach. Those who are strangers to the faith laugh at these doctrines as foolish, but I will show that they are full of understanding and wisdom. And I shall give an answer, since I have set my hope on your words.
"And do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth," and so on. That is: do not take true knowledge out of my heart.

"And I walked in a broad place, because I sought out your commandments," and so on. He walks in a broad place even when he is afflicted, the one who says, "In affliction you made room for me," and again, "Afflicted in every way, but not hemmed in." For he has the spaciousness that comes from the Word, which no one who sins has. That is why Paul says to the Corinthians about himself, "You are not hemmed in by us," but about them, "You are hemmed in by your own affections." For deeds of wickedness hem the worthless man in within himself.

By the same author. Love for God creates spaciousness in human souls, for love, it says, is not hemmed in. Love for God means seeking and keeping his commandments, for the Lord says: "If you love me, keep my commandments."
