So it is right that the one who seeks God's commandments walks in a broad place, that is, lives his life in spaciousness. For the one who loves the Lord bears all things and endures all things. Naturally, then, he suffers no constriction.

"And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and was not ashamed," and so on. Paul too says: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek."
"And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved [?]" It is necessary to remember the sayings of God, so that we may keep the law of God concerning self-control.

"This has become mine," and so on. He means the divinely inspired Scripture. For the righteous man, it is not only spoken but also comes to pass, since he adds accomplishment to meditation. That is why he is also said to seek out the ordinances: he does not meditate on them in passing. Accordingly, the other translators write "I kept" instead of "I sought out."

"You are my portion, O Lord; I said that I would keep your law," and so on. Folly is the portion of the fool. In the same way, prudence is the portion of the prudent, and righteousness the portion of the righteous.

"I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your saying," and so on. The face of God is the imprint of his being, as has often been said. Some long for the Lord with their whole heart, so that when the heart has become pure they may behold him, and by gazing on him may receive mercy. Such a person might speak these words, in keeping with the teaching. See how great is the one who will see the face of God. Let Jesus teach you, when he says: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

"I considered your ways, and turned my feet to your testimonies," and so on. What he says is this: I never spoke rashly without first considering whether I ought to speak or keep silent. I never did anything rashly without considering whether the action was fitting. For our ways lie in our thoughts and in our actions. So he says: I did everything with careful thought. And so, as I walked, I turned my feet to your testimonies, so as not to walk outside the testimonies of God, for I had devoted my whole mind to your commandments.
"I was made ready and was not troubled, to keep your commandments," and so on. Freedom from passion naturally keeps the heart untroubled. It comes to us from a right way of life and true doctrines.

"The cords of sinners have entangled me, and I have not forgotten your law," and so on. Successive and intertwined sins are called "cords." Those who have set out to weave sin are forced, because of it, to add another sin as well. So David added murder because of his fornication, and Cain joined a lie to the murder of his brother. Yet even when these sins had entangled him, he says that he did not altogether forget God's law. For he looked to repentance, turned back, and broke the cord of sin.
"At midnight I rose to give you thanks for the judgments of your righteousness," and so on. This should be said to those who neglect prayer at night.

"Their heart has curdled like milk, but I have meditated on your law," and so on. Cheese was not always cheese. In the same way, the demons once existed when they were [not?] evil. And if milk is older than cheese, clearly virtue is also older than wickedness, for David likened wickedness to cheese. "It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your ordinances," and so on. It is as if he said: I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions and distresses. [?] worthy to be shown your ordinances, which cannot be learned in any other way.
"Let the proud be put to shame, because they unjustly acted lawlessly against me," and so on. Shame tends to bring the sinner to awareness of his sin.

"Let those who fear you turn to me, and those who know your testimonies," and so on. He asks [?] that such people turn to him and come to him, so that he may share with them the grace that is in him. "Let my heart be blameless in your ordinances, so that I may not be put to shame," and so on. [?] He does not yet have such a heart, so he asks for it, as in "Create in me a clean heart, O God." And how will it be "blameless" (in the other translators, "perfect" [?])? He added, "in your ordinances." And from this it follows that he is not put to shame, for every sin deserves shame.
"My eyes have failed for your saying, as they said: When will you comfort me?" and so on. Comfort is the soul's rest from its toils.

"For I have become like a wineskin in the frost," and so on. In many places in Scripture one finds the [body?] figuratively likened to a wineskin. What the righteous man says, then, is this: "I have put to death my members that are on the earth. By the divine word I have cooled the heat of the body. I am no longer hot with appetite for the belly or for [?] pleasures. I have put to death and cooled my members on the earth." "How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment for me on those who persecute me?" and so on. For the days of human beings on earth are few, [and in them?] he prays that Satan may quickly be crushed under his feet.

By the same author. All the days of human beings are few. "Since, then, I live only a short time on earth, I wish to see those who persecute me judged, and I beg you not to put it off." And who are the ones against whom he prays that judgment may come? Those who persecute us are Satan and the spiritual forces of wickedness. Even when a human being seems to persecute us, the one who persecutes in this way is not a human being, but the devil, whom he imitates.

"Lawless men told me idle tales, but [?] like your law," and so on. He means either the old wives' [tales?] of the Jews' teachings, or the [?] of human beings, and the babbling of the [wise?] of this age. Many undertake to interpret the divine Scriptures, both those in the Church and those outside it: heretics and Jews, and Samaritans too. But not all of them speak well. Rare is the one who has grace from God for this. Many promise to speak, but they do not speak well, and they live lawlessly. So if they say anything, it is idle talk and babble. A vigorous, strong and saving word cannot dwell in the soul of a lawless man.
By the same author. This text should be used against those who draw on outside wisdom and promise to teach about the knowledge of God.
"They almost made an end of me on the earth, but I did not forsake your commandments," and so on. That is: I almost became earthly when I was tempted by my enemies.

"According to your mercy give me life, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth," and so on. He asks not to be [handed over?] into the hands of those plotting against him, to an [untimely?] death [?]. The life he asks for is not yet eternal life, but the present one. Yet he asks for it not as an end in itself, but as something that will help bring about a good end. "For if I live," he says, "I shall keep God's commands." Through these commands it is possible also to gain eternal life.
By the same author. The mouth of God is the prophets, who served as ministers of his testimonies, commandments and ordinances.

"Forever, O Lord, your word abides in heaven," and so on. "In heaven" means "among his holy powers." For everything there is in order, and there is no transgression of the word. By "heaven" he does not mean the heaven that passes away, even though everything in it moves in order. He means the heaven that is said to be God's throne. On earth, by contrast, the word does not even abide. It has no place where there is fornication and impurity and the other passions. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? He did not say "for ages of ages" or "of the age," for after the age, heaven and earth will pass away. He meant the age in which "the word is abiding." For a perfect person may seem to be on earth while having his citizenship in heaven. So the truth is in him always.

"Your truth is from generation to generation. You founded the earth, and it abides," and so on. The earth has been founded on this truth. All who are saved from the earth are built on this cornerstone, which has been laid as a foundation. That is why the earth abides: it has an unbreakable and secure base and foundation. And the truth has illumined the day that it made, as God shone upon it. It remains in the same order, without change.

For all things are your servants, etc. If all things are servants of God, how can Solomon say of the ant in Proverbs: "Though it has no farm, and has no one to [?] it, and is under no master, it prepares its food in summer"? God is called master in two ways: either as creator, or as one who is known. That is why Paul too says: "Having been set free from sin, you have become slaves [?] to God", which clearly means by virtue and knowledge. [?] "your fruit for sanctification, and the end eternal [?]." If the ant has no share in such an end, it clearly has no share in this servitude either. So the ant is rightly said not to be under a master, in respect of [?] this kind of mastery.

[?] Unless your law had been my meditation, I would then have perished in my humiliation, etc. It is truly [?] not to perish when one is placed in difficult circumstances [?], as in martyrdom. Unless someone has meditated beforehand on the law of God, he perishes.
[?] Of all consummation I have seen an end; your commandment is exceedingly broad, etc. More than all the [?] from outside, the words of God's commandments broaden the soul and lift it up [?].

[?] How I have loved your law, Lord! It is my meditation all day long, etc. The law is meditated on not only in words and sounds but also in [?] actions. For when someone reads, understanding what is said and doing it, neglecting it in no [?] action but in everything doing what the law wills, that person, speaking and reading and doing, meditates on the law of God. Here, then, it says, "It is my meditation all day long," but in the first psalm it says that the one who is to be blessed must meditate on the law not only by day but also by night. Why did it perhaps leave out the night here? Because human life here is mixed, and for this reason we now have both day and night; but when we become holy and blessed, night will not follow on for us, but we shall be in [?] that day. See, then, that the one who is journeying here, that is, who is not yet perfect in his way of life (for conduct in the world is a journey), does not yet journey purely, but is sometimes in day and sometimes in night: in day when he does what the law requires as he ought; in night when he does not yet carry out the law with his whole heart (even if he [?] meditates on the law), or also when he acts contrary to what he ought. So the one who is beginning, or making progress, meditates on the law day and night; the one who has been made perfect is not in night but in day, as Paul says: "The night is far gone, the day has drawn near; let us walk decently, as in the day." And again: "So then we are no longer of night or of darkness, but we are children of light and of day."

You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment, for it is mine forever, etc. Whoever has been stripped of [?] the passions and has come to share in knowledge becomes more cunning than the demons, often repeating Paul's saying: "For we are not ignorant of his designs."

By the same. By "enemies" he now means those who lay claim to [?] the commandments and hate us, though we do not hate them in return. He means the Jews of the circumcision; for the Christian has been made wiser than they are in the commandment of God, understanding and keeping the law spiritually. For this reason I can understand more deeply the Lord's saying: "Love your enemies." For those are our enemies who "have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge."

I have understood more than all who teach me, for your testimonies are my meditation, etc. The Scriptures were theirs first; they were entrusted with the oracles of God. They profess to have become teachers, since they were the first to receive the law and the prophets. So we who come from the Gentiles say: "I have understood more than all who teach me." Why? "Because your testimonies are my meditation." I find new testimonies beyond the testimonies that have often been spoken of. For my meditation is the testimonies of Jesus Christ; I have received these very testimonies, and that is why I have understood more than all who teach me. The man of the Church called them enemies, and called them teachers; now he calls them elders as well.

I have understood more than the elders, for I have sought out your commandments, etc. I use this text against old men who think that length of time and dispassion are what procure the knowledge of God.

I have held back my feet from every evil way, so that I may keep your words, etc. We used to walk in evil ways, being once "foolish and disobedient, led astray, enslaved to various desires and pleasures," and so on. Those were evil ways. This saying of the man of the Church is a perfect one. For as long as we still sin, we cannot say these things; for it is by holding back our feet from every evil way that we shall keep the words of God. What words? Those in the law, when we understand them spiritually and recognize Jesus Christ, who is proclaimed through them. "I held back my feet" shows the freedom of choice. For he spoke the verse as though it were in his own power to move his feet to walk, or to hold them back.

I have not turned aside from your judgments, for you have given me law, etc. I always remembered your tribunal. And in the ninth psalm he says: "Appoint a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are men." For Moses gave laws concerning the letter to those who could not receive the coming of the New Covenant; but Jesus Christ, when he came, gave me the Gospel as law and showed me that the law of Moses is spiritual.
How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth, etc. The mind that delights in knowledge and is nourished by it is called a mouth.

From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way of unrighteousness, etc. I have become understanding through your commandments, which mark out for me what I must do; and indeed I not only keep away from every way of unrighteousness, but have also come to hate it.
[?] I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness, etc. He has called unchangeableness an oath.

[?] By the same. What is "I have sworn" doing here? [?] "He made a covenant with his chosen ones." And when God had made this covenant with his chosen ones, the believer accepted it and, as if by oaths between God and [?] himself, made his covenant, so as to establish and keep the judgments of his righteousness. I establish them, he [?] says, in my soul; and when I establish them, [?] that saying of Solomon in Proverbs: "The thoughts of the righteous are judgments." Those are the judgments of the righteousness of God, [?] which came about when I swore and established them in [?]. Here "to establish" means to determine firmly, and "to swear" means to resolve unchangeably and to choose, with firm assurance, to keep the [?] work inviolate.

[?] Be pleased with the freewill offerings of my mouth, and teach me your judgments, etc. The things we were not commanded to do but [?] do by our own choice, these he calls the freewill offerings of our mouth: for example, if I practise virginity, which I was neither commanded nor [?] to do, but [?] judged it better to do of my own free will. Be pleased with this, then, Lord. And likewise in other matters one may find [?] such things in our life, some of which we do because we are commanded, while others we do of our own free will.

[?] My soul is in your hands continually, and I have not forgotten your law, etc. You will ask how the soul of David is continually in the hands of God: whether as in righteousness or as in knowledge. Perhaps the former. For it belongs to angels to see the face of God continually, that is, to contemplate him, but to men to be able to act righteously continually in deed; and that is what being in the hands of God means. For [?] right-doing in thought belonged to Christ alone, who did no sin (clearly in deed), and no [?] was found in his mouth; [?] it is clear that this refers to thought, from which the overflowings of the heart proceed. [?] I entrust my soul to you always, [?] you as its guard, defender and pilot; [?] that is why I have not forgotten your law, so that I may not [?]. Everyone who has dedicated himself to God commits his soul into his hands, as he also said elsewhere: "For you are my defender, [?] Lord; into your hands I will commit my spirit." [?] Whoever divides himself among pleasures and bodily passions and the cares of this life does not commit his soul into the hands of God.

[?] By the same. Aquila renders thus: "My soul is in my [?] constantly and continually, and I have not forgotten your law"; Symmachus: "My soul is in my [?] always"; and the Fifth agrees with the Seventy.

Sinners have laid a snare for me, yet I have not strayed from your commandments, etc. Sinners weave many and various snares for the righteous: for Joseph, the Egyptian woman and his brothers; for Daniel, those who had received authority from Darius. But these did not stray from the commandments of God, and so they rose above the snares.

I have inherited your testimonies forever, for they are the joy of my heart, etc. Those who rejoice in the commandments of God and embrace righteous action always inherit his testimonies, gaining them as their lot and portion in place of everything in the world, and rejoicing in whatever they may suffer for their sake.

I have inclined my heart to carry out your statutes forever, for the sake of the reward, etc. I inclined it knowing that a reward is laid up, and that reward is the kingdom of God: "What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him."
By the same. The reward of the statutes is the knowledge of them.

I have hated the lawless, but I have loved your law, etc. The lawless man, insofar as he is lawless, is hateful; but insofar as he is the image and handiwork of God, he is to be loved. It is in keeping with this second sense that we have been instructed to visit those in prison, and that the law commands us to do good to evildoers. Here, however, he may be speaking of words and laws that David hated.

By the same. He did not hate lawless people, for his life showed that it was not lawless people he hated. He did not hate Absalom the parricide, nor Saul (of whom God said, "I regret that I anointed Saul as king"), who plotted against David in various ways, nor any other lawless person. That is why, when he said "the lawless," he did not add "people." As a holy man he hated what deserves hatred: lawless words, lawless doctrines, such teachings, the disposition by which people sin. That is why he set the law that he loves over against the lawless words. It is in this sense that we have been commanded to hate even father and mother, that is, to turn away from them when they urge us toward impiety or try to turn us away from martyrdom for Christ. For otherwise we have been commanded to love even our enemies. And since God calls us to hate even our own soul, in the same way we must also hate lawless people, so that we may turn them back by improving ourselves and not becoming like them.

Turn away from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God, etc. Unless the demons turn away from us, we are not able to carry out the commandments of God; for it is these above all that they oppose, because these become for us the means to the knowledge of God.

Uphold me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my [?] expectation, etc. "For affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character, and proven character hope, and hope does not put us to shame."

By the same. "According to your word": that is, according to your promise. For you promised in the law to defend those who keep it. So count me, who have this aim, worthy of your providence, so that having attained my hope I may [?] be filled with shame. Here "word" means the promise; it amounts to saying: Grant me the salvation promised to me.

Help me, and I shall be saved, and I shall meditate on your statutes continually, etc. For even though he said, "You are my helper and my protector," he still needs unceasing help. For as long as we are here, "I shall be saved" is not yet complete; it will be when we live the life of the angels of God. For then too comes the meditation on the statutes face to face, [?] not according to the shadow but according to the truth.

I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved your testimonies, etc. We call "transgressors" those who have been taught the word and, after being taught, kept it, but then fell away and transgressed. But he sees that all people have starting points toward goodness, even if they were not taught; so that not only those who fall away after coming to faith are called transgressors, but also those who sin in any way whatever. The sinners of the earth are the people who have sinned on earth. For there are other sinners, sinners of heaven, against whom our wrestling is directed: "against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." For they sinned there first, and afterwards do the same on earth too.

Nail down my flesh with the fear of you, for I have been afraid of your judgments, etc. The one who is nailed is crucified. So I look for the cross, and I ask whether the cross is perhaps the fear of God. For the Saviour also said: "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me." We have often drawn distinctions between fear and love, and have said that the one who loves is more perfect than the one who fears, and that fear is necessary as an introduction. But where "perfect love" enters, "it casts out fear." Since, then, the righteous man is found nailed by God through fear, I ask whether perhaps, while he is being crucified, he fears, nailed through fear, in order to put to death his members that are on earth; but when perfect love comes, he is taken down from the cross, buried, and raised from the dead, so that he may walk in newness of life, no longer according to fear but according to the love that is in Christ Jesus.

I have done judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who wrong me, etc. How, then, was Job handed over to those who wronged him, when he had done judgment and righteousness, as the Lord himself testified? It is his soul that he does not want handed over to them; for the righteous man knows how to despise body and possessions.

I am your servant; give me understanding, and I shall know your testimonies, etc. No slave of sin is a servant of God. So let the one who serves in every action and thought, doing everything according to his word, say: "I am your servant." Being such a man, the Prophet asks to receive as the wages of his service: "Give me understanding." For there is an understanding given by God, which is stored up with God as in a treasury. For, it says, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and the rest of the good gifts that follow, will rest upon him.

It is time to act for the Lord; they have scattered your law, etc. The time is a season of success for the Lord, namely to execute vengeance. The lawless have annulled your law and set it aside. Symmachus: "It is time to act for the Lord, for they are scattering your law." Aquila: "They have made it void."

Therefore I kept myself upright in all your commandments; I have hated every unjust way, etc. Whoever has not succeeded in all the commandments has not hated every unjust way either. And if the one who fears the Lord hates injustice, and this man has not hated it, he does not fear the Lord. And the one who does not fear is not blessed, since "Blessed is the one who fears the Lord." Whoever loves the commandments of God hates all wickedness as opposed to them. For virtue and vice cannot be reconciled, any more than light and darkness, health and sickness.

Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out, etc. Since your testimonies are great and full of meaning, they are wonderful, and for this reason I do not attend to them casually; rather, my soul searches them out intently. For while I contemplate them, I see that I fall far short of knowing them, and I apply myself to them a second time; then, seeing again that I am barely at the introduction to them, I intensify the search as far as it is open to me, until I possess the purest truth of their knowledge.

I opened my mouth and drew in spirit, for I longed for your commandments, etc. Whoever opens his heart through the practical life draws in the Holy Spirit, who reveals to him the mysteries of God. The mouth of my soul is the mind. So, having closed it to evil thoughts, I opened it to good ones, and drew in the Spirit of understanding, of grace and of wisdom.
By the same. So the supply of the Spirit is the reward for declaring and fulfilling the commandments of God, so that we have only to open our mouth and at once draw in the Spirit from heaven.

Direct my steps according to your word, and let no lawlessness lord it over me, etc. Lawlessness is said to rule over the one who sins in thought, but to lord it over the one who transgresses in deed. Or perhaps lawlessness rules over those who sin a little, but lords it over those who sin the most.

My eyes have sunk into streams of water, because I did not keep your law, etc. He now figuratively calls the temptations that come in [?] thought "waters," and from these Solomon turns us away, saying: "Keep away from strange water, and do not [?] from a strange spring."

[?] By the same. Our eyes sink into streams of water, [?] the unstable affairs of life, [?] so there is need to be drawn up from there and to look clearly [?] at the abiding things of the age to come. By the same. Symmachus renders thus: "My eyes sank into divisions of water over those who do not keep your law."

Your zeal has wasted me away, because my enemies have forgotten your words, etc. What zeal did I [?] take up whenever I saw someone who had forgotten your words! Not simply zeal, but burning [?] and fiery zeal, a very conflagration, if I saw any people forgetting your words. It was this zeal that the disciples remembered, spoken in a psalm in the person of the Lord: "Zeal for your house has consumed me."

Your word is thoroughly tried by fire, and your servant has loved it, etc. The law of God, he says, is unadulterated, as having been refined by the Spirit himself. That is why it holds no flattery and no irony, but openly reproves those who sin and braces those who [?]. "For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart." Let us too, then, since we are servants of God, love this word, in no way gambling with it or adulterating it (as Paul also hinted), but offering it pure, just as we received it from the Spirit's smelting. By the same. The fire-tried word of God burns up wood, hay and straw, consuming wicked habits.

Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and your law is truth, etc. Righteousness among men is decreed for a short time. Eternal righteousness is righteousness in the proper sense: whomever you justify, you confirm eternally and justly. But human righteousness is not like this, for it is temporary and fails in many things. And your law is truth itself, utterly true in all things. Truth is also understood as rightness, as in the verse: "You are righteous, Lord, and your judgments are upright." Affliction and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation, etc. He says "have found me" as though the afflictions and distresses were seeking us out. Or perhaps those who afflict are called afflictions, and those who bring distress are called distresses; for Scripture has the custom of naming states in place of those who possess them. So in Paul: "Love never fails"; and in Solomon: "Evil counsel has forsaken the instruction of youth and has forgotten the divine covenant." Scripture also often does the reverse, and names the one who is naturally fitted to receive virtue in place of the virtue. For in Proverbs it says, "The uninstructed have hated wisdom," instead of virtue. And Paul: "Do not be shaken from your mind," that is, from such and such an opinion. In afflictions your commandments were my meditation, consoling me and lightening the pain. For these are joined to those who labour at virtue; from their teaching I learn courage and bear painful things nobly. Symmachus too translated it in this way: "Afflictions and hardships seized me, but your commandments delighted me." And Aquila thus: "Affliction and constraint found me; your commandments are my enjoyment."

Your testimonies are righteousness forever; give me understanding, and I shall live, etc. Understanding comes before knowledge, so that the one who has knowledge is also understanding, but the one who has understanding does not necessarily have knowledge as well.
I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, Lord; I will seek out your statutes, etc. Whoever loves God with his whole heart cries out with his whole heart.

By the same. A cry is not a loud voice, but the greatness of what it conveys to God. For the righteous man raises a great voice to God when he asks for heavenly and great things. So too righteous Abel, though dead, still speaks: "For the voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground," to show that the righteous man cried out to God with a great voice. And to Moses, when he was being pursued by the Egyptians, God says: "Why do you cry out to me?"
I rose early, at the untimely hour, and cried out; I have hoped in your words, etc. The untimely hour is a spiritual disposition of a settled state that is eager for knowledge.

Those who persecute me with lawlessness have drawn near, but they have gone far from your law, etc. We are taught by this saying what happens to the one who persecutes the righteous: the nearer he draws to persecuting the righteous, the farther he gets from the law of God. And the farther he is from the law, the farther he is also from life, because the law is our life.

You are near, Lord, and all your ways are truth, etc. He himself draws near in this way; but unless we too, as he draws near, actively draw near to him, we will not enjoy his nearness. That is why sinners are far from God: "Behold, those who put themselves far from you shall perish." But the righteous man actively draws near to God.
By the same. Righteousness is near to the one whose nature inclines him to act righteously. But it is much nearer to those who have actually gained righteousness and knowledge through practice.

[?] you founded them forever, etc. Knowledge came to me from your testimonies, since I began to revere God from the start. For I was helped by having understood the testimonies handed down, and so I was [?], and I was launched toward knowledge, and [I knew?] that you founded the testimonies forever. [Since?] God founded the testimonies, [?] never ceases to be founded; rather, what is founded and built upon lives. And what does he build upon it? Ordinances, commandments, statutes, judgments, wisdom, knowledge. In this way he completes the building with all good [?], with words of wisdom and with knowledge of understanding. If these are [laid upon] the foundation, a person has [the building] of himself complete, worthy for God to dwell in him and [walk] in him.

[Look on] my humiliation and rescue me, for I have not forgotten your law, etc. It is a blessed thing to be humbled [before?] God, for James says: "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you." [If], then, we are humbled in this way, then even if demons plot against us, and even if people who hate virtue make war on us, we have God to [deliver us]. We need only make sure not to forget his law, [and not] grow weary in our afflictions.

[Salvation is] far from sinners, for they have not sought out your statutes, etc. If the salvation of rational nature is the knowledge of God, and [this] comes about in pure souls, it is rightly said [?]: "Salvation is far from sinners." For "wisdom will not enter a soul that plots evil." Where judgment is near, salvation is also near; and where salvation is far off, judgment is far off too. Why? Because [he] did not seek out your statutes. For your salvation does not flee from us; we flee from it. "For the Son of Man," who is salvation, "came to seek and to save what was lost."

[Your] mercies are many, Lord; give me life according to your judgment, etc. "The mercy of a human being is for his neighbor, but the mercy of the Lord is for all flesh." For even the most righteous person needs God's mercy when measured against God's exact judgment, since even the fact that someone seems to have become righteous comes about by God's mercy. [What] has anyone done that is worthy of eternal blessedness? [Yet] God does [nothing?] without judgment, not even give life. And his mercies are many, because those on whom they [come] are many.

Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies, etc. "Blessed," he says, "are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

By the same. The word "many" hints at enemies both visible and invisible, whose persecutions and afflictions take various forms. Some pretend to be friends and hold out pleasures to us; others lay their hostility bare and bring every [kind] of temptation upon us. But let us not turn aside from the testimonies of God, in which he solemnly testified to us: "Through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of heaven."
I saw the senseless and wasted away, because they did not keep your words, etc. "Zeal for your house has consumed me."

See how I have loved your commandments, Lord; give me life in your mercy, etc. On this ground he calls upon God and says to him: I appeal to your face. For I am confident that, when you turn your face toward me to look at me closely, you will see how I have kept your commandments, for you will find the imprints of good works in me.

Rulers persecuted me without cause, and my heart stood in awe of your words, etc. By "rulers" he means the world-rulers of this darkness. "For," he says, "the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me." By "world" he does not mean the system made up of heaven and earth, but those who live a worldly life.

By the same. The verse has its particular meaning for David: he was pursued by Saul for no reason and out of envy, yet out of fear of God he refrained from taking revenge. But it also applies to everyone, because there is no other way to escape unharmed from the hostile rulers except by being guarded by the fear of God.

Seven times a day I praised you for the judgments of your righteousness, etc. Just as the eighth day is a symbol of the age to come, since it contains the power of the resurrection, so the seventh is a symbol of this world. Perhaps, then, David praised the Lord because he knew the principles of righteous judgment that govern this sensible world.

By the same. Throughout his whole life the righteous person is enlightened and will live in a perfect day, one that no night interrupts. He praises God seven times because he has risen above the world, having passed beyond the world that came into being in six days. Then, having come into the paradise of God and having contemplated the principle of God's creation and providence, he gives thanks for the judgments of God's righteousness, the judgments according to which each thing received its own varied creation and providential care.

Great peace have those who love your law, and for them there is no stumbling block, etc. If the little ones are made to stumble, then the little ones do not love the Lord. For he says, "Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble." But those who love the Lord are not made to stumble. The little ones do not love the Lord, and that is why they do not know the reasons for what happens, and they stumble over these things. The peace meant here is not peace with the invisible enemies but peace with God, and for them there is no stumbling block. For the law levels the road of virtue for them, removing every obstacle of sin. Or it is also peace with those of the same faith, even if those people often do not wish to be at peace with them.

I awaited your salvation, Lord, and I loved your commandments, etc. Blessed is the one who waits for the salvation of God and who also loves his commandments. Such a person advances into a perfect life, to the height of blessedness, the blessedness that was allotted to the apostles themselves, to whom he said: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like people waiting for their master."

Let my petition come near before you, Lord; give me understanding according to your word, etc. Through the earlier letters he was journeying toward God and was not yet near him. But when he reached the end of the present passage, at the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, then he prays that his prayer may draw near to God and reach him. As for drawing near to God, we should know that we have found the following differences. The more perfect person draws near to God himself. The lesser person, who comes close to him in rank, does not draw near to God himself but has a prayer that draws near to him. So you would find this said about Moses: "Moses alone shall draw near to God, but the others shall not draw near," while in this case you find a prayer saying, "Let my petition draw near," and so on. It is now worth considering what the difference between these is. God is not in a place; he is a power that cannot be spoken, uttered or seen. If God is not in a place, and yet it is sometimes possible to draw near to God, clearly we draw near to him by what is invisible in us. And what is invisible in us? The hidden person of the heart, whom Scripture has called "the inner man." It belongs to him, then, to draw near to God. And one can draw near through Jesus Christ, especially if we understand that Christ is righteousness, that he is truth and wisdom, resurrection and the true light. For without these one cannot draw near to God, nor without the peace that guards the heart and the thoughts, which is Christ. The more someone falls short of these, I mean righteousness and wisdom, the farther that person is from God.

Let my request come before you, Lord; rescue me according to your word, etc. He asks that his request be so approved, firm and blameless that it may come before the Lord. I will know whether my request has come before you if I am rescued by you according to your word, my request and your wisdom. For the person who has risen above all passions and has withdrawn as far as possible from the vice that makes us worthless has been rescued by God according to his word. In place of "my request," Aquila has "my petition" and Symmachus "my supplication." So he asks for two things: understanding of the sacred words, and release and freedom from the evils of this life. And these are things we need as well.

My lips will belch forth a hymn when you teach me your statutes, etc. Belching generally happens to those who have eaten their fill. When we are full, we belch out the flavor of the food we have taken in. The divine word, then, knows of spiritual food, for the Word himself says that he is bread: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven; whoever eats this bread will live forever." And the Word also says that he has flesh, in the saying: "Whoever eats my flesh has life in himself, for my flesh is true food." If, then, we are filled with this bread, which is the Word, we will belch forth a hymn. Sometimes prayers will also be belched forth, for the same thing must also happen through prayers, "when you teach me your statutes." For if I am not taught your statutes, I cannot belch forth anything of this kind.

By the same. Just as singing psalms belongs to those who are cheerful (for he says, "Is anyone among you cheerful? Let him sing psalms"), so singing hymns belongs to those who contemplate the principles behind the statutes. Singing psalms is fitting for human beings, but singing hymns is fitting for angels, or for those who live an angelic life. That is why the shepherds living out in the fields did not hear angels singing psalms but singing hymns and saying, "Glory to God in the highest," and so on. Cheerfulness, then, is the soul's freedom from passion, which comes from God's commandments and from true doctrines; and a hymn is a giving of glory.

My soul will live and praise you, and your judgments will help me, etc. He confined the life of the soul to the time to come, for "our life is hidden with Christ in God." Then it will praise God in the full sense.

I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments, etc. The Lord first turns back the soul that has gone astray as righteousness, and then also as wisdom, since the straying of the soul is vice and ignorance.
Psalm 119

"A Song of Ascents," etc. Only those who ascend in their life and in their reasoning are at home among the Ascents and the mysteries in their songs. We conjecture that the first Song of Ascents was sung among the people whenever war was expected; the second, when they were preparing and needed allies; the third, when, having engaged the enemy, they had in some way gained the upper hand; the fourth, when they were hoping for final victory; the fifth, when they had succeeded; the sixth, while they were returning; the seventh, once they had returned; the eighth, while they were restoring the temple; the ninth, after peace had come, when they describe who is blessed, since they have recovered their own people and are with them; the tenth, when they were enjoying deep peace, when they say that they have often been attacked, but that the enemy have never been able to prevail against them; the eleventh, when they were now at leisure for divine things and understood their depths; the twelfth, as not being puffed up over what they had come to know; in the thirteenth they pray for the restoration of Christ; in the fourteenth, for the restoration of the Church; the fifteenth concerns their duty, once they have reached the house of God, to stand in it and bless the [Lord], lifting up their hands to the holy places, so that they too may be blessed by the Lord.

"In my distress I cried to the Lord, and he heard me," etc. God hears those who are afflicted for the sake of virtue and knowledge in the affliction of captivity and the hardship it brings. By "crying" he means the return of a soul, crushed and humbled, to the one who is able to rescue it; and God hears it at once.

"Lord, rescue my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue," etc. Over and over he begs God to be freed from such plots. If we must flee those who are deceitful and treacherous, how much more the swindlers who instill wicked doctrines! One might say that those lips are especially unjust which lead away from virtue and draw toward vice. That is precisely why this prophet asks that his very soul be rescued.

"The arrows of the mighty one, sharpened, with the coals of the desert," etc. Nothing is so fitting against the opposing powers as the arrows of Christ, which are set against the flaming arrows of the evil one, and the coals that burn up wood, hay and straw. And if there is an arrow of love—as the bride says in the Song: "For I am wounded with love"—then there is also an arrow of justice, courage, temperance and the other virtues; wounded by these arrows, the peoples fall beneath God.

By the same. He who says, "You have made me a chosen arrow," is the chosen arrow among many arrows, just as he is the chosen son among many sons. God would not have a quiver for a single arrow—the quiver of which he says, "And in his quiver he hid me." All, then, are arrows of the mighty God, sharpened, and set against the arrows of the evil one.

"Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt among the tents of Kedar," etc. It does not belong to the same person to say, "Do not take me away in the half of my days," and, "Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged." Or perhaps in the former place he means the days which the fear of the Lord adds, according to Solomon—days made by the Sun of righteousness, in which Abraham too died full of days. Here, however, he laments with regard to the gift of the senses [?]. For he too has "the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary" for the sake of those who are helped—if indeed David, according to Luke in the Acts of the Apostles, or according to Paul as well, was sent forth "to serve his own generation."
By the same. "Kedar" is interpreted as "darkening." So he says: I have dwelt among the tents of darkening, that is, of the body of death, and this soul of mine, he says, has sojourned long.
Psalm 120

"I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come," etc. He says: I lifted up my eyes to the mountains—the holy angels—expecting to be helped by one of them; but my help came from the Lord, "who made heaven and earth." For he did not add "who made heaven and earth" without purpose. If he himself made both heaven and earth, he says, he can bring help everywhere, even in a foreign land, and stretch out his hand even among barbarians.

"Do not let your foot be moved, and may he who keeps you not slumber," etc. Do not be overturned, he says, nor be made to stumble, and then you will have God stretching out his hand to you. So the beginnings must come from us, and God is ready to stretch out his hand.
"The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night," etc. This, I think, is the sun that rises on the sown ground and dries it up; and in the same sense, "the fool changes like the moon."
"The Lord will keep your going in and your going out, from now and for ever," etc. The going out is the one from vice to virtue; the going in is the one from virtue to the knowledge of God.
Psalm 121

"I rejoiced at those who said to me, 'We will go into the house of the Lord.' Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem," etc. Those who said to the righteous man, "We will go into the house of the Lord," can themselves also say, "Our feet were standing"—to those who had said it to them: the Son and the Holy Spirit, and holy angels or human beings who by their way of life are making the journey to the house of God well.
By the same. "Our feet were standing": the future is spoken of as past, as also in "They divided my garments among themselves," and in "They gave me gall for my food."

"Jerusalem, built as a city whose sharing is together," etc. When the believers are of one heart and soul, and the members have the same care for one another, they are Jerusalem, and like a city whose sharing is together.
"For there the tribes went up," etc. He prophesies about the tribes that were to go up to virtue and the knowledge of God; for all the tribes have attained virtue and the knowledge of God.

"For there thrones were set," etc. About these thrones it is said in the Gospel too: "You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." About the thrones in Jerusalem Jeremiah says this: "And the Lord said to me: From the face of the north evils will be kindled upon all who dwell in the land; for behold, I am calling all the kingdoms from the north, says the Lord, and they will come, and each will set his throne at the entrances of the gates of Jerusalem, and against all its walls round about, and against all the cities of Judah. And I will speak to them in judgment concerning all their wickedness, in that they forsook me and sacrificed to foreign gods and worshiped the works of their own hands."
Psalm 122

"To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven," etc. In the bodily heavens God dwells as creator, through his richly varied wisdom; in the intelligible heavens, as righteousness, knowledge and wisdom.

"Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us," etc. The servants of the masters—the Father and the Son—are spirit and body; the maidservant of the mistress—the Holy Spirit—is the soul. And the three are the Lord our God, for the three are one. The eyes of servants, then, look to the hands of their masters for when they will give orders by a sign of the hand. Or else the hands of the masters, the Father and the Son, are the angels of each, and the hands of the mistress, the Holy Spirit, are the Spirit's own powers.

By the same. The eyes of those who have the spirit of slavery leading to fear look to the hands of masters and to the hands of a mistress; but the eyes of one who has the spirit of adoption look to the Lord God.
"For we have been greatly filled with contempt," etc. Symmachus renders it thus: "For we have been glutted with much scorn."
By the same. "God chose what is despised in the world"; that is why the despised must be given seats in the Church. And this can console those who are despised.

"Our soul has been filled exceedingly; reproach for those who prosper, and contempt for the proud," etc. Notice that these are sinners, and yet they prosper. Symmachus renders it thus: "Our soul has been glutted with much, as the prosperous spoke against us and the proud held us in scorn." Aquila: "Our soul has been filled to the full with the mockery of those who reproach us, with the contempt of the proud."
Psalm 123

"If the Lord had not been among us, let Israel now say," etc. It is likely that one of the priests, standing on one of the steps, would say something like this to the people when they came to the temple at dawn: "Let Israel now say, 'If the Lord had not been among us'"; and that Israel, doing as it was told, would begin with "The Lord was among us" and continue with the rest of the psalm. Let it be said—"If the Lord had not been among us"—not by just anyone, but by the true Israel, whose Lord he is, as one of them says: "For us there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him"; as Paul also said, "For I too am an Israelite," and, "Are they Israelites? So am I." And it is likely that this psalm was said by the people at the priest's command whenever the people, having been in danger in war or from some plot by the nations, had been saved and had defeated the enemy—especially if they had come back after fighting bravely with the help of some extraordinary divine manifestation. And let Israel also say, "Often have they fought against me from my youth," as is said in Psalm 128.

"Then they would have swallowed us alive," etc. They swallowed Judas the betrayer alive, for before the betrayal he had the Life that said, "I am the life"; but those who have been nurtured in wickedness from the beginning they swallow dead.
"Then the water would have drowned us," etc. By "water" he figuratively means the temptations that drown the soul; and these same temptations are also called thoughts.
"Our soul has passed through a torrent," etc. By "torrent" he again means the thoughts, because they do not last, but leap upon the mind all at once and then dry up again.

By the same. "And the word of the Lord came to Elijah: Go from here eastward and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan. And you shall drink water from the brook, and I will command the ravens to feed you there. And Elijah did according to the word of the Lord, and stayed by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan. And the ravens brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening, and he drank water from the brook. And after some days the brook dried up, because there had been no rain on the land."

"Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters," etc. We have been rescued from the snare of the demons who hunt us, since Christ crushed the devil and granted us to tread on snakes and scorpions and on all the power of the enemy, a power that prevails only against the negligent. For we have received the grace of the Spirit, and we are nourished by the blood and body of Christ.

By the same. The opposing powers hunt for the soul of the righteous. Their snares are the people they work through, who provoke us and invite us to sin, and all the material things that invite us to sin. But a sparrow does not fall into a snare without the Father who is in heaven.

"The snare is broken, and we have been rescued," etc. The Old Testament breaks the snares of action by legislating, "You shall not commit adultery"; the New destroys the snares of thought by commanding, "You shall not desire." Yet in the case of Abimelech of Gerar, he destroyed the snare of action, not allowing him to touch another man's wife; in the case of Joseph, the snare of thought, for Scripture does not present him as having desired another man's wife. Blessed is he whose snare of action the Lord has broken, but more blessed is he whose snare of thought he has destroyed, and in whose mouth no guile was found.
Psalm 124

"Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion," etc. Those who come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, bear the image of the heavenly one, and by trusting in the Lord they become like that Mount Zion.

By the same. If by trusting in the Lord one becomes like Mount Zion, then another might by some other means become like Mount Horeb, and another like Mount Sinai; and from the opposite qualities one might be like a mountain of Egypt, or a mountain of Babylon, and other such mountains among the enemies. Or else, just as those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion, so those of lesser rank are like the mountains round about her.

"Mountains are round about her, and the Lord is round about his people," etc. The mountains round about Jerusalem are, I think, divine powers. For "the angel of the Lord encamps" round about those who fear him; but round about "his people" is "the Lord" himself. So the people of the Lord is different from those who fear the Lord; for "House of Israel, bless the Lord" is one thing, and "You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord" is another.

"For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous," etc. It is the work of the Lord, who is round about his people, not to let the rod of sinners reach the lot of the righteous. And the people of the Lord is righteous.
By the same. If the lot of the righteous is the knowledge of God, he will not leave the righteous in ignorance, lest it become for them a cause of ignorance.

"So that the righteous may not stretch out their hands to lawless deeds," etc. Note the words "stretch out": this happens in lawlessness. But if, hypothetically, the rod of sinners were left upon the lot of the righteous, the righteous would stretch out their hands to lawlessness. We will make use of these words if during persecution many deny God and sacrifice to idols, saying that, since those who deny him were not righteous, the Lord left the rod of sinners upon their lot, so that they stretched out their hands to lawlessness. "For from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
Psalm 125

"When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted," etc. The apostles are foretold as going to say these things about themselves and about those among the Gentiles. And after this he speaks about sowing and reaping.
By the same. Captivity is the passing of a rational nature from virtue and knowledge to vice and folly.

"Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation," etc. The mouth was filled with joy and the tongue with exultation, and from them flow joy and exultation. When this has happened, those of the Gentiles who are being taught say: "The Lord has done great things for them." And about themselves they say in thanksgiving: "The Lord has done great things for us; we have been made glad." "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept"—but "when the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, our mouth was filled with joy." When we have carried out the words "I set a guard over my mouth," and "The mouth of the righteous meditates wisdom," and "Open your mouth with the word of God," and words like "Our mouth is opened to you, Corinthians," then we shall truthfully say also, "Our mouth was filled with joy."
"Then they will say among the Gentiles, 'The Lord has done great things for them,'" etc. "For after this he appeared on earth and lived among men."

"Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like torrents in the south," etc. Above, the two verses were spoken as though the return from captivity had already taken place; but now the Prophet says this as though he were still in captivity—the former, I think, prophesying about the apostles, the latter speaking in the person of the Gentiles. For the words from "The Lord has done great things for them" to "like torrents in the south" belong to those among the Gentiles.
"Those who sow in tears will reap in exultation," etc. Those who carry out the practical life with toil and tears sow in tears; those who partake of knowledge without toil will reap in exultation.
Psalm 126

"Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman has kept watch in vain," etc. This text should be used against thoughts of pride. Unless the Lord builds, through the help he gives, those who build have labored in vain.

By the same. First, "the Lord built the rib that he took from Adam into a woman." And since he did not build together with Cain when Cain built a city named after his son Enoch, Cain the builder labored in vain. So too those who set out from the east and said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower," labored in vain at their building, since the Lord was not building with them. And the Hebrews in Egypt groaned, I think, because they were laboring in vain at building, since the Lord was not building with them.

By the same. Those who built the house in Jerusalem labored in vain; that is why it was destroyed. It would not have been destroyed if the Lord had built it. But those who build the house of God, which is his Church—the apostles of Christ and the teachers appointed by him—have not labored in vain, for the Lord built it. In another sense, too, the heterodox build a house, but not with the Lord, doing harm to the Church; that is why they have labored in vain. And the same holds for the Jews.

By the same. Insofar as the soul is a house, it has God within it as master of the house; but if it becomes a temple, it has Christ within it as God. Through the practical life it gains him as master of the house, through natural contemplation as king, and again through theology as God. The other two necessarily accompany the third, just as the first accompanies the second; but the second and the third do not now necessarily accompany the first.

"It is in vain for you to rise early; rise up after sitting, you who eat the bread of sorrow, when he gives sleep to his beloved," etc. Just as sleep withdraws us from the things of the senses, so too the contemplation of God withdraws us from them.
By the same. Just as when we are asleep we do not even know that we are sleeping, so too when we are contemplating we do not even know that we have entered into contemplation.

By the same. If the practical life stands for bread, and sleep for knowledge, then it is fitting that sleep is given to us after we have eaten the bread of sorrow; for only the knowledge of God can relieve the weariness of the practical life.
By the same. If sleep usually warms the body, knowledge is rightly called sleep; for it makes all who possess it fervent in spirit.
By the same. Just as sleep digests food and nourishes the body through its juices, so knowledge nourishes the soul, teaching it the principles of the practical life.

"Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward of the fruit of the womb," etc. The inheritance of the Lord is not daughters but sons, who are the reward of the fruit of the womb. Such are the righteous sons. That is why they will appear three times a year before the Lord God. No unrighteous son is a reward or an inheritance of the Lord.
Psalm 127

"Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways," and so on. Many are the ways of the Lord, and those who walk in them are blessed. Along them one can travel on to him who said, "I am the way," as one goes from the many pearls to the one pearl of great price. If all who fear the Lord are blessed, those who do not fear the Lord are not blessed. Those who have cast out fear, however, are not blessed in this way. Those who fear the Lord walk in his ways, and if anyone does not walk in them, he does not fear him.
By the same. If the fear of the Lord adds days, then all who fear the Lord are blessed.
By the same. If the one who walks uprightly fears the Lord, then all who fear the Lord are blessed.

"[You shall eat] the labors [?] of your fruits," and so on. The greater [?] the labors of the fruits, the greater [?] the food in the age to come. The labors of the limbs, that is, of the hands, are called [?] fruits. So the labors of the fruits are good, and so is the food [?] by which we ascend to the living bread.

"Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house; your sons like young olive shoots around your table," and so on. No [?] of God will [seek to obtain?] these things, for what this speaks of is spiritual, not bodily. When the vineyards and olive groves of the righteous are blessed, we must interpret the wife and the sons figuratively [?], or else literally [?]. Or we may say that the wife is wisdom and the sons are [?]. The wife who is a good portion, or the [?] valiant woman of Solomon, is a fruitful vine, especially when she is a good keeper of the house. But a wife of the [opposite?] kind comes from the vine of Sodom. To a wife who changes for the worse one might [say?]: "How have you turned to bitterness, O [?] vine?"

By the same. The wife of the mind is wisdom. "Love her," it says, "and she will keep you. [Honor?] her, so that she may embrace you," and you will gain wise [offspring?] from her. And: "Call wisdom your sister." It calls her a sister because she too comes from the Father of all. One should remember [?] how Abraham called his own wife [his sister], wholly [?] of one who wishes wisdom to be [?]. "Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord," and so on. The [man?] who is so called because he fears the Lord has a field [?], and [?] on the sides of his house the [?], and his sons as young olive shoots around his table.
"[May you] see your sons' sons," and so on. And [?] says: "A good man will leave an inheritance to his children's children [?]."
Psalm 128
"Many a time have they fought against me from my youth."

"[Let] Israel [now say]," and so on. One who has been [fought against?] since childhood, and who has conquered his enemies even though he was often [attacked?], will say these things. So will the one who says: "[God] who has fed me from my youth." "[They lengthened] their iniquity," and so on. [Compare?] this: "Woe to those who drag their sins along as with a long rope, and their iniquities as with the strap of a yoke [?]." The further someone lengthens his iniquity, the further he removes himself from God. "Let them become like grass on the housetops, which withered before it was plucked," and so on. The teaching of the lofty things raised up against the knowledge of God is grass on the housetops, which withers before it is plucked. It fills neither the hands with good deeds nor the bosom with knowledge. Those who pass by do not speak of it as the one did who said, "I will turn aside and see this great sight."
Psalm 129

"Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord," and so on. He has cried to the Lord from the depths within himself, not from the surface. "I have cried to you" differs from "I have cried toward you," and it may mean: I have spoken of God greatly and with a great voice (great, that is, in the intellectual sense). The wicked man honors the Lord with his lips while his heart is far from him. But the blessed man, because the Spirit cries out in his heart, has cried to the Lord from the depths.
By the same. The one who searches the depths of God is the one who cries to the Lord from the depths.
"Let your ears be attentive," and so on. By the Lord's ears he means his power to hear prayers.

"If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand?" and so on. Sins committed in thought make the mind impure. If they separate it from the knowledge of God, then no human being will be found worthy of knowledge. "For who will boast of having a pure heart?" Or who will dare to claim that he is clean of sins? "And no one," it says, "is clean of filth, not even if his life lasts but a single hour."

"For with you there is propitiation," and so on. The propitiation for iniquities that is with the Lord is Christ, for "he is the propitiation for our sins." "For your name's sake I have waited for you, O Lord," and so on. Endurance for the sake of God's name is better than endurance for any other reason. And the soul that has come to the word of the Lord endures in a praiseworthy way.

"My soul has waited for your word; my soul has hoped in the Lord," and so on. Hope naturally arises from tested character, tested character from endurance, endurance from affliction, and affliction from self-control and temptations. The cause of all these is the fear of God, which is yoked to right faith. And faith is assent to things not yet grasped.

"And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities," and so on. The mind is set free from sins or iniquities of thought at the moment it is found worthy of knowledge. For [practical?] [?] does not take away the thoughts of the heart, only the impassioned thoughts.
Psalm 130

"[Lord], my heart has not been lifted up, nor have my eyes been raised," and so on. These are the words of a righteous man who, though endowed with great and wonderful gifts, is not puffed up, not exalted beyond measure, not [?], but stays humble-minded even in these. "[If] I was not humble-minded, but exalted my soul. Like a weaned child upon its mother, so you will repay upon my soul," and so on. Isaac and Samuel were weaned, and so was this man, who imitated them and those [like] them. The soul is not exalted by some weaned person exalting it. Rather, it is [exalted?] toward its own mother, of whom it is said: "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother," and what follows.
By the same. The Lord gives the soul of the weaned one the reward for [having ascended?] so far.

"Let Israel hope in the Lord from this time forth and forever," and so on. In the song [before?] this one it was said: "From the morning watch let Israel hope in the Lord." In this one, until when? [?] "From now and forever." For after that one enjoys the things hoped [for].
Psalm 131

"Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness," and so on. The Lord remembers the one in whom [meekness?] arises, and does not remember the one in whom it does not. If the Lord remembers meekness, then great freedom from anger is needed for anyone to receive the Lord. For meekness is an untroubled state of the irascible part, which arises when one is deprived of perishable pleasures.
By the same. In place of "meekness," Aquila rendered "ill-treatment," Symmachus "affliction," and the Fifth version "humiliation."

"Until I find a place for the Lord," and so on. The place of the Lord is the pure mind. "We found it in the plains of the forest," and so on. He is speaking prophetically about wisdom, which is Christ.

"Your priests shall be clothed with righteousness, and your holy ones shall rejoice," and so on. Just as one puts on righteousness, so too one puts on self-control, courage, love, patience, and the other virtues.

"Like the ointment on the head that runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron," and so on. The ointment is the Holy Spirit, the head is the mind, and the beard is reason, and reason encompasses the heart. The beard of Aaron is the reason that walls off the passions and offers the virtues to God as a priest. The grace of the Spirit runs down even to the hem of his garment. That is, through practical virtue it passes on to moral philosophy as well. For the hem of the garment is its end.

"Like the dew of Hermon that descends upon the mountains of Zion," and so on. In Deuteronomy Moses calls this mountain Hermon, but the Phoenicians call it Sanior and the Amorites San[?]. It lies beyond the Jordan. There is a story that the apostate angels met on this mountain to deliberate about their apostasy and made compacts there.

By the same. The mountains of Zion are the saints who look out toward lofty things, and the dew descends upon them. Hermon means "turning away of beasts." They also say that the Jordan once had its source there. This too signifies the grace of holy baptism. For that grace always descends upon the saints, and through it the intellectual beasts are turned away.
Psalm 133

"Behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God," and so on. "You who stand," it says, "in the house of the Lord" and do not fall "like one of the princes," but who take care not to fall, "bless the Lord."
By the same. The contemplatives are in the house of God, while those devoted to the practical life are in the courts of the house of our God.

"In the nights lift up your hands to the holy places, and bless the Lord," and so on. In place of "to the holy places," one translator has "in holiness," and another "in a sanctified way." By saying "in the house of the Lord" he showed that no one is forbidden to lift up holy hands anywhere at all, but that it is especially fitting to do so in places consecrated to God.
Psalm 134

"Praise the name of the Lord; praise [the Lord], you servants, you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God," and so on. Those who praise are none other than those who stand, and they praise nowhere else than in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. Note that it says "the house of the Lord" but "the courts of our God." Note too that above it said "bless," but now "praise." And in the Hebrew there it had only "who stand in the house of the Lord," but now it adds "in the courts of our God."

"For I have known that the Lord is great, and our Lord is above all gods," and so on. [?] says in the story of Jethro: "Now I know that the Lord is great above all the gods." But the Prophet says first "[For] I have known that the Lord is great," and then "and our Lord is above all the gods." "Whatever the Lord willed, he has done in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the deeps," and so on. Whatever the Lord has made in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in the deeps, is good, since it was made by the will of God. But there may be something in heaven, such as the spiritual forces of wickedness; or on earth, such as sinful men; or in the seas, such as the wickedness of the dragon; or in the deeps, such as the wickedness of those appointed to go there. That evil is not what [the Lord] made by his will, for "out of the mouth of the Most High shall not come forth evil and good." By the same. Just as heaven is the dwelling place of the holy powers, so the earth is the dwelling of human beings: "For the heaven of heaven is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the sons of men." The demons opposed to us dwell in the seas, in the figurative sense, and in them the dragon too was formed to be mocked. In the same way the subterranean demons dwell in the deeps, in the allegorical sense.

"[He] brings up clouds from the end of the earth; he made lightnings for the rain," and so on. A cloud is a rational [nature] entrusted with the principles of Providence. Lightning is spiritual teaching, which leads the souls of others back from vice to virtue. "And he gave their land as an inheritance," and so on. If our inheritance is the knowledge of God, how can the adversaries be said to possess it? And you will [answer?] that perhaps they are said to possess it not because they know it, but because they prevent us from reaching it. "Blessed be the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem," and so on. He who dwells in a pure heart dwells in Jerusalem. He said that the Lord dwells in Jerusalem. He did not mean to confine the divine nature there. He knew that at that time the divine manifestation was there, in the temple of Jerusalem.
Psalm 135
"Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever," and so on. Those who suffer hardship in this age naturally need mercy in this age too.
"Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy endures forever," and so on. The word "confession" signifies thanksgiving and glorification. But it is also used of the confession of sins, as here.

By the same. He is the God of gods: of those to whom the word of God came, according to the Scripture that says, "I said, You are gods," and "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." This is because of his great love and close bond with them. Of the demons, however, he is God because he created them. The Apostle also says, "If indeed there are many gods and many lords in heaven and on earth." But those called gods after the Trinity are gods by participation in divinity, while the Savior is God by essence, not by participation. The words "for his mercy endures forever" are added as a refrain. Since he always shows mercy, those who sing the refrain rightly say "for forever," and so on.

"To him who alone does great wonders," and so on. It shows him continually doing good and working wonders. It states two, three and four things about him: that he does them, that they are wonders, that they are great wonders, and that he alone does them. This is said not to set aside the Son but to set him apart from the demons. And what are these wonders that he alone does? At the beginning of the psalm, after all, he spoke not about power but about goodness. Why, then, does he now turn here to speak of power? Because these wonders belong not only to power but also to goodness and love for humankind.

"To him who established the earth upon the waters," and so on. If the earth is the foundation of the water, how has the earth been established upon the waters? And how can Job be telling the truth when he says, "who hangs the earth upon nothing"? Perhaps the earth below the abyss hangs upon nothing, while the earth above the abyss, on which we live, was established upon the abyss. In that case the abyss lies in the middle of the earth, contained as in a vessel. That is the answer if one wants to defend the literal history. As for the deeper meaning, he says: "Glorify him who established rational nature upon true knowledge." In the Gospels the Lord calls rational souls "earth" and knowledge "water." One can learn this from the seed that fell into the good earth, and from the river of living water that flows from the belly of the one who has believed. The rest of the psalm also follows this second interpretation. The moon and stars give light to this earth while it still lives in ignorance and cannot yet be lit by the sun of righteousness. Again, Egypt, a symbol of vice, is overtaken when the firstborn, understood spiritually, are destroyed. Pharaoh is punished by being drowned in spiritual waters. And Israel travels through the desert hungry, thirsty and tempted, which is a symbol of the practical life, hurrying toward the land of promise, which they say is the knowledge of God.

"[To him who] shook off Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea," and so on. He wanted to show how easily they were drowned, and so he used this [expression?]. The army too shares in the punishment and is chastised, because they shared in the sins committed against the Jews and took part in the pursuit.

"For in our humiliation he remembered us," and so on. When the Lord remembers us as impure, he remembers us under the aspect of righteousness. When he remembers us as pure, he does so under the aspect of wisdom. But it must be understood that these aspects are predicated with reference to the [?] of the things that have come into being, which presents Christ as creator.
"He who gives food to all flesh," and so on. The flesh that is nourished by God is the flesh that will see the salvation of God.
Psalm 136

"By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept when we remembered [Zion]," and so on. These men's longing for [their homeland?] is great. Why did they sit by the rivers? Because they were captives taken from [?] enemy country, and they camped outside walls and cities. "On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments," and so on. All the souls that sit in shadow and ignorance, it must be understood, [have] unfruitful reason, since they have hung up the instruments that serve the practical life.

"For there those who took us captive asked us for the words of songs, and those who led us away [said]: Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion," and so on. I [know?] that the demons too compel us to recite psalms and spiritual songs that contain some commandment we have transgressed. They want to hear us and laugh at us for saying things we do not do.

"Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who said: Empty it, empty it, down to its foundations," and so on. The words "Empty it, empty it, until the foundation [is reached] in it [?]" are given as spoken by the enemies. [This shows?] that those who wrestle against us try to lay hold even of the natural seeds of virtue. These seeds he figuratively called a foundation, laid down in the soul itself from the beginning. The enemies' aim is that the mind should fall completely from virtue and, as the proverb says, go about more naked than a pestle, clothed neither in Christ nor in the wedding garment.

"Blessed is he who will seize your infants and dash them against the rock," and so on. All who destroy the soul's wicked thoughts according to the teaching of Christ dash the infants of Babylon against the rock.
Psalm 137

"O Lord, you have tested me and known me," and so on. And in what follows, too, as though the heart were laid bare in temptations, it says: "Test me, O God, and know my heart." The fifth edition says "you have searched out" here, and "search out" in what follows. For as gold is tested in the furnace, so are acceptable people tested in the furnace of humiliation. And it is written in a psalm: "You have tested us as silver is refined by fire." Once you have understood this, you will know that only the righteous person, and everyone who has been tested, is known, as being in Christ from God. This is also clear from the words: "Test me, O Lord, and know my heart."
