By the same. God foreknows all things, yet he still tests us. He does this not in order to know, but to make those who endure more proven. And so that no one would suppose that he comes to know by testing, he added: "You have understood my thoughts from afar." For he knows our thoughts even before they are stirred, or rather long beforehand. How then could he need a test to learn anything for himself?
"You have traced out my path and my measuring-line," and so on. For those who walk a good path, God traces out the measuring-line, and God has foreseen all the measures of their way.

"For there is no deceit on my tongue," and so on. "There is no deceit on my tongue," he says. This means: my words are not superficial but come from the depths and from the heart. But the heart of fools is in their mouth. By the same. He used "tongue" figuratively for the heart.

"Behold, O Lord, you have known all things, the last and the ancient," and so on. Consider why the things in the middle have been passed over in silence. It is because evil lies in between: it exists neither at the beginning nor at the end.

"Your knowledge has been made too wonderful for me; it is mighty, I cannot attain to it," and so on. These are the words of a wise teacher who has helped many people and has dispensed the wonderful mysteries of knowledge.

"If I go up to heaven, you are there; if I go down to Hades, you are present," and so on. He says this as one who is able to travel and flee to heaven and to Hades, and to fly to the uttermost parts of the sea. It is likely that the soul can do this once it has come to exist by itself. Examine alongside these words the passage in Deuteronomy that runs as follows: "This commandment is not too hard for you, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, so that you should say, 'Who will go up to heaven for us and get it?' Nor is it beyond the sea, so that you should say, 'Who will cross to the other side of the sea for us and get it for us, so that we may hear it and do it?' The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart and in your hands, so that you may do it." Compare also these words from [Amos?]: "Not one of them who flees shall escape; not one of them who tries to save himself shall be saved. If they dig down into Hades, my hand shall drag them up from there; and if they go up to heaven, I will bring them down from there. If they hide on the top of Carmel, I will search them out and take them from there. If they sink out of my sight into the depths of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it shall bite them. And if they go into captivity [?] the sword, and it shall kill them."

"And I said: Surely darkness will trample me, and the night is light in my delight," and so on. The ignorance of the heart is darkness (for, he says, "their senseless heart was darkened"). If so, then the one who is the cause of this darkness for us is fittingly also called darkness himself. He tries to darken the delight we take in knowledge, but God does not allow it and lights up the darkness: "For the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it." For we acquired ignorance through evil, and we have taken on knowledge through virtue.

"For you have possessed my kidneys," and so on. Blessed is the one whose kidneys have become the Lord's possession. "My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret," and so on. He called the soul a "bone," which God alone made.
"Your eyes saw my unformed substance," and so on. The unformed soul is the one that has not been given form through virtue and knowledge.

"And in your book all shall be written," and so on. God's book is the contemplation of bodies and of incorporeal things, and a pure mind is by nature written in it through knowledge. In this book are also written the accounts of Providence and Judgment. From this book God is known as Creator, Wise, Provident and Judge. He is Creator because of the things brought from non-being into being. He is Wise because of the reasons laid up in it. He is Provident because of the things that help us toward virtue and knowledge. And he is Judge, in turn, because of the various bodies of rational beings, the manifold worlds, and the ages that encompass them.
"Days shall be formed, and no one in them," and so on. They shall be formed in knowledge, and no one will be outside knowledge, so that God may become all in all.
"I awoke, and I am still with you," and so on. "[Awake,] O sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you." Awakening, therefore, is the return from evil to virtue.

"I hated them with a perfect hatred," and so on. The perfect person hates evil and keeps away from all wickedness. If so, then anyone who shares in any of their wickedness at all has not perfectly hated evil.
"Test me, O God, and know my heart," and so on. If God is a consuming fire, then clearly he tests the souls of men in his aspect as fire.
PSALM 139

"Who devised injustice in their heart; all day long they drew up battles," and so on. The demons draw up their battle lines against us through thoughts. Sometimes they stir up desires and sometimes anger. At other times they stir up anger and desire together, and from these comes what is called the compound thought. But this happens only at the time of acedia. The other thoughts come at intervals and take turns with one another. On that day, however, no other thought takes over from the thought of acedia. First, this is because it lingers. Second, it holds almost all the other thoughts within itself.
"They sharpened their tongue like a serpent's," and so on. He calls the keenest thought "sharpened." The thought that snatches the mind away into blasphemy is of this kind.

"Who plotted to trip up my steps," and so on. The demons often do not present wicked ideas to us bare. They do not want the mind to see plainly how irrational these ideas are and throw the thoughts away. Instead, they sow their wicked ideas along with other ideas that seem good. They do this only with the perfect, who have no passions. Into those who are passionate and impure they throw thoughts even openly, and these people are unable to drive them away.
"Coals of fire shall fall upon them," and so on. This fire and these coals burn up wood, hay and straw, consuming wicked habits.

"I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the poor and justice for the needy," and so on. This is a prophecy about the coming judgment. At that judgment the ungodly will be handed over to the fire, and the righteous will be received into rest. Solomon also drew benefit from this and said: "For God will bring every work into judgment." The psalm ends on a good note, since it is also entitled "For the end," and it speaks of the hope laid up for the righteous: "The upright shall dwell with your face." In place of "with your face," Symmachus says "beside your face." This means seeing God face to face with a purified mind.
PSALM 140

"Let my prayer be directed like incense before you," and so on. The prayer that is directed like incense belongs to the one who can say: "We are the fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing."
"Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth," and so on. Nothing guards our heart as well as the fear of God, since it is by the fear of the Lord that everyone turns away from evil.

"But let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head," and so on. By the oil of a sinner he means doing good not for the sake of knowing God but for glory from men. This is what it means for someone who gives alms to sound a trumpet.

"Sinners shall fall into his net," and so on. The net is the varied punishment drawn up out of the depths of wickedness. But this net belongs to the age to come. The net of the present age is spiritual teaching, which leads to virtue those who have strayed from godliness.
PSALM 141

"With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord," and so on. Fire by nature rises upward. In the same way, the voice of the righteous by nature rises to the Lord and, as it were, calls on him to grant what one asks of God.

"I will pour out my supplication before him; I will declare my affliction before him," and so on. He asks only for great and heavenly things and prays with a new spirit. So he is confident in pouring out his supplication before the Lord, for it has nothing lowly or [?] in it. Such things are found in the supplications of those who babble, who ask for things unworthy of God and do not pour them out from a pure heart. The verse belongs to the bold speech of a saint, and a sinner could not fittingly say it. The next verse, too, belongs to one who is afflicted in every way but not crushed. He boasts in the afflictions that produce endurance, because he walks the narrow and hard way that leads to eternal life.

"On the way by which I walked they hid a snare," and so on. Our enemies plot against all the virtues. In courage they hide the snare of cowardice. Into meekness they throw rashness. Into almsgiving they bring showing mercy for the sake of onlookers rather than for God. Into fasting they bring fasting for the sake of men. All this concerns the practical life. But what could one say about contemplation, and about how many snares the enemies lay for orthodox doctrine through the heresies?
"Refuge has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks after my soul," and so on. Whoever has lost this refuge cannot say: "In affliction you made room for me."

"I cried to you, O Lord; I said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living," and so on. If our Lord is wisdom, and he himself is the portion of the living, then the portion of the living is wisdom. Wisdom is the reason they are called living, and this wisdom is Christ.
"Deliver me from those who persecute me," and so on. Constant temptations drive the mind away from knowledge.

"Bring my soul out of prison," and so on. Not everyone can say, "Bring my soul out of prison." Only those can say it who, through purity, are able to give themselves to the contemplation of created things even apart from this body.
PSALM 142

"O Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication in your truth; answer me in your righteousness," and so on. Whoever is confident that he worships God in spirit and in truth, and no longer in type, may say: "Give ear to my supplication in your truth."

"And do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living will be justified before you," and so on. When the Lord enters into judgment with man and says, "My people, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you?", no one living will be justified. No one living will be justified before the Lord. Before men, however, a person may sometimes be justified, and not only before unjust men but even before other righteous men. A verse akin to this one supplies the reasons for not being justified: "So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged."
"My soul is like waterless ground before you," and so on. The waterless ground is a pure soul that seeks spiritual knowledge.
"Hear me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed," and so on. When a person suffers from acedia for too long, his spirit fails. Similar to this is the verse: "When my spirit was failing within me."

"Let me hear your mercy in the morning, for in you I have hoped. Make known to me, O Lord, the way in which I should walk, for to you I have lifted up my soul," and so on. He is seeking the contemplation of the age to come, which divine Scripture is accustomed to call the kingdom of heaven.

By the same. He can say this about the [?] way that leads to virtue. Or he can say it about the way one travels after departing this life, which is the way to the tree of life, guarded by the cherubim and the flaming sword.

By the same. The land of the living and the level land are the same: the good land, into which the good Spirit of God guides those who are worthy. From this we have learned the dignity of the Spirit. For just as God is called good, so is the Spirit. And just as he begged God to guide him, so he also asks to enjoy the Spirit's guidance. Then nothing will seem steep or difficult to him, and he will travel a way that is straight and smooth and free from error.
PSALM 143

"Blessed be the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war," and so on. Whoever has been taught by the Lord how to fight the opposing power knows the reasons of the virtues and vices and the differences between thoughts. He knows the marks of dispassion [?] and its definitions. He also recognizes the reasons behind nocturnal fantasies and dreams. Some of these arise from the rational part of the soul when the memory is stirred, others from the irascible part, and others from the desiring part. But we have dealt with these things more precisely in [?] 1.

"Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow," and so on. For "man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them," and so "his days pass away like a shadow." Things here are like children at play. The one who judges today is judged tomorrow. The one who is haughty in his rule is often led away by the executioner. The rich man ends up in poverty. The one who had no hope and no name often rules over everything. The changes are frequent and the reversals unpredictable.

By the same. Vanity is a most wicked habit of the rational soul. Through it the soul prefers perishable pleasures and despises the eternal and incorruptible ones. "O Lord, bow your heavens and come down; touch the mountains, and they shall smoke," and so on. God's touch is spiritual teaching, which drives out of souls the smoke that wickedness has stored up in them.
"Send out your arrows, and you will throw them into confusion," and so on. These arrows are set against the fiery arrows of the enemy.

"Rescue me and deliver me from many waters, from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of injustice," and so on. The mouth of the heterodox has spoken vanity because of their great [?] doctrines. And because of their wicked deeds, their right hand is a right hand of injustice. The foreign sons think that certain things are on the right side, when in fact they belong to injustice. This is why the devil stands at their right hand, as he did at Judas's.

By the same. The prophet also says: "Yet I will speak judgment to you: why does the way of the ungodly prosper?" And again David says: "My steps had nearly slipped, for I was envious of the lawless when I saw the peace of sinners."

"O God, I will sing a new song to you," and so on. Whoever makes the new covenant sings the new song to God. Or it is whoever has received from Jesus in the upper room the new bread of the new covenant and the cup.

"Whose sons are like young plants grown up in their youth," and so on. The sons of the man who is blessed because he fears the Lord are "like young olive shoots around his table." But the sons of the foreign sons are "like young plants grown up in their youth." The blessed man has no daughters, but they have daughters who are adorned and decked out like the likeness of a temple. He has sons of sons, but they do not. Moreover, he has no storehouse or barn, but they have "full storehouses, overflowing from one into another." According to the Gospel, too, the birds of the air, which the heavenly Father feeds, have no storehouse or barn. And again, these people have prolific sheep that multiply nowhere else than in their streets, and fat oxen like those of Egypt's plenty.

"They called the people blessed who have these things," and so on. The blessedness of the unjust is a life without sorrow and with much wealth. But the blessedness of the righteous is dispassion of soul together with the knowledge of God.
PSALM 144
"I will exalt you, my God," and so on. Spiritual exaltation is the thanksgiving of a pure mind for the good things that have come to it from God.

"Every day I will bless you," and so on. "Even in hardships and temptations," he says, "I will bless you, O Lord"; that is, continually. For we owe him for many things. He made us when we did not exist. He made us what we are. He sustains us now that we exist. Every day he provides for us, both in common and individually, both secretly and openly, even when we do not know it. But it is fitting to sing his praise continually not only for these things but also for the majesty of his glory and for his pure essence. For this too we owe him praise and blessing, constant thanksgiving, worship, and unceasing service. To show this very thing, the Prophet added:

"Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and there is no limit to his greatness," and so on. God's greatness is contemplated as being in Christ and in created things, and there is no limit to his greatness. Perhaps this also shows God's providence, which reaches from infinity to infinity, toward the things that have come into being through him.
By the same. The contemplation of all created things has a limit. Only the knowledge of the Holy Trinity is without limit.

"And his compassion is over all his works," and so on. If God's compassion is over all his works, how can there be some whom it does not reach? It follows that God's compassion extends to them as well. Unless perhaps his compassion reaches his works, but not in every case the works of his hands.

"Let all your works confess you, O Lord, and let your holy ones bless you," and so on. Here he calls rational natures "works," for they are by nature able to confess God. Whether some confession also rises up from the rest of creation, God alone would know.

"Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages," and so on. If the kingdom of God is the contemplation of the ages that have been and that will be, then it is rightly said: "Your kingdom is a kingdom of all the ages."
"The Lord preserves all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners," and so on. The destruction of a sinner is the separation of a rational soul from the whole of a life lived in evil.

"My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name forever and to the age of ages," and so on. All flesh that blesses the name of the Lord forever and to the age of ages will clearly be seeing the salvation of God forever and to the age of ages.

By the same. Paul also says: "Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of human hearts." A tablet of flesh, then, is a rational soul that readily receives the law of God. But there is also flesh that is blamed, as in the verse: "My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh." And again Paul says: "Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God." For here flesh signifies evil.
PSALM 145

"Who keeps truth forever, who executes judgment for the wronged, who gives food to the hungry," and so on. He said "truth" meaning the one who is true, naming the person who shares in a disposition after the disposition itself. In the same way, "he loves mercy and judgment" means the merciful person and the one who judges justly. And in Paul, "love does not boast" stands for the one who has love. In the same way you will find people named after the worse dispositions they possess.

"The Lord sets the prisoners free; the Lord gives wisdom to the blind; the Lord raises up those who are broken down," and so on. Things do not bind the mind, nor do our ideas of things. What binds it are the passionate ideas of things. The Lord created gold, and he himself made woman, and nothing God has made stands in the way of human salvation. Rather, fornication and greed bind the mind, forcing the ideas of things to linger in the heart.
By the same. Clearly he calls blind those who see neither their own good deeds nor the failings of others.
"The Lord will reign forever," and so on. Christ reigned before the ages without flesh, and he also reigned eternally in the flesh. The Holy Spirit proclaims these things as good news to the Church.
PSALM 146

"The Lord builds up Jerusalem and will gather the scattered people of Israel," and so on. Those whom evil scatters, virtue gathers. So too the Lord says in the Gospels: "And whoever does not gather with me scatters."

"Who counts the multitude of the stars," and so on. The number by which God counts rational beings shows the differences in the states of the stars. The names he gives them signify different kinds of spiritual knowledge. But of the creeping things in the sea he says: "There are creeping things without number." How could spiritual number be applied to those who creep on their bellies and are slaves to pleasures, whose "anger is like that of the serpent, and the venom of asps is under their lips"? And again Solomon says that many have been wounded by evil and countless are those it has slain.

"The Lord lifts up the meek, but brings sinners down to the ground," and so on. We must ask from where he brings sinners down. He tells us where by saying "to the ground." Perhaps he brings them down by making them live in the earthly body of humiliation. He lifts up the meek, then, whom he had earlier brought low. But he brings down to the ground the sinners who were on high before they sinned.
"Who covers the heaven with clouds," and so on. The heaven and the more divine things are clothed and covered with clouds, as far as which the truth reaches.
PSALM 147

"For he has strengthened the bars of your gates," etc. The bars of the gates of Jerusalem, held together by the Lord, are, I think, the rational arguments for the truth that is contemplated and grasped, which set it forth powerfully.

By the same. The bars of Jerusalem are the practical virtues, which prevent the enemies from slipping in; those of Zion are the heavenly doctrines and the right faith in the worshipful and holy Trinity, since Jerusalem signifies the soul and Zion the mind. For Jerusalem is interpreted "vision of peace," and Zion "watchtower."

"He who makes your borders peace," etc. The borders of Jerusalem are all peace; outside its borders there is no peace. Therefore whoever is not in peace is outside the borders of Jerusalem. By the same. They say that the borders of peace are the dispassion of the soul.

"And filling you with the fat of wheat," etc. There is something similar in the eightieth psalm: "And he fed them with the fat of wheat." The grain of wheat is the Saviour; that is why it is wheat with which God fills Jerusalem.

"He who sends his word to the earth," etc. Here he speaks of "earth" allegorically: perhaps of us, who carry the treasure in earthen vessels; but it is better to understand it of the Son of God, the one in the flesh, which so great a Lord was willing to enter.

"He who gives snow like wool, who scatters mist like ashes," etc. God is said to "give" in two ways: either by permitting or by acting. It is as if someone said of the sun that it is what makes both day and night, but makes day by shining and night by withdrawing. Here, then, God's "giving" must be understood in the second sense, since by sending his word he melts these things.

"He will send out his word and melt them," etc. Snow and ice, mist and cold, befall the rational nature through the absence of the Sun of righteousness; and these the Word of God, when he was sent, melted. "For I came," he says, "to cast fire upon the earth."
PSALM 148
"Praise the Lord from the heavens," etc. Praise is a hymn to God upon the contemplation of the things that have come into being.
"Praise him, all you stars and light," etc. Here "light" symbolically signifies rational nature; for "You," he says, "are the light of the world."

"Praise him, you heavens of heavens, and let the water that is above the heavens praise the name of the Lord," etc. Heaven, spiritually understood, is a rational nature that carries the Sun of righteousness within it.
By the same. The water above the heavens signifies rational natures, separated from the waters that are in the heavens.
"And he will exalt the horn of his people," etc. A horn is a pure mind.
"A hymn for all his holy ones," etc. A hymn is amazement, joined with glorifying, at the contemplation of the things that have been made and done by God.
PSALM 149
"Sing to the Lord a new song," etc. He sings a new song who has put off the old man, which is corrupted according to the lusts of deceit, and has put on the new man, created according to God.

"His praise is in the assembly of the holy ones," etc. Just as "praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner," so neither is it in an assembly of evildoers, but in the assembly of the holy ones; and it belongs in such an assembly rather than in a single person or in a few.

"Let Israel rejoice in the one who made him, and let the sons of Zion exult in their king," etc. Since "made" is said of the human being according to the image, and "formed" of the one from the dust, holy gladness also lies in what is according to the image; that is why Israel is commanded to rejoice in the one who made him. And Christ reigns over the sons of Zion, that is, Wisdom, Word, Truth; let them exult in him.

"Let them praise his name in the dance," etc. If the many, in the same mind and the same judgment, with one accord, with one soul and one heart, praise the name and the distinctive character of the king, they praise his name in the dance, in harmony.

"Let them sing psalms to him with timbrel and psaltery," etc. Those who have put to death their members that are on earth, and have led the principalities and powers up onto the tree to be crucified with Christ, sing to God with the timbrel; those who are whole and in harmony in spirit sing with the psaltery.

"For the Lord takes pleasure in his people, and he will exalt the meek with salvation," etc. The Lord takes pleasure in his own portion, which is his people, and not in the people of some other ruler of this age. And he will exalt the meek into the land which the meek inherit, not the land below, but the one on which the Jerusalem above stands; for God will exalt the meek with salvation, and the holy ones will boast in glory. In what kind of glory? Fittingly, in the glory of which he says, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord"; or in glory such as Moses had when the appearance of his face was glorified, and of which Paul says, "And we all, with unveiled face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory."

"And they will exult upon their beds," etc. They will exult upon their beds for whom "the night is far spent, and the day is at hand"; who also walk decently, as in the day, "not in revelling and drunkenness, not in debauchery and licentiousness."

"The exaltations of God are in their throat," etc. Those whose throat is not an open grave have the exaltations of God in their throat; and two-edged swords are in the hands of those who stand ready to punish all disobedience and who pull down every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.
"And two-edged swords in their hands," etc. Swords are thoughts and actions of the soul that arise from evil and ignorance.
By the same. A sword is a rational mind that cuts the soul off from evil and ignorance.

"To execute vengeance on the nations, rebukes on the peoples," etc. "Vengeance on the nations" means on those of other beliefs; "rebukes on the peoples" means on those who sin in their way of life while being reckoned members of the Church.

"To bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles," etc. Whoever convinces the teachers of those of other beliefs, and those among them who are thought distinguished because of their supposed ability, binds their kings with fetters, so that they may not advance in their teaching, and their nobles with iron manacles, so that they may no longer keep hold of the one they long held captive because he was easily deceived.

By the same. A bond, spiritually understood, is the dispassion of the rational soul; or the fear of the Lord, which turns away from evil; or spiritual teaching, which does not allow the mind to travel toward evil; or spiritual love, which prefers nothing to the knowledge of God.

"To execute upon them the written judgment," etc. The holy ones execute a written judgment, worthy of the Scripture that is in the Spirit, upon the kings and nobles mentioned before; and all the things mentioned before are glory for all God's holy ones, so that whoever does not have them is not a holy one of God.
PSALM 150

"Praise God in his holy places," etc. Let no one who has gone out of the holy places praise God; for "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?" And the foreign land is whatever is not holy. Or else: since what is holy must not be given to dogs, nor pearls thrown before swine, and the praise of the Lord is holy and a pearl, God must be praised among the holy, and neither among dogs nor among swine.

"Praise him in the firmament of his power," etc. Where there is a firmament of faith, and a building like the one built upon the rock by a wise man, and Christ, the power of God, there let God be praised, as in the firmament of God's power. And let these things be present both in the one who speaks and in the one who hears.

"Praise him for his mighty acts," etc. Just as the soul of the righteous blesses God in every place of his dominion, so he must also be praised for the mighty works he has established and ordered. Let them understand these, so that both the one who speaks and the one who hears may share in them. For the things continually accomplished through his saints are beyond words.

"Praise him according to the abundance of his greatness," etc. When each greatness of God has been understood, each of the creatures will also be understood, and so will the abundance of his greatness, each part of which has no limit.

"Praise him with the sound of the trumpet," etc. We must make a trumpet according to the spiritual sense of the instructions about making trumpets in Numbers, so that we may praise God with its sound. Such trumpets, I think, are also meant in the words "For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible," and in "With the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God he will descend from heaven." There is also the feast of the new moon of the seventh month, a memorial of trumpets, in keeping with which it is said: "Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the auspicious day of our feast."
By the same. A trumpet is a contemplative mind, or a mind entrusted with spiritual teaching.

"Praise him with psaltery and lyre; praise him with timbrel and dance; praise him with strings and organ; praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation," etc. A lyre is a practical soul set in motion by the commandments of Christ. A timbrel is the putting to death of the desiring part for the sake of the good itself. A dance is the harmony of rational souls who say the same thing and have no divisions among them. Strings are the concord of virtues and instruments, once the discordant voice [?] has been removed. An organ is the Church of God, made up of contemplative and practical souls. A well-sounding cymbal is a practical soul fastened to the longing for Christ. A cymbal of jubilation is a pure mind inspired by the salvation of Christ.

By the same. Many strings harmoniously put together, each musically set in its own place, are the many commandments and the doctrines about many matters, which have no discord with one another. And the organ that contains them all is the soul of the one who is wise in Christ.
By the same. Whoever speaks with the tongues of men or of angels but does not have love is not a well-sounding cymbal.

"Let everything that has breath praise the Lord," etc. If, according to Solomon, the breath of human beings is the light of the Lord, let every rational nature that breathes this light praise the Lord.
